News.title: Man in his 30s fighting for his life after early hours attack outside popular nightclub – as suspect arrested
News.content:
BAR ATTACK Man in his 30s fighting for his life after early hours attack outside popular nightclub – as suspect arrested







Next

A MAN is fighting for his life after an early hours attack outside a popular nightclub – as cops arrest a suspect.

The man – in his 30s – was assaulted outside Antix in Bristol in the early hours of Saturday, November 14 at around 4.45am.

Avon and Somerset Police described his injuries as life-threatening after he was raced to hospital.

The force said the victim had attended the venue before being required to leave with a friend before the shocking incident took place.





A man in his 40s has been arrested in connection with the incident and has been released on conditional bail, they added.

Officers are now appealing for witnesses after launching an investigation into the “serious assault”.

A police spokesperson said there “were a number of people at the scene who may have information who could assist us”.

“We are now appealing for any witnesses who have not yet spoken to the police, those with information about the incident, or CCTV, dashcam or mobile phone footage which could assist our enquiries, to contact us,” they added.

Antix is described as an independent, family-run bar and nightclub in the centre of the city and opened in 2005.

News.title: Man, 24, arrested on suspicion of ‘attempted murder’ after being seen in ‘blood-stained clothes’ – as OAP seriously hurt
News.content:
OAP ‘ATTACK’ Man, 24, arrested on suspicion of ‘attempted murder’ after being seen in ‘blood-stained clothes’ – as OAP seriously hurt







Next

A MAN has been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder after he was reportedly seen in blood-stained clothes.

Officers scrambled to Bridgend, South Wales, at around 3.55pm on Friday following reports of a man with bloodied clothing.

South Wales Police said the man – a 24-year-old from Waterton – has been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder.

The force added a 67-year-old man – also from Waterton – had been raced to hospital as in a “serious condition”.





Both men are known to each other and to police, with officers not looking for anyone else in connection to the incident.

The 24-year-old man is currently in police custody.

A spokesperson said: “An increased policing presence will be seen in the Waterton area whilst officers carry out their investigation into this incident.”

News.title: Two men, 18, rushed to hospital after ‘stabbing’ in popular park – as urgent probe launched & locals warned ‘stay away’
News.content:
‘KNIFE’ HORROR Two men, 18, rushed to hospital after ‘stabbing’ in popular park – as urgent probe launched & locals warned ‘stay away’







Next

TWO teenagers have been rushed to hospital after an alleged stabbing in a popular park.

Cops launched an urgent probe after the incident just before 5pm today at Alexandra Park in Oldham, Manchester.

Officers and emergency services scrambled to the scene and two men aged 18 were treated for injuries consistent with a stabbing, said cops.

The men have been taken to hospital however their injuries aren’t believed to be life-changing or life-threatening at this stage, police added.





Locals have been urged by cops to “stay away from the scene” so officers can carry out their work.

No arrests have been made at this time, said the force.

However there is a scene in place and specialist resources remain in and around the park whilst the investigation continues, according to Greater Manchester Police.

Cops have urged any witnesses or anyone with information to come forward immediately.



Detective Inspector Kelly Paterson of Oldham CID said: “Thankfully the two men that have been injured are not believed to have life-threatening injuries at this time however knife crime has absolutely no place in our communities and on our streets.

“We are currently appealing for any witnesses who may have been in and around the ‘Lions Den’ area of the park and may hold vital information for our investigation.

“Communities may be concerned by this incident however I’d like to reassure you that our officers will maintain a robust presence in and around the park as we carry out our enquiries.

“There will be a scene in place until at least tomorrow as our enquiries are ongoing.



“I urge people to stay away from the scene to let our officers carry out their work.”

News.title: Wife, 34, said she was ‘so proud’ of husband before he murdered her and their 3 kids – as son begged ‘don’t kill me’
News.content:
'PURE EVIL' Wife, 34, said she was ‘so proud’ of husband before he murdered her and their 3 kids – as son begged ‘don’t kill me’







Next

A MUM who was shot dead alongside her three young children gushed that she was “so proud” of her husband days before he killed them.

Isaac Luechtefeld gunned down his wife, Raquel, and their three young children – Enoch, 5, Hannah, 3, and Job, 1 – before turning the firearm on himself in Plant City, Florida.



A terrified young boy could be heard pleading for his life in a chilling 911 call moments before Luechtefeld carried out the horror murder-suicide.

Emergency dispatchers heard the youngster screaming, “daddy, please don’t kill me,” just before a loud gunshot rang out.



Days earlier, Raquel celebrated her husband online after he was praised in a magazine for his work as a mechanic.

She wrote: “So proud of my hubby! He was one of the master techs featured in the Kenworth Diesel magazine release!”

Read more US news COLD BLOOD Surgeon who kept 'murder bag' to be executed after killing man in billing grudge



Luechtefeld was described by colleagues as “someone that just about everyone in our shop looks to for guidance and assistance with their repairs and diagnostics” in the article.

The couple, both 34, shared a joint Facebook account housing dozens of smiling snaps of them and their growing family.

Seemingly loving posts can also be found all over their timeline.

Isaac had publicly raved about his wife on the page, writing under a photo of their wedding day that his memories are “beautiful only because your [sic] in them.”



In a 2015 post, he wrote: “I love you Raquel Luechtefeld! It’s almost impossible for me express how happy I am and how much I love you!”

The couple went on a date night just days before the ruthless murder-suicide.

The 911 dispatcher heard a male voice say “sorry buddy” moments before a loud bang, according to Hillsborough County Sheriff Chad Chronister told reporters of the 911 call.



He continued: “In the distance, we can hear a small child begging for his life, ‘dada, dada, daddy please don’t shoot me, daddy please don’t kill me’.”

Minutes later, cops raced to the home where they conducted a perimeter search and spotted a lifeless child lying on the floor.

Inside, deputies made the harrowing discovery of Luechtefeld, Raquel, and their three young children with gunshot wounds.

Chronister added: “When you become a deputy sheriff, you expect to see awful things. But what the deputies encountered here today is nothing short of pure evil.”

He revealed officers who responded to the scene were left “completely shook”, adding that impacted deputies have been ordered to take time off and offered peer support.

The 911 dispatcher who listened in as the horror unfolded over the phone was also left “emotionally traumatised”.

Chronister urged anyone battling a mental health crisis to reach out for support, pointing residents towards the Crisis Center of Tampa Bay.

He said: “As we approach the holidays, we know that some of this community will struggle, will be overwhelmed with emotions.

“I’m making the plea to all of you, if you need help, simply have the courage and strength to ask for it.”

Both the gunman’s mum and Raquel’s sister told The New York Post they had been completely blindsided by the tragedy and there was “no indication” that he was suffering from mental health issues.



Luechtefeld’s mum, Beverly Apticar, called the tragedy a “shock,” saying: “This is something that nobody saw coming, and this is not who Isaac was.”

The Luechtefelds had been married for 14 years after meeting in Colorado and moved to Florida six years ago.

Raquel Luechtefeld’s sister said the family had celebrated her sibling’s birthday just a week ago with a surprise party at their parents’ house and said her brother-in-law had seemed his “normal self.”

Rebecca Uribe said: “He was such a good dad, and he was such a good husband. All of this blindsided us.”

She described the children as “so happy, so full of love, full of affection, confident” and revealed they had been homeschooled by the couple.

“They love their dad, they love their mom, they had full trust and confidence in their dad. They loved him so much.”

News.title: Moment fare dodger punches cop so hard he ‘leaves teeth marks on knuckles’ – as thug says ‘I should’ve hit him harder’
News.content:
Next

THIS is the shocking moment a thug fare dodger punched a cop so hard he ended up with “teeth marks” on his knuckles.

Shemar Robinson, 24, left a police officer with lasting facial injuries after the sickening attack at Dollis Hill Station in London, on November 19.



Footage shows vile Robinson making his way throughout the barrier as one cop challenges him and tries to grab his arm.

Robinson then turns and smashes the officer in the face before raising his fists again against other officer.



A second policeman then raises his taser and orders the thug to lie on the floor before Robinson is arrested.

Graphic footage shows the station floor is spattered with the injured officer’s blood as a colleague tells Robinson: “You really think that was a good idea.

“You’re on probation and you’re going to start punching a police officer in the face. Look at all this blood, that’s from him.”

During his interview Robinson, wearing a black and white Adidas tracksuit, is seen beaming a broad smile, as he laughs as he says he meant to hurt the officer.



He expressed pride at having the copper’s teeth marks on his knuckles.

Robinson admitted he had “no remorse” and said: “I should have hit him harder.”

A clip of incident showed drops of blood from the injured officer, who had been previously wounded that week, on the floor of the station’s ticket hall.



The officer’s wounds required hospital treatment, including stitches and may have given him permanent scarring.

Yesterday Robinson, of no fixed address, admitted inflicting grievous bodily harm, possession of cannabis, a class B drug and fare evasion.

He was remanded in custody and will be sentenced at Harrow Crown Court on a date to be fixed.

It was the third time Robinson had been arrested this year for assaulting police.

Detective Chief Superintendent Luke Williams, who leads policing in the area, said: “This officer was violently assaulted simply for doing his job – trying to prevent someone breaking the law.



“He has been spoken to by senior officers who have thanked him for his bravery and resilience.

“We will continue to provide him with support as he begins to recover from his injuries.

“This is the second time this officer has been injured in the line of duty this week and it is a testament to his commitment that his main priority was getting back out alongside his colleagues on the frontline.

“I am particularly concerned that this is not the first time Shemar Robinson has shown a propensity for targeting police officers.

“While this time his guilty pleas led to his remand ahead of sentencing, on more than one previous occasion he has been bailed, only to go on and carry out a similar act of violence or criminal damage aimed at the police.



“This awful incident highlights the repeated challenges faced by officers, who continue to encounter the same individuals committing offences despite repeatedly being brought before the courts.”

News.title: EU graduates could hit UK with £1.5billion in unpaid uni fees as hidden cost of Burnham’s Brexit ‘reset’ deal revealed
News.content:
OWE NO EU graduates could hit UK with £1.5billion in unpaid uni fees as hidden cost of Burnham’s Brexit ‘reset’ deal revealed







Next

EU students could leave Britain on the hook for an eye-watering £1.5 billion in unpaid university fees, new research suggests.

The bombshell figures heap fresh pressure on Andy Burnham’s Brexit deal – which threatens to be derailed altogether because of a massive row over uni fees.



The PM unveiled his new agreement at a summit in Brussels on Friday, which included a youth mobility scheme and a new deal on food checks.

But Brussels are threatening to blow up the entire deal unless the UK agrees to cut university tuition fees to the same rate British students pay.



They have set a six month deadline.

Worried universities say it could leave them with a gaping £500 million funding blackhole.

And in a fresh twist, new figures from Reform UK suggest that EU students could leave British universities a staggering £1.5 billion in unpaid student loans.

Reform’s Education chief Suella Braverman said: “It is disgraceful that Andy Burnham is willing to spend hundreds of millions cutting student fees for foreign students while allowing British youngsters to be ripped off with mountains of debt.”

“I will not hesitate to reverse his sell-out and put our own students first.”

Reform UK is proposing to ban foreign students that fail to pay back their student loans from entering Britain.



The party’s number crunchers say 172,000 European students owe a total of £6.2 billion to UK universities.

Of these, 43,700 have failed to make a single loan repayment in the past 12 months – costing £360million, according the figures from the Student Loans Company.

This is the equivalent of one in four EU graduates.

If they do not pay back any of their fees they will end up owing £1.5 billion of debt owed to UK universities, according to the analysis.

The figures emerged as universities warned Mr Burnham’s Brexit deal would “come at a cost”.



The University of Manchester’s vice chancellor Professor Duncan Ivison said: “If nothing was done to compensate or provide additional funding, it would take £500m we estimate, out of the higher education sector at a time where there’s a lot of pressure on the sector.”

Vivienne Stern, the CEO of Universities UK, said universities are facing “a lot of financial strain” because of rocketing inflation.

They have effectively subsidised teaching British students this by charging foreign students more – and any cut in these fees risks a blackhole, she warned.

She told The Sun on Sunday: “You can’t go on like this.

“We could not maintain the reputation we have got for an excellent university system if we continue to chip away at the income that universities get for teaching.



“We agree it would be a good thing to get a solid basis for EU students to study here and UK students to study in Europe.

“But it has to be financially sustainable for UK universities too.”

Mr Burnham had promised not to “re-run” Brexit arguments when he was standing to be an MP in the Leave-backing constituency of Makerfield.

Yet just six months on, the PM has reignited the Brexit wars and said all options are on the table – including rejoining the EU.

Remainer Labour MPs are gleeful at the volte-face, with one talking The Sun on Sunday: “We are winning”.



But privately, many are terrified that any moves to tear up the Brexit vote after the next election will hammer the party in their old Red Wall heartlands in the North and Midlands.

And several Cabinet ministers have warned the PM to be careful in what he unleashes – but they have been gagged from speaking out publicly.

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told the BBC that “all options will be on the table” including rejoining the EU bloc.

Nigel Farage blasted the Labour PM for openly plotting to reverse the Brexit vote.



He said: “There’s something incredibly ironic, and indeed rage-inducing, about an unelected prime minister reneging on the manifesto pledges his party came to power on, trampling on the largest democratic exercise ever seen in Britain, while selling us a stitch-up.

“The whole thing is deeply immoral.

“The majority of British people don’t want open door immigration with 450 million people nor do they want to fritter away £750 million a week to the EU.

“Burnham appears determined to betray the emphatic message given to all politicians in 2016 – all so he can distract from the endless failures and inaction of his own government.”

No10 denied the new Brexit deal could be torpedoed because of the row over university fees.



But in a car-crash BBC interview defending the deal, Cabinet minister Angela Eagle lost her rag and ended up shouting down the line at interviewer Justin Webb.

When the presenter dared to ask her about fears the Brexit deal could plunge British universities into economic turmoil, she insisted the Treasury would take a look.

Before fuming: “You’ll just have to be patient because these things take time!”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

A government spokesman said: “The food and drink, emissions trading and Youth Experience deals agreed at the summit stand on their own, and dates for implementation are set out in the joint statement agreed by the UK and the EU.

“Both sides are now taking them through their respective legal processes, while tuition fees are a separate negotiation.”

News.title: Hotel Chocolat urgently recalls Christmas boxes over salmonella warning – as customers urged ‘do not eat’
News.content:
CHOC ALERT Hotel Chocolat urgently recalls Christmas boxes over salmonella warning – as customers urged ‘do not eat’







Next

HOTEL Chocolat has urgently recalled some of its Christmas boxes over a “potential risk” of salmonella.

The British chocolate manufacturer said the recall involved a “small number of products as a precautionary measure”.

They added it was “associated with a pistachio paste ingredient used in manufacture”, stressing “salmonella has not been detected in any finished Hotel Chocolat products”.



The products recalled include some of the brand’s Christmas chocolate boxes purchased between October 2 and October 8.



The Food Standards Agency asked customers to check whether any purchased products match specific lot codes in the recall notice.

No other Hotel Chocolat products are included in the recall.

Symptoms caused by salmonella usually include fever, diarrhoea and abdominal cramps.



The Food Standards Agency said people experiencing these symptoms “should stay away from work, school or nursery until you have stopped having symptoms for at least 48 hours to avoid passing it on to others”.

In its recall notice, the chocolate manufacturer said: “Hotel Chocolat is recalling a small number of products as a precautionary measure due to a potential risk of salmonella associated with a pistachio paste ingredient used in manufacture.

“Salmonella has not been detected in any finished Hotel Chocolat products.

“However, following notification within our ingredient supply chain that raw pistachios used in the manufacture of the pistachio paste may be linked to a salmonella contamination incident, we have taken the decision to initiate this precautionary recall.”



The Food Standards Agency said customers should not eat any affected products.

In a statement, it added: “Instead, return them to the store where you purchased them where you will be given a replacement or refund.”

News.title: Dad of 12, 49, killed after being repeatedly punched in brutal kebab shop attack following row over spilled sauce
News.content:
FATAL ATTACK Dad of 12, 49, killed after being repeatedly punched in brutal kebab shop attack following row over spilled sauce







Next

A DAD-OF-12 was killed after being repeatedly punched in a brutal kebab shop attack following a row over spilled sauce, a court heard.

Young John Mongan had travelled to Welshpool, Wales, with his family to celebrate his son’s engagement when the horror unfolded on June 27.



The 49-year-old was with his wife and adult children – including his two youngest daughters – when Martin Slezak, 23, unleashed a brutal assault.

The family visited a kebab shop at the end of the evening with CCTV footage showing Mongan backing out onto Church Street before he is knocked unconscious.



Slezak continued to rain blows on Mongan as he lay motionless on the street before a friend intervened.

But following a short altercation, Slezak then turned viciously kicked Mongan in the head while his family watched on in horror.

Despite the best efforts of paramedics and members of the public, Mongan was sadly pronounced dead at the scene.

Caernarfon Crown Court heard how the violent confrontation stemmed from the spilling of some sauce in the kebab shop, reports North Wales Live.



Slezak was subsequently arrested and charged with murder the following day.

He denied murdering Mongan – arguing he had acted in self-defence and the defence of others – but was found guilty of manslaughter following a two-week trial.

On Friday, Slezak, from Welshpool, was put behind bars for 10 years.

Senior investigating officer Detective Superintendent Rhys Jones called the incident a “sustained and violent attack”.

He said: “In continuing to assault Mr Mongan as he lay unconscious, Slezak demonstrated a shocking intent to cause serious harm to someone unable to defend himself.



“Throughout our investigation he has denied this intent, displaying a complete lack of remorse for his actions or the impact on Mr Mongan’s wife and children.”

Following the verdict, Mr Mongan’s family said: “Young John Mongan was a father who would do absolutely anything for his children.

“We knew that we could depend on him, he was our security, guidance and the person who would always be there to help us through anything that life sent our way. That has been taken away from us.



“There will be birthdays, weddings, family celebrations, Christmases and countless other occasions when his absence will be felt. There will always be an empty space where our father should be.

“His two youngest daughters, who were there that night and witnessed it all, will never have their father there to walk them down the aisle on their wedding days.

“He will never see them dressed as brides, never give them away, never share in their happiness or be there to offer them his advice and protection as they build their own lives.

“These are moments that every father hopes to experience, and our father has been cruelly deprived of these.

“His grandchildren adored him. He was everything to them. They have lost a grandfather who loved them unconditionally and who was such an important part of their lives.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“They have been robbed of years of love, laughter, memories and time with him. They will never get to experience all the things that our father should have been there for as they grow older.

“The person who killed our father did not just take one life. He took away a husband, a father, a grandfather and the heart of an entire family.”

News.title: Jennie Bond: 'King Charles reached out to Meghan after her dad Thomas Markle was arrested'
News.content:
Jennie Bond: 'King Charles reached out to Meghan after her dad Thomas Markle was arrested'

Royal expert Jennie Bond said the King had been in contact with Meghan after her father was arrested in the US on a federal charge of possessing child sex abuse material

View 4 Images The King is said to have reached out to Meghan Markle (Image: Getty Images)

King Charles reached out to Meghan Markle after the shocking arrest of her estranged father, according to a royal expert.

‌



‌



Former BBC royal correspondent Jennie Bond said the King had been in contact with Meghan after Thomas Markle was arrested in the US earlier this month on a federal charge of possessing child sex abuse material. Speaking to Sky News, she suggested the family communication was a positive sign, despite the ongoing rift between Prince Harry and his brother, Prince William.

‌



Asked about the prospect of a reconciliation between the royal brothers, Jennie said: "No sign of that at all, no thawing of the estrangement between the brothers. But yes, there is communication between Harry and Meghan and the King.

‌



View 4 Images Thomas Markle after his arrest (Image: Pinellas County Sheriff's Office via Getty Images)

"I'm pretty sure that the King communicated with Meghan after her father was arrested and showed sympathy for her in that predicament. So there is communication.

"No meetings that we know about, but you know, the most crucial aspect of reconciliation is that any meetings that may or may not have taken place - and I think probably they haven't - but any communication remains private."

‌



She added: "And so far, that appears to be the case, and that gives some hope for the future."

Jennie also praised Charles for trying to maintain relationships with both his sons, despite their long-running family tensions.

‌



View 4 Images Royal expert Jennie Bond said Charles 'showed sympathy' for Meghan (Image: @SkyNews/X)

She said: "I've no doubt that [...] it's very, very difficult for Charles to try to keep both sons on board, and he has great loyalty towards William, who has stuck by him all this time. But I think actually that Charles has done a pretty good job of that, and he's on reasonable terms with both his sons."

‌



The comments come after Thomas Markle, 82, was arrested in Florida on November 6. Investigators seized around 78 items from two storage units in California, and he is accused of possessing child sex abuse material.

He was initially released under electronic monitoring but was returned to custody after prosecutors alleged he had cut off his ankle tag. He remains in custody and denies the allegations.

‌



View 4 Images Prince William and Harry have had long-running tensions (Image: Getty Images)

In the latest development, a US judge ruled on November 19 that Thomas was mentally competent to face the charges following an independent psychiatric assessment.

Article continues below

His next preliminary hearing is scheduled for December 1, although this could change if he is indicted before then.

Meghan previously said she was "deeply distressed" by the allegations against her father and explained that her decision to keep him away from her children had been about protecting them.

News.title: Man dies after horrific electrocution while hanging Christmas lights at London shopping centre
News.content:
Man dies after horrific electrocution while hanging Christmas lights at London shopping centre

The man was rushed to hospital after reportedly being electrocuted while hanging the Christmas decorations at Brent Cross Shopping Centre - he died the next day

View 2 Images Brent Cross Shopping Centre in London (file) (Image: Shutterstock / MN Nourzay)

A man in his 40s has died after he was reportedly electrocuted while hanging decorations on a 25ft Christmas tree at Brent Cross Shopping Centre.

‌



‌



The injured contractor was rushed to hospital on Wednesday morning but tragically died the following day.

‌



Management at the north London shopping centre warned retail workers the centre would be closed on Wednesday - but many still turned up for their shifts, only to find the doors locked.

‌



One member of staff at a cosmetics shop said all staff were "very upset" following the news, adding that the news came after they had already left for work.

"We received a message from the management at Brent Cross about the incident but, [I was] already on the way to work," the worker told Metro.

‌

"It's a terrible thing to happen and we are all very upset about it."

‌



Another worker added: "His poor family; we are thinking of them. We had to close and lost money, but that's not so important when someone has been hurt like this."

One told Metro: "The lights and the circuit must have shorted. Our lights are still not working, we are almost working in the dark."

‌



David Pinto-Duschinsky, Labour MP for Hendon, said he was "incredibly sad" to learn a man had died.

Paying tribute, he wrote: "I've just seen the incredibly sad news that the man who was electrocuted at Brent Cross has died.

‌

‌

News.title: Maths brainteaser is so hard it leaves teens in tears – can you solve it?
News.content:
Maths brainteaser is so hard it leaves teens in tears – can you solve it?

A viral maths brainteaser has left a teenager in tears, but there's a surprisingly simple algebra solution to the tricky word problem. Can you crack the exam puzzle?

View Image Maths puzzles can be incredibly frustrating (Image: athima tongloom via Getty Images)

For many of us, maths puzzles are something we were much better at back in school – when we were doing them regularly and the rules were fresh in our heads.

‌



‌



Once exams are over and we’re no longer practising, that problem-solving muscle can get rusty, and even familiar-looking questions can suddenly feel harder than they should. Algebra is often the first skill to vanish.

‌



As soon as we stop rearranging equations and “solving for x”, the letters, symbols and steps can seem to disappear from our brains. With that being said, we have a tricky brainteaser to help you brush up on your algebra.

‌



But be warned – this puzzle shared by Math Tutor has been deemed so tricky that it's been leaving teens in tears. Grab a pen and some paper and give it a go if you dare.

Question

Content cannot be displayed without consent

The question reads: "One number is 5 more than another number. Three times the greater plus twice the lesser is 30. Determine the numbers."

‌



The girl in the clip expressed her frustration, saying the question was "messing" with her because she couldn't work out what it was asking her to do. It certainly sounds tricky, but breaking it down into straightforward algebra makes it far more manageable.

Ensure our latest DWP headlines always appear at the top of your Google Search by making us a Preferred Source. Click here to activate or add us as Preferred Source in your Google search settings

‌



Answer

The next part of the TikTok video walked viewers through how to tackle the problem, so if you'd rather not have it spoiled, you might want to stop reading here!

You can begin by translating the written question into basic algebraic expressions. The first part of the puzzle states that "one number", which we'll call X, equals the sum of five and another number, Y.

‌



This gives you: x = 5 + y.

Given that X must be greater than Y based on the first statement, we can work out what the next line is asking. It tells us that three times X plus twice Y adds up to 30, meaning: 3x + 2y = 30.

‌



Next comes solving the equations. It's not the simplest of tasks, but it's perfectly achievable with a bit of algebraic knowledge.

Start with the second equation, substituting X with its value from the first equation: your new equation therefore reads 3(5 + y) + 2y = 30.

Article continues below

You then expand the brackets, giving you 15 + 3y + 2y = 30, or more neatly, 15 + 5y = 30. To simplify further, subtract 15 from both sides to get 5y = 15.

Divide 15 by 5, and Y equals three. Going back to our original equation to wrap up, if Y equals three, then X has to be eight because X = 5 + 3.

News.title: Woman buys £19 diamond from TikTok and is blown away when jeweller appraises it
News.content:
Woman buys £19 diamond from TikTok and is blown away when jeweller appraises it

A woman bought a 'shady' diamond from TikTok Shop, and she was determined to find out whether it was real or not, so went to two separate jewellers for their verdicts

View 2 Images She got a diamond from TikTok shop and assumed it was fake (Stock Image) (Image: Getty Images/Image Source)

When you think of diamonds, you likely think of fancy jewellery shops and maybe even picking out an engagement ring. However, one woman bagged herself a diamond on TikTok Shop for just £19.

‌



‌



Due to this rock-bottom price, shopper Maggie didn't expect much when parting with her cash. However, she wanted to do it for the plot anyway. She jokingly referred to her diamond as "shady," saying that she was going to "see whether it's real or not".

‌



Maggie told her audience: "I'm going to take it to two different jewellers to authenticate it, so let's see if I got scammed, or if it is actually a real diamond after all."

‌



Ensure our latest Mirror headlines always appear at the top of your Google Search by making us a Preferred Source. Click here to activate or add us as a Preferred Source in your Google search settings.

The first jeweller Maggie went to wasn't "able to tell whether it was a lab diamond or not because apparently you need special equipment to do that".

‌



So she went to another one, who told her that the diamond's clarity wasn't VVS because you could "see loads of marks in there".

VVS means tiny internal features are extremely difficult to spot under 10x magnification. They sit just below Flawless (FL) and Internally Flawless (IF) on the clarity scale and are divided into VVS1 and VVS2.

‌



The jeweller then confirmed that the diamond was lab-grown, and Maggie responded, "Really?!" expecting it not to be the real deal at all.

She added: "So apparently that diamond is real; I am shocked at that." The shopper explained that while the jeweller believes the diamond is real, they have suspicions that the "IGI certificate is fake".

‌



View 2 Images She was shocked it was real (Stock Image) (Image: Getty Images)

Maggie explained: "He said he knows this because it said on the IGI certificate that it was VVS2, which is like, clear, no little specks in it, but he said that it's a very, very cloudy diamond and it's also a very poor cut.

‌



"So, essentially, it isn't a very good diamond, but it is still a real lab diamond."

Even though Maggie managed to get a lab-grown diamond at such a bargain price, she would rather have a "beautiful diamond" around her neck or on her finger than the cloudy one.

Article continues below

And in the comments section, people agreed. Some believe the price was so low due to the cloudiness of the stone that Maggie received.

One theorised: "Most labs are super high clarity, and nobody buys low clarity ones, so this is the only way to get rid of them". And another said: "Not a good diamond then. I wouldn't bother with it, to be honest".

News.title: EMILY THORNBERRY: 'Our place is in the EU - Labour must be bold in manifesto'
News.content:
EMILY THORNBERRY: 'Our place is in the EU - Labour must be bold in manifesto'

Emily Thornberry, the chair of the Commons' foreign affairs committee, said she thinks Britain should be back in the EU and called for Labour set out what sort of re-entry deal it would seek in its next manifesto

View 3 Images Emily Thornberry said Labour should let the voters decide on rejoining the EU (Image: Thomas Krych/ZUMA Press Wire/REX/Shutterstock)

The UK-EU Summit on Friday was a diplomatic coup, and I congratulate Andy and Keir for their hard work in getting us to this point.

‌



‌



A deal signed by Boris Johnson on Christmas Eve was never going to cut it, so it’s right that we untangle the mess the Tories got us into. At long last, we’ve injected some common sense into our relationship with our closest neighbours.

‌



If someone tries to tell you this is all about Frazzles and bendy bananas, ignore them. Instead, think pet passports, being able to export cheddar to the French, and protecting our industries from cheap Chinese goods made by some of their dirtiest industries.

‌



It’s also about the future. Youngsters who frankly never voted for Brexit will once again be able to travel, work and study in Europe.

View 3 Images 'The UK-EU Summit on Friday was a diplomatic coup' (Image: Nicolas Economou/NurPhoto/Shutterstock)

And there will be more deals to win in the future: Made in Europe, access to electricity markets, digital partnerships and greater collaboration on electronic data.

‌



But the problem with being outside the bloc is that we end up in a permanent state of negotiation, because we always have to play catch-up, rather than having a seat at the table.

That’s why I think we should simply be back in the European Union. Polling from Best for Britain and YouGov shows that a majority of Brits, including a third of Reform voters and 40% of Tory voters, now support rejoining. It seems the public are coming round to the idea.

‌



When Andy became PM, he finally ended the conspiracy of silence over Brexit and opened a new chapter for Britain and the EU. It’s not about relitigating the arguments of the past, it’s about charting a new path forward. And there’s nothing wrong with taking stock of where we are as a country, where we are as a world plagued by conflict and competition, and deciding that having a voice in the room is much better than being the outcast peering in. These summits are an important start, but they are not an end unto themselves. At some point, we are going to have to decide where it is we want to end up when the dust settles.

Personally, I think Labour should just be bold, set out exactly what sort of re-entry deal it would seek to secure for the country, slap it on our next manifesto, and let the voters make the final call.

‌



Lessons from Finland and Estonia

For Putin and his cronies, Britain is the great enemy these days.

But while the Russians won’t be rolling tanks over the hills here any time soon, they are fighting our friends in Ukraine, who are defending the cause of freedom for all of Europe. If Ukraine fell, we know Russia wouldn’t stop there.

‌



View 3 Images 'If Ukraine fell, we know Russia wouldn’t stop there' (Image: Supplied)

I’ve just come back from Finland and Estonia, where they are preparing, should Russia take its second step.

‌



Even in Britain, Russia has been attacking us just below the threshold that would require an armed response, trying to test us: from arson attacks on the former PM’s home to cyberattacks on our infrastructure, worsening the cost of living.

Why? Because they want to sow fear, division and chaos. That’s why we must improve our resilience at home, continue to support our troops abroad, and refuse to accept anything other than a just and sustainable peace in Ukraine.

‌



Putin must be stopped.

North London’s New James Bond

There has been lots of speculation about who would take over as the next Agent 007. One name making the rounds was actor Jack Lowden, who has been keeping North London safe while filming the hit Slow Horses series. Although Richmond’s Robert Pattinson ultimately landed the top job last Monday, as far as the people in my patch of the city are concerned, Jack, you’ll always be our James Bond.

Article continues below

A Christmas Angel

Just to clarify, contrary to the gossip, Angel Tube Station WILL be open this Christmas. That’s great news for Christmas shoppers, because it’s the best place to go. Saying that, I think the ban remains on Norwegians skiing down the escalators. The slopes have been closed since 2007!

News.title: Major UK motorway closed as serious crash causes chaos near airport
News.content:
Major UK motorway closed as serious crash causes chaos near airport

Drivers have been urged to avoid the area and allow extra time for their journeys as police investigate the collision, with recovery work and debris clearance needed before the motorway can reopen

View Image A crash shut the M42 northbound near Birmingham Airport, with drivers reporting a "huge fire" (Image: Getty Images)

A major crash has shut part of the M42 near Birmingham Airport.

‌



‌



Police closed the northbound carriageway following the collision between junctions J5A and J6. Emergency services, including police, paramedics and firefighters, are at the scene.

‌



Drivers described seeing a “huge fire" following the crash, which involved a pick-up truck and a van at around 12.35pm, BirminghamLive reported.

‌



The cause of the crash and whether anyone has been injured is yet to be confirmed.

National Highways confirmed the closure. The statement read: “The M42 in the West Midlands is closed northbound between J5A (Birmingham Airport, NEC, A4545) and J6 (Bickenhill Interchange) following a collision and subsequent vehicle fire.

‌



“West Midlands Police, Fire and Ambulance Services attended the scene. West Midlands Police will be carrying out collision investigation works, which are expected to take several hours.

“Once the investigation is complete, vehicle recovery and debris clearance will be required before the carriageway can reopen. National Highways Traffic Officers are on scene assisting with traffic management.”

‌



West Midlands Police also urged drivers to plan ahead and allow extra time for their journeys. Its statement said: “If possible, please avoid the area and plan an alternative route.

“We will provide further updates in due course.”

News.title: Streeting calls Putin a 'cold-blooded killer' as he meets Zelensky in Kyiv
News.content:
UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky following continued Russian attacks on Ukraine on Friday evening and overnight.

Zelensky has justified Ukraine's repeated attacks on a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, describing it as a "fair response" to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in Ukraine.

He rejected a claim from Russia that the bridge, which links Russia to the peninsular it illegally annexed from Ukraine, was "exclusively civilian" in use.

Streeting and Zelensky hugged upon meeting and the British defence secretary explained he had come to Kyiv to see what support Ukraine needs for winter.

The BBC's Sarah Rainsford reports from Kyiv.

Read more on this story.

News.title: Catherine talks openly about how cancer changed her in documentary on BBC
News.content:
The Princess of Wales has spoken about how "cancer does change you," in a forthcoming documentary called Heal to be shown on the BBC.

"It changes your body, it changes you physically - but there is a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you," says Catherine in the first glimpses from the documentary, which features her private thoughts on her illness and recovery.

The highly personal film, to be screened on BBC One on 29 November, will see Catherine share her experiences of cancer, saying: "Healing is a journey."

It includes new footage of her completing the Three Peaks Challenge earlier this year, which involved climbing the highest peaks in England, Scotland and Wales over a day.

"It's clear we're not meant to carry life's challenges alone," says Catherine's voice-over, accompanied by images of other cancer patients and the princess hugging her own family, including Prince William.

"It is often through pain that we realise there is a greater beauty that lies beyond that," she says, once again reflecting the sense of change from her cancer experience.

News.title: 'We're not meant to carry life's challenges alone', Catherine says in first clip
News.content:
The Princess of Wales' cancer journey is set to be depicted in a new BBC documentary "Heal" that will air next weekend.

It follows Catherine announcing in January 2025 that she was in remission after having revealed her diagnosis less than a year prior.

She has since spoken openly about her illness and treatment although has never disclosed publicly what type of cancer she faced.

The new documentary will include footage of her completing the Three Peaks Challenge earlier this year.

"It changes your body, it changes you physically - but there is a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you," she says.

More on this story.

News.title: Spitting Image co-creator Peter Fluck dies aged 85
News.content:
Peter Fluck, co-creator of award-winning satirical puppet show Spitting Image, has died aged 85.

His family said he died in the early hours of Saturday at home in Cornwall, following a recent illness.

Spitting Image was immensely popular and sometimes controversial, running from 1984-1996 across 18 seasons, and featured puppet caricatures of celebrities, politicians and royals, including former Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher and Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother.

"The spirit that Spitting Image brought to the country was epoch defining," a family statement said.

"With Roger Law ('Luck and Flaw'), he brought a unique cutting edge to caricaturing that later evolved into a production company that created the TV series Spitting Image," it added.

"Peter's creative life continued after the series for many years from his studio in Cornwall. He was a private man who eschewed fame and attention."

The show won several awards, including one Bafta TV award and two Emmys and at its peak drew an audience of 15 million.

Fluck was born in Cambridge in 1941, and created the show alongside childhood friend Roger Law, who he met while studying at Cambridge School of Art.

Following school, both Fluck and Law moved to London and set up as freelance illustrators, and in 1976 set up their partnership 'Luck and Flaw' back in Cambridge.

News.title: Who will be Robert Pattinson's 'Bond girl' - and does the role need to change?
News.content:
After months of speculation, we finally have a new Bond. The question now is - who will play Robert Pattinsonâs leading lady?

Whatâs clear is that Pattinsonâs announcement as 007 has completely upped the game.

He's one of Hollywood's biggest stars, so all eyes are on Amazon MGM to see whether they go for an equally big name as a âBond girlâ, or if they'll take a chance on someone a little less well known.

Whoever is cast opposite him, though, needs to have a "very strong identity of her own", believes film critic Larushka Ivan-Zadeh - "someone distinctive, sexy, complicated".

Showbiz reporter Catrina Rose agrees: "I'd love to see a Bond girl who's just as interesting and unpredictable as he is."

And then, some say the whole concept of a Bond girl is outdated and the role needs to evolve for a new era. So what can we expect?

News.title: Can AI really help spot Black Friday deals? We put it to the test
News.content:
Whether it's scrolling through endless choice, spotting fake reviews, or working out if a "deal" is a deal at all, Black Friday sums up a lot of online woes.

Retailers promise bargains - but the sheer number of offers can leave us feeling no closer to finding the best deal.

It's an area where generative AI products, such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini, have promised to help.

But are they any good at finding Black Friday deals? We had a go ourselves a week ahead of the big day.

Figures suggest relatively few UK shoppers currently go to AI tools for help.

A recent YouGov survey of 19 countries found the UK ranked second-last in the proportion of people who said they had used AI to help them shop.

Crucially, 36% of respondents who said they would be shopping around Black Friday didn't plan to use an AI tool at all.

But the survey suggested a growing number of people were considering it - and tech firms have released features to capitalise on this.

Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping for UK users in November and OpenAI launched a Shopping Research tool on ChatGPT days before last year's Black Friday.

In the US, Google recently launched Universal Cart, with AI-powered features such as price tracking and identification of relevant promo codes.

But there has been criticism that fact-checking AI ends up taking more time, while some brands are working to try to make sure their products show up in chatbot answers.

We asked four models to find a 55-inch TV deal, using the free versions of many of the most popular tools.

While this was not a rigorous scientific test, the experience we had produced mixed results.

News.title: These dead pets were meant to be cremated - then their bodies appeared on a livestream
News.content:
The livestream begins.

A man â bald, goateed, wearing red-tinted sunglasses â walks down a cracked back road, guiding the camera towards a cluster of plastic-wrapped objects that spill out of the tall grass.

Names are written on the packages â Brandon; Ira; Lucky; Sweet â and numbers. One says 29kg (4.5 stone). Another says 2.5kg. Through the plastic you can make out what appears to be fur, claws and a flattened ear.

It's a mass dumping, the man explains. "We have about 25 animals here that have been dumped in bags. A couple of cats, some dogs."

"Purebreds," says the woman filming.

Warning: This story contains images some might find upsetting

In the weeks since that video was streamed on Facebook, Chris and Geraldine Taylor, who run animal rescue NGO Luna and Furry Siblings (LAFS), say they have uncovered 15 dumping sites in the suburbs of Bulacan, near the Philippines' capital of Manila.

In total they've unearthed the remains of some 170 dead pets. Belgian Malinois, golden retrievers, pugs, puppies and cats have been found dumped off service roads, sealed in septic tanks, floating in rivers and buried in vacant lots.

Many of these animals are thought to have been sent to cremation businesses in the expectation they would be turned to ash.

Now, many grieving owners are having to confront a distressing reality: their beloved pets may not have received the send-off they paid for. The urn in their home may not contain their pet at all. And they may in fact see their so-called fur child again, jettisoned like common waste on the side of a highway.

One saw the livestream and wrote on Facebook: "I think one of those pets is mine." Below, they attached a photo of a beaming Alsatian.

News.title: 'I was exhausted': Two days in the shoes of a tradwife
News.content:
Dressed in an unfamiliar long skirt, Poppy Jay is standing in a chicken coop faced with an angry cockerel as she checks for eggs.

As a director and writer, Jay is normally behind the camera, but today she's in front of it, trying out life as a tradwife.

The Tradwife - short for traditional wife - movement sees women embracing traditional gender roles in the home, such as cooking, cleaning and child rearing, while submitting to their bread-winning husbands.

While tradwives say they are bringing back old-fashioned family values, the movement has faced controversy. Its critics say tradwives fuel inequality and diminish women's empowerment by reinforcing archetypal gender roles.

For three days, Evangelical Christians Molly and Aaron Edwards welcomed Jay, a proud feminist, into their Yorkshire home to show her their lifestyle for the BBC One documentary Young, British and Tradwife.

On two of the days, the couple - who have seven children - allowed Jay to take on the homely duties that are usually Molly's responsibility, so Jay could try out the tradwife life.

"I was exhausted," Jay exclaimed when she spoke to BBC News.

During her stay, she helped Molly cook, home school the children, tend to the garden and brave the chicken coop.

She was given a book called The Gift of Womanhood to study the night before and asked to wear a dress.

"What struck me was how hard Molly works - like any mum of seven," Jay said. "She is a devoted mother, she cooks and cleans, she's doing endless loads of washing. She's barely got a moment to herself and I felt like I was getting in the way."

News.title: England run up record win over New Zealand in rugby union's Nations Championship
News.content:
England (19) 37

Tries: Slade, Van Poortvliet, Earl, Chessum, Atkinson Cons: F Smith (2), M Smith Pens: M Smith (2)

New Zealand (5) 12

Tries: De Groot, B Barrett Cons: McKenzie

England's revival roared up a gear as they beat New Zealand by a record margin after former captain Lewis Moody led the hosts' response to the haka.

Moody, who was diagnosed with motor neurone disease last year, stood at the centre of a flying V formation that England had adopted for their victories over the same opponents last year and in the 2019 Rugby World Cup semi-final.

In terms of margin, this win trumped both - and the other seven England victories in the teams' 121-year rivalry.

And the hosts were full value for it. They dominated the All Blacks from the start.

Henry Slade crossed for the opening try in the fourth minute and only England's own mistakes prevented them taking a bigger lead than their 19-5 advantage into the break.

Beauden Barrett marked his 150th Test appearance by rounding off a coast-to-coast Kiwi try to cut England's advantage to 24-12. But his team never really threatened to reel in Steve Borthwick's men.

England introduced five forwards off the bench in the immediate aftermath of that 55th-minute score and, with Ellis Genge in fearsome carrying form, they had more than enough to see out victory in comfort.

Seb Atkinson took a delayed pop pass from Marcus Smith to stroll in for England's fifth try just after the hour.

The hosts finished the game camped down in the New Zealand 22m in search of a sixth score while choruses of Swing Low rolled around the stands.

For New Zealand, who suffered a shock defeat by Wales last weekend, it is a result that suggests a long Test season, which included four Tests against South Africa, may be catching up with them.

By contrast England, who could still end up in next weekend's Nations Championship grand final depending on results, are riding a wave of confidence.

News.title: UK should only rejoin EU if it innovates on technology, Blair warns
News.content:
Former prime minister Sir Tony Blair has said Britain should only rejoin the European Union if it reforms - and allows more innovation on technology.

Speaking to The Sunday Times, external, Sir Tony said: "I was painted as saying Britain should just go back and rejoin - I'm not saying that - it's heavily conditioned."

Sir Tony was a prominent opponent of leaving the EU, and told the paper: "I do think Brexit was a real mistake."

But he added the debate was different now than it was in 2016.

Referencing the need for technology innovation, he said Europe could and "probably are" moving in the wrong direction.

He said: "The problem if we go back and join Europe is that; I can't say that the technology revolution is the single biggest thing, and then if Europe moves in the wrong direction on technology innovation, which they might do and presently probably are doing, that it's a good idea for Britain to rejoin. That's what's changed in this last ten years."

He argued Britain should have an ambition to reform the EU.

But he added that we have to be "prepared to walk away from that negotiation" and need to make our own economy and tech sector strong.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham this week agreed what he called a "win-win" deal with the EU.

The agreement covered British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen also announced that the trading bloc and the UK are launching a digital partnership, including areas like artificial intelligence (AI) and quantum technology.

The EU and Britain "have enormous potential to innovate together", she added.

News.title: Village votes to 'leave UK' over migrant plan
News.content:
Villagers vowed "this is only the beginning" after voting overwhelmingly to "leave the UK" in protest at plans to house migrants at a former airbase.

Residents in Barnham, Suffolk, held a symbolic poll on Saturday to decide whether or not to declare independence.

The referendum was called after RAF Barnham, near Bury St Edmunds, Suffolk and Thetford, in Norfolk, was earmarked by the government as a site to house up to 931 male asylum seekers.

Two-hundred-and-fifty-seven people - 94% of those who took part â voted in favour of leaving, 16 voted against and one vote was spoiled.

Following the result, which is not legally binding, residents unveiled a flag - a Stone-curlew against a Suffolk blue background - to celebrate the village's newfound "independence".

Barnham is the second village to hold a symbolic poll over migrant housing plans, after residents of Piddington in Oxfordshire voted to leave the UK in September.

John Bauer, chair of the parish council, has said the Suffolk village will now declare itself the Bailiwick of Barnham.

News.title: Man charged with attempted murder after Bradford councillor stabbed
News.content:
A man has appeared in court charged with attempted murder after a Bradford councillor was seriously injured in a stabbing.

Councillor Ibrar Ali was attacked at about 11:00 GMT on Thursday on Thornbury Avenue, before being driven to nearby Manse Street, according to West Yorkshire Police.

Arfan Ali, 32, of Thornbury Avenue, is also charged with assault and possession of an offensive weapon in a public place. At Leeds Magistrates' Court earlier, he was remanded into custody until he appears at Bradford Crown Court on 21 December.

Councillor Ali remains in hospital in a serious but stable condition, police said.

Councillor Ali is a Your Bradford Independent Group representative for Bradford Moor ward and was first elected in May.

He works as a community development manager at charity The Leap, and was one of the founders of Leeds Road Festival.

Speaking after Thursday's incident, his family thanked police, paramedics and members of the public who "courageously provided first aid and assistance at the scene" and asked people to "keep him and his family in your duas [prayers]".

News.title: Staff gagging clauses lifted ahead of probe into culture at data watchdog
News.content:
Non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) signed by staff at the UK's information watchdog will be lifted to allow them to speak out about its culture, the government has confirmed.

Ministers are expected to publish the details of how an independent review of the working environment at the Information Commission will be carried out next week.

It follows the departure of the watchdog's boss five months ago amid allegations of sexually inappropriate behaviour.

A government spokesperson confirmed that NDAs, known as "gagging clauses", would not be enforced by the Information Commission, saying the regulator "will not use the terms of any agreement to prevent people from participating in the review".

The government "will set out further details on the review, including its terms of reference and the independent reviewer, shortly", they added.

The Information Commission is one of the UK's most high-profile regulators charged with the crucial task of regulating AI, data protection and Freedom of Information requests.

It recently won a court battle with TikTok after it fined the social media platform Â£12.7m for misusing children's data, and has penalised bodies including the Ministry of Defence after an email blunder exposed the details of interpreters fleeing Afghanistan.

But it has been without permanent leadership since Information Commissioner John Edwards resigned earlier this year.

It came after an independent investigation found a "case to answer" over reports of alleged inappropriate behaviour towards staff including claims of sexual harassment.

The Information Commission said the investigation found Edwards' behaviour "fell short of the conduct expected from a public official".

In a resignation statement posted on his LinkedIn page in June, Edwards said he disagreed with how the investigation had been carried out but accepted his position had "become untenable".

The statement continued: "I have accepted that there have been occasions where I exercised poor judgement and made attempts at humour that were inappropriate and caused offence."

Freedom of Information requests have found that since the start of Edwards' tenure in 2022 to the present, 16 current and former employees have signed non-disclosure or confidentiality clauses costing more than Â£354,000.

Nine of those , externalincluded a "non-derogatory clause" which legally prevents employees from making negative comments publicly.

While this is a small proportion of the more than 1,000 staff employed by the commissioner, government advice stipulates that public bodies should only use confidentiality clauses "when necessary" and that they should "not seek to stifle or discourage staff from raising concerns".

Since 2025, new laws also mean they cannot be used to silence employees subjected to harassment or abuse.

After Edwards' departure, the government announced a review, external into the Commission's culture and governance, with the then-Secretary of State for Science, Innovation and Technology Liz Kendall telling a committee of MPs she was "absolutely appalled at what the independent investigator found - sexual harassment and bullying".

Five months later, the investigation has not begun.

In recent weeks, the two major civil service unions, the PCS and FDA, have pushed for an external examination of the events leading up to Edwards' resignation in meetings with government officials.

The unions have also asked for those who signed non-disclosure agreements with the ICO to be released from them so they can contribute to the review.

The PCS union says other concerns had previously been raised with them about Edwards, including a bullying complaint, which was investigated at the time.

An internal staff survey, published in August and released under FOI, external points towards wider issues at the Commission, with 14% of all employees reporting they had either personally experienced bullying, harassment and discrimination.

Multiple current and former employees have also told the BBC of experiencing or witnessing incidents of bullying or harassment.

PCS General Secretary Fran Heathcote said the union's members at the Commission "have been failed for too long by a toxic leadership culture that has allowed bullying and harassment to persist, leaving many staff fearful of speaking out".

Heathcote said she welcomed the "positive engagement" the union had received in recent weeks from the Commission and officials at the Department for Culture Media and Sport (DCMS), which oversees it.

But she added: "For the review to command the confidence of staff, it must be genuinely independent, robust in its approach, and prepared to identify where accountability lies."

Conservative MP Caroline Dinenage, who chairs the DCMS select committee, said the Commission "needed a firm new direction" after the departure of its former boss.

"Instead, a leadership vacuum has compounded what went before at a rudderless organisation where it seems the worst behaviours in the workplace are not being challenged," she added.

She said it was "vital" the government brought in "someone who can set a new tone and is dedicated to changing attitudes and protecting staff" to head up the Commission.

A spokesperson for the Information Commission said its commitment to an independent review reflected its "ongoing commitment to listening and learning from the events of the past year and those leading up to it".

"Our new Board, appointed this summer, has been working exceptionally hard to provide fresh leadership, ushering in a new governance structure and a new strategy," they added.

"It is committed to listening carefully to the review's findings and recommendations, and building on the positive work on our culture already taking place across the organisation."

News.title: Former journalist and Lost Lives author David McKittrick dies
News.content:
The renowned journalist and author David McKittrick has died at the age of 77.

McKittrick was best known for his work during the Troubles, and the book Lost Lives.

The book detailed the people who died as a result of the Troubles.

It was first published in 1999 after several years of research by McKittrick and co-authors Seamus Kelters, Brian Feeney and Chris Thornton.

Lost Lives won the Ewart-Biggs Memorial Prize for the promotion of peace and understanding in 2000.

At a later stage, David McVea joined the project.

A death notice for McKittrick said he was the "beloved husband of Pat, much loved father of Julie and Kerry, cherished grandfather of Daniel and Emma and the dear brother of Arlene and Freda".

"He will be sorely missed by all his extended family and friends," it added.

Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) leader Claire Hanna MP paid tribute to McKittrick, describing him as an "outstanding journalist".

"David McKittrick was the outstanding journalist reporting in Northern Ireland throughout the Troubles," she said.

"Calm, empathetic and rigorous, he combined exceptional integrity with an unrivalled network of contacts.

"Throughout decades of conflict, he preserved his humanity and remained true to his moral compass."

Hanna added that her "thoughts are with David's family, friends and former colleagues at this sad time".

News.title: Scouts say they face £1m tourist tax cost for overnight trips
News.content:
Scout groups are warning they could face an additional annual bill of Â£1m as a result of the government's proposed tourist tax for England.

The overnight levy would allow councils and regional authorities to charge visitors an additional fee for their accommodation, including campsites, raising money to be spent on local services.

The increased cost from the Visitors Levy could price some young people out of joining Scout camps and other trips, the group said.

Dwayne Fields, the UK's Chief Scout, has called for youth groups to be exempted and said the charity - which sees more than 1.4m overnight stays a year - would be "firmly opposed to any proposal that would see local mayors tax Scouts and other voluntary youth organisations".

The Ministry of Housing, Communities & Local Government told the BBC that local leaders who introduce the levy "will have the option to exempt certain types of accommodation in their areas, including accommodation which is often used for trips by youth groups like Scouts and Girl Guides - such as camping pitches".

They added money raised from the levy will "stay local and be invested in the visitor experience and local growth including in high streets, parks and events".

Labour mayors have indicated they would cap the levy at 5% but the legislation contains no maximum limit.

In a statement, the Scout Association said the tax, if set at 5% across the country, could cost the charity Â£1.04m a year and force volunteers to deal with onerous paperwork.

They worked this out by assuming the levy would be set at 5% for all the 1,423,344 annual overnight stays across Squirrels, Beavers, Cubs, Scouts, Explorers and volunteers.

Girlguiding would also be subject to the levy.

In a statement, Fields said: "We strongly support investment being made available to strengthen local communities. Well-crafted legislation can unlock that opportunity.

"But we are firmly opposed to any proposal that would see local mayors tax Scouts and other voluntary youth organisations for camping trips that equip young people with skills for life, while burdening volunteers with the role of unpaid government tax collectors."

News.title: Bad Girls star Helen Fraser dies aged 84
News.content:
British television, theatre and film star Helen Fraser, who was perhaps best known for her role in the hit prison drama Bad Girls, has died.

The actress, who also appeared in episodes of Coronation Street and The Royle Family, reportedly died on 10 November at Yaxley House Care Home, in Eye, Suffolk. She was 84.

Born in Oldham, Greater Manchester, she had lived in Wickham Skeith, in Suffolk, with her late husband Peter Handford.

From 2004 until 2019, she was also an ambassador for East Anglia's Children's Hospices (EACH). The charity said it was "deeply saddened" by her death and would "remember her with enormous fondness and gratitude".

"Helen was very special to us and a wonderful ambassador, supporter and friend who worked tirelessly to champion our cause," a spokesperson said.

"Whether fundraising, attending events, opening our shops or rallying our volunteers, Helen brought incredible warmth, empathy and joy.

"She had a wonderful way with people and made a lasting impression on all those fortunate enough to spend time in her company."

The actress first trained at the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art in London before making her breakthrough in the 1963 film Billy Liar.

But it was her role as the tough prison officer Sylvia Hollamby in the long-running ITV show Bad Girls that made her a household name among British audiences.

Fraser appeared in more than 90 episodes across all eight series, from 1999 to 2006, and later reprised the role in the West End stage version of Bad Girls: The Musical.

Fraser's funeral will be held at West Suffolk Crematorium on 4 December at 13:30 GMT, according to a death notice published by the East Anglian Daily Times, external.

Attendees are asked to make donations in her honour to East Anglia's Children's Hospices charity.

"We feel truly honoured that EACH will benefit from donations made in her memory at her funeral," the charity's spokesperson added.
