World.title: Anthropic worker claims to have solved a Holy Grail of math problems with the help of AI
World.content:
Anthropic worker claims to have solved a Holy Grail of math problems with the help of AI

toggle caption i Seth Wenig/AP

A mathematician who works for artificial intelligence giant Anthropic claims he has solved a Holy Grail of math problems with the help of the company's AI tool Claude.

It marks the second time in recent months that an AI company or someone linked to one claims to have cracked a famed unsolved math problem.

Levent Alpöge, a member of the company's technical staff, made the announcement Friday by way of a four-page explanation posted on his website. He said that he believes by working with Claude, he has found a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis.

Sponsor Message

"Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line," Alpöge wrote. "No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line."

Formulated in 1859, the Riemann Hypothesis centers on the distribution of prime numbers — those that are only divisible by one and themselves — as they grow towards infinity.

Alpöge said his discovery came late Sunday night. He messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to ask about "my ability to announce," as the San Francisco-based company was about to make major news with its stock market debut.

A day after the company's initial public offering — the most valuable in history — Alpöge revealed he'd solved the problem that has proved elusive for more than 150 years. Anthropic did not respond to an email from The Associated Press requesting comment on Alpöge's claim.

Alpöge released his and Claude's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis within 17 million lines of Lean code, a programing language that allows people to program proofs of mathematical theorems. Traditionally the findings buried in that code would be published in a formal paper, said Alex Kontorovich, distinguished professor and department chair of mathematics at Rutgers University.

Sponsor Message

"Usually when somebody gives you a paper, that's also kind of code for a proof and you have to actually read the paper, follow it yourself, figure out if you believe every single line in that paper. And when you're done, you should have a deep understanding of why something is true," he said.

He said Claude followed that code and said the proof is true.

"Does that mean I understand it? Not yet. But the computer is extraordinarily picky, way pickier than I am and so if you can satisfy the computer, there's a very, very good chance you're going to satisfy me too," he said. "But I have to do the work."

Hours after the announcement, the Riemann Hypothesis remained listed as unsolved on the Clay Mathematics Institute's website. The institute had selected the hypothesis back in 2000 as one of seven Millennium Prize Problems and offered a reward of $1 million for the solution.

The assessment process of whether the problem has actually been solved takes time, explained Martin Bridson, president of the institute.

"This is an announcement of historic significance, which holds the promise of a dramatic transformation in the perception of what is possible in the struggle to extend the human understanding of mathematics," he said in a statement. "But the journey from today's announcement to a place of real understanding will be long and difficult."

Alpöge said he is "presenting the world with a complete argument before having mastered a massive neighbourhood around its mathematics." He said more than 250,000 pages came out of his work with AI.

In September, OpenAI said its technology was key in a similar breakthrough with Navier-Stokes, an equation that governs the flow of fluids.

"Navier-Stokes fell and now the Riemann Hypothesis," said Kontorovich. "There's some kind of out-of-body experience where I'm looking at myself saying, 'Yes, the Riemann Hypothesis has been solved,' and kind of trying to comprehend what the hell these words are coming out of my mouth."

Sponsor Message

Anthropic made a blockbuster Wall Street debut this week, through which it raised a record-breaking $81 billion at a $1.5 trillion valuation.

Amodei has projected an optimistic vision for AI's future in which the technology leads to significant advancements in math and science research while simultaneously warning about the potential risks AI poses.

World.title: Hegseth reportedly moves to restrict defence ties with Canada, but Ottawa sees no change
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has reportedly issued a classified directive restricting military co-operation between the United States and Canada — something that Canadian government and military officials were not aware of and have seen no evidence it has been put into practice.

The Washington Post reported late Friday that the directive was circulated last week in a secret memorandum. The report cited U.S. officials familiar with the decision.

Three Canadian defence officials speaking on background on Saturday said they were aware of the reports and were looking to substantiate them, as well as seeking clarification because there's been no change at the military operational level between the two countries.

A Republican senator attending the Halifax International Security Forum confirmed the existence of the memo and the restrictions but downplayed their impact, saying they have no effect on operations between the two countries.

"It does limit general flag officer meetings to those that advance [U.S. Department of War] objectives," said Sen. Mike Rounds, who sits on the armed services committee.

U.S. defence officials — uniform and civilian — must seek permission before attending social events or think-tank conferences.

The measures were drafted months ago but only signed recently, Rounds said, adding that it's unfortunate they were leaked.

The intent, however, was to put pressure on Canada.

U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds speaks to reporters in the U.S. Capitol Building on Monday in Washington, D.C. Rounds on Saturday confirmed the existence of Hegseth's memo and the restrictions, but downplayed their impact. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)

"Look, we really want you to bring up your defence spending," Rounds said, before quickly adding the U.S. delegation at the conference had a chance to be briefed on the latest measures.

"We just had a chance to talk with our Canadian friends, and they indicated and laid out the roadmap that they're using to significantly increase their defence spending."

Democratic Sen. Chris Coons of Delaware says he was irritated by Hegseth's directive and its impact on relations with Canada.

"This is a completely unnecessary insertion of a negative tone," said Coons, who is also in Halifax and sits on the Senate foreign relations committee.

"I'm relieved this has no significant operational impact, but at the end of the day, as we've got our adversaries globally pulling together and working more closely — Iran, North Korea, China, Russia — the United States should be doing nothing to further aggravate some of the distance and division between the United States and Canada."

Defence Minister David McGuinty, who is also at the security forum, said the two countries continue to work "hand-in-glove" on various missions such as stopping the flow of illegal drugs in the Caribbean and on new policy initiatives such as integrated air and missile defence.

"It's the first time we heard of this — just yesterday," McGuinty said, referring to the directive. "It's clear there's some sort of document we haven't seen. I'm not aware of the contents of it."

Minister of National Defence David McGuinty rises during question period in the House of Commons on Parliament Hill in Ottawa on Nov. 3. McGuinty says Canada and the U.S. continue to work 'hand-in-glove' on various military missions and new policy initiatives. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

There was no mention of the directive from the Americans at the security forum dinner Friday night, according to two of the confidential defence sources, one of whom wondered if the congressmen and senators were even aware of it.

CBC News is not identifying the sources because they were not authorized to speak publicly.

The existence of such a directive would only add to mounting tensions between the long-standing allies over trade and defence spending.

Canada, U.S. working on trade deal

The move comes as the Trump administration and the government of Prime Minister Mark Carney inch toward a trade deal that could see some relief in key sectors such as automotive and steel and aluminum.

The military and defence ties between Canada and the U.S. are deep, long-standing and would be difficult to restrict at an operational level without harming the security of the U.S. itself in one fashion or another, said one of the sources.

Cross Country Checkup is asking: Is it OK to start travelling to the United States again? Leave your comment here and we may read it or call you back for this Sunday's show

The two countries co-operate in the defence of North America through NORAD. In Europe, they are founding partners of NATO and work side by side with the other 30 members of the Western alliance. They also work together in the Indo-Pacific in joint military exercises.

A third source said it would also be difficult and counter-productive for Washington to, for example, restrict access to U.S.-made weapons systems and equipment, which Washington has been eager to sell and pressuring Canada to buy.

WATCH | Carney says he's examined risk of U.S. military action in Canada: Carney says he examined 'extreme tail risk' of U.S. military action in Canada | Duration closed caption 8:20 Prime Minister Mark Carney said in an interview with the New York Times that he's studied the risk of a U.S. military attack on Canada. Matina Stevis-Gridneff, the newspaper's Canada bureau chief, said Carney took several seconds — 'a pregnant pause' — before responding as to whether such a scenario had crossed his mind.

Officially, the scope of Hegseth's restrictions is unclear, according to the Washington Post report. Since the memo is classified, the Department of War has not identified which military programs or activities might be affected.

In a statement to CBC News prior to Rounds's comments, the Pentagon's chief spokesperson, Sean Parnell, ruled out restrictions on operational level matters, but was vague on what precise impact the memo would have.

"The Department of War is taking steps to ensure its engagements with Canada advance tangible U.S. defence objectives and ultimately support a reinvigorated defence relationship," Parnell said in a written response.

"DoW is prioritizing opportunities for bilateral cooperation that strengthens the defence of our Homelands and shared hemisphere, while supporting Canada's ability to meet NATO obligations. This guidance does not impact defence intelligence co-operation, our binational NORAD command or our co-operation through NATO."

The response left open questions about bilateral military exercises, training exchanges, defence planning and other forms of co-operation.

But even on that level, Canadian officials say they've seen no evidence thus far of any restrictions and point to the notion that the memo has been in circulation for a week.

WATCH | Pentagon withdraws from Canada-U.S. defence board: Pentagon withdraws from Canada-U.S. defence board | Duration closed caption 2:33 The Pentagon has announced it has paused its participation in a joint Canada-U.S. defence board that's been around since the 1940s, accusing Canada of not making enough progress on its commitments. Canada says it's always ready for constructive discussion on how to strengthen mutual security.

Last spring, the Trump administration paused U.S. participation in the Permanent Joint Board on Defence (PJBD) with Canada.

Halting the activity of the decades-old board, a bilateral advisory group that co-ordinates continental security and recommends defence policy to both governments, was considered largely symbolic because it met infrequently.

Canada has been routinely criticized in Washington over its lacklustre defence spending.

There has been change under Carney, and Canada has now hit the NATO target of spending two per cent of GDP.

Carney, however, has publicly stated he wants to diversify both the country's trading relationship and where it sources its military equipment. He has said it's not good for more than 70 cents of defence equipment dollars to be going to one market — the United States.

World.title: Montreal police arrest 2 ex-officers for alleged assault, criminal harassment, breach of trust
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM) announced Saturday in a news release that it arrested two of its own officers in connection with allegations of discriminatory and racist acts by police officers at Station 39.

The arrested officers were released under the promise to return to court, where they will face charges of assault, criminal harassment and breach of trust, according to the SPVM.

The two officers had previously been placed on administrative leave, and were among seven who were fired on Nov. 2. Two were dismissed from Station 21 and five from Station 39, according to Montreal police Chief Fady Dagher.

The firings were the result of an internal disciplinary investigation that was carried out at the administrative level of the SPVM.

Other related criminal investigations are still being handled by the SPVM's Division des normes professionnelles.

Montreal groups praise arrests

In an email to CBC News, Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada thanked the police officers who "had the courage to defy the code of silence."

"The trust that Montrealers have in their police force is paramount," she said. "The work continues, and justice must take its course."

For Fo Niemi, executive director of the Center for Research-Action on Race Relations in Montreal, the arrests are reassuring.

"It validates everything we had hoped would take place," he said. "The whole country is watching this."

Niemi says the arrests are a step in the right direction towards protecting the public and rebuilding its trust in police.

"If you want to uphold police values and standards you must report the misconduct of others," said Niemi, speaking to police officers. "You must denounce injustice inside, committed by your colleagues."

He says the charges could also help set a precedent for how police officers are held to account going forward.

Alain Babineau, director of racial profiling at the Red Coalition, a Montreal group that works to dismantle systemic racism, said that it's very rare that charges against police officers are brought forward.

He agrees that the arrests are positive, but said that "it's only a beginning."

Babineau says that the practice of street checks facilitates racist and discriminatory behaviour by police. The Red Coalition is calling on the SPVM to end the practice.

"That kind of power has to be put in abeyance," he said.

World.title: 11 killed in burst of violence in northern Mexico after capture of cartel leader
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A burst of violence in Mexico's Sinaloa state after authorities captured cartel boss Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as El Chapo Isidro, left at least 11 people dead, authorities said Saturday.

Meza Flores, one of the FBI's 10 most wanted fugitives, was captured and flown to Mexico City on Saturday after a heavy firefight between Mexican forces and cartel gunmen overnight left residents of the city of Guasave terrorized and trucks and businesses burning.

Mexico's defence cabinet on Saturday afternoon said that seven alleged cartel gunmen and four Mexican soldiers were killed.

Meza Flores climbed the cartel ranks to lead the Beltrán Leyva cartel and later became the leader of his own group, the Meza-Flores Transnational Criminal Organization. The United States had a $5 million US reward offer for information leading to his arrest, and he was wanted for trafficking drugs to the U.S. and illegally carrying firearms.

Mexico's government said in a report early Saturday that intelligence from the U.S. helped with the capture of Meza Flores, but provided few details about how authorities in Mexico and the U.S. co-ordinated to detain him.

Meza Flores was also a key ally to Los Mayos, a faction of the Sinaloa Cartel, which was designated as a foreign terrorist organization by the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump last year. His capture represents a blow to the cartel as it fights with another faction for control of the northern Mexican state.

The Trump administration and Mexican authorities both celebrated the arrest as a security win, but experts warn it could set off another wave of violence in a region already ravaged by cartels.

Night of terror after forces moved against cartel

The capture of Meza Flores and his No. 2 in the city of Guasave set off a wave of violence overnight, terrorizing civilians. Calm appeared to set in Saturday morning.

Videos show screaming civilians fleeing gunfire at a baseball game, burning cars and businesses, and circling helicopters shooting at homes below. Such shows of force by cartels are common following the capture or killing of leaders.

Vehicles on fire on a highway near Los Mochis, Sinaloa, on Friday following the announcement of El Chapo Isidro's arrest. (Yohari Leon/Facebook/Reuters)

Guasave resident and firefighter Paola Sánchez said thousands of people were terrorized late Friday night as they took shelter from intense gunfire in grocery stores and other locations.

"Last night, many businesses were burned, including Oxxo [convenience] stores, kiosks and pharmacies, along with cars and trucks," Sánchez told The Associated Press.

The city's firefighters had to take shelter at their station and wait until Saturday morning for orders from their superiors to dispatch the first crews to check whether any businesses or vehicles were still burning, she added.

"Everything looks calm today," she said.

Mexican Security Secretary Omar García Harfuch wrote on X Saturday morning that armed forces would remain deployed in Sinaloa state to protect civilians.

This undated image released by the U.S. Department of State shows Fausto Isidro Meza Flores. (U.S. Department of State/The Associated Press)

U.S. pressure on Mexico to crack down on cartels

Meza Flores's detention marks another high-profile capture of a cartel leader as Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum faces pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump to crack down on cartels.

Sheinbaum has gone after illegal groups more aggressively than her predecessors, and homicides have dipped significantly in her two years in office.

WATCH | El Mencho's killing briefly caused mayhem in Mexico: Thousands stuck in Mexico as cartel chaos calms | Duration closed caption 7:01 Calm has started to return to Mexico following the killing of the powerful cartel leader known as El Mencho, but travel advisories remain and Canadians are waiting for flights to resume. Meanwhile, Mexico's president said authorities tracked a romantic partner of the drug kingpin to start the operation that left about 30 cartel members and 25 troops dead.

Both the U.S. and Mexican governments celebrated the capture on Saturday, with the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) commending Mexican authorities.

"The capture of El Chapo Isidro delivers a significant blow to a ruthless criminal organization that has used extreme violence to traffic deadly drugs, including fentanyl, a designated weapon of mass destruction, into American communities," the DEA said in a statement.

"This operation underscores the critical importance of intelligence sharing in targeting dangerous cartel leaders."

García Harfuch called the detention "an important step in pacifying Sinaloa."

Firefighters hose down a burning cargo truck on a highway between Guamuchil and Guasave in Mexico's Sinaloa state on Saturday, following overnight violence after Mexican authorities captured Meza Flores in Guasave. (Martin Urista/The Associated Press)

Mexican authorities said they used "stealth and surprise" to capture Meza Flores, establishing a security perimeter around the building where he was located. After coming under attack with guns and explosives from suspected cartel operatives, armed forces personnel entered a home and detained him, they said.

Video shared by authorities shows heavily armed men in camouflage escorting a man who appears to be Meza Flores through a dimly lit house and putting him in the back of a truck.

'Kingpin strategy' causes more violence, experts say

Sheinbaum's government has immobilized a number of cartel kingpins. Chief among them was Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes, known as El Mencho, who was killed in Guadalajara state in February. Similar to the aftermath of the capture of Meza Flores, that dramatic operation resulted in a burst of violence and burning cars.

Members of the Mexican army stand guard outside the Specialized Prosecutor's Office for Organized Crime in Mexico City on Saturday. (Paola Garcia/Reuters)

Mexican security analyst David Saucedo said the capture of Meza Flores marked another instance of the governments of Mexico and the U.S. increasingly falling back on a longstanding security strategy, which critics warn could fuel more violence in the long run.

The so-called "kingpin strategy" relies on taking out top capos as a way to combat cartels. But experts say it often triggers violent power disputes among groups, like the one underway in Sinaloa.

"What is evident is this is a product of pressure from the United States," Saucedo said. "What they do is capture high-profile kingpins — the leaders — but they don't dismantle the entire organization.

"They arrested the No. 1 and No. 2, but the entire network of hit men, street-level drug dealers, businesses and political and police connections remains intact."

World.title: Etsy faces backlash over including AI model training in new policy update
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Some Etsy sellers across Canada are removing products from the platform amid criticism for introducing artificial intelligence model training as part of a policy change.

Tsuki Matsuba, in Vancouver, B.C., is pulling her custom stationery products from Etsy ahead of a new AI policy the company is rolling out next month.

"It felt like a kick in the teeth," said Matsuba.

There is a line of language within an update to the company’s terms and agreements rolling out Dec. 16 that says Etsy, its third party partners and vendors can use sellers' content to "develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies."

One of the largest accounting and consulting firms in the world, KPMG, reported in 2025 that 88 per cent of tech executives surveyed believe tech companies that embrace AI will develop a competitive edge over those who don't.

It also showed 68 per cent of respondents expect a moderate to very high return on investment related to AI investments — 10 per cent of more.

Canadian backlash

After seven years working in animation, Matsuba said AI was one of the major factors in losing her job in that industry.

She fears shop owners on Etsy are "being forced" to choose between earning holiday income and remaining on the platform under terms that allow their content to be used for AI training.

More Etsy shop owners across Canada are removing products and original artwork from the platform due to concerns that their work will be used to train AI.

Artist Tina Nawrocki, in Ottawa, wrote on X that she is "closing down" her Etsy shop due to the company’s "new predatory AI practices."

Halifax-based artist, The Calendork, announced it has removed all artwork from its Etsy shop while remaining open due to the "new insane AI policies."

'Should have done more'

Etsy’s head of customer operations, James Ossman, said in a statement that respecting its sellers’ work is "central" to the way Etsy runs its business.

He said sellers’ "creative work belongs to them," and Etsy doesn’t use that work to train "AI models designed to copy their original work or replace their creativity."

WATCH | Indigenous artists affected by Etsy's fur ban: Etsy to ban the sale of fur, with some Indigenous artists affected most | Duration closed caption 2:27

The company plans to continue discussing the policy change with sellers to "clarify what we mean and our intent in the Terms," said Ossman.

He also said that the company "should have done more" to communicate changes coming with Etsy’s updated policies with the platform’s sellers.

But for Matsuba, those discussions won’t change her decision to stop selling her products on the platform.

"My business is completely AI free," she said, "I don’t want to participate in developing AI further."

World.title: UN talks on AI in warfare end with no commitment to binding rules
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

UN-backed talks this week on regulating AI in warfare ended Saturday with nations agreeing to further discussions, but without a consensus on developing firm rules on how to rein in deadly autonomous weapons.

Proponents for regulations including UN Secretary General António Guterres had called for a legally binding treaty within a short time frame on AI weapons like drones that could identify and kill without human involvement.

The discussions ran Monday to Friday at a Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons meeting in Geneva. More than 100 countries that are party to the convention, including Canada, were expected to take part.

Though most countries supported working towards the treaty, some military powers like the U.S. and Russia resisted committing to binding rules that would limit them in developing such high-tech weapons. That resulted in a softened agreement to "elaborate" a possible accord on such lethal autonomous weapons systems by 2028.

Izumi Nakamitsu, the UN high representative for disarmament affairs, hailed a "significant achievement" but acknowledged a "glass half full or half empty" scenario, citing Guterres's hopes for a legally binding deal this year.

However, some advocacy groups bemoaned the blocking of stronger language at a time when AI is increasingly becoming a factor in deadly strikes.

"States have agreed it is sufficient to just talk about the issue, for the 14th year, while these weapons enable atrocities," said Max Tegmark, a machine learning specialist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and founder of the Future of Life Institute.

Superpowers resist binding rules

The outcome is disappointing but expected, said Branka Marijan, senior fellow at the Centre for International Governance Innovation and senior researcher with anti-war organization Project Ploughshares.

Marijan says military superpowers like the U.S. and Russia have resisted legally binding rules.

"There is a real issue here of political will. There's just no political will among the major militaries to have legally binding instruments and hard laws," she said.

AI is being used increasingly in conflicts around the world to gain advantage in battle.

Both Russia and Ukraine are using AI to track targets and plan attacks in the war entering its fifth year. In Ukraine, there are reports that autonomous drones operated by Russia have killed civilians, while Ukraine has also reportedly tested such weapons.

The U.S. has made a major push to increase its use of AI in combat, and is testing advanced fighter drones that fly themselves.

WATCH | The future of AI-powered military weapons: AI drone warfare is here. Should Canada buy in? | Duration closed caption 6:05 Governments are spending billions on the autonomous arms race — should Canada join in? For The National, CBC’s Jennifer Yoon examines the future of AI-powered military weapons, what it means for international humanitarian law and where Canada fits in.

The need for regulation has become more urgent as the world sees this "incredibly dangerous move" towards the development and deployment of increasingly capable autonomous weapons systems — without any guardrails, Marijan said.

"I think there's extreme scenarios, but there are very immediate risks and concerns if you think about the fact that each country could deploy these systems now and there are no real constraints," she said.

CBC News reached out to Global Affairs Canada and the Department of National Defence for comment.

In a statement sent to CBC News earlier this month, the Department of National Defence said the Canadian Armed Forces supports the development of autonomous functionality on the condition that it would be "operated within a responsible chain of human command and control and commits to uphold the reliable and lawful use of such weapon systems."

Canada was among the countries that agreed to a declaration on how to govern use of artificial intelligence in warfare at a military AI summit in Spain in February.

In 2025, Canada also supported a UN resolution calling on countries to lay the groundwork for possible negotiations on a treaty governing the use of lethal autonomous weapons systems.

The UN's Nakamitsu called for countries to begin work towards a deal as early as Monday and "start thinking about how to get as strong as possible [an] instrument to prohibit and regulate lethal autonomous weapon systems."

World.title: Israeli settler violence at unprecedented levels during Palestinian olive harvest
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

"It’s so random and doesn’t have any rules. You don’t know where it could come from, or in which intensity. Which weapon, how many?"

Wala Zoran is talking about attacks by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank during the annual olive harvest.

We met her on Oct. 11 while she was standing with a group of fellow Palestinians, warily watching some settlers standing alongside Israeli soldiers on the other side of an olive grove in the village of Abu Mash’al. One settler had a rifle slung across his back.

Zoran and her family, including her elderly grandparents, were attacked by settlers in the grove the day before while trying to harvest their olives.

"They started throwing big stones at us and we realized that we can’t take the olives — we can’t take anything, actually," she said. "We started running, but they were so close. Everybody was hit with the stones, like my father, my sister. I was. My cousin was shot in the leg, actually, and had to spend the night in hospital."

Wala Zoran and her family were attacked by settlers on Oct. 10, while trying to harvest their olives in the West Bank village of Abu Mash’al. (CBC)

This despite their efforts to avoid a confrontation.

There have been more settler attacks against Palestinians and their property during this year’s olive harvest than in 20 years of record-keeping by the United Nations.

Like many Palestinians, Zoran’s family has changed how they harvest in a bid to stay safe. They try to gather their olives in quick bursts, not waiting until the big tarpaulins they put on the ground to catch the olives are full before ferrying them back home.

They also wait to begin picking until other families from the village are able to join.

But safety in numbers isn’t working.

Israeli soldiers and settlers are seen side by side in Abu Mash’al in the Occupied West Bank. According to the United Nations, Israeli settler attacks, often with Israeli military protection, numbered close to 400 for October alone. (CBC)

'People depend on olive oil here'

Zoran lives in France but returns home to help her family with the annual harvest. She’s worried her parents will have to make another attempt this year to finish the harvest.

"People depend on olive oil here," she said. "We can’t just say, 'OK, I don’t feel like doing it this year.'"

The olive industry contributes up to 15 per cent of agricultural GDP in the Palestinian economy.

A family harvests olives in the Palestinian town of Beit Surik, on the western edge of the occupied West Bank. Some groves lie behind the separation barrier built by Israel in the early 2000s, which snakes onto Palestinian land in some parts, cutting farmers off from their trees. (CBC)

On the other side of the family's olive grove, the IDF soldiers eventually left after lobbing tear gas into the trees where a few Palestinians had remained.

The settlers then gathered up the olives left behind and drove off with them in the direction of what’s known as an outpost.

All Israeli settlements in the occupied territories, including East Jerusalem, are illegal under international law. Israel continues to expand them while also tolerating — and often facilitating — a growing number of outposts, small camps from which Jewish extremists try to push Palestinians from their land. Even Israel considers them illegal, at least on paper.

More than 180 outposts have been created since 2023, according to the Israeli settlement watch group Peace Now, many of them close to Palestinian population centres.

Political analyst and researcher Ibrahim Rabaya’a says it’s one reason violence is surging during this year’s harvest. He describes the speed with which the outposts are spreading as a "strategic escalation" by settlers emboldened by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanhayu and his far-right government.

"We are talking about … a very organized process, very organized players," said Rabaya’a during an interview at his home in Ramallah. "[The settlers] are well-trained. They are working in general as an army, militias."

'Every single day we have attacks'

It's especially striking how emboldened the settlers are compared to even a year ago — whether in groups of two or three harassing Palestinian herders and their livestock or forming battle lines in large numbers, masked and terrifying.

CBC News witnessed the latter while visiting Abu Falah, one of a cluster of villages in the central West Bank, on Oct. 13.

WATCH | Palestinians risk their lives to pick their olives: Palestinian farmers risk their lives to pick their olives | Duration closed caption 9:56 Israeli settler attacks on Palestinian olive harvesters in the Occupied West Bank have reached a 20-year UN record high. CBC senior international correspondent Margaret Evans goes into the groves and finds lives — and a way of life — dangerously at risk.

We arrived just a few hours after settlers had descended from a hilltop outpost above the town and taken axes to dozens of olive trees.

The residents had blocked the road leading from the base of the hill into the town with heavy stones to stop the settlers from going any further by vehicle.

When the Palestinians led our news crew to see the damaged trees on foot, the settlers spotted us and started back down the hill, some on foot, running at full speed with sticks and slingshots. Others were driven down in the backs of white pickup trucks. They were masked and dressed in black.

When the call went out to Abu Falah’s residents to defend their groves, they picked up rocks of their own on the way, moving through the olive trees to the outer perimeter, later firing firecrackers at the settlers as they advanced.

"Every single day we have attacks and every single day we’re out in the field defending people," said Diyaa Murra, a university student volunteering with the Palestinian Red Crescent.

Palestinian emergency services are under increased pressure during the harvest, with the Israeli NGO Yesh Din charting more than 25 settler incidents a day during the harvest, from vandalism to physical assault.

Ambulances try to position themselves in areas where repeat attacks take place to avoid being delayed by Israeli military checkpoints or imposed closures.

"I think the only way to defend ourselves from the settlers is to engage with everybody in defending the village," said Murra, who was born in Abu Falah. "So I decided to work with the Red Crescent to be part of the defence system. That’s the only way."

The melee continued in Abu Falah until the Israeli Defence Forces (IDF) arrived, firing tear gas canisters in the direction of the Palestinians retreating from the bottom of the hill.

WATCH | Israeli settlers attack and beat Palestinians, U.S. journalist: Israeli settlers attack and beat Palestinians, U.S. journalist in West Bank | Duration closed caption 2:32 Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine says hardline Jewish settlers attacked her along with Palestinian olive farmers in the West Bank, and continued to kick her while she was on the ground. Settler violence has spiked since the start of the annual Palestinian olive harvest.

A few days later, the settlers attacked Abu Falah again, making international headlines after a U.S. photojournalist for the Washington Post named Heidi Levine was severely beaten by settlers who surrounded her.

Violence affects livelihood

Before we left Abu Falah on the day we visited, we counted at least 40 settlers involved in the attack clearly visible and back up on top of the hill.

Yet we witnessed only one arrest: a Palestinian man handcuffed and blindfolded as Israeli soldiers led him toward a military vehicle.

Later, we learned the father of five had been held for three days and fined for throwing stones.

The Palestinians say they have little else with which to defend themselves.

"[Palestinians know] most of the settlers are protected by the army," said Mohammad Ahmad, a Palestinian American waiting for the olives he managed to collect to be processed at a mill in Silwad, a town about 10 kilometres from Abu Falah.

"Even the young settlers [… ] under the age of 18 and 17 years old, they have weapons, you know."

Olives picked in the West Bank are processed at a mill in Silwad, a town about 10 kilometres from Abu Falah. (CBC)

Ahmad says this season’s violence is impacting livelihoods and yields, including his own.

"I have never experienced or felt the way we’re feeling right now, because of the settlers and because of what’s going on," he said. "And we’re not allowed to reach most of our lands."

Tensions with IDF

Many Palestinians are required to co-ordinate access to their own olive trees with the IDF, depending on where they’re located.

On Tuesday, the IDF issued a statement on social media saying that 90 per cent of what it called "co-ordinated harvests" had been completed. It also denied claims that security forces were deliberately preventing the olive harvest.

The Palestinian Farmers Union responded, saying that as of late October, 55 per cent of the overall olive crop "remained inaccessible or unharvested."

Israeli forces arrived early in the morning of October 21st, keeping the Palestinian villagers of Deir Jarir from reaching their olive groves. (CBC)

Israeli security forces can often declare areas of confrontation between Palestinians and settlers closed military zones.

That’s what happened when our crew arrived in Deir Jarir, another town in the central West Bank, on Oct. 21.�

After settlers ambushed an initial attempt to harvest olives, the Palestinians invited Israeli and international activists to accompany them on a second try, hoping they might offer protection.

But when they arrived at the muster point carrying ladders and olive rakes, the villagers found an armoured vehicle and a handful of IDF soldiers blocking the road.

"They are telling us that our farms are closed military zones and we cannot leave, and we’re stuck here," 72-year-old Abu Asif told CBC News.

The IDF has said its security forces operate to "prevent friction and violence, enabling residents to harvest safely."

In some instances, Israeli soldiers themselves have uprooted entire olive groves, saying they could be used by Palestinians to hide in and as a launching point for attacks.

Palestinians say it’s simply one more way Israel is trying to remove them from their land.

"Our life under occupation has always been difficult," said Abu Asif. "But this time, this season, it’s the most difficult and the hardest."

'The Palestinians are defenceless'

Prime Minister Netanyahu has dismissed the settler attacks as the work of a "small minority."

But Israeli lawyer and peace activist Daniel Seideman says that what’s happening in the West Bank couldn’t be done without Netanyahu's "knowledge, consent and blessing."

"The Palestinians are defenceless," he said in an interview at his office in Jerusalem. "The military is either in bed with the settlers, doing the settlers' bidding or turning a blind eye and saying, 'This isn’t our responsibility.'"

"It’s clear that the settlers see this as a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to ethnically cleanse the West Bank," Seideman said, adding that he didn’t use the term lightly.

Seideman spoke to CBC News ahead of last month’s Israeli election, which many believed would see Netanyahu’s tenure come to an end. At the time of publication, it's still unclear who will ultimately form a government.

Analyst Ibrahim Rabaya’a says while a change in government could rein in some of the settler violence, few Palestinians believe it would slow the de facto annexation of the West Bank.

"It is also a strategy for other political players in Israel, but they try to do so without bringing anger from international society," he said. "What we can [call] silent annexation."

Political analyst Ibrahim Rabaya’a says the proliferation of settler outposts in the West Bank is one reason violence is surging during this year’s olive harvest. (CBC)

None of the other main Jewish political parties are on the record supporting a Palestinian state, although Yair Golan’s Democrats have indicated they would potentially support it in the future.

The olive harvest is a favourite target for Israeli hard-liners, precisely because it is such a potent cultural symbol of Palestinians' connection to the land.

Israeli flags everywhere

Rabaya’a says that in addition to the daily hardships of living under occupation, the settlers have been trying to increase psychological pressure on Palestinians.

Over the past several months, Israeli flags have started appearing along the main road from Ramallah up to the northern cities of Nablus and Jenin.

WATCH | Settlers use Israeli flags as intimidation tactic in West Bank: Settlers are using Israeli flags as new intimidation tactic in the West Bank | Duration closed caption 2:30 Video reviewed by CBC News shows Jewish settlers surrounding a Palestinian shop in the West Bank with Israeli flags — part of a new intimidation tactic described by one analyst as 'psychological warfare.'

And along that road in the town of Luban al Sharqiya, settlers arrived one night in October to completely swamp a Palestinian roadside café with Israeli flags.

The owner, Muayad Hussein, who lives with his family in a house just behind the café, says that when he heard them, he was too afraid to come out.

He showed CBC News the images captured by his security camera: dozens of young Jewish extremists pounding the flags into the ground. An Israeli police car can be seen parked on the other side of the road. Someone hands out drinks as they work.

Hussein told us one of the settlers from a nearby outpost warned him that if he took the flags down, they would come back.

He’s afraid they will. So the flags remain.

World.title: Judge awards damages to both sides in lawsuit after neighbours' dispute over loose dogs 'spun out of control'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A judge has awarded an eastern Manitoba couple sued by their neighbour $10,000 in damages, and their neighbour $1,000, after an "unfortunate series of events" unfolded over dogs allowed to run loose on an unfenced property.

The couple — a man and woman, named as the defendants in a lawsuit filed with Manitoba Court of King's Bench — purchased their "dream property" along the Winnipeg River, in the rural municipality of Alexander, in 2015, Justice Sheldon Lanchbery wrote in a Nov. 16 decision.

The property has a large forested area, with walking trails, that shielded them from their neighbours, and offered an escape from the "hustle and bustle of the real world," Lanchbery wrote.

Around 2017, a woman — the plaintiff in the suit — purchased the adjacent property to the east, and decided it would be "a great location" to raise rescue dogs, the decision says.

Though she lacked prior experience in handling rescues, she registered a business as a dog rescue — an idea that "originated during a course of employment on an Indigenous reserve," where dogs roamed freely, Lanchbery wrote.

She decided to also let the dogs she rescued roam on her new property.

"The dogs in question are best described as feral," Lanchbery wrote, and their "aggressive tendencies" continued post-rescue.

Justice Sheldon Lanchbery decided against awarding legal costs to either party, saying in his decision they 'were painfully aware this was not their finest hour.' (Jaison Empson/CBC)

Although the municipality had bylaws in place to restrict the number of dogs a landowner can have on their property, the woman "far exceeded that number," the judge wrote.

"The evidence as to the precise number is inconsistent," but she had at least seven prior to the COVID-19 pandemic, Lanchbery wrote.

The couple said they "did not dare go walking" in the forested area of their property because of the dogs.

The man in the couple testified one of the woman's dogs bit his shin. He also suffered a contusion on one of his hands after he punched the animal, Lanchbery wrote.

'A lot of talking, but not a lot of listening'

The woman had a dog kennel on her property, but the dogs were not always kept there and were not leashed when outside it, the decision says. The woman believed the dogs "should be able to roam," which included defecating on the couple's property.

There were early attempts to resolve the conflict, which Lanchbery described as "a lot of talking, but not a lot of listening."

Accusations "flew back and forth," and "a first-year law student knows what follows next," wrote Lanchbery.

Building a fence between their properties could have solved their problem. Justice Sheldon Lanchbery

Security cameras were installed, and both parties started to photograph and film each other near the property line.

Land surveys were also ordered and boulders were placed near where the dog owner believed the property line was, but another survey done by the couple showed she was incorrect, the decision says.

The woman then approached the couple to ask if they would help pay for a fence to keep her dogs from entering their property.

The couple refused, in part because they felt it was the woman's responsibility to control her dogs, Lanchbery wrote.

He quoted American poet Robert Frost, who "knew fences make good neighbours."

"Building a fence between their properties could have solved their problem," wrote Lanchbery.

Both sides guilty of trespassing

Disputes continued between the parties. The woman purchased a "large, cumbersome" dock, and instead of putting it on her own property, she placed it on the couple's.

"I find if the dock was to be placed in the Winnipeg River, the easiest unimpeded point of access to transport the dock into the Winnipeg River was on the east side of … [the dog owner's] property, not on the west side [closer to the neighbours]," wrote Lanchbery.

The couple put up "no trespassing" signs, " adding to … [the dog owner's] frustration," he wrote.

The woman later accused the couple of trespassing and filed her lawsuit, after the man threw broken boards from the dock into her dog kennel.

One of her dogs suffered an eye injury, but the judge said evidence suggested it likely wasn't from the boards.

The man admitted he had thrown the boards into the kennel, but denied the dog was present when he did so. There was no evidence the dog was in the kennel at the time, Lanchbery wrote.

The judge concluded, however, that both parties were guilty of trespassing — the couple by throwing the deck boards into the kennel, and the woman by letting her dogs run loose.

He awarded the couple $10,000 in aggravated and general damages for the woman's failure to control her dogs, which was ongoing behaviour, compared to the couple's single instance of trespassing, he said.

He also awarded the couple an extra $100 because the woman placed her dock on their property, and parked cars there too, which he said was "an inconvenience at best."

Lanchbery awarded the dog owner $1,000, saying the man's conduct in throwing the boards was "especially egregious" given that he has previous military experience, including training other members in hand-to-hand combat.

The couple's lawyer had argued that given that background, the man had actually "exercised great restraint in not injuring" the woman's dogs, but the judge rejected that argument.

"Removing boards from [her] dock and propelling them into a run are an intentional act of intimidation," he wrote.

The judge decided awarding legal costs to either party was not justified, given their conduct throughout the dispute.

"When the testimony concluded in this action, the litigants were painfully aware this was not their finest hour," he wrote.

World.title: The pros, cons and risks of using AI as your personal assistant
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Imagine a chatbot that can not only recommend a great restaurant in your area, but can also book a reservation, put it in your calendar and email an invitation to your friends.

In recent months, that scenario has become reality, with some of the world's biggest AI developers launching digital personal assistants they say will make users' lives easier.

The companies behind these new mass market agents say they are remarkably capable, safe and easy to use.

But cybersecurity experts say the more advanced tasks come with more risk that something could go seriously wrong.

What are AI assistants, and how do they work?

Three of most well-known ones on the market — Meta's Muse, OpenAI's dots and Anthropic's Claude Duet — all debuted within weeks of each other and all have similar capabilities.

Muse can be spoken to as if it were a chatbot and instructed to send emails, book travel, make purchases and more on your behalf when connected to third-party apps like Shopify and Ticketmaster.

It can handle multiple tasks at once and continue working through them even while the app is closed.

LISTEN | Tech columnist on her experience using Muse: The Current 21:24 What could possibly go wrong with Meta's Muse? Meta's personal AI agent Muse is now one of Canada's most downloaded apps, and has attracted millions of users since it was first launched in September. It acts as a personal assistant and can help with things like paying bills and ordering food, but it relies on a lot of your personal information. We speak with the Wall Street Journal's personal tech columnist, Nicole Nguyen, who has tried the app and tells us why she finds it both incredible and terrifying at the same time.

OpenAI says users can instruct dots to do "nearly anything" by messaging or calling them through ChatGPT. They can be connected to other devices and over 4,000 apps, and even have the ability to use your laptop.

Anthropic's Claude Duet has been pitched as more of a proactive agent for work than as an assistant to take on personal errands.

The agent can take on simple administrative tasks, like scheduling meetings, and more complex projects, like creating financial reports or building web apps, according to the company's product announcement.

While Muse is free, dots and Claude Duet each require a subscription. Claude Duet isn't available in Canada yet.

How do AI personal assistants keep your personal info safe?

CBC News reached out to Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic to ask how they protect users' privacy and prevent their personal assistant agents from going beyond the scope of the tasks they're assigned, along with what advice they'd give users to prevent this from happening.

A spokesperson for Meta said Muse runs on its own dedicated computer in the cloud that is designed so users' data is securely stored, referring CBC to a blog post by software engineer Tarek Sheasha outlining the safeguards built into Muse.

They also referred CBC to another blog post that says Muse checks with users before taking on sensitive actions, like sending an email or making a purchase, and shows a complete audit trail of everything the agent has done.

A spokesperson for OpenAI referred CBC to a blog post outlining its safeguards, which includes encryption for users' content and account security systems that monitor for suspicious use.

OpenAI also monitors dots as they plan and carry out actions "looking for potentially harmful behavior, such as acting outside your instructions or trying to bypass safeguards," the blog post says.

OpenAI also notes that users can give dots custom rules, such as to never send emails, and says certain actions require a user's confirmation each time, such as permanently deleting data and installing or running software from an unrecognized source.

A spokesperson for Anthropic said Claude Duet was built to enable people to stay in control of what it does, and so their information is handled with discretion.

The model never sees users' passwords, browser cookies or sign-in tokens, and Claude Duet is instructed never to share sign-in credentials, credit card and bank account numbers and government ID numbers — even if you ask, the spokesperson said.

What can go wrong?

Some users have reported getting more than they bargained for when putting these high-powered assistants to work.

A Montreal man asked Muse to handle his Facebook Marketplace transactions. But after listing a keyboard for sale, Muse gave out his home address to a stranger without his knowledge.

When the buyer showed up, Muse even told him the seller was there even though he wasn't home.

"Muse doesn't check with me, it doesn't tell me this guy has messaged and then it gives the guy my address, agrees to his price and literally tells him to come right now, that's the crazy part," Matt Robb told CBC News last month.

WATCH | Meta AI agent gives out man's address: He used Meta’s AI agent Muse for Marketplace sales. Then it set one up behind his back | Duration closed caption 2:39 Matt Robb started using Muse, Meta’s AI agent, to handle Facebook Marketplace transactions. But after listing a keyboard for sale, he got more than he bargained for. One expert advises people to really look at what they’re letting Muse access.

Asked how something like this could happen, a spokesperson for Meta pointed CBC to a social media post made by Robb about his ordeal, where he explained he had clicked "allow always" instead of "allow one time" when asking Muse to handle his Marketplace transactions on his behalf going forward.

While these agents can be innovative and exciting tools, they should be used in a limited way and given very specific instructions in order to avoid these kinds of mishaps, said Claudiu Popa, a Toronto-based certified cybersecurity professional with privacy consulting firm Datarisk Canada.

"Unless you tell them very specifically what they can and cannot do you're going to have unpredictable results," he said.

"That's the issue with all AI agents, and this issue is going to continue for the foreseeable future."

David Shipley, CEO and co-founder of Beauceron Security in Fredericton, said he hasn't let these agents get near his computer at all.

"I absolutely do not trust this technology," he said.

Shipley compared trusting them with your personal errands to a monkey's paw wish, referring to the classic horror story that serves as a cautionary tale to be careful what you wish for.

"You might wish for it to do a certain set of actions and it's going to go and do those actions, but perhaps not in the way that you intended it to do that."

Why have Canada's biggest banks blocked AI assistants?

With a client's authorization, AI agents can also connect to bank accounts and credit cards to monitor balances and transaction histories and give tips on budgeting.

But concerns over AI agents accessing sensitive information have also prompted Royal Bank, TD Bank, CIBC and Bank of Montreal to block them from directly accessing their clients' online bank accounts and other information.

The CEOs of RBC and BMO recently warned that third-party AI agents are not to be trusted with personal banking information.

WATCH | Canada's banks ban AI agents from access client accounts: Why banks are banning AI agents | Duration 1:23 As privacy fears and security concerns rise, some of Canada's biggest banks are hitting the brakes on clients using personal AI agents — with most outright banning them.

Those warnings should give people pause about using these agents entirely, given that banks "have been among the more fervent adopters of digital technology over the last 30 years," Shipley said.

But Popa said he thinks these AI personal assistants can be used in a limited way without compromising your personal information, such as for tasks like research or writing emails — not sending them — for you.

"You can't necessarily trust an outside AI agent with your private information. So sharing calendars, emails, all sorts of personal information and personal files, that is for me, it's not a line that I would let it cross."

World.title: De la Espriella calls on US to prosecute Petro in response to call to “resign now”
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called on the US Justice Department to “investigate, prosecute and hopefully jail former President Gustavo Petro after the latter called on the people to “rise up” and “restore real democracy.”

De la Espriella addressed the nation at the end of a day of anti-government marches that mobilized tens of thousands of people throughout Colombia.

Petro led the march in Cali and called on his supporters to “rise up,” call a general strike and force the president to “leave now,” less than four months after De la Espriella took office.

Reiterating fraud accusations and the president’s business ties to paramilitary warlords and drug traffickers, the former president told the crowd that “it is not about waiting until 2030; an illegitimate government must leave now.”

A government whose policy goes against the people must leave now. A government whose policy builds hunger and death for the people of Colombia must leave now. Life must be restored, democracy must be restored, and the slogan “Abelardo, resign now!” must become the slogan of the majority of the Colombian people. An agreement will eventually be made to transition back so that the Constitution of Colombia and the laws in favor of the Colombian people prevail. But from here on out—and that is why we must move to a national strike, that is why we must move to a general strike—within the people’s right of expression and decision, an illegitimate government that goes against the interests of the Colombian population must leave now. Gustavo Petro

De la Espriella told Petro that he would never accept they “attack democracy, promote a coup d’état or attempt to destroy Colombia, just as he did when he was a guerrilla fighter.”

The president claimed that the former President and congressional opposition leader Ivan Cepeda “have no moral authority whatsoever. However, as I tell you, I will not accept them attacking democracy, attacking institutionality, or promoting a coup d’état in an attempt to destroy Colombia.”

De la Espriella repeated his threat to extradite his predecessor if requested to do so by the administration of his ally, US President Donald Trump.

I make a direct call to the judicial authorities of the United States so that investigations related to acts of corruption, drug trafficking, or any other criminal conduct move forward with full rigor and the independence of the judicial system in the United States. Petro’s government was a criminal enterprise, and international laws and provisions were violated. The United States has jurisdiction to investigate him, prosecute him, and hopefully imprison him. Let the North American justice system act, let the whole truth be known, let the evidence be examined, and let those found responsible answer before the law without regard for anything other than the application of the law. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president has tried to criminalize the opposition and the former government ever since taking office in August without much success.

World.title: Colombia rejects US proposal to conduct joint strikes against drug trafficking: NYT
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella rejected a US plan to conduct joint military operations, anonymous US officials told the New York Times (NYT).

According to the NYT, De la Espriella told the US government he supported working with the US military, but lacked congressional support invite US soldiers on Colombian soil.

The conversation would have taken place in the week ahead of US defense secretary Pete Hegseth’s visit to Colombia on Wednesday.

In a response, the president and the defense secretary said that the alleged US plan was “fake news.”

“I have not rejected any proposal of the Government of President Donald Trump,” De la Espriella said on social media platform X.

Colombia and the United States maintain strong and increasingly close cooperation in the areas of security, intelligence, and the fight against drug cartels and narco-terrorist organizations. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president confirmed that congressional approval would be required for him to invite foreign troops into Colombia.

Between visits to Venezuela and Ecuador, Hegseth briefly stopped in Colombia, and met with Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora and Foreign Minister Omar Bulla.

The defense secretary expressed his support for the government’s plans to combat drug trafficking.

“You, sir, are never going to have a stronger partner than President Trump, Secretary Hegseth an the War Department,” Hegseth told Bula.

Both the US and the Colombian governments have assumed a militaristic approach to drug trafficking, contrary to their predecessors.

World.title: “Basic food stuffs exempt from sales tax:” De la Espriella on tax reform bill
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella rolled back his government’s plan to impose sales tax on basic food stuffs in an attempt to seek approval for his tax reform in Congress.

In an address to the nation, De la Espriella said that “basic household goods will be exempt from VAT. I made that clear from the very beginning.”

Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo and Finance Minister Miguel Gomez last month announced the introduction of a 19% sales tax on basic food stuffs and the creation of a mechanism that would allow the poor to recover this money.

The radical proposal was necessary to prevent Colombia from defaulting on debt, said Gomez.

However, “after several analyses, they adjusted the proposal to protect the basic food basket, which required a greater effort on the part of the government,” the president said Sunday.

De la Espriella’s tax reform, which will have to pass before December 16, got stuck in Congress after the coalition Liberal Party said they wouldn’t support taxing the basic food basket.

Also the far-right Democratic Center party opposed the measure, which almost immediately triggered calls for a national strike.

The president suggested that he would cut expenses he blamed on the leftist “criminal organizations” that won the 2022 elections with former President Gustavo Petro.

My true tax reform is the fight against corruption, against the criminal organizations that squandered the state’s resources for so many years. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“There is still a lot to do, but you can’t fix that disaster in three months,” said De la Espriella.

Contrary to campaign promises to reduce the State apparatus, De la Espriella proposed a 2027 budget that increased state spending.

On top of that, the government has been talking to the International Monetary Fund about a credit line that would support his increased spending.

World.title: De la Espriella replaces director of earthquake reconstruction fund as scandals mount
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked the director of the Miracle Fund, which was to reconstruct the parts of Colombia destroyed by an earthquake in August, over excessive wages and hardly any progress.

De la Espriella decided to sack the director, befriended businessman Jaime Andres Uribe, after the opposition revealed he had given himself a COP39.4 million ($11.9 thousand) salary.

The labor cost of the 26 Miracle Fund staff was COP765.5 million ($231.2 thousand), revealed opposition Senator Kamelia Zuluaga (Pact0 Historico), who had filed an open information request.

The fund additionally estimated it needed an annual COP8.9 billion ($2.7 million) for the 130 people that were supposed to be hired.

The president responded on Twitter, claiming that “the salaries that have been announced for the Milagro Fund are NOT in line with my austerity policy. I DO NOT APPROVE THEM! I have ordered that this absurdity be reversed immediately.”

Hours later, De la Espriella said he accepted the resignation of Uribe and said that former Housing Minister Luis Felipe Henao would assume the leadership of the reconstruction effort.

Henao became controversial in 2020 when a photo appeared of him and late drug trafficker José Hernandez, a.k.a. “El Ñeñe,” who allegedly helped finance the campaign of former President Ivan Duque.

Henao’s wife, Luz Stella Murgas, was recently appointed director of business association ANDI.

The government’s response to the earthquake has been fiercely criticized as it has failed to effectively begin reconstruction efforts in western Colombia, where the 7.4M earthquake destroyed more than a 100,000 homes an much of the regional economy.

World.title: Colombia’s foreign minister apologizes to Democrats for “inappropriate and disrespectful” comments
World.content:
Colombia’s Foreign Minister Omar Bula apologized for “inappropriate and disrespectful” comments he made in 2020, when he claimed that US Democrats “thrive in illegality.”

In a letter to the Democratic Party, Bula offered his “sincere apologies for comments I made in past social posts concerning leaders of the Democratic Party.”

The foreign minister referred to comments he made between November 2020 and September 2024 in which he claimed that “the globalists and US Democrats love everything illegal” and claimed their party “had turned into crap.”

In the letter, Bula stressed that his “perspective has evolved since then, and those messages do not reflect the views I hold today. Nor do they, in any way, represent the position of the Government of Colombia under President Abelardo de la Espriella.”

I value the contributions that Democratic leaders have made to the friendship between our countries and welcome the opportunity to continue building on that work together. Foreign Minister Omar Bula

After a stunning electoral defeat of the Republican Party, which lost control over both houses of the congress, Bula called for “mutual respect and bipartisanship” regardless of “political differences and electoral cycles.”

Starting in January, when the new Congress takes office, the Foreign Ministry will depend on the support of the Democratic majority for any type of financial aid or formal bilateral agreements.

World.title: De la Espriella failed to make Colombia secure in 90 days
World.content:
Colombia’s far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella failed to live up to his promise to “recuperate” state-control of conflict regions through a “shockwave” of hardline security measures within 90 days in office.

His first three months in office ended this week, and by almost every metric violence is rising.

Non-state armed groups and organized criminal groups alike have staged a series of attacks on security forces and their infrastructure, likely in retaliation for aggressive security actions that have included bombings carried out by Colombian aerial forces (which have killed at least 8 minors).

It would seem the shockwave is being carried out by not-state, rather than state forces.

According to new data published by the country’s Ombudsman’s Office and police, extortion, homicides, acts of “terrorism”, kidnappings, and attacks on security forces have all risen since De la Espriella assumed the presidency. Thirty-eight members of the police or military have been killed, and 213 wounded in attacks by criminal groups.

Child-recruitment by non-state armed groups has also risen dramatically: 131% higher than former President Gustavo Petro’s first 90 days in office.

Although De la Espriella has made concrete changes from the policy of his predecessor — destruction of coca is up, and the right-wing president has dismantled previously ongoing negotiations and peace processes with some criminal groups — much of his administration’s security policy has been more about optics than substance.

The president has released videos of himself walking among the bodies killed by aerial bombings, and has taken to showing up in affected cities wearing a pistol on his hip, and carrying a walkie-talkie.

During an operation in Cucuta, in the province of Norte de Santander, on November 10, De la Espriella spoke with military officials armed, wearing a military uniform and a red military-style beret.

The same day, The National Liberation Army, ELN, the largest remaining rebel group in the country, carried out a drone attack on a military base in the north of the same department that killed at least one soldier and wounded 4 others.

His Ministry of Defense released a video of him interrogating and mocking a member of FARC-dissident group the 33rd Front, telling him “welcome to Patria Milagro,” the miracle country —a slogan from his campaign during elections.

In September, paramilitary group the ACSN shut down large parts of the northern coast, including the city of Santa Marta. In a show of power, the ACSN even defied a response-deployment by Colombian military forces to the region to continue the forceful shutdown as the military largely stood by powerless.

De la Espriella has since militarized both Santa Marta and Cucuta, a measure which seems to have had little effect on the day-to-day operations of non-state armed groups in the regions.

De la Espriella has also repeatedly requested help from the US, and invited them to participate in his security crackdowns. In September, the President met with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio to sign a series of agreements he calls the “Barranquilla Accords.” Colombia agreed to give US companies preferential treatment regarding mining contracts, particularly involving rare earth minerals, in return for US security assistance and drone technology, among other things.

De la Espriella has attempted to align Colombian and US interests in security in the region, and talked repeatedly of extraditing “high priority targets,” to the US rather than charge them under Colombian law.

At a press conference with Rubio, De la Espriella announced what he called a “21st-Century Plan Patriot.”

Named after an aggressive security operation by former right-wing President Alvaro Uribe, the president said the agreement with the US will “modernize aircraft, radars, drones, helicopters, anti-drone systems, air defense, mobility, intelligence, cyber defense, special forces, and maintenance and operations.”

Armed groups currently operate in 24 of Colombia’s 32 provinces — roughly 75% of the country. That was true before De la Espriella took office, and the president’s promise to change that within three months has so far yielded little to change that.

World.title: Three months after 7.5M earthquake struck Colombia, “reconstruction hasn’t begun”
World.content:
Human rights officials warned on Tuesday that the reconstruction of west Colombia, which was partially destroyed by an August 10 earthquake, fails to show progress.

In a statement, the Ombudsman’s Office warned that “difficulties persist in providing assistance to and supporting the recovery of affected communities, particularly with regard to housing, access to essential services, the protection of rights, and funding for response measures.”

The top human rights official of Pereira, Leonardo Fabio Reales, told Caracol Radio that “the reconstruction of the city has not begun. There isn’t even a rough outline of what is planned to be done after the earthquake.”

Pereira is among the hardest hit by the 7.4M earthquake that destroyed more than 123,000 homes, and hundreds of hospitals and schools.

More than 450 people continue to live in tents in temporary camps that were set up in Pereira and cities like Buenaventura, according to the Ombudsman, which raised the alarm over “the lack of clear protocols for closing shelters and providing housing alternatives for departing residents, alongside infrastructure and security deficiencies in several facilities.”

Promised rent assistance, which would allow those who lost their homes to temporarily find residence, has also been insufficient.

“More than a month ago I received a million pesos ($304) stipend, although this was supposed to be three, I haven’t received any news,” Pereira resident Christian Castañeda told France 24.

“They’ve announced a so-called ‘Miracle Fund,’ but so far we’ve only seen billboards—no major progress,” said Castañeda, whose mother is one of more than 3,000 people who have yet to receive financial aid.

This Miracle Fund was set up a few weeks ago with an initial COP625 billion ($190 million) budget, which is only a drop in the COP59.29 trillion (18 billion) bucket that the government must get together for the reconstruction process.

“I’m not sure whether the Miracle Fund is working with the diligence and sense of urgency that are required, nor am I sure that they are doing so in the most transparent way,” said House Representative Catherine Juvinao, a member of the congressional commission that monitors the recovery process.

According to Senator Alejandro Toro, local governments from parts of the country that weren’t affected by the earthquake have also tried to receive emergency funds.

Sixteen departments were listed as affected—16, when everyone knows only 5 were actually impacted. It turns out that among these 16, certain departments reported every single public building and school as damaged. For instance: in Caqueta, according to the governor, there are more affected municipalities than families. No one knows the true number of victims in Caqueta; the press didn’t cover a single damaged house there. In Bolivar, along the Atlantic Coast, 11 families were reported affected—and do you know how many total people were listed under those 11 families? 467 people from 11 families! That averages to 43 people per family! Come on, that is completely false! That is a lie; it’s not as if every household belongs to [vallenato singer] Diomedes. They also reported about 189 damaged schools, which would mean 12 or 13 damaged schools per family… impossible. This same issue occurred across other departments—16 departments, including Sucre!

Senator Alejandro Ocampo

Ocampo said he would continue his lawsuits against the foundation of First Lady Ana Lucia Pineda, Colombia Luz y Sonrisas, which has failed to comply with court orders ordering transparency on what it has done with money collected in response to the earthquake.
