World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Sheinbaum in China, Rodríguez at the mic and a kingpin behind bars
World.content:
President Claudia Sheinbaum spent most of the week in Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. That left Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez running the mañaneras from Monday on. The Minnesota Vikings, meanwhile, were pumping thin air into a chamber in the Midwest to prepare for Sunday night’s kickoff in Mexico City.

It was a relatively calm week at home while the president was abroad. That changed Friday night, when Mexican special forces captured an alleged drug kingpin on the FBI’s Top 10 Most Wanted list, sparking violence in Sinaloa.

Didn’t have time to catch Mexico’s top stories of the week of Nov. 16? Here’s what you missed.

Sheinbaum touches down in Shenzhen

Sheinbaum left Mexico City’s airport at 11 p.m. on Saturday for a 12:35 a.m. flight to Tijuana. She then boarded China Southern Airlines flight CZ8032 to Shenzhen. It was another commercial flight, in keeping with the austerity symbolism started by her predecessor. She arrived at 11:30 a.m. Monday local time and went straight to the Tequila Coyote’s restaurant to meet Mexicans living in China, whom she called “extraordinary.” The economy-class journey also struck a chord online: Bloomberg reported that a hashtag about her arrival was seen 10 million times on Weibo.

Sheinbaum pitches Plan México at APEC

In a 13-minute speech at the APEC CEO Summit on Tuesday, Sheinbaum told more than 2,000 business and political representatives that Mexico “guarantees conditions for investment.” She said the government and private companies expect to invest US $432 billion in infrastructure under Plan México between 2024 and 2030. She also described the plan as having a “humanist vision.”

Mexico News Daily noted that foreign direct investment hit a record of almost $35 billion in the first half of 2026, though growth was only 2.1%. Insecurity, USMCA uncertainty and the recent judicial reform are seen as deterrents. On Thursday, she gave a four-minute address at the Leaders’ Meeting, calling this “a decisive moment for humanity.” Mexico will host APEC in 2028.

Meetings with Xi, Carney, Trump and more

Sheinbaum told Chinese President Xi Jinping on Tuesday that her visit marks “a new era” in bilateral ties, focused on science, technology, clean energy and health. Neither side’s readout mentioned Mexico’s new tariffs on Chinese goods. She also revealed she had asked Xi for a panda for Chapultepec Zoo.

She also met Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney that day, and both reaffirmed support for renewing the USMCA. Carney said bilateral trade is up 18% this year.

On Wednesday came the one many were watching: a roughly 20-minute meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump, her first formal in-person talks with him. Sheinbaum said trade negotiations are “very far along” but gave no timeline for a deal. Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard said 56 technical meetings have been held. Trump’s recent tariff threat over the migrant caravan went unmentioned, and the two agreed to meet again at next month’s G20 summit at Mar-a-Lago.

She also met leaders from Vietnam, Australia, Singapore and Peru, plus the IMF’s Kristalina Georgieva. At her closing press conference, Sheinbaum called the trip “very productive and very successful” but said Mexico has no plans for a free trade agreement with China.

Rodríguez takes the mañanera podium

With the president away, Interior Minister Rodríguez led this week’s morning press conferences. On Monday, the mañanera featured World Bank data showing that Mexico’s monetary poverty rate fell from 35.3% in 2018 to 21.1% in 2025, with 17.3 million fewer people in poverty projected by the end of 2026. Officials also touted a CB Global Data poll putting Sheinbaum’s approval at 69.8%, the highest in Latin America.

Sheinbaum joined Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday’s mañanera by video link, and on Thursday, Rodríguez praised her boss’s “composure” and “firmness, without confrontation or subservience.”

Mexico ranks fourth in APEC tech exports

An APEC report showed that Mexico ranks fourth among APEC economies in the share of exports that are medium- and high-tech goods, at 70.6%. Only Taiwan, Hong Kong and South Korea rank higher. Mexico sits ahead of China (61.6%), the United States (46.5%) and Canada (31.7%). APEC projects regional growth of 3.4% this year and 3.1% in 2027.

Revolution Day parade

Hours after landing from China, Sheinbaum presided over the parade marking the 116th anniversary of the Mexican Revolution. She invoked the 1917 Constitution and defended democratic freedoms. She also accused political opponents and foreign interests of trying to weaken her administration and delegitimize the 2027 midterms. Pageant floats and military contingents then rolled through the Zócalo and down Paseo de la Reforma.

What’s going on with the peso?

The peso sank past 19 per dollar on Thursday, hitting 19.04, its weakest level in 17 months. Bloomberg tied the move to Banxico’s dovish stance, after a 25-basis-point cut to 6.25%, and expectations of another Fed hike in December. That would narrow the interest-rate gap that supports the carry trade. The peso is down about 5.5% this year.

The November MND Peso Index™ offers some context. It found the peso 4.2% undervalued at 18.67 per dollar, versus a 0.7% undervaluation in October. The swing was driven almost entirely by depreciation.

Mexico and US lose measles-free status

The Pan American Health Organization revoked the measles-free status of Mexico, the United States and Bolivia after 12 months of continuous transmission. Canada lost its status a year earlier. Mexico has recorded 20,601 cases over 2025 and 2026, but only 14 are currently active, down from a February peak of 1,314. The government aims to end the outbreak in the second half of 2027 and regain recognition in 2028.

Migrant caravan trudges north

A caravan of about 1,500 migrants left Tapachula last Tuesday, and Trump threatened to double tariffs on Mexican goods if it isn’t stopped. By Tuesday, it had shrunk to 781 people in Mapastepec, Chiapas, as migration officials urged people to go home. On Thursday, Rodríguez responded to U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin’s remarks by saying Mexico “will continue detaining” people involved in smuggling.

Former Iguala mayor sentenced

José Luis Abarca, Iguala’s mayor during the 2014 Ayotzinapa tragedy, was sentenced to 60 years on Nov. 10 by a federal judge in Tamaulipas. He and 25 co-defendants, including the police chief, were convicted of six counts of aggravated homicide and attempted murder. Those charges stem from the attack on a bus carrying the Los Avispones soccer team. Abarca is already serving 20- and 92-year sentences. His lawyer argued police control had been ceded to then-Gov. Ángel Aguirre.

‘El Chapo Isidro’ captured in Sinaloa

Friday night’s big news came from Sinaloa. Mexican special forces captured Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro,” and two other leaders of his organization.

The FBI lists Meza Flores on its Top 10 Most Wanted list and had offered up to US $5 million for information leading to his arrest. Agents came under fire from gunmen using explosives during the raid in Guasave, according to the Defense Ministry. Violence erupted afterward, with civilians fleeing gunfire at a baseball game and vehicles burning on a highway near Los Mochis. The Mexican government said U.S. intelligence helped, giving few details. The three were flown to Mexico City.

Looking ahead

The aftermath in Sinaloa is the story to watch, as violence following the capture may not end quickly. On trade, Sheinbaum and Trump are due to meet again at the G20 in Florida next month. Sheinbaum has said talks are “very far along,” but no deal date has been set, and the U.S. has still not agreed to any tariff reductions for Mexican automobiles, steel or aluminum. Financial markets, meanwhile, will be watching the Fed’s December meeting and Banxico’s decision on Dec. 17 for clues about whether the peso’s slide continues. Back at the Estadio Azteca, the Vikings and 49ers will find out Sunday whether their different altitude strategies paid off.

Mexico News Daily

This story contains summaries of original Mexico News Daily articles. The summaries were generated by Claude, then revised and fact-checked by a Mexico News Daily staff editor.

World.title: Mexican special forces capture top FBI fugitive ‘El Chapo Isidro,’ unleashing a night of fire in Sinaloa
World.content:
Listen to this article

Mexican special forces on Friday detained Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, a cartel leader known as “El Chapo Isidro,” who was one of the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation’s 10 most-wanted fugitives.

The arrest on Friday night in the municipality of Guasave in the northern state of Sinaloa triggered a violent reaction, with cartel operatives setting up narco-blockades and engaging in gun battles with military forces.

Se informa que, derivado de la coordinación entre organismos de inteligencia de la Secretaría de la Defensa Nacional y de los E.U.A., realizada en el marco de la cooperación bilateral con ese país, el 20 de noviembre del presente año, Fuerzas Especiales de la Guardia Nacional (Lobos) y del Ejército (Murciélagos), en coordinación con elementos de Fuerzas Especiales del Ejército comisionados en la Secretaría de Seguridad Pública del Estado de Sinaloa, detuvieron en el municipio de Guasave, Sin., a Fausto Isidro N (a) “Chapo Isidro”, jefe de la organización delictiva “Beltrán Leyva” y aliado al “Cártel del Pacífico” facción “Mayos”, a Germán N (a) “Serafín”, segundo al mando de esa organización delincuencial y a José N, operador financiero de este mismo grupo delictivo. (a) “Chapo Isidro”, cuenta con una orden de aprehensión en México por delincuencia organizada y por cometer delitos contra la salud, y una orden de extradición a los E.U.A. por asociación delictiva para distribuir droga en territorio estadounidense; además, se encuentra en la lista de los 10 fugitivos más buscados por el F.B.I. La operación para estas detenciones, fue realizada por fuerzas militares de élite, las que una vez ubicado con precisión el objetivo, mediante el empleo de diversos ingenios tecnológicos, la desarrollaron en 3 fases, de la forma siguiente: Arribo al área del objetivo: se realizó utilizando el sigilo y la sorpresa por diferentes vías de acceso terrestre al área de la detención. Establecimiento de la seguridad y captura del objetivo: esta se realizó a inmediaciones de la ubicación de los detenidos, mediante la colocación de un dispositivo de seguridad interna y externa, para evitar la huida o la llegada de refuerzos, habiendo sido agredidos con disparos de armas de fuego y explosivos, por lo que la fuerza de detención ingresó a la casa habitación para capturar a las personas indicadas. Evacuación del objetivo: confirmada la identidad de los detenidos, se procedió a su evacuación a la Ciudad de México, en una aeronave de la Fuerza Aérea Mexicana, para ser puestos a disposición de las autoridades ministeriales competentes. Derivado de esta detención, se registraron bloqueos en los municipios de Ahome, Guamúchil, Guasave y Navolato, para lo cual, en coordinación con autoridades locales, se activó el plan antibloqueo, movilizando fuerzas de seguridad para restablecer el tránsito en las vías de comunicación y proteger a la población. #NoticiadeÚltimaHora #ComunicadoDePrensa #EjércitoMexicano #FuerzaAéreaMx #GuardiaNacional — @Defensamx (@Defensamx1) November 21, 2026

Meza Flores, 44, is the leader of the Beltrán Leyva Organization and an ally of the “Mayos” faction of the Sinaloa Cartel, according to the Ministry of National Defense (Defensa), which announced his arrest in a statement early Saturday. He is considered one of the most powerful drug traffickers in Sinaloa, with the Reforma newspaper describing him as “the main active capo” in the state.

U.S. authorities have described him as the leader of the Meza-Flores Transnational Criminal Organization (TCO) and a former high-ranking leader of the Beltrán Leyva Organization.

In its statement, Defensa said that the Beltrán Leyva Organization’s second-in-command, Germán N, alias “Serafín,” and a financial operator of the same group identified as José N were also detained in the operation in Guasave carried out by elite National Guard and Mexican Army special forces. The ministry said the three suspects were arrested at a home in Guasave, a coastal municipality in northern Sinaloa that includes a city of the same name. It said that “stealth and “surprise” were used in the operation to detain the three men, who were subsequently transferred to Mexico City on an Air Force plane.

Defensa said that the capture of Meza Flores was the result of coordination between Mexican and U.S. intelligence agencies. It said he was wanted in Mexico on organized crime and drug trafficking charges and noted that he is subject to a U.S. extradition request.

In 2017, U.S. authorities announced a reward of up to US $5 million for information leading to Meza Flores’ arrest.

In February 2025, the U.S. State Department said that “for over 20 years, the Meza-Flores TCO has been responsible for smuggling multi-ton quantities of heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine, and marijuana into the United States.”

It noted that in May 2012, Meza Flores was indicted in the U.S. on drug trafficking and firearm charges and in November 2019 “a federal grand jury returned a superseding indictment charging … [him] with additional drug trafficking and firearms violations.”

On Saturday morning, the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) said that the capture of Meza Flores “represents a significant victory against one of Mexico’s most violent criminal networks.”

“For decades, this organization has fueled bloodshed and instability in Mexico while trafficking deadly drugs, including fentanyl, into the United States, posing a significant threat to American lives and communities,” the DEA said on social media.

“#DEA commends Mexican authorities for this decisive operation and remains committed to dismantling the violent criminal organizations responsible for trafficking deadly drugs into our country.”

In a social media post earlier on Saturday, federal Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said that the arrest of “El Chapo Isidro” and the two other cartel suspects was “an important step” toward the “pacification of Sinaloa,” a state that has been plagued by Sinaloa Cartel infighting for more than two years.

However, it was violence rather than peace that immediately followed the arrests.

‘A night of terror’

The Defense Ministry reported that narco-blockades were set up in several Sinaloa municipalities, including Ahome, Guasave and Navolato, in response to the arrests on Friday night. Vehicles were set on fire to create the blockades on major roads in Sinaloa, including Federal Highway 15. Gas stations and convenience stores in Guasave were also set ablaze.

There were also gun battles between cartel henchmen and Mexican military forces. Video footage showed that military helicopters opened fire on ground targets in Guasave. Reforma reported that the helicopters targeted criminal cells seeking to “rescue” Meza Flores.

Mexico’s military captured FBI-wanted cartel leader ‘El Chapo Isidro’ in Guasave, Sinaloa. Armed clashes erupted as helicopters opened fire, vehicles burned and roads were blocked. Gunfire also halted a baseball game, sending players and fans scrambling for cover. https://t.co/URhPOTN512 — Al Jazeera English (@AJEnglish) November 21, 2026

Authorities did not say whether anyone was killed during what media outlets described as a “night of terror” in Guasave and other parts of Sinaloa.

Shortly after 9 p.m. Friday, the Sinaloa Security Ministry (SSP) said that federal forces had come under attack in Guasave. In a social media post, the SSP instructed local residents to stay indoors.

A Mexican Pacific League baseball game between the Algodoneros de Guasave and the Venados de Mazatlán at Kuroda Park in Guasave was suspended amid gunfire in the city. CNN reported that an official broadcast showed players from the two teams “fleeing the field mid-game,” while baseball fans “scrambled out of the stands as a barrage of gunfire rang out.”

The arrest of Meza Flores is another high-profile blow against organized crime, following the fatal wounding of Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) leader Nemesio “El Mencho” Oseguera Cervantes in a military operation in Jalisco in February.

Mexican authorities have arrested more than 74,000 people for allegedly committing high-impact crimes such as homicide and drug trafficking since President Claudia Sheinbaum took office in October 2024. Among the other cartel figures who have been detained are Audias Flores Silva, an alleged high-ranking member of the CJNG known as “El Jardinero” (The Gardener), and Axel Alfredo Cárdenas Rodríguez, son of a Gulf Cartel leader known as “El Contador.”

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Mexico’s forgotten cactus spirit: An interview about colonche with César Iván Ojeda-Linares
World.content:
We all know the cactus fruit and have maybe tasted its juicy flesh and hard seeds protected by a spiny skin. But most of us have never tried — or even heard of — the fermented beverage that can be made from it.

César Iván Ojeda-Linares, a researcher at the Instituto de Ecología of the Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México (UNAM), takes us on a journey through Mexico’s prickly pear landscapes, where he encountered colonche, a traditional fermented drink made from the fruit. He explores its connections with the people who make it, the vessels in which it ferments, and why this heritage is at risk.

What first drew you to Mexico’s fermented drinks?

During my master’s degree, I was studying evolutionary developmental ecology, and I went to Japan for a research stay. There, I realized I wasn’t enjoying working only with models, genes and model plants as much as I had expected.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Secretaría de Turismo Zac (@zacatecas_travel)

One evening, I was invited to a sake tasting by my mentor at Kyoto Sangyo University. I saw the diversity of sake and thought, “This is amazing — Mexico has a diversity of drinks, too.”

I returned to Mexico wanting to investigate fermented drinks, the plants used to make them and their relationships with people and microorganisms. Early in my doctorate, I noticed that plants and fermentation were often studied separately, and people were missing the big picture. What interested me was how people select or manage something invisible: microorganisms.

How did colonche become part of that research?

When I was applying for my doctorate, I wanted to study many things. I was living in Michoacán, a central region in Mexico, and I included pulque, mezcal and fermented corn drinks in my plans because of corn’s symbolic and cultural importance in Mexico.

Then I was reviewing an old book about Mexico’s drinks and came across colonche. There wasn’t much information. When I searched scientific databases, I found at most two articles at that time and only two records of yeast strains isolated. So I started looking for where it was made.

How did you find the colonche producers?

At first, I went to Guanajuato and couldn’t find anything. I would ask about colonche, and people would say they had no idea what it was.

Then I got hungry and stopped somewhere selling gorditas, in a community called La Chirimoya. After eating, already feeling a little discouraged, I asked whether they knew about the colonche fair. A woman told me, “My friend organizes it.”

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Casa Mercedes (@casamercedesgto)

That was the connection. I went there, began taking notes, met producers and started my fieldwork. I think I interviewed about 13 producers in the community at that time.

The landscape also astonished me. We were walking among nopales more than 3 meters tall. They rose above us and provided shade. Getting to know the producers and the territory was an exploration of a landscape that was new to me.

For someone who has never tried it, what is colonche — and how do people make it?

Colonche is a fermented drink made from prickly pears, especially the red fruits producers call cardonas. There are many ways to prepare it.

The one I particularly like comes from Laguna de Guadalupe, Guanajuato. Producers collect the fruit and peel it where they harvest it. They take it home, squeeze out the pulp, and put it into their pots to ferment. Some of those pots are more than 80 years old.

There is a detail I find beautiful: The peels are left where the fruit is harvested, and cows come along and eat them. Their mouths become stained red — it looks as though they are wearing lipstick.

In San Luis Potosí, I encountered another method. Producers heat the fruit in a metal pot to extract the pulp. Some add anise or other spices. To start fermentation, they may add colonche saved from the previous season or locally produced pulque. Many colonche producers there also make pulque.

In Zacatecas, I encountered a woman who heated the fruit juice and added aguardiente. She had spent time in the United States and, after being deported, did not know how to prepare colonche, so that was the method she used.

From a microbial perspective, what is happening in the pots used in Guanajuato?

Part of the microbial community carrying out fermentation is in the pots themselves. Producers do not necessarily need to add a starter culture or a fermentation “mother.” Their pot is, in effect, their fermentation mother or starter.

Those pots have been in families for generations. Their porosity gives yeast small spaces where they can remain and become active again when liquid and suitable conditions return.

There is another layer to this relationship: the pottery itself. San Felipe Torres Mochas, near Laguna de Guadalupe, specialized in making these pots. That production has been declining, and fewer people make them now. So the pot connects the microorganisms, the family and a local craft tradition.

Hopefully, the producers of these containers will survive or maintain the tradition; otherwise, it will shift to plastic containers and it might be a loss of flavors or aromas.

How does heating the juice and adding a previous batch change the fermentation?

Heating kills some of the wild yeast and bacteria, and it also changes the material they will ferment. It is no longer the same juice coming directly from the fruit, and that changes the possibilities for other yeast to establish themselves. It is like an open space to conquer.

Using a previous batch is also interesting because it involves selection driven by humans. Certain groups of yeast and bacteria survive and are carried over to the next fermentation, reproduced from one fermentation to the next.

In a study we published, we found much lower microbial diversity in the inocula — the material used to start fermentation. That allows us to identify selection for particular, more limited groups of microorganisms. So in a broad sense, the producers are selecting a consortium of microbes that helps them to reproduce what, culturally, they conceive as a good colonche.

What interests you about people selecting organisms they cannot see?

Selection is well studied in plants and animals. With corn, for example, you can see changes in the grain, its size and its uses — whether it is for pozole, tortillas or popcorn.

With microorganisms, it is fascinating because you are not selecting something you can see. You are selecting something you can taste or smell, and you are not selecting only one species; you select a community.

What pressures have you seen on colonche production?

There are fewer producers now than when I began. Some have died, and others have stopped making colonche because of poor seasons for prickly pears and other social and environmental conflicts.

The spaces where people collected fruit are also being fragmented. Land that was used for gathering and communal resources is being divided into plots. In some places, large areas once covered with nopales are being converted to bean monocultures.

Some producers have also told me that colonche no longer comes out the same — that it does not taste the way they remember it, mostly because different environmental factors changed the flavor of the cactus prickly pear fruits.

What did working with Comcáac producers in Sonora teach you about fermentation’s relationship with a landscape?

I worked in Punta Chueca in the northern state of Sonora with Indigenous Comcáac producers who make a drink from cardón fruit. We held a fermentation workshop: They explained how they made it, and I brought a microscope so we could see what was growing in the fermentation. Most of the producers were women, and they invited their children to participate.

One of the most valuable lessons came when we were collecting fruit. I asked why they did not collect fruit that had not opened. They explained that it was not fully ripe, and that if animals had not visited it, fermentation took much longer. They described bats, bees and flies visiting the fruit.

I have not been able to evaluate that relationship directly because of limited time and funding. But their understanding connects fruit availability, animal visitors and fermentation. So, I really see that Indigenous communities have a very detailed way to characterize how these interactions occur, and it has different layers of understanding their relationship with the environment, even with invisible beings such as microbes.

The drink is also part of their New Year celebrations and rituals associated with asking for rain and good harvests. Defending the territory therefore means defending not only the land, but also food systems and practices that depend on it.

Why is colonche difficult to separate from the place where it is made?

It continues fermenting, which makes transporting it difficult. I used to carry samples to the laboratory in a cooler. Once, I closed a container without leaving a way for the carbon dioxide to escape, and it burst. The car’s trunk was covered in red liquid and smelled for weeks.

That is part of what makes it so local. You need to visit the place to know the drink, the people and the ecosystem. In one sense, that protects its uniqueness. At the same time, it limits how widely it can become known.

I think drinking this beverage is a privilege: a chance to enjoy good conversation while taking in the landscape. I know that globalization encourages people to seek out new tastes, and that the “gastronomification” of food fuels this desire. But some things give a place its magic, and colonche is certainly one of them here. Perhaps part of that magic lies in enjoying it in the landscape and among the people who give it life.

Katy Alivraz is a contributor to Mexico News Daily.

World.title: Chicano baby: The Mexican lowriders challenging gang stereotypes
World.content:
Every Sunday, a special kind of meetup takes place in downtown Mexico City: a few dozen men and women gather in oversized white shirts and baggy jeans with blue bandanas hanging from their pockets, all sporting gleaming silver lowrider bicycles.

Inspired by the Mexican-American Chicano communities of 1960s and ‘70s California, their style is often associated with cholos: a Los Angeles street culture that has long been stereotyped as synonymous with gang violence.

But that’s exactly what this group wants to challenge. They are here to represent a subculture shaped by migration and marginalization, honor its heritage and scrap the stigma of violence attached to it.

“We represent culture, that’s it,” Hiram, a member for two years, explains.

Most members in this report chose to be identified by first name only, citing privacy reasons.

“We are not violent, we are not a gang. We’re here so people can see us, see we’re not bad guys.”

Finding support and love

This wanna-not-be gang is strikingly intergenerational. There are little kids in gangster white face paint running between the bikes, veteran-looking men covered in tattoos, a mother and her teenage son — a real family, as the group’s name “Mexican Family” would have it.

“Many of us come from a dysfunctional family; we find support and love from people who aren’t blood. That was the primary purpose of creating this group,” explains el jefe, Babo, who founded the group three years ago.

The members meet every week, tinker and ride their bikes — all hand-wrought from different bicycle parts and adorned with jewels — pose with passersby and invite people to try their bikes.

Contrary to what its aesthetics would suggest, not all of them share the Chicano identity.

At its origin, Chicano was used as a derogatory term for the Mexican-American working class in the U.S. before activists in the 1960s and ‘70s reclaimed the identity as a symbol of resistance and pride.

Some members of the group are Mexican-American, others have been deported from the United States over the years, and many of the youngsters are just Mexican.

What brings them together is a shared love of lowrider bicycles and cars, as well as an appreciation for what Chicano identity symbolizes.

“It’s tradition, history, resistance,” explains a young Mexican member with no ties to the U.S., who goes by the name Estonet. “Chicano means keeping Mexican culture alive anywhere in the world.”

Tessie joined a year ago to spend time with her teenage son, a lowrider fan. She wants people to stop associating the club with gangs. The point, she says, is to “go slow and happy on a bike, no matter which one it is.”

But the stigmatization of this culture mostly comes from its association with the cholos.

Unpacking the term ‘cholo’

Cholo also began as an insult, a colonial-era slur for people of mixed Indigenous and European descent, before Mexican-American youth in Los Angeles reclaimed it as a style, taking visual influences from Chicano culture such as the lowrider bicycles and cars.

Over time, however, police discrimination and popularization through gangster films such as “Blood In Blood Out” (1993) made the term synonymous with dangerous gangs.

“For better or for worse, culture changes,” el jefe continues. “The cholo has more to do with gangs, with prison.”

Some members’ own pasts are not far removed from those associations.

Hiram, who self-deported from the United States nearly two years ago after getting into a car accident and fearing imprisonment, says most of the older members of the group used to be in gangs.

“Arriving somewhere that receives you with open arms is very hard… you don’t know the problems you had, the gangs you were in.”

Joining the group, he says, has been “like going back to the place where something was missing.”

1 of 11

A family affair

Juan, who brought his lowrider car to one of Mexican Family’s Día de Muertos parades with his teenage daughter, shares the same sentiment. “We grew up in the street, but we’re here because we don’t need the street anymore,” he says.

“Ten years ago, you could not have seen us here all together, from different barrios,” he says, alluding to the fact that many of them were members of different street gangs here in the city.

For Alvin, who grew up without papers in the U.S. and voluntarily came back to Mexico five years ago, his membership in the group is a family homage.

“My father was a cholo. I grew up watching my dad with all the bikes, these cars,” he says.

In this way, Mexican Family seems to have also become an asylum for men with troubled pasts to start anew, without forgetting the culture that raised them.

Toeing the line between bravado and vulnerability, the group could be accused of glorifying the violence attached to gang aesthetics. But perhaps what it does best is hold space for the complexity of an identity crossed by a multitude of borders, subject to poverty, marginalization and all too often, violence — and seek to redefine it as a community united by culture, pride and family.

Mathilde Hourticq is a multi-platform journalist based in Mexico City covering breaking news, subcultures, youth issues and many other things in between. Her video-journalism has appeared on the Associated Press, AFP, and Press Association.

World.title: ‘Trading Places’: A new podcast by Mexico News Daily
World.content:
The team at MND is excited to be launching a new podcast series to complement our existing “Confidently Wrong” podcast and “MND Hits the Streets” series of videos.

Cesar Martinez will be joining me as the co-host of Trading Places. Both Cesar and I have, in fact, traded places. I was born in Wisconsin and now live in San Miguel de Allende, Guanajuato, after having lived, studied, worked, or traveled in Mexico for over 30 years. Cesar was born in Mexico City and now lives in Los Angeles, California. Cesar has spent over 40 years living in the United States, between Texas and California.

Each episode, Cesar and I will speak about Mexico with a different person of Mexican heritage (first and second generation Mexican Americans) living in the United States. We will reflect on how the guests’ perceptions of Mexico have evolved and changed (and why) as well as their current thoughts on the country, its leadership and its future. We will explore if they are feeling more of a pull towards (or away) from Mexico, and if so, why. We will review how their children’s views on Mexico differ from their own, and how theirs differs from those of their parents. We will, of course, also discuss the evolving relationship between the United States and Mexico, and what that means for both countries.

The goal of the podcast is to encourage the nearly 40 million Mexican diaspora living in the United States to reflect on their own relationship with Mexico and hopefully inspire them — each in their own way — to build a stronger connection with the country. We believe that there is a significant opportunity for the U.S. population of Mexican descent to have an outsized impact on the economic growth and overall well being of Mexico and want to provide a platform to share inspiring case studies and stories.

Please tune in, get informed, and get inspired!

Check out the first episode of MND’s Trading Places here:

We Both Left Our Home Country—for Opposite Sides of the Border | Trading Places - Episode 1

World.title: Is education the biggest challenge facing Mexico? A perspective from our CEO
World.content:
Let me start with why I’m writing about this, because I know education can often feel like a heavy or hopeless topic. I’m not here to lecture. I’m writing because this is as much a business issue as a social one. Mexico became the largest supplier of goods to the U.S. in 2023 and now accounts for over 18% of U.S. imports. That partnership depends on a Mexican workforce that can keep learning as technology changes, and reading and learning are foundational to that workforce. When that foundation weakens, it affects Mexican families, the companies that employ them, and the U.S. businesses and consumers who rely on them.

The U.S. and Mexico don’t face the same problem. In the U.S., student achievement is slipping from a higher level. In Mexico, the problem is structural: Too many students never build strong reading and math foundations to begin with. I also see an opportunity here. Used practically and skillfully, artificial intelligence could change what’s possible in education. For example, early studies show well-designed AI tutors can help students learn faster, and simple tools on a basic phone can reach classrooms short on teachers and resources. It’s no cure-all, but it gives us something new to work with.

I was perhaps a bit slow in recognizing the scale or seriousness of the education problem here in Mexico. Having done business in the country for over 30 years now, to be honest most of my interaction in the business world was with professionals in corporate environments — people who went to private schools and had college degrees. Of course in non-business settings I interacted with people of all walks of life and different levels of education throughout the country, but the scale of the problem didn’t really hit me until we purchased MND and I began researching more about Mexico’s educational results and the impacts its having on productivity and growth.

I have written about how Mexico’s education problem is translating into a productivity problem (which ultimately translates into an economic growth problem) here: Mexico has a labor productivity problem: Our CEO’s perspective and here: Productivity brings prosperity: Is Mexico really failing at both? A perspective from our CEO.

Mexico’s public schools have always had their challenges, but when compared against other OECD countries, the country was doing OK, and the results were slowly getting better. But this year’s recently released PISA results squashed just about any reason for optimism. Mexico’s results, compared to other OECD countries, are getting worse. Compared to its own prior years’ results, the country is losing ground in all three focus areas of testing: reading, mathematics and science. The statistic that most jumped out to me was that only half of Mexican 15-year-olds can read at a high enough level to enable further learning. I recently wrote about it here: Mexico fails the 2025 PISA evaluation: A perspective from our CEO.

To make matters worse, the workplace is quickly evolving. The old basic assembly and manufacturing jobs that lifted so many people out of poverty around the world aren’t what they used to be. Automation and robotics are doing an increasing amount of that work, forcing workers to learn new skills or be replaced and be out of work. Artificial intelligence is quickly proving to be a superpower for those who have the education to learn and apply it, and a massive potential disruptor to those who do not. Last year, I wrote a three-part series on why and how I think Mexico needs to start evolving its economy, given what is likely coming in technology disruption:

The thought of a workforce that is no longer needed for most manufacturing jobs and yet unable to learn new skills to find other types of work should scare all of us. The question is, what can be done about it? The solutions are not easy, but the team at MND is committed to helping do our part. Here are some specific examples of what we have done so far, and what is coming:

1. We had our team do a deep dive report, beyond the most recent PISA scores, to get a data-driven view on how Mexico is doing in educational attainment and results. We wanted to create and publish a data-driven baseline as a starting point on a topic that can very quickly get emotional in the absence of solid numbers. We published that report recently as part of our ongoing Mexico Well-being Series.

2. As a follow-up to the PISA results and the MND report, I recently took a trip to the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia to learn more. Why UPENN? Because they are one of the leading universities in the world in education policy, training leaders from across the world (including Mexico) on how to improve educational systems. They also have a rock-star, world-renowned professor named Dr. Sharon Ravitch who is on the leading edge of researching how AI could be an accelerator for kids (and school districts, and countries) to improve educational results. I met with Dr. Ravitch and reviewed with her my concerns about Mexico’s educational system and what I think is one of the biggest challenges holding back Mexico.

3. Dr. Ravitch was concerned about the PISA scores, inspired by our reporting, and understood the challenge facing Mexico. She has had both personal and professional connections with the country and wanted to help. So she gathered a group of Mexican and Mexican American doctoral graduates of an executive doctoral program at UPENN’s Global School of Education. The group, who hail from across the U.S., has studied issues related to education and equity. They offered to create a special series of articles for MND diagnosing the problems and suggesting a range of practical solutions, while taking into account the reality of where Mexico is today and the challenges and opportunities created by AI.

Starting this week, MND will be publishing a weekly installment on this topic. The team has worked hard to ensure that these articles are written to educate, inform and inspire action. They are not written for federal government policymakers, but rather for the rest of us who are concerned about the problem and looking for ways to contribute. They are written for locals and foreigners living in Mexico hoping to help, for the Mexican diaspora living abroad who want to make a difference, and for business and NGO leaders seeking suggestions and solutions.

4. Of course, Mexico News Daily also continues to publish articles for children on our MND Kids platform. This site is in both Spanish and English and provides students, parents and educators an easy-to-use digital tool to teach reading via real MND news stories about Mexico that have been rewritten for kids. If you haven’t checked it out yet, you can join the thousands already using the platform here: mndkids.com.

If the importance of this topic resonates with you, please follow the series each week, share it with someone who could help, and tell us how you’d like to be involved — whether as a contributor, partner, volunteer, school connection or supporter. Just put your thoughts in the comments or write to us directly at mndadmin@mexiconewsdaily.com. The more people who engage, the faster we can turn good ideas into real results for Mexican students.

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.title: Brazil Investing Rules for Foreigners in 2026
World.content:
The paperwork has shrunk since 2025, but the tax bill has not, and a few answers still sit with a broker rather than in a public rule.

Guide: Investing Guides

A foreigner can buy Brazilian shares and bonds in 2026 with less paperwork than before 2025, but a new 10% tax on dividends has changed the sums. The rules sit in a joint resolution of the securities regulator (the CVM) and the central bank (the BCB), which took effect on Wednesday 1 January 2025.

This guide sets out what the official texts say about accounts, taxes and currency charges, and it marks every point we could not confirm. It is journalism, not tax or investment advice, and a licensed Brazilian broker must confirm how your own case is treated.

Key Facts Accounts. Individuals investing their own money from a non-resident real account need no local representative or securities-regulator registration.

Dividends. Law 15,270 taxes dividends sent abroad at 10% from 1 January 2026.

Currency tax. The IOF currency tax is zero on foreign investors’ portfolio inflows, returns and dividend payouts.

The paperwork has shrunk since 2025, but the tax bill has not, and a few answers still sit with a broker rather than in a public rule.

In plain English CVM: the Comissão de Valores Mobiliários, Brazil’s securities regulator.

the Comissão de Valores Mobiliários, Brazil’s securities regulator. BCB: the Banco Central do Brasil, the central bank.

the Banco Central do Brasil, the central bank. CPF: the number the tax authority, the Receita Federal, gives each taxpayer.

Free download · Expat checklist Get the free checklist as PDF Moving to Brazil 2026: the step-by-step checklist. This guide condensed into 2 printable pages with tick boxes and the key official links. Email address Get the PDF Your checklist is ready. Download the PDF checklist

What Changed on 1 January 2025

Joint Resolution 13 of the CVM and the BCB, dated Tuesday 3 December 2024, took effect on 1 January 2025. It revoked Resolution 4,373 of 2014, the rule that had governed foreign portfolio investors for a decade, along with seven other texts.

Registrations made under the old rule need no update and stayed available for consultation for one year after the new rule began. Foreigners may use the same instruments and face the same sign-up requirements and trading limits as Brazilian residents.

WatchRating below investment grade (BB); public debt at 93% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

As a rule, a foreign investor must name a representative in Brazil, which has to be a financial institution, and must register with the CVM. Individuals are exempt from both when they invest their own money from a non-resident real account in their own name, subject to the CVM’s own sign-up checks.

How a Foreigner Opens an Account

The usual route is a CNR, a real-denominated account for people who live abroad, at a Brazilian bank or broker, and the institution decides which documents to ask for. Our guides to

opening a Brazilian bank account and to buying shares on the B3, São Paulo’s stock exchange walk through that step.

The resolution bars foreign investors from investing residents’ money through a real account in Brazil. It also forbids receiving or paying money for these investments through accounts held abroad.

Individuals who invest outside a CNR, still with their own money, may skip the representative up to R$2 million (about US$336,000 at the 5.9488 reais per dollar close of the RT market-data service on Friday 20 November 2026) in total monthly contributions per intermediary. Above that line the full requirements apply.

The Receita Federal, Brazil’s tax authority, issues the CPF, the taxpayer number for individuals, and the joint resolution itself does not mention it. Foreigners living abroad must apply in person at a Brazilian consulate, says the government’s gov.br service portal.

Dividends Now Carry a 10% Withholding Tax

Law 15,270, signed on Wednesday 26 November 2025, applies a 10% income tax at source to profits and dividends sent abroad from Thursday 1 January 2026. Brazil had left dividends untaxed since 1996, so for many foreign holders this is the biggest change in years.

Planalto Palace in Brasília, the seat of Brazil’s federal government (Marcos Oliveira/Senado Federal, CC BY 2.0).

Profits earned up to the 2025 financial year are exempt if their payment was approved by Wednesday 31 December 2025. Foreign governments that grant reciprocal treatment, sovereign funds and foreign pension entities are also exempt.

The law lets a foreign beneficiary claim a credit when the company’s own tax rate plus the 10% passes a set ceiling, and the claim must come within 360 days of each financial year. Our

dividend tax explainer works through an example.

Interest on equity, a payout many Brazilian companies use instead of dividends, is taxed at source too. The consolidated text of Law 9,249 now shows 17.5%, after a 2025 supplementary law (number 224) changed it from 15%.

Gains, Government Bonds and the IOF

We could not confirm from an official text how gains on share sales are taxed for foreign investors, so ask your broker how it treats them. The 10% dividend tax above is the one change we could verify in the law itself.

Income from federal government bonds bought since 16 February 2006 carries 0% withholding for non-residents under Law 11,312. The exception covers residents of countries that levy no income tax or less than 20%, and it applies only to deals within the rules of the National Monetary Council (CMN), the government’s financial rule-setter.

Under Decree 6,306, the IOF is zero on foreign-exchange deals that bring a foreign investor’s money into financial and capital markets, return it, or send dividends and interest on equity abroad. The government raised other IOF rates in 2025, and the official text lists 3.5% on residual outflows and 0.38% on residual inflows.

Notes on the decree’s opening line and on those two rates cite a 2025 legislative decree suspending part of the rule and a Supreme Court case (ADC 96), so we cannot say which version applies today. The three zero items above carry no such note of their own.

Tesouro Direto and What Is Not Confirmed

Tesouro Direto is the Treasury’s retail platform for government bonds. We could not read an official Treasury page on whether non-residents may use it, and banks reportedly differ, so we make no claim either way.

We also could not confirm the current IOF rate on other transfers, the full capital gains rule for foreigners or the tax treatment of every fund structure. Each answer should be confirmed in writing by the institution that will hold your assets.

Questions worth putting to a broker are which account type it will open, how it withholds tax on dividends, and which IOF category applies to a transfer. For background on becoming a Brazilian tax resident, see our guide to

taxes for expats and the earlier investing guide, and keep up with Brazil news.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need a CPF to invest in Brazil from abroad?

The joint resolution does not mention a CPF. Brazil’s government says foreigners abroad apply for one in person at a consulate, so ask your institution what it requires.

Is there a tax on the money I bring in?

Decree 6,306 sets the IOF at zero for foreign investors' inflows into financial and capital markets. Other currency deals can be charged, so ask the bank which category yours falls under.

How much is the dividend tax for foreigners?

Dividends sent abroad are taxed at 10% from 1 January 2026, under Law 15,270. Profits approved for payment by 31 December 2025 stay outside it.

Can a foreigner buy Tesouro Direto?

We could not confirm it from an official Treasury page. Several banks reportedly offer it to non-resident clients, so ask your institution directly.

Is this tax or investment advice?

No. It reports what Brazilian official texts say, and a licensed Brazilian broker or tax adviser must confirm your own case.

World.title: Mercosur Opens Asia Door Through Singapore
World.content:
A free trade deal with Singapore is live, but Brazil's broader push into Southeast Asia is slower, narrower and more cautious than the headline suggests.

File photo, 6 November 2019. The Singapore National Stadium in Kallang, the venue for Brazil's two friendlies, seen from the Singapore Flyer. Photo: Dietmar Rabich, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Trade: Southeast Asia

Brazilian exporters of oil, grain and meat gained a tariff-free door into Southeast Asia on 1 August 2026, when a free trade agreement (FTA) with Singapore took effect for Brazil. Brazil’s presidency put it into force through Decree 13,081 of 27 July.

It is the first FTA that Mercosur, South America’s trade bloc of Brazil, Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay, has struck with a Southeast Asian country. Talks with Vietnam and Indonesia move more slowly, and nothing is signed with either.

Brazil’s trade ministry data show Singapore bought US$7.4 billion of Brazilian goods in 2025, more than any other member of ASEAN, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations. Across all 11 members (ten plus Timor-Leste, which joined in 2025), Brazil exported US$24.4 billion and imported US$14.1 billion, leaving a surplus of US$10.3 billion.

The trend has strengthened this year, according to the ministry’s Comex Stat database. From January to October 2026, exports rose 10.3% to US$21.9 billion, while imports fell 8.8% to US$11.1 billion.

Mineral products, a customs category that includes crude oil and iron ore, led 2025 exports at US$8.6 billion. Brazil buys mostly machinery and electrical equipment from the region, worth US$5.1 billion.

Not every market is growing: exports to Malaysia fell 17% to US$2.4 billion from January to October 2026, while sales to Singapore rose 10% to US$6.5 billion. Brazil’s imports from Singapore dropped 74% to US$0.8 billion over the same period.

File photo, 2023: container stacks at the Port of Salvador, Bahia, one of Brazil’s export gateways. Photo: Samory Pereira Santos, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

The Singapore agreement was signed in Rio de Janeiro on 7 December 2023, after five years of talks. It took effect for Singapore and Paraguay on 1 February 2026, for Uruguay on 1 March and for Brazil on 1 August.

Singapore removed tariffs on all Mercosur exports at once. Mercosur will open 95.8% of its tariff lines, 25.6% immediately and the rest in steps of 4, 8, 10 or 15 years.

Mercosur kept 433 sensitive lines, or 4.2% of the total, outside the deal. They include electrical machinery, plastics and optical instruments.

Argentina’s ratification is the missing piece: its Congress finished approval in late August with 234 deputies in favour and 4 against, and Law 27,819 appeared in the Official Gazette on 15 September. The deal takes effect there only after Argentina deposits its ratification with Paraguay, the treaty’s depositary, a step we could not confirm.

Vietnam is already a large partner, with bilateral trade of US$7.4 billion in 2025, according to Brazil’s trade ministry. Brazil sells it maize, cotton, soy, wheat and pork, and buys steel goods, tyres, telecom equipment and footwear.

Mercosur and Vietnam formally launched talks at the bloc’s summit in Foz do Iguaçu on 20 December 2025. Brazil’s trade board, Camex, had replaced a broad 2020 mandate in September 2025 with a narrower one for a preferential trade agreement (PTA), which cuts tariffs gradually on selected goods.

A public consultation from 1 April to 15 May 2026 showed strong export interest in animal proteins, instant coffee, leather, paper and pulp, and industry worry about more imports from Vietnam. The ministry says it will insist on robust rules of origin, keep its trade-defence tools and may add bilateral safeguards.

The first round ran five days in Buenos Aires and closed on 28 August 2026, where Argentina’s Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno received the delegations. No date is published for the second round, and the ministry calls the talks an early phase.

Indonesia’s talks have fared worse. Mercosur and Indonesia launched negotiations for a comprehensive economic partnership agreement (CEPA) on 16 December 2021, according to Brazil’s foreign ministry.

On 9 August 2026, Indonesia’s trade minister Budi Santoso said the CEPA had made little progress and proposed a narrower preferential deal. He blamed differences among Mercosur members and asked Brazil to help build consensus.

He spoke after meeting Brazil’s trade and industry minister Márcio Elias Rosa on 7 August in Jaipur, India, at a meeting of trade ministers from the BRICS group of emerging economies. Elias Rosa welcomed the proposal, and Brazil will study it; nothing is signed and no date is set.

President Lula set out Brazil’s aims at the East Asia Summit, an annual gathering of Asia-Pacific leaders, in Kuala Lumpur on 27 October 2025. “Automatic alignments and situations of dependence are traps the Global South needs to escape,” he said, in the presidency’s text (translated here from Portuguese).

He added that “the rapprochement between ASEAN and Mercosur has potential to integrate the production chains of two regions of great economic complementarity.” Brazil is a sectoral dialogue partner of ASEAN under a 2024-2028 action plan.

For exporters the mechanism is simple: lower tariffs make Brazilian goods cheaper in Singapore, the region’s biggest buyer of them. A guide for Brazilian firms explains how to claim the cuts.

The record shows no negotiation between Mercosur and ASEAN as a whole, and Brazil’s mandate for Vietnam rules out a comprehensive deal for now. More coverage sits in the Southeast Asia section.

Sources: Brazil’s trade ministry, Comex Stat (https://comexstat.mdic.gov.br/); Siscomex (Brazil’s foreign-trade portal) pages on Mercosur-Singapore (https://www.gov.br/siscomex/pt-br/acordos-comerciais/mercosul-singapura) and Mercosur-Vietnam (https://www.gov.br/siscomex/pt-br/acordos-comerciais/mercosul-vietna); Presidential Decree 13,081 (https://planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/_ato2023-2026/2026/decreto/d13081.htm); Brazil’s foreign ministry, Indonesia-Mercosur statement (https://www.gov.br/mre/en/contact-us/press-area/press-releases/joint-ministerial-statement-for-the-launch-of-negotiations-towards-a-comprehensive-economic-partnership-agreement-between-indonesia-and-mercosur); Brazil’s presidency; Indonesia’s trade ministry.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can Brazilian companies use the Singapore deal now?

Yes, it has applied to Brazil since this summer. Exporters should check which tariff lines Mercosur excluded.

Is Brazil negotiating with all of ASEAN?

No. The record shows talks only with individual members, and only Singapore has produced a signed agreement.

Why is Brazil’s Vietnam deal narrower than the Singapore one?

Brazil wants gradual, selective tariff cuts and keeps protections for local industry, which worries about more Vietnamese imports. Its public consultation made that concern plain.

World.title: Codelco Offers Investors 60 Mining Sites
World.content:
Chile's state copper miner is asking private money to help find its next mines, while its own output falls and lawmakers argue over who stays in control.

File photo. A haul road inside the Chuquicamata copper mine, Calama, Chile, 2016. Photo: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

CHILE · COPPER

Codelco, Chile’s state-owned copper miner, has offered private investors about one million hectares of mining concessions that it holds but has not developed. Chairman Bernardo Fontaine presented an initial portfolio of 60 properties this week at Asia Copper Week, an annual industry conference in Shanghai.

He spoke at the closing dinner, where about 2,500 industry representatives gathered, and framed Codelco as a long-term partner, not only a seller of metal. The offer matters to US readers because the Chilean Copper Commission (Cochilco), the state copper research body, said in its third-quarter 2026 market report that Chile’s mine output will fall 8.4% this year, to 4.94 million tonnes.

Codelco already explores with BHP, the global mining group, on the Anillo project in the Antofagasta region. It has also signed an exploration memorandum with India’s Adani Group, a large conglomerate, for the Kaburkaala project and works with Pucobre, a Chilean copper company, on the Tovaku project.

Under the plan, Codelco would contribute its mining rights and geological knowledge, while partners would be expected to bring money, technology and experience. Terms would be negotiated project by project, and Codelco has not said what share it would keep, which properties would go first or which partners it has in mind.

His talk was titled “The Next Great Frontier of Copper: From Competition to Collaboration”, and it ended with an invitation. “We invite you to choose Chile when you assess where to invest, and Codelco if you are looking for a long-term partner,” Fontaine said.

He added that “the copper of the future will not be found by waiting.” In his words, it “will be discovered by exploring, investing and building together.”

The urgency sits in Codelco’s own numbers. On 28 August 2026 the company reported 564,000 tonnes of fine copper (pure metal content) for January to June, against 634,000 tonnes in the same months of 2025, a fall of 11%.

On 5 November Codelco said its 2024 and 2025 records had overstated production by more than 40,000 tonnes (preliminary figures), a week after it dismissed eight executives and professionals over the reporting errors on 29 October. The audits by KPMG and EY, two international audit firms, are unfinished, and no completion date has been published.

In a radio interview, Fontaine said that Codelco’s “future production will keep falling unless we can undertake a very broad action of partnering with private companies.” That is the argument behind the Shanghai offer.

Chile’s Law 19.137, in force since 1992, sets the conditions under which Codelco may form associations with third parties over certain mining properties. Fontaine has said its procedures are long and bureaucratic and can take years.

Finance Minister Jorge Quiroz said on 11 November 2026 that state control of Codelco will never be lost. He called private capital a long-term idea, not privatisation, in the debate on private capital.

Cristián Tapia, a deputy of the centre-left Party for Democracy (PPD) who presides over the lower house’s Mining Committee, backs partnerships “as long as Codelco can hold the majority control of these shares.” That is the one condition he set.

Marco Antonio Sulantay, a deputy of the conservative Independent Democratic Union (UDI), welcomed the call for private capital but said it should be open to investors from every country. Daniel Valenzuela, an independent deputy sitting with the conservative National Renewal (RN) bench, called private capital a good strategy because “to keep indebting Codelco would be a tremendous irresponsibility.”

Cochilco expects output to recover by 3% in 2027, to 5.08 million tonnes, but that rebound is not guaranteed by any new mine. For US buyers, whose power grids, electric vehicles and data centres all run on copper, new supply from Chile’s idle ground would depend on partners willing to pay for the search.

No one has yet said how investment, risk and control of new projects would be shared across Chile’s copper industry. The next dated marker is 1 December 2026, when the Central Bank of Chile publishes the October IMACEC, its monthly economic activity index, a first read on mining’s weight in the economy.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Codelco being sold to private investors?

No. The offer concerns undeveloped mining rights, and Chilean officials say state control of Codelco itself will not be lost.

Who could invest?

Codelco has named no partner from this offer. One lawmaker said any call should be open to investors worldwide, not only Chinese ones.

Why does this matter outside Chile?

Chile is a leading copper supplier, so the way its state miner finds new ore affects future supply. Who pays and who controls new projects is still undecided.

World.title: Ecuador Airliner Skids Off Runway, No Deaths
World.content:
A passenger jet slid off the paved surface in southern Ecuador and nobody was reported hurt. No authority has yet said why it happened.

File photo, 2020. Aerial view of Quito, Ecuador's capital.

Ecuador

An airliner arriving from Quito, reported to be a Boeing 737-500, left the runway while landing at Santa Rosa, in El Oro province in southern Ecuador, on the night of Friday 20 November 2026. No injuries or deaths have been reported, but no authority has yet said what caused it.

A passenger jet slid off the paved surface in southern Ecuador and nobody was reported hurt. No authority has yet said why it happened.

Santa Rosa Regional Airport serves the town of Santa Rosa in El Oro province, near the Peruvian border. The flight was domestic, and the aircraft left the paved surface during landing.

The mayor said 63 people were aboard. Leonel Tenesaca, the airport supervisor, put the number of passengers at 65, and the crew count has not been published.

ECU 911, Ecuador’s national emergency service, reported no injured and no dead in the early hours of Saturday 21 November and described the event as a forced landing. Firefighters from Santa Rosa and Machala, the provincial capital, went to the airport.

File photo: downtown Guayaquil, Ecuador, with an airliner in the sky.

Preliminary accounts name Aeroregional, an Ecuadorian airline, as the operator. We found no statement from the airline or the airport operator, and no official has confirmed the flight details.

The DGAC (Dirección General de Aviación Civil, Ecuador’s civil aviation authority) issued two NOTAMs, formal notices to pilots, between the night of 20 November and the early hours of 21 November. The last, at 01:48 on Saturday, closed a runway until Saturday night because of the incident, and the DGAC has not said which runway or what caused it.

Aviation regulators call this kind of event a runway excursion, meaning an aircraft leaves the paved surface while landing or taking off. Many end without serious injury, as this one appears to have.

In such cases investigators normally examine the tyres, brakes and wheels, the flight recorders, the crew’s actions, and the runway surface and weather. Rain was reported in Santa Rosa that night, but no official has linked it to the incident, so the tyre explanation should be read as a first lead only.

The people most affected are the passengers and crew who lived through the emergency, and anyone booked to or from Santa Rosa while a runway is closed. Damage to the aircraft and whether an investigation has been opened have not been stated by any official.

For readers in the United States, the route was domestic, and no reports of foreign passengers have emerged, although the nationalities of those aboard have not been published. More reporting on the country is on our Ecuador page.

Was anyone hurt when the plane left the runway?

No injuries or deaths have been reported, ECU 911 said in the early hours of Saturday 21 November. The passenger count differs between two local officials.

What caused the plane to leave the runway?

The cause is not established. The mayor of Santa Rosa said a tyre apparently burst on landing, which is a preliminary account that still needs technical evaluation.

The civil aviation authority closed a runway until Saturday night 21 November because of the incident. It has not said which runway or when normal flights resume.

World.title: Brazil Cancer Chain Pivots to Clinics
World.content:
A cancer-care chain that spent 2026 negotiating with creditors says its future lies in clinics, not hospitals, while court approval and a shareholder dispute remain open.

BRAZIL · COMPANY NEWS

Oncoclínicas, a Brazilian private cancer-treatment chain, will build its recovery around outpatient clinics once a court approves its debt plan, chief executive Carlos Gil said in an interview published on Saturday 21 November 2026. The company is trying to restart after a financial crisis that cost it doctors and some hospital leases.

Oncoclínicas filed for an out-of-court restructuring, known in Brazil as “recuperação extrajudicial”, on Monday 13 July 2026 to renegotiate about R$5.1 billion (US$0.86 billion) of debt, converted here at 5.907 reais to the US dollar, the rate of 21 November 2026. Brazilian law lets a company agree a plan with its creditors and then ask a judge to make it binding.

The crisis led to the loss of doctors and the end of some hospital lease contracts. In March 2026 Gil replaced founder Bruno Ferrari as chief executive, at first on an interim basis.

In a formal filing known as a notice to the market on Friday 30 October 2026, the company said creditors holding more than R$3.5 billion (about US$0.59 billion) had joined the plan, or 61.6% of the debts it covers. Those covered debts total about R$5.7 billion (about US$0.96 billion) and leave out amounts owed between companies of the same group.

Gil put support at 77% of the covered debts, above the legal quorum, the minimum the law requires. But joining a plan is not court approval, which still rests with the 3rd Bankruptcy and Judicial Recovery Court of the Central Civil Forum of São Paulo, the court handling the case.

Gil said the company prepared itself during the talks with creditors “precisely so that this resumption would be possible operationally” (our translation from Portuguese). He described the plan as “a large extension of the debt, allowing the company to recover over time”.

The plan offers different kinds of agreement depending on the creditor profile, Gil said, with longer maturities at its centre. Medicine-supply agreements are a significant part of it.

Several existing commercial partners are waiting for court approval before they return, Gil said, and new partners have signalled they want to work with the company in the recovery. Sales of hospitals and diagnostics units are already under way to raise cash.

Gil said Oncoclínicas “has been divesting these hospitals, really focusing on oncology clinics and on its large footprint in Brazil, being present in all regions” (our translation). The company has not said how many hospitals remain for sale or at what prices, nor how many clinics it will run once the sales end.

Under the current format the plan does not provide for immediate dilution of shareholders, meaning a cut in the share of the company they own. Gil said “there could be a conversion later on, but not at this moment”, and that “there is nothing planned at this moment in terms of capitalization” (our translation), with talks possible after court approval.

The company has not said what a later conversion of debt into shares would look like. That question matters most to minority shareholders, who are already in a separate fight.

The securities regulator CVM (Comissão de Valores Mobiliários) decided on 25 August 2026 that a mandatory tender offer, meaning a buyout offer to minority shareholders, is required under the company’s bylaws. Josephina III, a fund linked to the investment firm Centaurus Capital, would have to launch it and contests that duty.

A federal court on 23 October 2026 provisionally suspended the fund’s duty to launch the offer. A São Paulo court suspended the shareholder meeting set for Friday 6 November 2026, and the company had announced no new date at the time.

For readers abroad, the shares trade on B3, the São Paulo stock exchange, as ONCO3. Gil says the cash for the plan’s commitments will come largely from treating patients again, so creditors and drug suppliers depend on clinics reopening at scale.

The wider picture sits in the Brazil news section. No next dated step is confirmed, because court approval is undated and no new shareholder meeting date had been announced.

Do shareholders lose value under the plan right away?

Not under the current format, which does not provide for immediate dilution. A later conversion of debt into shares is possible, but the CEO says nothing is planned yet.

It would make the agreement with creditors binding. The CEO says several commercial partners are waiting for it before they return, and no date has been given.

Patients, doctors, drug suppliers and creditors in Brazil are the groups most directly affected. Shareholders are affected too, through the dilution question and the tender offer dispute.

World.title: Ex-Official Warns of South African Division
World.content:
A former deputy finance minister says South Africa’s municipal elections offered little hope of change and warns of deeper polarisation as parties form city governments.

Photo: Evan Bench / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0)

Politics: South Africa

Mcebisi Jonas, a former South African deputy finance minister, warned in Cape Town on 19 November 2026 that South Africa’s politics risk deeper polarisation after this month’s municipal elections. He spoke at a University of Cape Town memorial event for Pravin Gordhan, a veteran African National Congress (ANC) minister who died on 13 September 2024.

Jonas served as deputy finance minister from 2014 to 2017 and now chairs MTN Group, a Johannesburg-based mobile operator. His warning comes while the parties that must now run the big cities are still bargaining over coalitions.

A former deputy finance minister says South Africa’s municipal elections offered little hope of change and warns of deeper polarisation as parties form city governments.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Government of National Unity (South Africa) Email address Follow

South Africans voted in municipal elections on Wednesday 4 November 2026, and the Electoral Commission of South Africa (IEC), the body that runs elections, declared the final results on Sunday 8 November. The ANC took about 31% of the vote, the Democratic Alliance (DA), the main opposition party and an ANC partner in national government, about 25%, and the uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) Party, founded by former president Jacob Zuma, nearly 10%.

National turnout was 52%, up 6.1 percentage points from 45.9% in 2021, the IEC said on 8 November. Many councils ended hung, meaning no party holds more than half the seats, so coalition bargaining rather than the ballot box now decides who runs them.

Jonas said he had yet to hear any party answer the question “build what?” as they bargain over coalitions, and had heard no “common vision for a better South Africa, for all its people”, and none “that transcends narrow political self-interest”. His own aim is “a more progressive partnership between the state, capital, labour and civil society”.

Cape Town City Hall above the Grand Parade. Jonas spoke at the University of Cape Town on 19 November. File photo: Martinvl / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

Jonas contrasted South Africa with other recent votes, saying those in Serbia, Brazil and the United States “bent power back toward the less powerful”. In his account, Brazil’s President Lula da Silva beat Flávio Bolsonaro, the former president’s son, in a runoff, Serbian students won a majority on 25 October, and the US Democrats won in the November midterms.

South Africa’s municipal elections, he said, signify less such a shift and more the risk of continued polarisation. He said the ANC’s campaign “appeared to be cribbed from a delinquent school child” saying “I’m sorry, I won’t do it again”.

He said the DA “seemed to be feeding off old tropes of racial competence”, while other parties “continued to fan the flames of xenophobia and populism”. He added: “It is no wonder then that there was no great excitement or propelling towards change in the South African elections.”

Jonas described the Government of National Unity (GNU), the ANC and DA-led national coalition in place since 2024, as “a shotgun marriage”, and said it “has become the political axis of white corporate interests in a cosy co-governance relationship with the political elites”. He called the arrangement “unmandated by the people of South Africa” but stressed: “This is not an argument against the private sector.”

Using IEC figures, he said only 29.2 million of about 39 million voting-age South Africans had registered, so the 52% turnout meant only about 37% of eligible people voted. That is Jonas’s own estimate; the IEC counted about 14.9 million ballots, which is closer to 38% of the same adults.

He said enthusiasm was strongest in the most privileged neighbourhoods, which “tipped the balance of power further against the historically disenfranchised”. He warned that consolidation of the most powerful elements along racial lines “risks provoking a counterreaction: a consolidation of the parties of the black majority”.

Add a weak state, xenophobia and “sectarian nationalisms”, he said, and “we are at risk of rolling back the democratic project”. He said the ANC “has no option but to go back to basics and consolidate its base”, and he pointed to high unemployment, low economic growth and stark inequality.

The effect for business is practical: companies and investors that deal with city budgets, services and contracts in Johannesburg, Tshwane (the Pretoria area) and Ekurhuleni (east of Johannesburg) must plan around coalitions that are still being negotiated. Johannesburg is South Africa’s biggest city and its business centre, so any firm with local contracts there is among those exposed.

No public reply from the DA or the ANC to the speech had been found as of 21 November 2026. The DA is a partner in the national government that Jonas criticised.

Under section 29 of the Municipal Structures Act 1998, the law governing councils, each new council must hold its first meeting, which elects the mayor, within 14 days of being declared elected, a deadline that falls on 22 November if counted from the IEC’s declaration. Cape Town’s council already met on Thursday 19 November and returned Geordin Hill-Lewis of the DA as mayor, because the DA holds 133 of its 235 seats, while the date for Johannesburg’s first meeting is not confirmed.

Mid-November talks included an ANC offer of the Johannesburg and Tshwane mayoral seats to ActionSA, the party led by Herman Mashaba, and a separate report describes the Johannesburg coalition talks. Jonas himself looks ahead to the national and provincial elections due in 2029, for which no exact date is confirmed.

What Prediction Markets Say Polymarket, a crypto-based prediction market, gives Herman Mashaba, the ActionSA leader, about 70% to be Johannesburg’s next mayor (21 Nov, 2:25 p.m. ET). About US$183,000 had been traded on that market. These prices are real-money bets, not polls. They show what traders expect, not what voters or councillors have decided. Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does Jonas’s view carry weight?

He served in government and now chairs a large company, so he speaks from both worlds. The speech is his own view, not the position of any party.

What is a hung council?

It is a council where no party holds more than half the seats. Parties must then agree a coalition before a mayor can be elected.

What does Jonas say should happen next?

He wants parties to say what they intend to build and to offer a shared vision beyond narrow self-interest. He also says the ANC must return to basics.

World.title: Tanzania Gold Mine Nyanzaga Is 88% Complete
World.content:
Construction is nearly finished and the cost forecast has risen, so the first gold pour in January 2027 is the next checkpoint.

File photo. A worker operates a drilling machine underground at the Shanta Gold mine, Tanzania, 2017. Photo: Deo photographer, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

Mining: Tanzania

Perseus Mining, an Australian gold producer, says its Nyanzaga gold mine in Tanzania is 88.4% complete and still on course to pour its first gold, the moment molten metal is first cast into bars, in January 2027. The company reported the progress on 27 October 2026, three weeks before the Tanzania Mining and Investment Conference, a government-organised mining forum, opened in Dar es Salaam.

Nyanzaga sits in the Sukumaland Greenstone Belt, a gold-bearing rock formation in Tanzania, and Perseus acquired the project in 2024. The company’s project page says Perseus owns 80% of it.

The project page puts the mine’s life at 16 years, including 14 years of production above 200,000 ounces of gold a year. Its ore reserve, the part of the deposit that can be mined profitably, stood at 4.0 million ounces in February 2026, according to the page.

Perseus said in its September 2026 quarterly report that Nyanzaga “remains on budget and on schedule to produce gold in January 2027”. Overall project progress reached 88.4% at the end of September, according to the quarterly report.

The company’s project page put it at 48% on 31 March 2026.

Perseus has spent US$407.6 million of the US$483 million approved construction budget, or 84%, and US$443.9 million in total once advance payments are counted. The construction budget is holding, but the total is rising: the investment decision, the final go-ahead in April 2025, set US$523 million, and Perseus now forecasts US$553 million to US$563 million.
