The protest, organised with the Marea de Residencias (Care Homes Movement), called for truth, justice and compensation for the victims and their families.

The protesters denounced the controversial protocols introduced under the regional government of Isabel Díaz Ayuso, which restricted hospital transfers for certain elderly care home residents during the pandemic. They also called for care homes to be fully publicly owned and run.

Critics have described the measures as discriminatory, while the regional government has defended its handling of the crisis.

World.title: Paolo Bulgari, Italian jewellery tycoon, dies aged 89
World.content:
Italian jeweller and businessman Paolo Bulgari has died in Rome at the age of 89, his family announced on Saturday, 21 November 2026.

 

The family paid tribute to him as "the greatest jeweller of our time", praising his humanity and his talent as an entrepreneur who loved Italy and served as its ambassador around the world.

Bulgari was the grandson of Sotirio Bulgari, who founded the eponymous jewellery business in Rome in 1884. Born in the Italian capital in 1937, Paolo belonged to the third generation of the family behind the luxury house.

From family workshop to global luxury empire

Paolo Bulgari joined the family business in 1960, initially working alongside his father, Giorgio. He developed a particular expertise in precious stones and became internationally recognised for his knowledge of gemstones.

In 1984, he became chairman of the company, working closely with his brother Nicola and nephew Francesco Trapani to expand the business internationally.

Under their leadership, Bulgari developed beyond its traditional jewellery business, adding watches, perfumes, leather goods and accessories to its portfolio. Its distinctive designs, often inspired by ancient Greek and Roman art, became synonymous with Italian luxury.

Italian film actress Gina Lollobrigida is pictured in Rome, Jan. 15, 1968, wearing a 833,333 pound, $2,000,000 garland of diamond flowers from the Bulgari Jewelry Firm of Rome AP Photo

The brand became particularly famous for its colourful gemstones, bold gold jewellery and distinctive use of cabochon-cut stones. Among its most celebrated admirers was Hollywood actress Elizabeth Taylor, whose association with the jewellery house helped cement its international reputation.

A woman looks at necklaces on display during a preview of the exhibition "Bulgari. The story, the dream" at St. Angel Castle in Rome, Tuesday, June 25, 2019. AP Photo

Sale to luxury giant LVMH

A major turning point came in 2011, when the Bulgari family sold its controlling stake in the business to French luxury conglomerate LVMH in a deal worth approximately €3.7 billion.

Paolo Bulgari later described the decision as painful, but said it was made partly out of responsibility towards the company's employees and concerns about the difficulties of managing the generational transition.

Security personnel stand outside a Bulgari boutique where South Korean Actress Kim Ji-won visited in Hong Kong on Wednesday, March 19, 2025. AP Photo

Despite relinquishing family control, he remained closely connected to the brand and continued designing jewellery well into his later years. He also enjoyed occasionally working behind the counter at the company's historic boutique on Rome's Via dei Condotti, sometimes introducing himself simply as a shop assistant.

Philanthropy and commitment to Rome

Beyond the luxury industry, Bulgari devoted considerable attention to social causes, particularly education and opportunities for young people.

In 2019, he founded the Paolo Bulgari Foundation with his wife. The organisation supports educational regeneration and vocational training in disadvantaged neighbourhoods of Rome.

One of its major projects involved the redevelopment of Largo Mengaroni, the main square in the Tor Bella Monaca district, completed in 2023 in cooperation with local schools, associations and the municipal authorities.

Paolo Bulgari is survived by his six children from two marriages. His funeral will take place on Monday, 23 November, at the Basilica of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme in Rome.

World.title: Latest news bulletin | November 21st, 2026 – Evening
World.content: Catch up with the most important stories from around Europe and beyond in this Euronews news bulletin. In just a few minutes, our newsroom brings you the latest news and breaking news across world affairs, business, politics, culture, entertainment and travel, with the context you need to make sense of a fast-moving day. Reported with the independence and the European perspective that define Euronews, this regular round-up gives you a clear and reliable overview of the stories shaping our world right now, wherever you are watching from.

World.title: Real Madrid outpace Bayern Munich in revenue race as both clubs post record figures
World.content:
European football's financial heavyweights are celebrating another record-breaking season. Real Madrid reported operating revenue of €1.221 billion for 2025-26, comfortably ahead of Bayern Munich's €988.2 million.

 

Real Madrid sets €1.25bn budget after record revenue

Real Madrid president Florentino Pérez announced the record figures at the club's annual general meeting, while presenting a budget of €1.25 billion for the 2026-27 season.

For the first time, the Spanish giants have surpassed the €1.2 billion revenue mark, a figure Pérez described as unprecedented for a sports organisation.

The club also recorded its highest-ever EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation), at €287.4 million. Net profit after tax reached €26 million, an increase of eight per cent compared with the previous season.

Pérez highlighted Real Madrid's international standing, citing Forbes, Deloitte and Brand Finance rankings. According to Forbes, the club is the world's most valuable football club for the fifth consecutive year. Deloitte ranks it first in revenue, while Brand Finance considers it the world's most valuable and strongest football brand.

Pérez said the club's partnerships with companies and technology providers would help it apply new expertise to its operations, particularly its sporting activities.

The figures underline the commercial strength of both clubs, although the Spanish giants remain out in front. Real Madrid's revenue increased by 3.1 per cent compared with the previous season, while Bayern recorded a more modest rise of around one per cent.

The difference amounts to approximately €233 million, although the clubs' published accounting figures are not entirely like-for-like: Real Madrid explicitly excludes player-transfer income from its operating revenue figure.

Real Madrid outstrip Bayern Munich in record revenues

Real Madrid's growth has been driven largely by its commercial operations and the redevelopment of the Santiago Bernabéu stadium.

Marketing generated €539 million, an increase of six per cent, while stadium revenue reached €363 million, up 11 per cent. Television rights and revenue from international competitions contributed a further €319 million.

West façade of Santiago Bernabéu Stadium in Madrid (Spain). Luis García, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

The stadium's commercial performance is particularly significant: its revenue has more than doubled compared with the final season before the redevelopment began in 2018-19.

Real Madrid have now recorded a profit for 26 consecutive financial years, according to the club.

Bayern close to the billion-euro mark

Bayern Munich are not far behind, having increased their consolidated revenue from €978.3 million to €988.2 million.

The club's sponsorship income was particularly strong, rising by almost €30 million to €268.4 million. Merchandising also reached a record €152.8 million.

However, the financial picture was more mixed when it came to profits. Bayern's operating result (EBITDA) increased from €187.8 million to €190.8 million, but its profit before tax fell by 16.9 per cent to €35.3 million. The group's net profit declined by 15.9 per cent to €22.8 million.

Bayern explained that the lower profit was largely due to exceptional revenue in the previous financial year from the European Championship and the Champions League final, which did not recur in 2025-26.

Bayern Munich's home ground, the Allianz Arena. AP Photo

CEO Jan-Christian Dreesen nevertheless described the results as another record year (source in German), emphasising the club's financial stability and its continued investment in the men's and women's teams.

Bayern also highlighted a decline in revenue from the Bundesliga's central media marketing, which fell by €10 million to €93 million. Dreesen said German clubs needed to address their competitive disadvantage in international television marketing.

Bayern reach a historic membership milestone

Away from the financial figures, Bayern celebrated another milestone: the club has surpassed 500,000 members for the first time.

According to Bayern, this makes it the largest sports club by membership worldwide. Its membership has doubled over the past 12 years, from around 250,000 in 2014.

The milestone also underlines the difference between the clubs' structures. Bayern is majority-owned by its members' association, FC Bayern München eV, while Real Madrid is entirely owned by its members, known as socios.

At Bayern, members also have voting rights at the annual general meeting, giving them a direct say in the club's affairs.

Two different models of financial success

Although Real Madrid currently have the larger revenue stream, both clubs demonstrate how Europe's leading football institutions are expanding beyond traditional sources of income.

Real Madrid have benefited considerably from their renovated stadium and global commercial reach. Bayern, meanwhile, have built particularly strong sponsorship and merchandising businesses while maintaining a cautious approach to spending.

The substantial difference in turnover does not translate into an equally large gap in profitability. Despite generating around €233 million more revenue than Bayern, Real Madrid reported net profit after tax of €26.3 million, only €3.5 million more than the German club's €22.8 million.

This suggests that higher revenues do not automatically result in significantly higher profits, as operating costs, player salaries, transfer spending, financing and other expenses also play a major role. Both clubs nevertheless ended the 2025-26 financial year in the black, demonstrating their ability to remain profitable while operating on a huge financial scale.

For Bayern, the next major target is clear: breaking through the €1 billion revenue barrier. Real Madrid, meanwhile, have already moved beyond it and are setting their sights on further growth.

World.title: Former Costa Concordia cruise ship captain released from prison on probation after nine years
World.content:
After spending more than nine years behind bars, Francesco Schettino, the former captain of the Costa Concordia cruise ship, left Rome's Rebibbia prison on Friday evening.

 

According to a report from the Italian outlet Quotidiano Nazionale (QN), the Rome Supervisory Court granted Schettino release under probation after a thorough review of his rehabilitation process and his conduct during his time in prison.

Francesca Carnicelli, a lawyer for Schettino, welcomed the decision, saying prison staff had given an extremely positive assessment of his participation in the rehabilitation programme.

"In our view, all the conditions were in place for this alternative measure to be granted, as it represents the correct continuation of the process after the conviction," Carnicelli said.

The case dates back to January 2012, when the Costa Concordia ship, owned by the Costa Crociere cruise line, struck rocks off the coast of Isola del Giglio in the Tyrrhenian Sea.

The impact ripped a hole around 35.59 metres long in the port side of the ship's hull, causing it to list heavily before it ran aground on a rocky outcrop near Punta Gabbianara, where it partially sank.

The disaster claimed 32 lives, including passengers and crew members.

In the subsequent legal proceedings, Schettino was sentenced to 16 years in prison

The sentence was upheld by the Florence Court of Appeals on 31 May 2016, along with a five-year ban from working in the maritime industry. The provisional compensation awarded to survivors who joined the proceedings as civil claimants also increased to between €40,000 and €65,000 each.

The conviction was finally upheld by the Court of Cassation on 12 May 2017.

World.title: Raccoon roast as a sustainable alternative to Germany's Christmas goose?
World.content:
He first came across raccoons while out fishing. For more than two years now, the small, button-eyed animals have been a permanent fixture on his restaurant menu – despite the fact that he is a vegetarian in his private life.

 

Chef Steffen Haaßengier now also teaches others how to prepare raccoon meat, offering cookery courses in Weimar, a city in the German state of Thuringia.

Chef Steffen Haaßengier with raccoon legs, red cabbage and Thuringian dumplings. Steffen Haaßengier

In 2025, the 42-year-old processed around 450 tonnes of raccoon meat. On special "raccoon barbecue days", he butchers up to 35 animals. Local hunters bring the raccoons to him after shooting them, and the veterinary authorities test them for diseases beforehand.

Tender meat with a distinctive flavour

In Canada, raccoons have long been considered a delicacy. "The raccoon has a very interesting, slightly sweet flavour of its own, somewhere between game and beef. It is tender, long-fibred meat, and you could also compare it to rabbit", says Haaßengier.

For seasoning, he recommends robust flavours such as rosemary, thyme, paprika, garlic and onion.

He says feedback from his guests is consistently positive. "Most people say they first have to get over the image they have in their heads. Many initially think of this small, cute animal, but there are lots of other small, cute animals, such as lambs, and they are cute too. But in the end, everyone likes the taste, and many even come back several times, bringing family and friends."

Raccoon on a lawn. AP/Gerald Herbert

To keep his customers interested, he is always coming up with new dishes. One example is his raccoon burger, which has become a firm favourite. It is served with homemade Canadian coleslaw and chips.

Raccoon burger with chips. Steffen Haaßengier

On Sundays, he always serves the classic "raccoon leg" with a red wine and lingonberry sauce. By now, he has built up a regular clientele who return every fortnight. He is currently working on a "lovely raccoon ragout".

The main argument in favour of raccoon meat, he says, is sustainability. "There is no factory farming involved, so there is no need for force-fed geese or other animals raised for their meat. There are plenty of raccoons anyway. They have to be culled because they are an invasive species. It is food for a good cause."

As for the price, he says, there is not much difference either.

Invasive species out of control

Originally native to North America, the raccoon is classified as an invasive species in Germany. As an omnivore, it poses a threat to native amphibians, reptiles and birds. According to the German Hunting Association, almost 290,000 raccoons were shot across Germany in 2025.

This "problem animal" can weigh between 3.6 and 13 kilograms and live for up to 16 years. During its lifetime, it can cause considerable damage, particularly to buildings, through faeces and urine contamination, as well as to gardens and native wildlife.

A group of raccoons: the invasive species continues to spread across Germany. AP Photo

The numbers are also rising in the German capital, Berlin. In the 2024/25 hunting season, 286 raccoons were shot, compared with just 103 in 2022/23. In neighbouring Brandenburg, around 30,000 raccoons were shot in 2022/23.

In East Germany before reunification, another invasive species was also a popular item on the menu: nutria. Its meat was considered a valued foodstuff, mainly available as a by-product of fur farming. The meat of the so-called "swamp beaver" was prepared in much the same way as rabbit or hare – as a roast, stew or pan-fried dish – or made into sausages. Nutria Bolognese was popular in school and workplace canteens.

Can raccoon with dumplings and red cabbage replace the traditional Christmas goose?

In Germany, a festive meal is traditionally a must at Christmas. While many families serve the classic potato salad with sausages on Christmas Eve, 24 December, the main Christmas holidays often feature roast goose, duck or beef roulades, accompanied by red cabbage and potato dumplings.

But does it always have to be the familiar classics? With raccoon numbers on the rise, an unusual alternative could soon find its way on to the Christmas dinner table: braised raccoon leg with dumplings and red cabbage. Could it catch on?

Steffen Haaßengier says it certainly could. "As a braised dish, raccoon leg can easily replace goose leg, roulade or duck." He adds that serving it would not mean abandoning any traditions.

On 6 December, his restaurant, Zum Lindeneck, in Weimar is hosting a St Nicholas feast. Alongside raccoon, badger will also be on the menu at Zum Lindeneck in Weimar, with both dishes offered at special prices.

World.title: Jair Bolsonaro hospitalised with abdominal pain while under house arrest
World.content:
Brazil’s former president Jair Bolsonaro has been admitted to intensive care with an intestinal obstruction, the hospital treating him said on Saturday, marking another health setback for the far-right leader, who was convicted of plotting a coup.

 

He was escorted to DF Star Hospital Asa Sul, Brasília, the capital of Brazil, by the military police.

According to his doctor, the former president has an "acute obstructive abdomen", Globo reports (source in Portuguese).

Bolsonaro remains in hospital under observation. Doctors have not ruled out the possibility of further surgery.

The hospital said in a medical bulletin that Bolsonaro remained “clinically stable, conscious, alert and breathing without assistance”. Doctors have inserted a gastric tube to provide nutritional support, adding that no date has been set for his discharge.

Bolsonaro taken to hospital after falling ill at home

Bolsonaro’s son Carlos, a senator-elect, described a night of vomiting and severe pain.

“I’m not a doctor, but I’ve never seen him like this,” he wrote on X, raising the possibility that his father could require another operation – potentially his tenth in less than eight years.

According to the Federal District Military Police, the former president, who is under house arrest, felt unwell, prompting a request for a medical assessment. A doctor visited Bolsonaro at home and confirmed that he needed to be taken to hospital.

Bolsonaro was convicted last year of plotting a coup after attempting to remain in power despite losing the 2022 presidential election to left-wing candidate Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. He has denied the charges, claiming he is the victim of a judicial witch-hunt orchestrated by the left.

The former president has undergone several operations and required repeated hospital treatment for health problems linked to the stabbing he suffered during the 2018 election campaign.

Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year-and-three-month prison sentence under humanitarian house arrest, granted by Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes in March.

"His health is deteriorating day by day," Carlos Bolsonaro said, blaming his father's condition on his lack of mobility and what he described as "psychological torture" inflicted by the state.

Brazil's Supreme Federal Court will rule in December on the constitutionality of a law that reduces Bolsonaro's prison sentence prison, as well as those of others convicted over the coup plot.

Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, Carlos's older brother, lost last month's presidential run-off election to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. The day after his defeat, Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes ordered the seizure of his passports as part of a money-laundering investigation.

Flávio Bolsonaro fled to the United States, where he refused to concede defeat. On Elon Musk's social media platform X, the former presidential candidate posted a message calling for support for his father.

World.title: Turkey seizes control of last major independent news channel amid fraud scandal
World.content:
Turkey's last operating independent TV news channel has fallen under state control, as President Recep Tayyip Erdogan scrambles to contain a wave of public fury over a $20 billion investment fund scandal that has swallowed the life savings of hundreds of thousands of people in the country.

Advertising

Sozcu TV vanished from the airwaves before dawn on Tuesday as police enforced a court order installing a state trustee, cutting the channel's transmission as it was broadcasting a programme on the latest revelations in the investment fraud scandal.

The move echoes a similar state takeover last month of Halk TV, another major independent broadcaster.

The silencing of Turkey’s two largest independent news channels has drawn sharp condemnation from opposition parties and human rights groups. While the government maintains that the judiciary operates independently, critics argue the court orders are politically motivated.

“This is part of a process of basically closing down all independent media that might risk reaching followers of the ruling party,” said Emma Sinclair-Webb of Human Rights Watch.

“The whole tactic of the Erdogan government has been to use court orders. The court orders are so problematic in themselves, so overreaching, so disproportionate, that this has nothing really to do with the legal process. This is all about a political crackdown.”

Turkey talks green at Cop31 while cracking down on activists

Sinclair-Webb noted that television remains the primary news source for most Turks, making both networks and individual journalists who question government policies prime targets.

Four journalist have been detained or placed under house arrest for reporting on the investment scandal.

Authorities accuse Sozcu TV of ties to followers of the late cleric Fethullah Gulen, whom Ankara blames for masterminding a failed 2016 coup. Four of its executives and officials have been detained. Halk TV faces separate corruption allegations.

Both broadcasters strongly deny the charges.

Investment scandal

The closing of the channels comes amid fallout from the collapse of more than 100 investment funds, which wiped out $20 billion, stranded more than 500,000 investors and triggered a stock market crash.

The scandal has implicated numerous figures linked to Erdogan’s ruling Justice and Development Party (AK Party).

According to recent polls, 80 percent of Turks are closely following the scandal, with a similar majority blaming the government.

On Thursday, protesters demonstrated outside the Capital Markets Board, the country's financial regulator, in Ankara.

Sweeping raids leave Turkey’s LGBTQI+ community fearing what comes next

Around 500 people are under investigation and more than 100 suspects have been jailed. Erdogan vowed this week that no one would escape justice and promised to expedite repayments to affected investors.

Political analyst Sezin Oney said the government is scrambling to control the public narrative as its reputation among its own voter base unravels.

“Up to now, AK Party and government circles were able to project to their base the idea that the opposition [is involved in] all sorts of corruption. So all of a sudden, that facade, that rhetoric has collapsed. Now it’s the government circles who are massively corrupt."

Debate moves online

Atilla Yesilada, a Turkey analyst at New York-based consultancy firm Global Source Partners, warned that the scandal has exposed deep flaws in financial oversight, threatening severe economic and political fallout for Erdogan.

“Turkey is heading for a recession because the institutional structure has completely collapsed,” Yesilada said. “In a free market economy, you really need regulatory boards to do their work which clearly, as we see in this instance, they don't. In fact, they enable or incentivise thieves [and make] their jobs easier."

Yesilada added that Erdogan lacks a clear path to resolve the crisis, as opposition figures release new allegations implicating AK Party associates daily.

Turkey's new opposition party offers hope, but its future is already in jeopardy

Following the state takeover of another broadcaster last year, the loss of Sozcu TV and Halk TV marks a grim turning point for Turkish media, Oney said. However, she questioned whether the government can successfully suppress public discourse.

“It’s the end of the road for TV journalism, you don’t have any oppositional voice or oppositional debate. But people talk, people think, one way or another. Because Turkey was a thinking and talking nation before, it's very difficult to stop [that]. It is just [being done now] on social media.”

The government has accelerated efforts to police online dissent, shutting down hundreds of critical social media accounts, although new ones are emerging just as rapidly.

Meanwhile Koza TV, a previously fringe station, has seen its ratings surge after becoming a new outlet for independent reporting on the scandal – although mounting regulatory fines make its future uncertain.

World.title: Podcast: Living on the breadline, France's 35-hour week and a divisive tax
World.content:
The French government's decision to raise the minimum wage has failed to satisfy protesters struggling to make ends meet amid the cost-of-living crisis. Also, did the introduction of the 35-hour working week actually help reduce unemployment? The evidence is mixed. And a look at the history of France's second-largest tax, the CSG, and why it's dividing politicians.

Advertising

French unions and workers have been protesting over the rising cost of living and wages that are failing to keep up with inflation. In response, the government has agreed to increase the minimum wage, known as the Smic, by 1.6 percent – putting an extra €24 a month into the pockets of the lowest earners. But the measure has failed to satisfy unions and public sector workers, who took to the streets again this week for a day of strike action. We hear what it's like to live on the breadline and the arguments for raising public sector wages. (Listen @0')

France introduced the 35-hour working week in 2000, aiming to reduce high unemployment by spreading work among more people. After five years of research, labour economist Elio Nimier-David has found that the reform failed to achieve its intended goals, while the question of how much people should work continues to divide politicians today. (Listen @19'20'')

The CSG, or general social contribution, was introduced in 1990 and is now France's second-largest tax after VAT, raising billions of euros to fund the country's social security system. But its broad reach and proportional rate have made it a political target, as presidential candidates debate how to ease the cost-of-living crisis and put more money back into people's pockets. (Listen @15'10'')

Episode mixed by Cecile Pompeani.

Spotlight on France is a podcast from Radio France International. Find us on rfienglish.com, Apple podcasts, Spotify or your favourite podcast app.

World.title: Getting rid of antibiotic resistance: Challenges and possible solutions
World.content:
If antibiotics stop working, even the smallest infection can be fatal. The WHO expects millions of deaths over the next 25 years. Can the "One Health" approach help combat antibiotic resistance?

"The threat is immense," said Jean Pierre Nyemazi, acting director of the World Health Organization's department of antimicrobial resistance, during a virtual press conference recently. "An estimated cumulative number of 39 million deaths directly attributable to AMR [antimicrobial resistance] would occur in the next 25 years."

It was, however, the stated goal of World Health Organization, or WHO, member states to reduce the mortality rate caused by AMR by 10% until 2030, Nyemazi added. "When we see the trend, the investments, the action, we don't think we are on the right track."

Without antibiotics, today's modern medicine would not exist

A world without effective antibiotics would be like traveling back to the days in which even the smallest infection was life-threatening, said Can Imirzalioglu, director of the Institute of Medical Microbiology at Justus Liebig University Giessen. "If antibiotics were no longer effective, modern medicine as we know it today would no longer be possible at all."

Imirzalioglu is not only an expert on antibiotic resistance but also on "One Health," a concept adopted in 2004 by experts in human medicine, veterinary medicine and nature conservation. It recognizes that the health of humans, animals and the environment is closely interconnected.

After all, antibiotics and antimicrobial-resistant germs are not just a problem in hospitals. They can also be found in animal shelters, in animal products, in waste water, in fertilizers and in plants. "One Health tries to keep an eye on all of this," Imirzalioglu said.

One Health: Pandemic prevention research in Africa To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

For hospitals and doctors' offices this means that antibiotics must be used as selectively and purposefully as possible. To this end, research is focused primarily on developing better and faster diagnostic methods.

In Germany, antibiotics were frequently prescribed against respiratory or urinary tract infections, Imirzalioglu said. But antibiotics are only effective against bacteria. If a virus causes the infection, they are ineffective.

Nonetheless, every antibiotics dose has consequences: it damages our gut microbiome. This consists of billions of micro-organisms, primarily bacteria, which are essential for digestion, metabolism and the immune system. "If we damage the [bacteria], resistant pathogens can spread and take their place," Imirzalioglu said.

Another problem was that such a spreading of resistant pathogens in the gut often went unnoticed and without causing symptoms, he added.

So people became "carriers of resistant pathogens, which they, in turn, release back into their environment."

In this way, resistant pathogens make their way out of hospitals via toilets and sinks into wastewater and, from there, into the Baltic Sea, where they are ingested by wild birds. This pathway was traced in a study by Katharina Schaufler , a veterinarian and microbiologist at the Helmholtz Institute for One Health (HIOH).

Why factory farming exacerbates the problem

Antibiotics have not only been used in humans on a large scale over a long time, excessive use in veterinary medicine has also led to resistance to nearly all available antibiotics, Schaufler said.

In 2006, an EU-wide ban on the use of antibiotics as growth promoters in animal feed came into effect. Since then, antibiotics may only be applied as part of veterinary treatment.

The problem is that due to factory farming the use of antibiotics for medical purposes is a permanent necessity. The mere fact that animals live together in confined spaces causes infections to spread rapidly.

Lack of space as well as boredom lead the animals to injure each other and this happens in an environment where, in Schaufler's words, "there's already a high level of bacterial pressure."

Through fertilizers, antibiotic-resistant pathogens enter the environment. "It has been proven that, for example, resistant bacteria can still be found on lettuce heads," the veterinarian said. Resistant bacteria were also found time and again on meat.

Zoonoses and the hidden pandemic risk in your backyard To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

National solutions are also falling short. In many countries, antibiotics are still a standard additive in animal feed, Schaufler said. And in such countries, antibiotics could be obtained in drugstores without prescriptions, Imirzalioglu added. Both say that all of this makes the global fight against antibiotic resistance more difficult.

Combating antibiotic resistance means preventing infections

Political will is of the essence when it comes to combating antibiotic resistance. Imirzalioglu works at Guardian , a project funded by the German Federal Ministry of Research, Technology and Space.

The aim of the project is to prevent outbreaks of diseases caused by resistant bacteria by monitoring and analyzing wastewater in the German state of Hesse.

At EU level, Imirzalioglu is also an advisor at the Antimicrobial Resistance One Health Network . He sums up his experience with policymakers: "The experts and working groups have great ideas, and then these are often scaled back or stifled during the initial stages."

Perhaps the lack of political will so far is one of the reasons why the WHO's Nyemazi is issuing an appeal to every individual: Preventing antibiotic resistance means preventing infections, through hygiene, regular vaccinations and doctor's appointments as well as taking medications in accordance with prescriptions.

This article was originally published in German.

World.title: Mexican special forces arrest drug kingpin 'Chapo Isidro'
World.content:
The alleged leader of the Beltran Leyva gang and one of the FBI's most wanted fugitives, known as 'Chapo Isidro,' was captured by the Mexican military following a raid and a shootout in the coastal Sinaloa state.

A gun battle between Mexican soldiers and alleged gang members in the city of Guasave, in the state of Sinaloa, ended with special forces detaining senior members of the Beltran Leyva drug trafficking network, Mexican officials said on Saturday.

The gang is aligned with one of the factions of the powerful Sinaloa cartel.

Authorities said the overnight raid resulted in capture of the suspected drug kingpin Fausto Isidro Meza F., better known as "Chapo Isidro," who is believed to be the leader of Beltran Leyva.

FBI offering millions for 'Chapo Isidro'

The 44-year-old Mexican national is one of the FBI's ten most wanted fugitives. The US law enforcement agency claims his group is responsible for smuggling "large quantities of heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine, fentanyl, and marijuana into the United States," and has offered a $5 million (€4.56 million) reward for information leading to his arrest.

He is also wanted in Mexico on charges including organized crime.

On Saturday, Mexican authorities said the raid was conducted due to "intelligence coordination" between Mexico's military and US agencies.

The three detainees were transported to Mexico City "to be placed at the disposal of the competent prosecutorial authorities," the military said.

It was not immediately clear if "Chapo Isidro" will be extradited to the US.

Roads blocked in Sinaloa

The troops used "stealth and surprise" to reach the area, establishing a perimeter around the drug dealer's location and then moving in from multiple directions, according Mexico's US embassy.

Unverified videos from Guasave, however, showed military helicopters firing at ground targets and sports fans scrambling for safety during a baseball game. Some of the violence in the western Mexican city seems to have taken place after Chapo Isidro was arrested, with drug cartels attempting to retaliate against the authorities and civilians for the move.

The military said security forces were deployed to restore traffic on roads and highways in Mexico's Sinaloa Image: Yohari Leon/REUTERS

Mexico's defense ministry confirmed cartel members set up roadblocks in the area, but added that security forces were assisting local authorities in restoring order.

The Guasave raid is only the latest in a string of high-profile moves against senior leaders of Mexico's illegal drug trade. Less than two weeks ago, Mexican navy announced the arrest of Rafael A., suspected of leading a cartel cell active in the states of Jalisco and Michoacan.

President ​Claudia Sheinbaum is facing pressure from Donald Trump, who has threatened to take military action against cartels on Mexican territory.

Editor's note: DW follows the German press code, which stresses the importance of protecting the privacy of suspects, victims and those who are associated with a criminal case, and urges the media to refrain from publishing their full identities in most cases.

World.title: Russian helicopter suspected of violating Finnish airspace
World.content:
Finland's Defense Ministry thinks the incursion is linked to a drone strike earlier Saturday on a Russian cargo ship, which is on a US sanctions list.

A Russian helicopter is suspected of violating Finnish airspace, the Nordic country's Ministry of Defense said Saturday.

The incident happened a few hours after a drone attack left a Russian cargo ship ablaze in the Gulf of Finland, the easternmost part of the Baltic Sea.

What do we know?

According to Finland's Defense Ministry, the incursion happened at 12:34 p.m. local time (10:34 UTC/GMT) off the town of Loviisa, on the southern coast.

"This alleged airspace violation may be linked to rescue or surveillance operations carried out by Finland following damage sustained by a cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland," public broadcaster YLE cited Defense Minister Antti Hakkanen as saying.

The ministry added the helicopter could have penetrated up to 4.1 kilometers (2.5 miles) into Finnish territory.

The Finnish Defense Ministry said there is no further danger to shipping or the public Image: Antti Hämäläinen/Lehtikuva/dpa/picture alliance

What do we know about the cargo ship attack?

Earlier Saturday, Finland — one of NATO's newest members — said a Russian cargo ship heading for Russia's Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad caught fire after being struck by drones in the Gulf of Finland.

The Finnish military said the Sparta II was damaged ⁠west ⁠of Russia's Gogland island, about 40 kilometers (25 miles) from Finland's coast, and later drifted into Finnish territorial waters.

Finnish ‌Border ​Guard Commander Ilja Iljin later told YLE that the vessel, which is known to have links to the Russian military, was struck by Ukrainian drones while in Russian waters.

"At the moment, ​there is no confirmed information ⁠about ​what cargo ​is on board, ​but it ‌cannot be ruled out ​that ⁠there is military materiel on ⁠board," ​Iljin said.

The ship is on a US sanctions list, according to a search of the Open Sanctions website.

The Border Guard later said the crew of the Sparta II was evacuating into a life raft and rescue boat.

Finland's Prime Minister Petteri Orpo is concerned about the Ukraine war spillover Image: Virginia Mayo/AP Photo/picture alliance

Orpo backs Ukraine against 'aggressor'

"The [Ukraine] war is spilling over into our neighbouring areas," wrote Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo on X.

Ukraine has the right to fight against the aggressor," he added.

The Finnish government has put temporary curbs on aviation and maritime traffic in the eastern Gulf of Finland.

The Defense Ministry said Finland had informed its allies about the incident.

World.title: EU and Indonesia sign trade deal
World.content:
A deal covering 730 million people promises lower tariffs and new investment opportunities as the European Union seeks to diversify trade ties amid growing global economic tensions.

The European Union and Indonesia signed a free trade deal on Saturday, describing it as a new chapter in economic relations between the two sides.

"This is one of the most ambitious deals the European Union has concluded in Asia," Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, said at the signing ceremony on Saturday.

"Together, we represent a market of 730 million people," she added.

The Indonesia-European Union Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) and the additional Investment Protection Agreement (IPA) are designed to reduce trade barriers and attract investment in strategic sectors such as electric vehicles, electronics, and pharmaceuticals.

The agreement comes after almost 10 years of negotiations and is part of a wider series of trade deals by the EU.

'Keeping the doors open when others are closing theirs'

The bloc hopes to reduce its reliance on individual economic partners as trade with both China and the US has become more difficult in recent years.

Von der Leyen also stressed the importance of international cooperation, saying that "in a time when others are closing their doors, we keep ours open."

In 2025, von der Leyen met with Indonesian President Pabowo Subianto to work on the agreement Image: Laily Rachev - Biro Pers Sekretariat Presiden

The deal sees tariffs on about 98% of EU exports to Indonesia to be done away with. The EU estimates that European companies could save more than €600 million (around €658 million) per year.

"The benefits for our exporters are concrete and measurable," Indonesian Minister of Economic Affairs Airlangga Hartarto said, hailing a "new chapter" in economic relations with the EU. He said the deal would benefit his country’s main exports to Europe, including palm oil, footwear and textiles.

Palm oil and deforestation had been major stumbling blocks during the negotiations, and the agreement includes mechanisms for cooperation on regulatory and sustainability issues as well as a dedicated protocol on palm oil to address environmental concerns.

The EU parliament is now expected to greenlight the deal while Indonesian authorities will also complete the ratification process so it can enter into force in 2027.

World.title: New EU budget proposal aims at tax gobal tech giants
World.content:
European Council President Antonio Costa has proposed a smaller EU budget for 2028-2034, including a 3% tax on major digital firms to ease member states' contributions. France has already rejected the plan as inadequate.

European Council President Antonio Costa has proposed a new draft for the next EU budget .

Among other things, he is suggesting a tax on big tech firms to ease the contributions of member states, some of which strongly criticised earlier proposals.

The EU budget is theEuropean Union’s shared budget and it is used for things ranging from agricultural subsidies, infrastructure projects to border control and defence.

A first draft for the 2028 to 2034 budget was proposed by the EU Commission in 2025 but was criticised, especially by a group of northern European members including Germany who wanted the budget to be much smaller.

Following that criticism, the European Council President has now suggested a new draft, which is smaller by €204 billion.

But divisions among member states appear to remain, with France immediately coming out against Costa’s new draft, saying it was "deeply disappointing."

The EU budget also covers financial aid for Ukraine Image: Hans Lucas/AFP/Getty Images

What’s the plan for the tech tax?

The proposal includes a string of new "revenue channels," explicitly intended to "to keep national contributions at a reasonable level," so that member state will have to contribute less than otherwise would be the case.

The biggest splash would likely come from a tax on companies with an annual turnover from digital activities of at least 50 million euros in the EU and 750 million euros worldwide.

Those firms would be subject to "an annual contribution corresponding to 3% of the annual net turnover from online advertising, digital intermediation services and user-generated data," according to Costa.

Aside from the tech tax, the "balanced basket of new own resources" also includes taxes on tobacco products and electronic waste.

What happens next?

Neither the EU Commission nor European Council President Costa will have the final word on the budget. Costa's plan will now be at the centre of hours of talks when EU leaders meet in Brussels next week.

"This is a realistic budget that addresses our new priorities while preserving our established policies," Costa wrote about his proposal. "I am confident that this proposal is a good basis for moving towards a final agreement."

But an initial reaction from France suggests that any final agreement might still be some way off.

The French presidency said the budget "falls well short ​of ‌what is needed, particularly on ‌the Common Agricultural Policy, ‌notably ​to guarantee income support for farmers."

"As it ⁠stands, ​this proposal ​from the President ​of the European ‌Council does not ​provide ⁠a basis for an ⁠agreement."

The EU was hoping to reach a general agreement on the budget by the end of 2026 with its formal adoption planned for 2027.

World.title: Russia strikes Zelenskyy's hometown, killing 2
World.content:
The attacks follow Russian President Vladimir Putin's vow of a "painful" response to Ukraine's attacks this week on the Kerch Bridge, linking Russian-occupied Crimea.

Russian ballistic missile strikes on Ukraine's southern city of Kryvyi Rih — President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's hometown — killed two people and wounded dozens of others, local officials said Saturday.

The attacks come amid little progress in talks to end the nearly five-year-old war and after Ukraine, on three occasions this week, struck the Kerch bridge linking Russian-occupied Crimea with Russia.

Russian President Vladimir Putin had vowed a "painful" response to the Kerch attack, as the bridge is vital for war supplies for Russian forces in the south.

Russia intensifies aerial attacks on Ukraine To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What do we know?

Among the dead in Friday evening's double-tap strikes on Kryvyi Rih were a 7-year-old boy and a 20-year-old woman, while several children were among the 60 wounded, the Ukrainian officials said.

Several fires broke out and damage was caused to about 25 apartment buildings, a hospital, schools and an industrial facility, Oleksandr Vilkul, the head of the city administration, wrote on Telegram.

Moscow, meanwhile, confirmed a further strike on Friday night in Kryvyi Rih.

Russia's Defense Ministry said a thermal power plant in the city was hit, along with a power substation in the region of Rivne, on the opposite side of the country.

Both facilities supply electricity to the industry supporting Ukraine's military, the ministry added.

Kryvyi Rih has been hit several times by Russia during the war Image: Press service of the National Police of Ukraine/Handout/REUTERS

What are the other latest developments?

Elsewhere in the nearly five-year-long war, Russia ​also struck a ​cargo vessel ‌near Odesa, which Moscow said was carrying dual-use goods ​for ⁠the Ukrainian military.

Eleven people, including two children, were wounded when a Russian drone attacked a five-story apartment building in the northeastern Kharkiv region, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said Saturday.

One person was wounded in a Russian attack on the capital, Kyiv, according to the service.

In Russia, local officials said Saturday that Ukrainian drone attacks wounded three people in the Bryansk and Belgorod border regions.

Finland, meanwhile, said it detected a drone attack on Saturday morning on a Russian cargo ship in the eastern Baltic Sea, prompting Prime Minister Petteri Orpo to warn that the war is "spilling over into our immediate vicinity."

After damage to Russia's Kerch bridge to Crimea, Zelenskyy warned in an interview with US broadcaster NBC that the structure "will not remain standing anyway."

World.title: Germany's religious freedom report: Authoritarian regimes, holy wars, and spies abroad
World.content:
Harassment, persecution, surveillance: Across much of the world, people of faith are facing growing pressure. A new German government report is unusually direct in criticizing China in particular.

The report spans more than 150 pages, but its conclusion can be summed up in a single sentence: "The global situation regarding freedom of religion and belief deteriorated during the reporting period," said Thomas Rachel, the German government's commissioner for freedom of religion and belief, and a member of parliament for the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU). Recently adopted by the Cabinet, the government's fourth report on the subject covers developments from 2023 to 2025.

The government has issued a dedicated report on freedom of religion and belief around the world. According to the report, this freedom is facing "increasing pressure" globally. The focus is not primarily on the suppression of religious institutions or structures, but on the situation of individuals who hold a religious belief, or none at all.

Faith in the Digital Age To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Authoritarian regimes increase pressure on religious communities

The importance of religious freedom is reflected in the way the government commissioner describes the issue: "Religion and faith are of great importance to four out of five people around the world and are central to their identity. People wake up with God and go to sleep with God. It is part of their everyday lives." Research by the Pew Research Center suggests that about 84% of the world's population identifies with a certain religion.

At a time when authoritarian regimes are gaining ground and expanding their surveillance capabilities, the report paints a bleak picture. The growing number of violent conflicts, the rise of authoritarian rule, and the spread of populism have led to "painful restrictions on freedom of religion and belief around the world."

The German government report does not attempt to provide a statistical tally of attacks or the number of people facing persecution. Instead, it examines 30 countries as case studies where, in the federal government's view, freedom of religion and belief is being restricted. These include about six countries each from Africa, Asia, and the Arab world. In Europe, the report focuses on Belarus, Russia, Ukraine, and Turkey, while in Latin America it highlights Mexico, Nicaragua, and Cuba. It also identifies shortcomings in five of the world's six most populous countries: China, India, Indonesia, Pakistan, and Nigeria.

India: Hindu nationalists force religious conversions To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Regarding India, the report refers to "Hindu nationalist efforts" that threaten the equal treatment of all officially recognized religions. It states that the generally peaceful coexistence of different faiths is "repeatedly overshadowed by tensions and, at times, violence." Both Muslim and Christian communities report growing intolerance and hate speech. According to the report, violent Hindu extremist groups have carried out a "large number of physical attacks" against Muslims, while the police and government authorities often respond inadequately.

In China, the German government identifies a "significant tightening of the legal framework of state control at the expense of freedom of religion and belief." According to the report, this particularly affects Uyghurs, Tibetans and churches that lack official state approval and are subject to harsh measures by the authorities. The law on the "Promotion of Ethnic Unity and Progress," which came into force on July 1, 2026, subordinates religion to "the formation of national identity" and patriotic education.

One of the countries where the situation has deteriorated most dramatically is Nicaragua, which has severely restricted freedom of religion and belief since 2018. The repression has primarily targeted the Catholic Church. According to the report, "intimidation, persecution, imprisonment, and expulsion" have forced around 130 priests and nuns to leave the country.

Exploring Africa's indigenous religions To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The reports reserves some of its sharpest criticism for Kirill, the patriarch of the Russian Orthodox Church. Under his leadership, the church has strongly supported Russia's war against Ukraine and portrayed it as a "holy war." According to the report, "weapons are blessed, Russian soldiers are absolved of their sins, and donations are collected for the war." It is perhaps the clearest example in the report of how religion can be used to justify oppression and violence.

Intimidation reaches beyond borders

The report explicitly addresses the threat posed by "transnational repression" (TNR), which it describes as a "growing global problem" that also affects Germany. The term refers to the persecution or intimidation of individuals by their country of origin beyond its own borders.

Ultimately, it argues, this amounts to a "continuation of domestic repression." Such "cross-border repression" has become considerably easier through the growing availability of digital means of repression, including smear campaigns on social media and spyware.

These forms of pressure range from physical attacks on individuals to digital assaults such as online intimidation and defamation. In some cases, repression is also carried out by threatening family members who remain in the country of origin. Russia and Iran, for example, are identified as the "main perpetrators of transnational repression" in Germany.

China is a particularly prominent example of religious and ideological tensions. Repression by Beijing in Germany primarily targets members of groups that the country's Communist Party classifies as "hostile to the system." These include Uyghurs, Tibetans, and members of the Falun Gong movement. According to the report, they are "also subject to surveillance and repressive measures in Germany," while relatives living in China are pressured.

Thomas Rachel hopes the newly published report will be "discussed in as many Bundestag committees as possible" and that members of parliament will "engage with the issue accordingly." Previous government reports on the subject have been debated in the Bundestag plenary at least once and, in some cases, twice.

Sweden: Hybrid warfare in a Russian Orthodox church To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Religion: A matter of German foreign policy

The issue's place within the German government has also changed during the current legislative term. Commissioner Thomas Rachel is now based at the Foreign Ministry, while both of his predecessors since 2018 were attached to the Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development. Today, Rachel says, the importance of religion is being "taken into account" in German foreign policy. He also points to his involvement in the Foreign Ministry's diplomatic training programs.

In doing so, the government led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) reversed a structural decision made by the previous center-left coalition, which was led from 2021 to 2025 by Chancellor Olaf Scholz of the Social Democratic Party (SPD). The Scholz government had reduced the issue's prominence by assigning it to the "Religion and Foreign Policy" division. Religion and foreign policy have now regained a more prominent place within government.

One example is the current foreign minister, Johann Wadephul, who has already visited the Vatican more often than his two predecessors combined. In addition, alongside Rachel, the ministry has for some time maintained a dedicated unit headed by an ambassador that deals with, among other things, "fundamental issues relating to religion and foreign policy."

World.title: COP31: UN Climate summit runs into overtime as deal remains elusive
World.content:
11/21/2026 November 21, 2026 Climate activist blames rich countries for COP failure

Harjeet Singh, the global convener of the Fill the Fund campaign and strategic advisor to the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative, said that COP31 could be a failure due to a lack of funding.

"COP31 is stuck for one simple reason: money. Europe and other rich countries came to Antalya with empty pockets," he wrote in a statement shared with multiple reporters.

"They've spent two weeks pushing electrification targets and demanding more ambition from developing countries, while refusing to pay for any of it," he added.

Singh accused wealthy countries of blocking a just transition mechanism and of ignoring calls to increase funding for the Adaptation Fund and the Loss and Damage Fund.

"You can't ask developing countries to transform their economies while they're drowning in disasters and debt," he wrote.

The climate activist stressed that the reason this COP failed wasn't a lack of solutions. It was due to "a lack of money and a lack of will from those who caused this crisis," he said.

World.title: La distancia entre el PP y el PSOE se estrecha al mínimo pese a la victoria de Feijóo en el debate
World.content:
Alberto Núñez Feijóo ganó con claridad, en opinión de los ciudadanos, su cara a cara con Pedro Sánchez. La encuesta de urgencia realizada por 40dB. para EL PAÍS y la SER no deja lugar a dudas: el 43% de los entrevistados señala como triunfador al líder del PP, diez puntos más de los que apuntan al socialista. Pero no todo son malas noticias para el PSOE, porque el acumulado del tracking diario de los últimos cuatro días estrecha al máximo la diferencia entre los dos grandes partidos, apenas siete décimas, equivalente a un empate técnico.

El aparente contrasentido se explica por las diferencias entre las muestras. Y por un detalle relevante: el debate, con una media de 10 millones de espectadores de audiencia, fue mucho más seguido por los votantes del PP. Un 61,5% del total de simpatizantes del primer partido de la oposición asegura que siguió el cara a cara hasta el final, mientras que entre los del PSOE baja hasta el 49%. La encuesta de urgencia fue elaborada con una muestra de 500 entrevistas en línea, recogidas entre las 23.43 horas del jueves, recién concluido el programa, hasta las 8.27 de este viernes 20. Esos datos se han incorporado hasta engrosar otro contigente mayor de 2.000 entrevistas que reflejan las intenciones de voto manifestadas en los últimos cuatro días.

En el debate, Feijóo se mostró mucho más convincente que Sánchez (47,9% frente a 38,8%) y algo más competente (43,5% frente a 40,9%). Pese a aparecer como derrotado, el actual presidente aún fue visto como más carismático que su contrincante: 46,8% frente a 39%. El duelo dialéctico fue seguido por casi tres de cada cuatro de los entrevistados, aunque no llegan a la mitad los que afirman haber asistido íntegramente

En las opiniones sobre el cara a cara pesa de modo determinante la simpatía política de los entrevistados. Entre los votantes del PP y Vox, Feijóo es visto abrumadoramente como triunfador. Sin embargo, tres de cada cuatro simpatizantes socialistas eligen a Sánchez, así como uno de cada tres del Frente Amplio (FA), la misma porción de los que manifiestan que no ganó ninguno de los dos.

Los 500 entrevistados por 40dB. tras el debate también manifestaron su intención de voto y esos resultados se incorporaron a los recogidos en los tres días anteriores hasta conformar una muestra de 2.000. Con esa perspectiva más amplia, y a pesar del revés del cara a cara, el PSOE consigue su mejor resultado no solo desde el comienzo de la campaña, sino también de toda la legislatura, en la que el instituto demoscópico ha realizado barómetros mensuales para EL PAÍS y la SER. De ese modo la diferencia entre los dos grandes partidos se reduce a siete décimas, la mitad de la ventaja que el PP logró sobre el PSOE en las anteriores elecciones de 2023. Lo que no impide que el conjunto del bloque de la derecha conserve su amplia distancia, con 189 escaños, 13 más que la mayoría absoluta.

Los socialistas ganan un punto en esta última entrega del tracking, sumarían un 31,2% y, aun con cinco décimas menos que en 2023, obtendrían tres escaños más que entonces, hasta 124. El PP, con el 31,9%, quedaría un poco por debajo de su cosecha en las anteriores elecciones y se anotaría 131 diputados, seis menos que en el Congreso saliente. Pero la tendencia general de los populares desde el inicio de la campaña apunta a una recuperación, cimentada sobre todo en el freno a las fugas hacia Vox. La encuesta incluso advierte un pequeño flujo en sentido contrario, de antiguos votantes de la extrema derecha que ahora se decantan por Feijóo.

Aun así, Vox sería la formación que más crece comparado con los anteriores comicios, casi cinco puntos, hasta situarse en el 17,1%. El Frente Amplio y las confluencias territoriales en las que participa siguen sin sumar mucho más allá del 5%, mientras que Podemos quedaría fuera del Congreso.
