World.title: Boy,11, electrocuted while playing hide-and-seek in Delhi, FIR filed
World.content:
An 11-year-old boy died in West Delhi’s Vikaspuri on Friday evening after allegedly suffering an electric shock inside a feeder pillar where he was hiding while playing, said police. While an FIR has been registered under relevant sections of negligence, electricity supplier BSES said that the cover of the electricity feeder was allegedly stolen and no complaint was filed.

The incident took place around 7:10 pm on Friday at the DDA Local Shopping Centre in Vikaspuri’s M-Block when a group of children were playing hide-and-seek, said officers.

Police received a PCR call regarding the electrocution of a minor and rushed to the spot, where the boy was found unconscious inside the feeder pillar, an outdoor electrical cabinet used for power distribution.

World.title: High turnout, voter deletions, and a brewing political contest in Ladakh
World.content:
Panchayat and Urban Local Body polls in Ladakh concluded Saturday with 70.03 percent turnout in Panchayat elections and 52.40 percent in municipal polls. The administration said this marked an improvement over the overall voter turnout of 67.8 percent recorded in the 2018 Panchayat elections.

Lieutenant Governor V K Saxena said the turnout reflected “an encouraging level of public participation in the democratic process and celebrates the true essence of democracy.” He added that witnessing everyone, “from the enthusiastic first-time voters to our respected senior citizens,” was a “powerful testament to people’s unshakeable faith” in the democratic process and local self-governance.

He also stated that these were the first Panchayat and municipal elections since 2018 and the first since Ladakh was made a Union Territory in 2019, adding that “it marks a proud milestone in self-governance”.

As per official figures, there are 192 panchayats in Ladakh. Of these, 55 have elected their sarpanches unopposed. There are also 1,428 panch constituencies, of which 1,186 have been declared elected uncontested, while about 212 panchs are yet to be elected.

Must Read | Amid push for UT body, why Ladakh groups are opposing local body polls

Meanwhile, climate activist Sonam Wangchuk and Apex Body Leh chairman Dorjay Lakrook alleged that “several voters faced deletions” in Saturday’s election, especially young voters who were not included in the voters’ list. Wangchuk also claimed he had been placed under house arrest, with security personnel deployed outside his residence, and was not allowed to step out even when he tried.



The activist marked his presence at the ongoing protest in Leh after the police deployment outside his residence was removed. Ladakh Police said in a post on Saturday that ADM Leh had passed a “prohibitory order” against Sonam Wangchuk and sought to clarify that he had not been placed under house arrest.

Hitting out at the Lieutenant Governor V K Saxena-led administration again, Wangchuk reiterated the demand to delay hill council polls scheduled for December 4. He also urged the Centre to reconsider the polls, alleging that the decision to push through elections despite the police’s opposition was aimed at “derail[ing] the ongoing talks” between the Ministry of Home Affairs and Ladakhi socio-political representatives.

“In the short term, the local administration may think that this will benefit them, but in the long term, the country will have to bear a national security cost. The prime minister and the whole country need to view this as a national security concern,” Wangchuk said.



Wangchuk stated that the government was upsetting people in a sensitive border region and “the Ministry of Defence should be more concerned about this because Ladakh has always supported them in previous wars and this sentiment should stay the same in the future. I believe that is bigger than the MHA, and the MoD should consider whether this is in favour of the country’s Security. Why are such patriotic people being distressed?”

He added that never in the history of the hill councils had elections been conducted in December. “We are not against any election, but forced elections without including the local people — how does that help bring faith in elected representatives?”

Meanwhile, Apex Body chairman Lakrook underlined that the basic principle of any election was maximum participation, “which is defeated by holding polling in this temperature in Ladakh,” citing the migration of a large part of the population from Ladakh to warmer regions.

World.title: Biryani cooking tips: Why birista cannot be replaced with caramelised onions
World.content:
Onions may seem like a simple ingredient, but how they are prepared can significantly affect a dish as complex and layered as biryani. While caramelised onions and birista are often confused with one another, they differ in their cooking methods, textures, and flavours, especially when it comes to creating the authentic taste and texture of a good biryani.

DISCLAIMER: This article is based on information from the public domain and/or the experts we spoke to.

What is the difference?

Although both preparations bring sweetness and depth of flavour, their textures and uses differ.



Chef Sandeep Panwar explains that caramelised onions are cooked slowly over low heat until they soften and develop a deep golden-brown colour. They have an almost jam-like texture and a pronounced sweetness, making them perfect for gravies, soups, sauces, and dishes that benefit from the rich, sweet flavour.

World.title: Presidential ordinance withdraws most privileges of KP MPAs, including protection against preventive detention
World.content:
PESHAWAR: President Asif Ali Zardari has promulgated five ordinances, doing away with most of the “privileges” of the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa lawmakers, including protection against “preventive detention” and providing a legal framework for special initiatives in the designated 12 districts and other districts in the province.

With the imposition of emergency in KP on Oct 11, an Area Representative and Development Council (ARDC) was formed to oversee 12 districts that were deemed to face intense security challenges, including the merged districts.

Two of the ordinances envisage setting up an executive committee with wide-ranging powers to oversee special initiatives, including developmental schemes, in the 12 designated districts and the rest of the province, respectively.

The committee will have powers to identify and recommend the executing agency for special initiatives in the designated and other districts, including military formations.

In a statement on Saturday, President Zardari’s office confirmed he had promulgated five ordinances pertaining to KP. Of these, the following four had been published in the Official Gazette on Nov 19 after their promulgation:

Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Societies (Registration) (Amendment) Ordinance, 2026;

Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Special Initiative Ordinance, 2026 (specific districts);

Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Special Initiative Ordinance, 2026 (other districts);

Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Provincial Assembly (Powers, Immunities and Privileges) Ordinance, 2026 (XI of 2026).

The fifth was the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Speaker and Deputy Speaker (Salaries, Allowances and Privileges) Ordinance 2026.

Through the amendment ordinance related to privileges of MPAs, drastic changes have been made in the KP Provincial Assembly (Powers, Immunities and Privileges) Act 2026, as 21 of its 40 sections have been omitted, including those providing protection to the MPAs against “preventive detentions” and offences related to “breach” of privileges.

The schedule of offences related to “breach of privileges” of the Assembly, its members and committees has also been omitted, thus leaving them without significant privileges.

It may be mentioned that Sohail Afridi — whose role as the chief minister was rendered non-functional due to governor’s rule — Speaker Babar Saleem Swati and other lawmakers have been in “preventive detention” since emergency was imposed, according to police.

KP Governor Faisal Karim Kundi also said last month that they had been placed under house arrest.

The important provisions omitted through the ordinance include sections 5 (attendance of MPA detained or arrested), 6 (members not liable to civil or criminal action), 10 (preventive detention), 11 (permission of speaker before arrest, detention, etc. of a member), 15 (power to summon), 22 (power to arrest), 31 (breach of privilege), 32 (breach of privilege to be an offence) and 34 (cognisance of offence).

Special initiative ordinances

The two ordinances relate to special initiatives in the 12 designated districts and the remaining districts in the province, respectively.

Both the ordinances provide for the establishment of an executive committee comprising a chairman, vice chairman and other such members as nominated by the prime minister, in case of designated district, and by the governor of the province, in case of the remaining districts.

For the designated districts, the Area Development Secretariat shall serve as secretariat of the executive committee, whereas for the other districts, the planning and development department shall serve as the secretariat of the committee.

Under the new laws, “special initiative” includes any work, developmental scheme, rehabilitation or reconstruction work, procurement of goods and human resources, consulting or non-consulting services or any other activity involving expenditure of public funds as determined by the executive committee.

The executive committee, in both the ordinances, has extensive powers including:

Identify an initiative as a special initiative of urgent or emergent nature;

Scrutinise and approve proposals, concept papers and PC-Is for the special initiatives;

Grant anticipatory approval for the initiatives, proposals, concept papers and PC-Is of the special initiatives;

Identify and recommend the executing agency, including military organisations and formations, for the execution of the special initiatives;

Provide a mechanism for the monitoring and evaluation of the special initiatives, including third-party monitoring and evaluation;

Review progress of the special initiatives;

Constitute committees or designate persons to carry out functions assigned to them by the executive committee;

Perform any other act to carry out the purposes of the ordinance.

The ordinances provide that the executive committee should meet at least once a month or as and when required.

The decisions of the committee shall be made on the basis of majority vote of its members, and in case of a tie, the chairman shall have the casting vote.

The chairman is also empowered to co-opt any other member or technical expert, to offer advice to the committee, as required.

Both the ordinances have overriding effect on other laws, including the KP Public Procurement Regulatory Authority Act 2012 and the KP Public Private Partnership Act 2020.

Moreover, no civil court shall have jurisdiction in relation to an act done, order passed, and any proceedings done under the ordinances.

Madressah registrations

Through the KP Societies (Registration) (Amendment) Ordinance, 2026, a sub-section 1-A has been included in Section 21, dealing with the registration of “religious madressahs”.

The newly included provision provides that madressahs which are or may be registered with the Directorate General of Religious Education, Ministry of Federal Education and Professional Training, shall not be required to be registered under the Act (Societies Registration Act).

World.title: At SCO moot in India, Musadik Malik declares climate change ‘enemy’ of civilisations
World.content:
Climate Change Minister Musadik Malik on Saturday declared climate change an “enemy” of civilisations as he highlighted its impact on South Asian countries at a meeting of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) in India.

Malik is in New Delhi on a three-day trip to attend the SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum, making him the first Pakistani minister to visit the neighbour since former foreign minister Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari attended an SCO meeting in May 2023.

Addressing the forum on Saturday, the minister said the enemy of this civilisation was not another civilisation but climate change, noting that Nepal’s representative also spoke about the issue.

Malik recalled the Aug 26 floods in Nepal, which claimed over 1,400 lives and left thousands of others missing, as well as the devastating 2022 floods in Pakistan.

He noted that those monsoon floods left 1,700 people dead and submerged one-third of the country, including almost the entire Sindh.

“Four days of rain caused Mohenjo Daro’s walls to fall; those walls that no one was able to break for 4,500 years, climate [change] and rain-induced floods did it.”

The minister remarked that humans were also an “enemy”, as they contributed to climate destruction.

“Do you know what is the meaning of Mohenjo-Daro?” Malik asked. “It means mound of the dead.”

Malik said the ancient site had, in a sense, opened its gates to the living during the 2022 floods, providing refuge to people displaced by the disaster.

He said people had sought shelter wherever they could find it, including parking lots and shopping malls, while mosques, temples, shrines and schools in Balochistan had also opened their doors to those affected by the floods.

“This is the power of civilisation. This is the power through which nations survive,” the minister noted.

During his speech, Malik presented three proposals for SCO, including the establishment of a network of cultural institutions, a digital repository to present the region’s historical and natural “gifts” to the world, and a climate-resilient heritage framework to address destruction caused by climate change in the region.

At the outset of his address, Malik said he had initially intended to deliver his speech in English but felt more inclined to speak in Urdu after considering his proximity to the tombs of Urdu poet Mirza Ghalib and Sufi saint Nizamuddin.

“It felt a little strange to speak in English. So, with your permission, I would like to speak in Urdu,” he said.

The minister pointed out that distinct identities were needed for dialogue, which could only take place between diverse voices.

“If there is one identity, one voice, then a monologue is needed. There is no need for dialogue,” he said, comparing it to waking up in the morning, looking in the mirror and speaking only to oneself.

“There is no beauty in that. Beauty is [in] the vase that has colourful flowers, the smell of different kinds. Today, we’re here to celebrate that colourful vase,” the minister said.

During his address, the minister highlighted Pakistan’s history and how its civilisation had been shaped by multiple influences, with connections extending across China, Central Asia, Iran and the Middle East.

“When we look at our history, all our roads lead to the north; Bukhara and Samarkand and Central Asia and Afghanistan. The entire history takes us to the north,” he said. “And when we talk about our prayers, our poetry, we are drawn towards the Middle East and Iran or Persia.”

Malik said diversity and the free flow of ideas and identities were something to be embraced. “There is wisdom there, in embracing it. We’re here to celebrate these things today.”

Meetings with Indian minister, others

Dr Malik arrived at Purana Qila in New Delhi for the second day of the inaugural SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum, according to a post shared by his office earlier in the day.

On the sidelines of the forum, Malik held separate bilateral meetings with representatives from various countries, including host India, Nepal, Iran and Tajikistan.

He met with Indian Minister for Culture and Tourism Gajendra Singh Shekhawat and Indian Secretary for Culture Vivek Aggarwal, state-run APP reported.

According to APP, the discussions focused on cultural ties and opportunities for promoting cooperation between Pakistan and India, with both sides exchanging views on matters of mutual interest and the importance of strengthening cultural and civilisational links.

During his meeting with Nepal’s Culture and Tourism Minister Khadga Raj Poudel, the climate change minister expressed deep grief over the loss of precious human lives in the August floods.

Malik emphasised that urgent global action was essential to address the growing risks of natural disasters caused by climate change.

In his meeting with Tajikistan’s Minister of Culture Sattoriyon Amonzoda, Malik underscored the strong historical and cultural ties between the two countries, the Pakistan High Commission in India said.

He reaffirmed Pakistan’s resolve to further strengthen these multifaceted ties, particularly through greater people-to-people exchanges.

In a separate meeting with the president of Iran’s Islamic Culture and Relations Organisation, Mohammad Mahdi Imanipour, Dr Malik underscored the deep-rooted historical and cultural bonds between Pakistan and Iran.

He reaffirmed Pakistan’s firm commitment to further expanding these fraternal ties across all spheres, the high commission said.

Meanwhile, Malik and Azerbaijan’s Culture Minister Adil Karimli expressed their commitment to further strengthening the long-standing fraternal ties between Islamabad and Baku.

Malik emphasised the need to enhance cooperation across all sectors of the bilateral relationship between the two countries.

The climate change minister also met with Kyrgyz Republic’s Deputy Minister of Culture and Youth Policy Askaraly Shukuralievich.

A day earlier, after arriving in New Delhi, Malik had described the forum as a “tremendous opportunity” for multilateral dialogue, saying that cultures and civilisations transcended geographical boundaries.

Speaking to Indian news agency ANI, he had said the gathering offered an opportunity to discuss shared history, geography, cultures and civilisations.

Malik’s India trip comes two years after India’s External Affairs Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar visited Islamabad for an SCO meeting.

Pakistan currently holds the rotating chairmanship of the SCO Council of Heads of State for the 2026-27 term and is scheduled to host the organisation’s summit in Islamabad in August 2027.

World.title: 4 guards of Sardar Khetran held after body recovered from Barkhan property
World.content:
QUETTA: Police said on Sunday they have detained four guards of former Balochistan minister Sardar Abdul Rehman Khetran following the reported recovery of a body from his property in Barkhan district.

A separate case has also been registered against the PML-N MPA and his two sons over the alleged murder, kidnapping and illegal confinement of one of his former guards in a private jail.

According to Koh-Suleman Deputy Inspector General (DIG) Ayaz Baloch, the four security guards were taken into custody during a search operation at Khetran’s fortified residence in Haji Kot on Nov 20. Weapons were also recovered from their possession, he said.

The operation followed the arrest of an employee responsible for managing Khetran’s land, whose identification reportedly helped police locate the burial sites.

Two decomposed bodies were recovered from a graveyard in the Tumnai area, around 40 kilometres from Barkhan, on Nov 19, police said. A third body was recovered during excavation at Khetran’s residence the following day.

Police have shifted the three bodies to Quetta for DNA testing. Khetran has rejected the allegations, describing the police action as “politically motivated”.

On Nov 18, Barkhan police registered a case against Khetran; his two sons, Islam Shah and Abdul Rauf; and three other accomplices on charges of murder, kidnapping and illegal confinement.

The first information report, seen by Dawn, was registered on the complaint of Pyara Khan Bugti, father of Khetran’s former guards, Sahib Din Bugti and Qamar Din.

The FIR invoked sections 34 (common intention), 302 (intentional murder), 342 (punishment for wrongful confinement), 343 (wrongful confinement for three or more days), 364 (kidnapping or abducting in order to murder), 365 (abducting with intent secretly and wrongfully to confine person), 368 (wrongfully concealing or keeping in confinement, kidnapped or abducted person) and 506 (punishment for criminal intimidation) of the Pakistan Penal Code (PPC).

The father alleged that his two sons were taken to a private jail four years ago, with Khetran saying that a man, accompanied by his brother and son-in-law, had complained against the brothers.

The father claimed that Qamar Din was released by Khetran a year ago, but he later found out through “people and the media” that Sahib Din was allegedly murdered.

He also accused the MPA of threatening him against reporting the matter to the police.

In July, Khetran was removed from his position as Balo­chistan’s minister for public health engineering.

Sources had said differences had emerged between Chief Minister Sarfraz Bugti and Khetran over several issues, with the rift reportedly deepening over time.

In Feb 2023, Khetran had been arrested after three corpses — of a woman and two young men — were discovered in a well near the minister’s residence in Barkhan, sparking protests over illegal prisons.

Khan Muhammad Marri, a former guard of Khetran, had said the bodies were of his wife Granaz and two sons, alleging they were kept in private jails. However, a postmortem examination determined the body belonged to a young woman, not his wife. A DNA report confirmed that the two other bodies were of Marri’s sons.

Shortly later, Granaz was recovered along with her 17-year-old daughter and a son, while three other sons were recovered from near Dera Bugti. A police surgeon had said evidence showed the teenage daughter was not only tortured but also sexually abused.

World.title: Security forces kill 15 terrorists in Balochistan's Mastung district: state media
World.content:
Security forces have killed 15 terrorists during two separate operations in Balochistan’s Mastung district, state media reported on Saturday.

According to security sources cited by Radio Pakistan, five terrorists were killed in the first operation, while 10 others were eliminated in the second one. Both were conducted against Fitna al Hindustan under ‘Operation Raddul Fitna 3’, which began in August.

The state has designated outlawed Balochistan-based groups as Fitna al Hindustan to highlight India’s role in terrorism and destabilisation across Pakistan.

Furthermore, several terrorist hideouts were destroyed during the operations, while a large cache of weapons and ammunition was also recovered, according to the report. It added that security forces also cleared the areas of Killi Pasand Khan, Musa Khan, Khorasani, and Kaftari of terrorists.

Security forces remain committed to eradicating terrorism from Balochistan, and operations will continue until the last terrorist is eliminated, security sources asserted.

Pakistan has seen a surge in terrorism, especially in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan, since the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan ended its ceasefire deal with the government in November 2022, vowing to increase attacks.

Last week, four troops, including a major, were martyred while 24 terrorists were killed in multiple intelligence-based operations (IBOs) in Balochistan and KP’s North Waziristan.

On Nov 1, a soldier was martyred while 17 terrorists were killed in two IBOs in Balochistan’s Kachhi and Kharan districts.

However, according to Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies , Pakistan recorded fewer militant attacks from Nov 6 to 12, but fatalities and injuries increased sharply, “highlighting the changing intensity and continued volatility of militant threat across the country”.

KP remained the principal centre of violence, accounting for 16 attacks and 44 fatalities. Balochistan recorded 13 attacks, resulting in eight deaths and 19 injuries, while the former tribal districts witnessed a “substantial” reduction in attacks.

World.title: CCD's school bag inspections in Punjab spark criticism on social media
World.content:
LAHORE: Punjab’s Crime Control Department (CCD) has started checking students’ school bags outside educational institutions for cigarettes, vapes and other intoxicating substances, drawing criticism from social media users over the involvement of law enforcement personnel in disciplining students.

After the CCD set up a checking point outside a college in Lahore on Friday, it issued a press release on Saturday announcing a special campaign across educational institutions in Punjab to protect children from drugs, cigarettes, vapes and other intoxicating substances.

A video of the department’s checkpoint set up on Friday to search students’ bags for any cigarettes and vapes was widely circulated on social media.

The move prompted a debate, with some social media users supporting the initiative as a measure to protect young people from drugs, while others questioned its legality, ethics and implications for students’ rights.

The CCD, established last year, has often been criticised by human rights advocates and civil society members for a high number of casualties among suspects. The Human Rights Commission of Pakistan (HRCP) has accused it of “extrajudicial killings”, which the department denies.

According to the press release by a CCD spokesperson, special checking desks have been established outside educational institutions, where students’ bags were searched to ensure that no intoxicating substances were taken inside, knowingly or unknowingly.

Students were also being briefed about the harmful effects of smoking and vaping, the spokesperson said, adding that the campaign aimed to prevent drug use in educational institutions and raise awareness about its physical, psychological, educational and social consequences.

He said parents and teachers had a key role in protecting children from substance abuse and urged them to monitor their activities and habits. This was also underscored by CCD on its Facebook page.

The department also appealed to the public to identify shopkeepers selling cigarettes and vapes to children, warning that cases would be registered against those suspected to be involved and they would be arrested in accordance with the law.

The spokesperson insisted that the initiative was part of efforts to encourage healthy lifestyles, maintain a safe educational environment and achieve the goal of a drug-free Punjab.

While the CCD asserted that parents welcomed the campaign, some internet users questioned the need to involve the law enforcement department in scrutinising students when teachers and parents could do the same.

Criticising the initiative, human rights lawyer Asad Jamal said on X that the Punjab government believed that every problem could be addressed through increased securitisation of public life.

“Today, it’s bags, tomorrow students will be bodily searched. Unconstitutional, unethical and unacceptable,” he wrote.

Former Punjab minister Arslan Khalid also questioned the presence of police personnel outside educational institutions, saying schools should not rely on police to discipline children.

“Parents and teachers are enough to teach discipline to the children. I will never want my children to have their school bags checked by police,” he posted on X.

In a reply to anchorperson Iqrarul Hassan, who voiced his support for the move, Khalid asked, “How is it a reasonable decision to allow police officers who regularly deal with hardened criminals, whose language and behaviour we are all familiar with, and who have no training in dealing with schoolchildren, to search our innocent children every day?

“If a child does something wrong, then a teacher or a father knows how to deal with them.”

Writer Ammara Ahmed wrote, “Virtue signalling by Punjab government has no end.”

In his post, Hassan linked it to the growing use of ice (crystal methamphetamine) and other drugs in educational institutions.

The TV personality said that as a father, he felt reassured by the measure, adding that although such steps would not be desirable under ideal circumstances, they had become necessary in view of the growing drug menace.

Television anchor Iqra Haris also termed it a “much-needed step”.

In June this year, Karachi’s South Zone police prepared an anti-drug policy in collaboration with the heads of 22 universities and schools to counter the growing threat of narcotics and vaping products.

Under the policy, anti-drug committees were to be formed in educational institutes, comprising heads of institutions, teachers, parents and law enforcers.

World.title: Internet provider expects submarine cable repairs to be completed by Dec 6
World.content:
Internet service provider Transworld Associates has said repair work on an affected international submarine cable is expected to be completed by December 6, with users likely to experience slower internet speeds during peak hours until the work is finished.

In an email to customers, the company said repair operations were actively underway and that the tentative timeline for completion was Dec 6.

“Further to our earlier notice on November 18, 2026, repair operations for the affected international submarine cable system are actively underway,” the company said.

Transworld said it had also scheduled a maintenance window during which its technical teams would address the existing cable issue. It added that alternative routing arrangements had been made to maintain connectivity during the maintenance activity.

“However, you may still experience slower speeds during peak hours,” Transworld said, apologising for the inconvenience caused to customers.

The development follows an earlier announcement by the Pakistan Telecommunication Authority (PTA) that a fault had been reported in the SEA-ME-WE 5 (SMW5) international submarine cable system, approximately 11 kilometres from Pakistan’s coast.

In a compliance report to PTA, Transworld acknowledged that not all SMW5 traffic had been catered for. The company informed PTA that 80 per cent of the affected traffic had been diverted to other cable systems.

The regulator warned that the fault could cause intermittent connectivity issues and a decline in service quality for some internet users.

The PTA had said Transworld Associates was coordinating with the SMW5 consortium to identify the fault and determine the estimated time for restoration.

Meanwhile, internet traffic was being rerouted through alternative international links to minimise disruption and maintain service continuity, the regulator had added.

Internet monitoring organisation NetBlocks had also reported a decline in connectivity in Pakistan, saying the incident was consistent with a fault in the SMW5 international subsea cable system.

Submarine cables are a critical part of international telecommunications infrastructure, carrying data between countries and continents. Faults in these systems can affect internet speeds and connectivity, particularly when traffic has to be redirected through alternative routes.

Currently, seven submarine cables provide internet connectivity to Pakistan: Asia-Africa-Europe 1 ( AAE-1 ), South East Asia-Middle East-West Europe 4 (SMW4) and India-Middle East-Western Europe (IMEWE), operated by PTCL; and South-East Asia-Middle East-Western Europe 6 (SEA-ME-WE 6), South East Asia-Middle East-West Europe 5 (SMW5) and Transworld Associates 1 (TWA-1), operated by Transworld Associates.

Cyber Internet Services operates the seventh cable named Pak­istan and East Africa Connecting Europe (PEACE).

In July this year, a fault in the same SMW5 cable system had caused widespread connectivity issues in Pakistan. The PTA subsequently announced that the fault had been repaired on July 3, following its detection on July 1.

Additional input by Kalbe Ali.

World.title: India's Congress warns of more protests against Meta after clashes with police outside its offices
World.content:
The youth wing of India’s main opposition Congress party on Saturday warned of more protests against Meta’s removal of some accounts and posts of its members, a day after clashing with police outside the US firm’s India offices.

Meta declined to comment on Friday’s unprecedented protests, which marked an escalation by the influential political group in the company’s biggest market by users.

Debate is growing in India about potential risks to free speech from the increasingly strict efforts of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government to remove social media content it objects to.

Modi’s government says it orders content to be taken down only if it breaches local laws, can harm public safety or national security.

Congress has long accused Meta and other social media platforms of curbing dissent online by removing party accounts, favouring Modi’s government.

Meta has said it restricts content in India to comply with local laws.

In Hyderabad on Friday, protesters carrying placards chanted slogans as they stormed into the building that houses Meta’s offices, smashing plants to the ground and clashing with police, according to footage released by the Indian Youth Congress’ X account.

Another video showed Congress workers spray-painting anti-Meta slogans on walls outside the building that houses its Mumbai office, clashing with security guards who tried to stop them.

In Gurugram near New Delhi, Congress workers chanted slogans and held banners reading “restore youth Congress accounts”, official online posts showed.

The Indian Youth Congress posted warnings on X that it would “storm your offices across the country and stage protests” unless Instagram accounts of its leaders are restored.

On Saturday, the Congress wing posted a video of its workers putting up a banner in central Delhi taking a dig at Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, referring to him as “Mark BJPberg” to allege the company’s favouritism towards Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party.

India’s IT ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Modi’s party accuses congress of vandalism

Telangana opposition politician K.T. Rama Rao criticised Congress workers over what he called vandalism at Meta’s Hyderabad office, saying it had undermined the city’s reputation as a safe destination for businesses.

Pradeep Bhandari, a national spokesperson for Modi’s ruling party, criticised Congress’ actions on Saturday, saying they had “not only vandalised and destroyed Meta’s office in Hyderabad” but were also “flaunting it on social media”.

“This is Congress Model: Vandalise offices of Private companies,” he wrote.

Two such accounts were restored after Friday’s protests, but thousands of accounts of journalists, creators and influencers critical of the government remain restricted, Manu Jain, who is in charge of social media for the youth group, told Reuters on Saturday.

Meta must explain how its algorithms restrict posts and must restore accounts taken down on government orders, he added.

Reporters Without Borders has said the removal of journalistic content from social media has been on the rise in India this year, and free speech activists say a new government rule gives social media companies hardly any time to review and decide on takedown requests.

In February, Modi’s government ordered social media companies to take down unlawful content within three hours of being notified about it, tightening an earlier 36-hour timeline.

Meta disclosures show that it restricted more than 5.4 million posts or accounts in India under local laws in the first half of 2026, second only to Indonesia and up from about 70,000 in the whole of 2025.

“The large majority of these items included instances where we were obligated to proactively restrict content … based on local law requirements,” Meta said.

World.title: Capt Safdar seeks Rs10bn in damages from Advocate Mian Dawood over 'defamatory' remarks
World.content:
LAHORE: Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz’s spouse and former MNA, retired Capt Muhammad Safdar, has served a legal notice to Advocate Mian Dawood, demanding an unconditional public apology, retraction of allegedly defamatory remarks, removal of videos and Rs10 billion in damages.

The notice, dated Nov 20, was issued through a Rawalpindi-based lawyer, Majad Ali Butt, under Section 10 of the Punjab Defamation Act 2024.

Advocate Dawood confirmed to Dawn that he had received the legal notice. He said an appropriate response would be sent to Safdar after examining the notice.

According to the notice, the dispute arose from Safdar’s public demand that former president of the Supreme Court Bar Association (SCBA), Ahsan Bhoon, produce his LLB degree, a matter it says is already before the Supreme Court and the Pakistan Bar Council (PBC).

Last month, PBC declared that the degrees of Bhoon and its other elected members were genuine.

The notice claimed that Safdar had said he would apologise if Bhoon’s degree proved genuine and that Advocate Dawood, an “unrelated third party”, responded with malice.

The notice cited three pieces of content, including a two-minute video uploaded on Sept 24 on YouTube, a news channel interview aired on Oct 29 and a video statement made after the SCBA elections held last month.

It argued that free speech cannot become a “licence for vulgar abuse”, and that Dawood was expected to show restraint.

The notice demanded that the lawyer publish, within 14 days, an apology on the same platforms and in leading English and Urdu newspapers, retract the statements, have the videos removed, pay Rs10bn and refrain from repeating the remarks.

Failing that, Safdar would approach the Special Tribunal under the Defamation Act, the notice warned.

In late September, Safdar called for verification of the degrees of prominent lawyers, including Bhoon, a close associate of Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar.

His remarks also came ahead of the SCBA elections. Bhoon heads the Independent Group, also known as the Asma Jahangir Group. Safdar had announced the formation of his own group, the Quaid-i-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah Group.

Subsequently, Bhoon filed a Rs5 billion defamation suit against Safdar over remarks questioning the authenticity of his LLB degree. The Punjab Defamation Tribunal had admitted the suit for hearing and issued a notice to Safdar.

World.title: Ramisa rape and murder: Sohel Rana mentions new name as charges framed
World.content:
A new name has surfaced in the Ramisa rape and murder case, with prime accused Sohel Rana telling reporters today that a man called "Dollar" was responsible for the rape and murder of the eight-year-old girl.

However, no further details about the person were immediately available.

Sohel made the claim while being escorted to the courtroom of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children Violence Suppression Tribunal.

"I am at fault, and Dollar is also at fault. I am not the only culprit," he told reporters.

Standing in the courtroom's dock, he shouted at the lawyers present in the courtroom after the hearing, and said, “I did not commit the rape; I only dismembered the body. A man named Dollar committed the rape. I have sinned, so punish me for that sin.”

At that time, Sohel further claimed that Dollar had promised to pay him Tk 2 lakh if he could bring the girl to him.

However, police officers present immediately stopped him from speaking further.

Sohel also claimed that his wife, Swapna Khatun, was innocent.

Earlier in the day, Sohel and Swapna were brought to the lock-up of the Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court in Dhaka.

Later, Judge Masrur Salekin of the tribunal framed charges against the couple in the case over the rape and murder of Ramisa in Dhaka's Pallabi area.

Both accused pleaded not guilty after the charges were read out, said Bench Assistant Pankoj Peter Gomes.

The judge also fixed tomorrow for the start of the trial, with the victim's father, Abdul Hannan Mollah, scheduled to testify first, he added.

On May 24, Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station submitted the charge sheet before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's Court in Dhaka, accusing Sohel of rape, murder and destruction of evidence, and Swapna of destruction of evidence and providing false information.

Several hours later, the CMM Court transferred the case to the Children Violence Suppression Tribunal for trial.

Ramisa, a second-grade student of Popular Model High School, was found beheaded on May 19 in the house of her neighbour, Sohel.

The following day, Ramisa's father filed a case with Pallabi Police Station, accusing the couple and an unidentified person.

According to the case statement, Sohel lured Ramisa into his room and raped her. Investigators said he later slit her throat and attempted to dismember the body to conceal the crime.

On May 20, police produced Sohel and Swapna before a Dhaka court, and court sources said Sohel agreed to give a confessional statement before a magistrate. The third and unidentified accused was on the run. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Aminul Islam Junaid recorded Sohel's confessional statement after police brought him to the magistrate’s chamber, said a court staff member.

Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station told The Daily Star that day, the prime accused had already admitted to the crime during primary interrogation.

On May 22, the Dhaka Bar Association decided not to provide legal assistance to the accused following an emergency virtual meeting of its executive committee, citing the gravity of the allegations.

The next day, the government appointed Supreme Court lawyer Musa Kalimullah as a state defence counsel to represent the accused to ensure a fair trial.

This report has been corrected at 4:43pm. In the earlier version, Sohel Rana’s comment was misreported. We regret the error.

World.title: Why Bangladesh must pivot to renewable energy now
World.content:
There are moments in a nation’s history when a crisis does more than create hardship. It reveals the weakness of an old system and opens the door to a better one. Bangladesh is now standing at such a moment.

The country is facing an energy crisis that no longer centres on power cuts. It is affecting factories, farms, schools, offices, exports, foreign currency reserves, and the daily life of ordinary people. What we are seeing today is not just a temporary shortage of gas or fuel. It is a signal that our energy system has become too dependent on imported fossil fuels.

More than 60 percent of Bangladesh’s energy demand is met through imports. LNG, coal, oil, and other fossil fuels have kept the country running for years, but this dependence has become risky and expensive. Global fuel markets are unstable because of geopolitical tension, supply chain disruption, and price volatility. For a country like Bangladesh, this creates double pressure: fuel supply becomes uncertain while fuel costs keep rising.

The government is now spending more than BDT 200 crore per day in energy subsidies. Annual energy import expenditure remains around USD 12 billion, putting serious pressure on foreign currency reserves. Nearly 70 percent of Bangladesh’s LNG imports come from Qatar. If supply is disrupted, Bangladesh can quickly face a severe shortage. In the power sector, daily gas demand exceeds 2,500 mmcfd, but supply sometimes falls to 850–900 mmcfd. This can create a power generation shortfall of 1,500–1,800 MW. Overall, the daily gas shortage exceeds 1,100 mmcfd, and peak-time electricity shortages may reach nearly 2,000 MW.

Bangladesh also has a weak Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The current reserve capacity is sufficient for only about 35–40 days, well below that of countries such as China and Japan. This makes the national energy system even more vulnerable.

Visual: Teeni and Tuni

The impact is already visible. In the readymade garments sector, gas shortages and load shedding are reducing productivity by 25–30 percent in many cases. This threatens export earnings, foreign currency reserves, and economic stability. The crisis has also reached ordinary households. Although Bangladesh declared 100 percent electrification in 2022, many rural areas still experience 10 to 20 hours of load shedding every day during summer. This affects education, small businesses, agriculture, and people’s dignity.

We have also seen long lines at fuel stations, schools moving online, and offices shortening working hours because of fuel shortages. These are not isolated events. They show how deeply energy insecurity can disturb national life.

Over the last 15 years, electricity tariffs in Bangladesh have been increased on many occasions, including more than 10 rounds of increases at both bulk and retail levels. This path is not sustainable. Fossil-fuel-based electricity depends on imported fuel, global prices, the availability of the dollar, subsidies, and repeated tariff adjustments. Solar power offers a different path. With a one-time investment, solar can provide stable energy for 15–20 years. Once installed, its fuel cost is almost zero.

The economic comparison is clear. A 1 MW HFO-based power plant produces electricity per year at a cost of nearly BDT 190 crore, with much of the cost paid in foreign currency. In contrast, a 5 MW solar project requires a one-time investment of around BDT 25 crore, after which fuel costs are practically zero. Each 1 MW of solar power can save around USD 325,000 per year in foreign currency.

This is why renewable energy should not be discussed solely in technical terms like decarbonisation, emissions, and sustainability. For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Despite Bangladesh’s potential, renewable energy contributes less than 5 percent to power generation, far below the global 30 percent target by 2030. Clear, measurable goals and timelines are essential for effective policy planning and investment decisions.

Renewable energy equipment imports face around 50–60 percent in duties and taxes, hindering local manufacturing growth. Policy reforms that reduce import duties and support local industry can accelerate renewable deployment and reduce dependency on imports.

For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Import duty is usually imposed to protect the local industry. But where local production is not yet significant, a high duty only increases project costs, reduces investment returns, and slows renewable energy expansion. Policy reforms can unlock this potential, making stakeholders feel their efforts directly contribute to progress.

India, Pakistan, Vietnam, and China have expanded solar and wind power by offering low or zero import duties, tax exemptions, and low-interest financing. Many countries have also reduced duties on lithium-ion batteries and energy storage systems. Bangladesh should learn from these examples.

The barriers are clear: high duties and VAT, high financing costs of 10–12 percent or more, limited access to easy loans, slow approval processes, net metering delays, high LC margin, weak Merchant Power Policy, lack of clear policies for rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, floating solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage, weak local manufacturing, and insufficient grid digitalisation. Addressing these collectively can accelerate Bangladesh's renewable journey, uniting stakeholders in a common goal.

One urgent reform is customs assessment. The current weight-based assessment system does not reflect the actual value of solar equipment. It can create artificial overvaluation and raise duties by three to four times. Bangladesh should shift to transaction-value-based assessment using pro forma or commercial invoice values, in line with international practice and WTO customs valuation principles.

The second urgent reform is the elimination of customs duty on renewable energy equipment. This should apply to Solar PV Module, Photovoltaic Cell, Solar Inverter, DC Cable, Data Logger, Aluminium Mounting Structure, Battery Pack, Battery Cell, BMS Circuit Board, PV DG Controller, Hybrid Controller, Solar Plant Safety Aluminium Walkway Mesh, Safety Accessories, and related components.

Current TTI rates are high. Solar PV Module carries 26.90 percent, Photovoltaic Cell 25.75 percent, Solar Inverter 28.73 percent, DC Cable 58.40 percent, Data Logger 37.25 percent, Aluminium Mounting Structure 58.40 percent, Battery Pack and Battery Cell 58.40 percent, BMS Circuit Board 31.50 percent, pack materials 37.25 percent, PV DG Controller or Hybrid Controller 89.08 percent, and Solar Plant Safety Aluminum Walkway Mesh 37.25 percent. These should be reduced to zero percent for renewable energy expansion.

The third reform is a tax holiday. Rooftop solar power producers and project companies should receive benefits comparable to those of utility-scale renewable energy producers. A practical structure could be a 100 percent tax holiday for the first 10 years, 50 percent for the next 3 years, and 25 percent for the next 2 years. This should apply to CAPEX, OPEX, IPP, and MPP models. A broader 10–20 year tax holiday for renewable energy projects should also be considered.

Bangladesh has a remarkable solar opportunity already waiting on its rooftops. About 7 percent of the country’s land is covered with concrete or other built structures. This means more than 10,000 square kilometres, or about 10 billion square meters of built surface. If only 30 percent is usable, that would give around 3 billion square meters. At 10 square meters per kW, this can create nearly 300 GW of solar potential. Bangladesh’s peak demand is only around 16–18 GW. The opportunity already exists on rooftops, factories, warehouses, schools, hospitals, government buildings, and commercial establishments.

Rooftop solar should therefore be relaunched nationwide with a clear business model. Utility-scale solar also needs support through unused khas land, transparent tendering, and grid readiness. Floating solar, river-based solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage should receive separate policy attention.

The suspended solar projects must also be revisited. A total of 31 solar power projects, with a combined capacity of more than 3,000 MW, were previously suspended or cancelled. Many were being developed by foreign investors, with more than USD 200 million reportedly already invested. If implemented, these projects could save around BDT 10,800 crore annually in energy import costs. They should be reassessed and revived quickly.

Energy storage is another missing pillar. Solar and wind need storage support to become more reliable. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and other storage systems should be reduced to zero. This will help stabilise renewable power and support future grid flexibility.

Electric vehicles can also become part of the solution. In China, Japan, and the United States, EVs are increasingly seen as mobile energy storage systems. A typical EV battery has a capacity of 40–70 kWh, enough to power an average household for 1–2 days. If Bangladesh had 1 million EVs, the country would have 40–70 GWh of distributed storage. This is several times higher than the daily peak demand gap. Solar-powered EV charging, vehicle-to-home, and vehicle-to-grid systems should be included in future energy planning.

If Bangladesh had 30–40 percent of the grid powered by solar, along with solar-powered EVs, the country would be far less exposed to global fuel market shocks. Long fuel lines, online schooling, shorter office hours, and industrial disruption could be reduced. Solar, storage, and EVs should now be planned together.

Finance will decide how fast this transition happens. Renewable energy projects cannot grow at interest rates below 10–12 percent. Long-term financing should be available at an interest rate of 3.5–4.5 percent. A 10–15-year financing facility at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent should be introduced. Bangladesh Bank’s green refinancing fund should be expanded. Rooftop and residential solar customers should be eligible for collateral-free loans. The LC margin for renewable equipment should be limited to 5%.

Net metering must be simplified. Approval should be completed within 15–30 days through a one-stop service. Approval, interconnection, inspection, billing adjustment, and utility coordination should all be simple and time-bound. Wheeling charges for renewable energy should also be kept reasonable and low. The Merchant Power Policy should be clear, simple, and investment-friendly so that industries and commercial consumers can directly procure renewable electricity.

Agriculture should also be included in the solar transition. Bangladesh can set a target to convert 1.5 million diesel irrigation pumps into solar pumps. This will reduce diesel imports, lower farmers’ production costs, and protect the environment. The program should include duty-free facilities, low-cost loans, investment support, and local service networks.

Waste-to-energy should also receive policy support. City corporations need clear rules, easy financing, and private-sector participation to enable urban waste management and distributed power generation to work together.

Bangladesh now needs a phased national roadmap for renewable energy.

In the short term, within 0–6 months, customs duty, VAT, and taxes on renewable energy equipment should be reduced to zero. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and energy storage should be withdrawn. Approval for net metering should be obtained within 15–30 days. Industrial and commercial solar installations should be eligible for special incentives. The 31 suspended solar projects should be reassessed. Wheeling charges should be rationalised. Solar, storage, and EV charging should receive urgent policy support. Collateral-free lines of credit should be introduced for rooftop solar. NBR should quickly implement assessment reform and a 0 percent duty.

In the medium term, within 1–3 years, renewable energy financing should be available at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent for 10–15 years. The LC margin should be limited to 5 percent. Land banks and grid infrastructure should be developed for utility-scale solar. Merchant Power Policy and MPPA should be simplified. Rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, and hybrid solar-storage projects should receive a 10–15-year tax holiday. A national program should convert 1.5 million diesel pumps into solar pumps. Rooftop solar should be made mandatory or incentive-based for government buildings, industrial zones, EPZs, economic zones, and large commercial buildings. EV solar charging and distributed storage policies should be developed. Renewable energy skill development and employment programs should also be launched.

In the long term, within 3–10 years, Bangladesh should aim to reach more than 10,000 MW of solar power by 2030. Offshore and onshore wind should be developed. Floating solar, river-based solar, and agrivoltaics should be implemented. A National Energy Storage Strategy should be prepared. Smart grid and power sector digitalisation should be accelerated. Local assembly and manufacturing of solar panels, inverters, mounting structures, battery packs, BMS, and EV charging equipment should be encouraged. Regional power trade should be expanded. The Renewable Purchase Obligation should be introduced. Fossil fuel subsidies should be gradually redirected to a renewable energy transition fund.

Image Visual: Anwar Sohel

The benefits can be large. Energy import costs will fall. Pressure on foreign currency reserves will decline. Industrial production costs will reduce. Export competitiveness will improve. The subsidy burden will decrease. New investment will grow. Renewable energy can create 20–25 jobs per MW through rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, solar pumps, EV charging, battery storage, smart grids, manufacturing, installation, operation, and maintenance.

The government may worry about revenue loss from tax and duty exemptions. But this should be seen as an investment. In the short term, there may be a limited impact on revenue. In the long term, Bangladesh can save far more by reducing fuel imports, lowering subsidies, saving foreign currency, strengthening industries, and attracting new investment.

Bangladesh’s energy crisis is a major challenge but also a historic opportunity. The crisis is not only a supply problem. It is a policy framework problem. Renewable energy, especially solar power, storage, and EV integration, can be among the most practical solutions for the country.

The question is no longer whether Bangladesh should adopt renewable energy. The real question is how quickly, how systematically, and how boldly the country can complete this transition.



Mohammad Ataur Rahman Sarker is a renewable energy entrepreneur and the secretary of the Bangladesh Sustainable and Renewable Energy Association.

Md. Tanvir Siraj is a renewable energy researcher.

World.title: The forgotten art of Bengali advertising
World.content:
I have never seen someone at a rustic village market, anklets jingling, shouting slogans for "Khol Company’s Ringworm Ointment." No smooth-talker has ever leaned in, fanning out thin booklets like a deck of cards, whispering rhythmically, "Here are the mysteries of Gopal Bhar, and here—the secret love letters."

I never hid colourful s of a reclining Gauhar Jaan, cigarette in hand, between the folds of shirts in my drawer. I did indeed rummage through my grandfather’s pockets to collect old tram tickets, but none of them bore that curious notice for "Ashtavakra Toothpowder." Perhaps the elders of the house witnessed a tram tearing through the heart of a half-awake city, bearing the Khadi Pratisthan’s pledge for cow protection—but there was no question of me witnessing such a sight.

An iconic early 20th-century  for Bukhsh Ellahie & Co., featuring classical maestro Gauhar Jaan holding a cigarette to promote their brand

Someone’s great-grandfather might have known which drummers came beating the kara and nakara to announce, "Tonight at seven, the Chaitanya-lila folk play commences." I never heard the name of a young "lad" like Dhiren Bal, who reportedly painted the  for "Himkalyan Hair Oil" at a three-way junction in Dinajpur.

While searching the Panjika (almanac) for the auspicious moment of a wedding, I never had the chance to chuckle at the suggestive illustrations for "Libido-Enhancing Tablets." On a morning shortly after Mahatma Gandhi’s assassination, I didn't sit with a newspaper wondering which artist, known only as "Munshi," had used swirling brushstrokes to sketch a portrait as a final tribute on behalf of some bankrupt cotton mill.

I saw none of this because I hadn't been born yet. Most of those who witnessed it are now gone forever. Yet, even without being born in that era, I have managed to 'see' it all. The old, withered newspapers and digital archives acted like Alibaba’s cave, revealing to me a lost jewelry box. To me, those vintage s were not just pages of history; they were the precious Sita-har, the Jhumko, and the Nak-chabi themselves. I saw those 'ornaments'—the lost illustrations—and through them, I glimpsed a world that has otherwise vanished.

Actually, on a sudden whim, I spent a long time digging through ancient newspapers and periodicals. My eyes kept getting stuck on the bizarre s still surviving on the faded, brownish-yellow newsprint of yore. I was looking, most of all, at the illustrations.

As I tasted this history, I remembered a book I read long ago: The Lost Tribes of Israel by Tudor Parfitt. Many believe that since the foreign invasions of Israel in the 8th century BC, at least twelve tribes went missing. Mr. Parfitt scoured the planet in search of them—a search that reportedly continues today. Some even believe the signs of those lost people are visible in the Afghans.

Looking at the drawings for old s, I felt I found a resemblance between those legendary lost tribes and these forgotten illustrators. That is why the book came to mind. It also felt as though there was no such mismatch that could prevent us from linking these unknown artists’ ghosts to their successors, even without a DNA test!

The connection might be clear, but can we not grant them even a small corner in the history of Bengal's illustrative arts?

Renowned figures like the artist Raghunath Goswami continue to say—no, those  drawings or ideas are not even worth considering. They claim it is a "mindless and indiscriminate simplification of art objects." They say the expression has neither grace nor form. Artistic value? Far from it!

For some reason, despite respecting the scholars' verdict, I grew stubborn. As I weighed the pros and cons, even the "ugly" artworks of those who drew s for ringworm cures or hair-growth tonics began to pull at my eyes. I saw in them plenty of humour, and plenty of heartache too. Nevertheless, I began looking for a way to have a long conversation with those early advertising artists.

A representative of a "vanishing species" like O.C. Ganguly (Arun Kumar Gangopadhyay) introduced me to a certain "madman." He had a crow's nest of hair. His lower garment was draped over his chest like a shawl. He wore a striped vest. His hands were shackled in massive iron rings.

It is precisely these kinds of s that art critics have referred to as brainless and ugly art. The  regarding the cure for insanity, however, dates back to 1952. Yet, long before that, a group of young artists from agencies had completely transformed the face of Bengali ads.

Apparently, such a madman would no longer need to be restrained. Why? Because the illness would be cured simply by administering "ABD Pills" and "Dutta Oil." Such was the claim of the "Bengali Asylum" of Dutta Nagar, Dum Dum, whose head office was at 29-A Vivekananda Road (Phone: Jorasanko 5220).

Seeing the address "Jorasanko" in that illustrated ad, I was immediately reminded of the Tagore family—specifically, their members who struggled with mental health. One was Birendranath Tagore, the fourth son of Maharshi Debendranath. He was brilliant at mathematics but suddenly fell victim to "wind-disease" (mental instability). The other was Somendranath, another brother of Rabindranath.

The Nobel laureate poet knew well which medicines helped the "insane." I learned of another —not for the ABD Pills of Dum Dum, but a special notice from "S.C. Roy & Co." at 167/3 Cornwallis Street. They advertised Dr. Umesh Chandra Roy’s world-famous "Great Cure for the Mad," priced at five rupees per bottle. The ad claimed that for over 70 years, this medicine had cured "millions of violent madmen and all kinds of nervous patients." This  would appear with a quote from the poet himself, saying: "...I have been aware of its efficacy for a long time." Was the "Great Cure for the Mad" then used on Birendranath or Somendranath? I know bringing up Rabindranath's name is somewhat irrelevant, but seeing these old drawings makes my mind wander in a thousand directions!

The illustrated  I mentioned was published in 1952—the day I saw the picture of the shackled madman in the paper. That drawing was made several years after legendary artists had already begun to dominate Bengali advertising. By then, Bengalis had seen hundreds of fantastic drawings for various products. A legend like O.C. Ganguly was earning forty rupees a month at Calcutta’s "Stronach Advertising" as early as 1937. An agency named "Paradise Advertising" existed in Calcutta in 1928. No one can really speak of agencies in East Bengal (now Bangladesh) before the Partition. We mostly know of the birth of agencies like Bitopi, East Asiatic, or Interspan in the 1960s. Clearly, advertising production in both Bengals (undivided India at the time) was centred in Calcutta. Be that as it may, an agency required an artist—someone to present the matter attractively to lure customers.

But not all sellers went to agencies. Instead, they took "ugly" creations (by today’s standards) made by local artists to make printing blocks for newspaper offices. The madman illustration is a classic example. The calligraphy in that ad was purely amateurish—something no professional agency would ever approve. Whether that ad ran before 1952 or if that was the first, I do not know.

It is undeniable that finding artists from the era before the establishment of agencies (pre-partition) is extremely difficult. Only a handful of artists signed their names on those ads, and even then, it was just a tiny first initial of their name and surname, usually in English. Pranabesh Maity, who drew ads in the 60s and 70s, had a more bitter experience. He claimed that even if artists signed, agency bosses would often erase the signature to imply that the agency was everything and the artist didn't matter.

This makes me think of the "Lost Tribes" and a piece by Premendra Mitra about the Patuas (traditional scroll painters). Premendra once had a great desire to find the lost Patuas of Kalighat. Briefly, the story goes like this—a young boy walking the streets of Kalighat would watch with wonder a specific style of indigenous painting. Ordinary men in dirty clothes sat cross-legged on mats in small roadside shops, painting those pictures. Yet, the walls of the shops were adorned with framed, colourful photographs of gods and goddesses. People coming to the temple preferred to buy the framed photos. Even so, the Patuas would sit down to paint whenever they found a moment’s respite between sales.

Then came a day when not only the scroll paintings but even the expensive printed pictures of deities vanished from those shops. The Patuas disappeared too. I don't know if that young boy was Premendra himself—since his childhood was spent in North India, having been born in Varanasi. But for a creative man like him to imagine that boy while thinking of the Patuas is not far-fetched. When a kind soul eventually went looking for those Patuas, he was utterly disappointed. He learned that they had been pushed out of the city. Their descendants had not become "useless" painters; some took jobs as labourers in jute mills or chose other professions. At most, unable to ignore the "blood connection," some practised their hand at painting the chalchitra (background canopy) of idols. Premendra tracked down a few of these "unfortunate" descendants and asked to see old scroll paintings. He was shocked to find they had almost nothing left. One or two pulled down a bundle of papers tucked into the thatch of their huts. Premendra saw the pathetic state of those soot-stained, discoloured papers—they were ready to crumble at any moment. Calling the insects "connoisseurs of art," a somber Premendra described how those paintings were being destroyed.

The author was accompanied by an art collector. His friend bought some paintings that were in good condition from the descendants for an unexpectedly high price. Later, he and others wrote about them. Premendra noted how his "self-satisfaction" was bruised. He commented that while many were becoming famous artists by adopting the Patua style, and those paintings were selling at major exhibitions to decorate drawing rooms—even impressing Pablo Picasso—the Patua sitting on a dirty mat in a narrow shop and the ordinary customer buying them for a pittance are nowhere to be found today.

Thinking of the early artists of Bengali advertising, I am reminded of Premendra Mitra's essay "Barbar Yuger Pore" (After the Barbaric Age), just as I was of The Lost Tribes of Israel. In it, I found no real difference between the forgotten Patuas and the nameless illustrators from the dawn of Bengali advertising.

The artists whose work I later came to know and appreciate were giants like Annada Munshi—whose ideas and illustrations revolutionised the look and feel of Bengali advertising. But I wanted to see what kind of "ugly and tasteless" creations (as labelled by later critics) Annada and his peers had replaced. Without seeing those, how could I understand the evolution of style?

Here, I must mention the artist Hemen Majumdar. He is never known to have drawn for s. Everyone knows that when art lovers discuss him, his paintings of "drip-wet Bengali women" inevitably come up. Who that woman was, was once a subject of intense speculation. A few know that he often painted while keeping a photograph by his side. Hemen had taken photos of his wife, Sudharani, in various poses as she returned from bathing in the family pond. His wife was his model. When giving the picture its final form, he would simply change Sudharani’s face and paint the face of a relative instead—much like modern-day Photoshop!

Essentially a romantic artist, Hemen Mazumdar never illustrated s himself. Yet, his signature style of depicting women was extensively adapted by other advertising artists.

Though Hemen was skilled at copying photographs, he knew the magic of glorifying them with colour. But that wasn't all. This was a man who was invited to design the gateway for King George V’s visit to India, who was a pioneer in publishing art journals, who painted the landscapes of Kashmir at the invitation of the Maharaja, who was the "Court Artist" of the Maharaja of Patiala, and who gave an artistic form to Mahatma Gandhi at the spinning wheel. He didn't just paint wet clothes!

At the same time, it is true that his skill at painting beautiful women was so popular that other artists, while drawing women for s, often mimicked Hemen’s postures—or those of the women painted by Raja Ravi Varma. Thus, even without drawing for ads himself, Hemen was "present" in this branch of art through the figures of women drawn in his style. Of course, bringing out the "wet-clothed" look or suggestive sensuality in black-and-white newspaper ads was a difficult task!

It’s worth mentioning that Hemen’s own work was occasionally used in advertising. An organisation called "Bengal Autotype" used to run ads featuring a sketch of Rabindranath Tagore by Hemen, accompanied by the Poet’s message. The advertisers even sold prints of that picture. The ad read: "A Wonderful Picture of Poet." Each print cost one rupee, with an additional 50 paise for postage. This ad appeared in the Visva-Bharati journal in the late 1930s, detailing the paper quality and dimensions.

In the eyes of some critics, the work of the "erotic painter" Hemen began to gain popularity in 1926 after a commercial firm in Mumbai bought his paintings to make calendars. The "forbidden" sword of the Hemen-style became a weapon for advertising illustrators too. One could easily call them followers of Hemen’s "voyeuristic" work. However, no matter how they were drawn, it's not as if the artists of the Battala press or the Patuas hadn't used such "swords" long before! Based on the consumer's mindset, this tradition seems never-ending—at home, abroad, and everywhere else.

Sandip Dasgupta has spent nearly three decades working in the editorial offices of newspapers and news portals. He has authored several history-based books, and a subject particularly close to his heart is the illustrations created by Bengali artists.
