World.title: At Rappler summit, human rights figures call for solidarity amid AI threats
World.content:
HUMAN RIGHTS. (From left to right) Amnesty International spokesperson Agnes Callamard, Norwegian Nobel Institute director Kristian Berg Harpviken, Norwegian Nobel Committee chairperson Jørgen Watne Frydnes, and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa speak at Rappler’s Social Good Summit on November 21, 2026.

MANILA, Philippines – Global human rights figures came together at Rappler’s Social Good Summit to emphasize the importance of collective action and community in fighting modern crises worsened by the threats of artificial intelligence (AI).

“Resistance matters, resistance can work,” Amnesty International spokesperson Agnes Callamard said on Saturday, November 21, when asked how to convince the public to side with human rights over profit-driven motives to the AI race.

Callamard pointed out that the public is part of a global majority willing to stand up to Big Tech.

“We must get together. Join organizations,” she added. “Collectively, we can fight back and hold the line.”

Callamard recalled how Navi Pillay, the most recent winner of the Nobel Peace Prize, faced a barrage of instant online hate after she was announced the recipient of the award.

The experience was familiar to Callamard, a former UN special rapporteur on extrajudicial executions, and fellow panelist Maria Ressa, both of whom were targets of online harassment during the Duterte administration. The two women have been vocal critics of former president Rodrigo Duterte’s bloody drug war.

“Women were attacked in the Philippines in 2017 at least 10 times more than men. What we did is we took the attacks down. It’s a curse because you feel it, but a blessing because you have the data,” Ressa, who won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2021, said.

“We studied it. We learned how to do it, and we turned it into a system where we can help others,” she added.

The closing panel, moderated by Rappler’s head of community Pia Ranada, discussed how AI has made warfare more efficient.

“If you look around us and we look at the various conflict zones, whether we’re talking about the geographical areas where war is playing out, or a conflict zone such as the struggle over where the reaches of AI are going to be allowed and not, I think we see that there is no lack of actors or individuals with enormous courage and integrity,” Kristian Berg Harpviken, Norwegian Nobel Institute director, said.

“There is no lack of organizations that are fighting back. And in the situation we are now, I think they are just more important than ever,” he added.

Jørgen Watne Frydnes, chairperson of the Norwegian Nobel Committee, said breakthroughs in fighting technology-driven threats can emerge from coalitions that set aside differences.

“What I hear is cooperation, it’s the necessity to cooperate, to lift your own perspective from your regional or local to global. And many of those campaigns that have succeeded, that did receive the Nobel Peace Prize, were campaigns that were able to take away the differences they had between them.

“Even though under our hardships, our trauma, war, terror, we continue, we continue as human beings. And that is a strength which is so inspirational,” Frydnes added.

This year’s Social Good Summit is themed “We, The Humans,” highlighting the importance of human rights, values, and community in the age of artificial intelligence. – Rappler.com

World.title: NU extends UAAP cheerdance reign with 3-peat; UE cops historic silver
World.content:
CHAMPS AGAIN. The NU Pep Squad bags its third straight UAAP Cheerdance crown.

(2nd UPDATE) The untouchable NU Pep Squad rules the UAAP Cheerdance Competition anew for a title three-peat and record-extending 10th championship, while UE wins its first silver medal in 24 years

MANILA, Philippines – The kings and queens of UAAP cheerdance still sit comfortably on their well-earned thrones.

For a record-extending 10th time in UAAP history, the NU Pep Squad is the UAAP Cheerdance Competition champion, adding another title three-peat to its dynastic history on Saturday, November 21, at the packed Mall of Asia Arena.

With its latest golden coup for double-digit titles, the Gab Bajacan-coached squad created a two-championship gap from the league’s long-tied second-placers, the legendary eight-time titlists UST Salinggawi Dance Troupe and UP Pep Squad.

Taking its act from Japan last year to Mexico on Saturday afternoon, NU embodied a tribal, ritualistic spirit, and took the capacity 21,126-strong crowd on an Aztec whirlwind, highlighted by a literal whirlwind toss to kickstart one of its multiple perfect pyramids.

Meanwhile, the UE Pep Squad — perennial middle-of-the-pack performers — finally broke a nine-year podium drought with a unique Chinese martial arts routine, embodying a true Red Warrior spirit for its first silver finish in 24 long years, or since Season 65 in 2002.

The UE Pep Squad barges into the top two with a Chinese-inspired routine.

Completing the top three, the FEU Cheering Squad extended its podium run to eight straight seasons with its third consecutive bronze medal after a deliberately paced Aladdin routine.

“We had such a hard time getting this routine going,” NU head coach Gab Bajacan said in Filipino. “In our practices, we hardly had a complete routine. We were really frustrated because we needed to present our own standard every time we practice, and we couldn’t do it.”

“So when we finished our routine as flawless and as perfect as possible, we were so happy because we never expected to complete our stunts, and we were all so nervous, especially the new ones. We just put our full trust in them, and they finally showed our strong “NU tribe” spirit.”

NU ruled the roost with 693.5 points, while UE earned its historic silver with 664.5 points. FEU completed the podium with 647.5 points, edging fellow contender Adamson with a fourth-best 636.5 points.

The San Marcelino standouts, who wowed the crowd with their extreme motorsports-themed routine, slightly missed the mark as they snapped a two-year podium run that produced back-to-back silver medals.

The FEU Cheering Squad lands on the podium with an ‘Aladdin’ theme.

In its ongoing pursuit of lost glory, UP placed fifth with 596.5 points, while La Salle broke a five-year, seventh-placer run with 565.5 points to land at sixth.

Following an error-filled curtain-raiser routine, UST plummeted to seventh with 537.5 points — its worst finish in 13 years. Meanwhile, Ateneo completed the field with its sixth straight last-place finish, far below UST at 469.5 points. – Rappler.com

World.title: The fellowship of the grind
World.content:
'It was moving to watch, and a little shaming that, in this industry and in this country, working musicians can depend only on each other'

In my first week of college in Manila, I went looking for the nearest, and cheapest, folk house in the University Belt. It was 1978 and the scene was in full bloom. Once my campus paper allowance kicked in, I graduated from the folk houses of Recto and Morayta to Ermita, the mecca, the venues we read about in Jingle Magazine: Kola House, Hobbit House, My Father’s Mustache.

Beer was cold and nobody minded the smoke. The sets ran from the ’60s canon of Bob Dylan, Peter, Paul and Mary, and Simon & Garfunkel, the gritty folk of Neil Young, the two-part harmonies of Seals & Crofts and Loggins & Messina, to the acoustic pop of James Taylor and Jim Croce, the bruised love songs of Jackson Browne, and the country-folk of John Denver.

But the folk house was never just about the music, particularly after the declaration of martial law in 1972. These intimate venues, usually a dim room with one singer and perhaps thirty listeners, became one of the few places where young people could gather, listen to “Blowin’ In The Wind” or “He Was My Brother” and other socially relevant songs, and not look over their shoulders. They provided sanctuary for the weary, the worried, and the dreamers.

Behind the performances was a grind.

Pendong Aban Jr. of Asin got his first gig at Charcoal House on Recto in the early ‘70s with his friend Keith. As Keith and Fred, they played two sets a night for P20 each. Charcoal House, however, was pang-masa, a student hangout; someone told them they were ready for Mabini, where the serious folk houses were.

At their audition at Pension Filipina, they watched God’s Ego, the heavy hitters known for spot-on Crosby, Stills and Nash covers. They realized they were not ready for Mabini yet.

By 1975, Keith and Fred were regulars at Kola House, My Father’s Mustache, Bodega, and Pension Filipina. Aban eventually went solo and did gigs in Japan. Back from a six-month stint, Aban alternated sets with a trio composed of Mike Pillora, Cesar Bañares, and a Manila-born singer with a big, soulful voice, Lolita Carbon. The three were Salt of the Earth, packing rooms with Peter, Paul and Mary covers. Aban’s solo set was eclectic, with covers of David Bowie’s “Space Oddity” and Dylan’s “Masters of War” and “Hurricane.”

Pillora, recalls Aban, invited him to play bass for the group, and that was the beginning of Asin. When “Anak” made Freddie Aguilar, another folk singer, a star, the labels came scouting the folk houses for the next big act, and one of them found the quartet.

A generation of Filipino musicians was made through gigs abroad, bands formed between sets, and countless auditions where competition was tight but friendly.

Chickoy Pura recalled those years at a recent benefit show his contemporaries staged for him at My Brother’s Mustache in Quezon City, perhaps the only remaining venue for folk songs and folk singers today. Folk singers of his time, said Pura, shared experiences, a bond, and sometimes guitars.

“Ang unang tanong sa iyo noong araw, ilan na ba ang pondo mo?” he recalled. A singer’s pondo was his stock of songs. Pura had maybe 15. Come back when you have 30, he was told. His first pay was a sandwich; later, P30 a night.

Today, he said, young players walk into bars with top-of-the-line gear. “Before, we looked for jobs on borrowed guitar sometimes.”

“We’re older now and some of our friends fell by the wayside, but we remember them with much affection and pride… You stop playing, you stop living,” he told the audience.

By the early ’80s, the mass market had drifted back to formula pop; the restless young channelled their restlessness through punk and heavy metal. Still, every eatery, canteen, or food court needed live entertainment, and folk singers came cheapest, although the songs have changed. I once sat through a lunchtime acoustic rendition of “Careless Whisper” in a busy student canteen.

The pioneers, their best years behind them, continue to make their living from shows that are few and far between. Those who landed record deals and delivered hit songs received meager royalties, if they came at all. The road takes its toll on voices and bodies, and many of them are well past retirement age. The medical bills begin to pile up.

What has never left is the fellowship. When one of them falls ill, the others play a benefit, as they always have, before small crowds of loyal, graying fans.

They were there that night for Pura. Lolita Carbon’s voice was powerful as ever, her stage presence still electric. It was also her birthday. The secret of life? “Basta masaya lang lagi dapat,” she told me after her set.

Lito Crisostomo, former lead guitarist for The Blank, Ang Grupong Pendong, and Asin, played Crosby, Stills and Nash classics with Erwin, his partner from their days in the circuit as Fat and Thin. For more than five hours, act after act took the stage: Bobby Mondejar and Friends, Corky and Kiko, Rene Vega, Albert de Pano, Koko Marbella, Pete Velasquez, Ding Laag, and Joel Yu. Special guests were Pido Lalimarmo, founding member of Side A and Artstart who now fronts an all-Steely Dan covers band Black Cows, as well as the Kakoy Legaspi Blues Collective, whose smoldering blues set prompted advertising maverick Vince Pozon to declare “may pag-asa pa sa kabataan.”

An extended jam on James Taylor’s “Steamroller Blues” rounded off the night of music and fellowship. By that time, it was almost 1 am but no one was in a hurry to leave. It was moving to watch, and a little shaming that, in this industry and in this country, working musicians can depend only on each other. The voice, the energy, the spirit, those things the grind could not take from them. – Rappler.com

World.title: Maria Ressa: Understand AI to defend ourselves from ‘predatory’ tech
World.content:
FIGHT BACK. Rappler CEO and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa delivers a speech during the plenary session of the 2026 Social Good Summit titled 'WE, THE HUMANS: Reclaim Our Future,' at BGC, Taguig City, on November 21, 2026.

'For those who are saying they cannot act: Don’t fall into learned helplessness. When you are the target, you are powerful,' Rappler CEO Maria Ressa says of the fight against artificial intelligence

MANILA, Philippines – Understanding artificial intelligence is essential to defending ourselves from the harms of the “predatory, extractive” technology, Rappler chief executive officer and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa said.

During the 2026 Social Good Summit on Saturday, November 21, Ressa warned that AI was built to “hack our biology” as the end goal of Big Tech is profit.

She explained that AI hacked people’s attention, intimacy, and agency, through machine learning in social media, generative chatbots, and agentic AI.

“What have we lost? Sustained attention… our ability to hold complexity, nuances, to move away from identity politics,” Ressa said in her speech, adding that AI is “shifting the evolution of our species.”

“The technology that we’re getting has essentially been predatory and extractive, like mining. How much data have been given, and where has it gone to?”

That defense should be complemented with building own technologies, according to Ressa. (READ: From Duterte to Big Tech: Maria Ressa’s blueprint on fighting back)

This is after Big Tech is “breaking the social contract” by taking and scraping content from news outfits, pushing the journalism industry to already “reaching market failure.”

In 2025, it was found that bots already drove 53% of internet traffic, according to the latest report of cybersecurity firm Imperva.

“For those who are saying they cannot act: Don’t fall into learned helplessness. When you are the target, you are powerful,” she also said.

Ressa also centered on the continued push to protect democracy by establishing facts and truth, in a bid to “reclaiming our future from the machines we built.” (READ: Maria Ressa on AI overreliance: ‘Don’t outsource the nuances’)

“When you don’t have facts and lies spread faster, you cannot actually solve any problem. Not climate change, not rule of law, not child safety. Because if you don’t have facts, you can’t organize. You can’t hold anyone accountable,” she said.

“The chain of facts is what makes a crowd or a mob into ‘we,’ the people. You break that, and there’s no ‘we’ left to reclaim anything.”

Citing the preliminary report of the United Nations Independent International Scientific Panel on AI, Ressa said AI is changing geopolitical powers.

Ressa is a co-chair of the 40-member panel, which assesses opportunities, risks, and impacts of AI.

“A few hold the future in their hands, five or six companies, and in terms of compute power, the US has 75% of the world’s compute power. China has 15%, and the EU (European Union), which has put in place the safety measures we need, has 5%,” she said.

She also said that the AI deployment is “far outstripping the ability of law, of audit, and of oversight.”

On Monday, November 16, California sued OpenAI, accusing the company of developing a dangerous product without adequate safety procedures or oversight after reports that its AI models had independently carried out cyberattacks. Among this cyberattacks was the July hack of the open-source platform Hugging Face.

In September, Australia said an OpenAI agent breached a government health data portal and gained unauthorized access to files.

“Can we stop impunity in tech?” she asked. – Rappler.com

World.title: Beyond the classroom, UPLB skaters carve out space in town with no skatepark
World.content:
WITH THE CREW. UPLB student and skate filmmaker Banchi Jimena (third from left) with his fellow skateboarders.

While skateboarding has gained national recognition through athletes like Olympian Margielyn Didal, access to dedicated skating spaces remains a concern for local communities

Tambay lang ‘yan (They’re just loitering). Banchi Jimena wants people to stop seeing skaters this way.

Banchi, 22, is a University of the Philippines Los Baños (UPLB) student and skate filmmaker. Los Baños has no dedicated outdoor skatepark, according to local skaters. So he and his friends skate wherever they can on campus.

One of their favorite spots is the rooftop of a parking garage near Christian School International. Others are hidden behind the Institute of Biological Sciences (IBS) building and the buildings around the College of Engineering and Agro-Industrial Technology (CEAT) in UPLB. Campus security has caught them several times.

“Kilalang-kilala na kami (They know us very well by now),” he said.

Jules, a UPLB student and beginner skater, ran into problems early. They had hoped to skate between classes as an eco-friendly way to get around. The roads turned out to be less suitable than they expected.

Finding people to skate with is just as hard. Banchi has seen a livelier scene in town and wants to bring it back. Jules usually skates alone and is still looking for others to learn from.

A town with nowhere to skate

Skateboarding has gained national recognition through athletes like Olympian Margielyn Didal. Access to dedicated skating spaces, however, remains a concern for local communities.

In Los Baños, skaters make do with spaces meant for other purposes. Finding other skaters is its own problem.

“Patay talaga ‘yung scene dito sa LB kaya sa Manila ako lagi (The scene here in LB is really dead, so I’m always in Manila),” Banchi said.

Before Banchi and Jules can skate, they first have to find somewhere to roll.

Banchi sees the search for spots as part of the fun. He compares skating to traveling, with a good street spot as the destination.

During his year off from school, his work took him to many places. He found new spots and made new friends along the way.

“Nakakapag-travel ka, na-enjoy mo pa ‘yung ginagawa mo (You get to travel, and you enjoy what you’re doing too),” he said.

Back in Los Baños, there are fewer options. Banchi said he has already explored most of the spots on campus.

Jules also found fewer places to skate than they expected. They usually skate in a parking lot within walking distance of where they stay. They also stick to places where skating is not prohibited.

Security is another concern. Banchi said guards treat skaters differently. Some understand skaters even if they don’t skate themselves. Others are only doing their job. In Los Baños, he said, guards have been less understanding.

Luckily, Jules has not been asked to leave a spot so far.

“Mahirap talaga. Pero kung skater ka, kumbaga, gagawa ka talaga ng paraan (It’s really hard. But if you’re a skater, you’ll really find a way),” Banchi said.

Still, a spot is only half of it. The other half is having people to skate with.

PASSION. Skate filmmaker Banchi Jimena holds his skateboard, camera, and filmmaking equipment. COMMUNITY. Banchi (left) says it’s important to have a crew who believes in you. Photos from Banchi Jimena’s Instagram page

A scene that went quiet

Banchi still remembers what the Los Baños scene used to be like.

“Dati, buhay na buhay (It used to be so alive),” he said.

Some of the skaters who anchored it can still be seen in front of CSI. Banchi looks up to them like older brothers. Most of them no longer skate.

So when he spotted someone skateboarding in town while out on a walk not long ago, he was glad.

“Nakakagulat na may nagi-skate pa pala dito (It’s surprising that people still skate here),” he said.

A few skaters still gather in the bayan. Jules has noticed that they usually come out only on weekends or on random days. When they do, they seem busy, which makes them hard to approach.

Jules ends up skating alone most of the time, learning without anyone around to guide them.

“My biggest challenge is finding a community and learning properly,” they said.

Banchi was not always sure he belonged either. When he started skating, he was the weakest in his group. He had always loved cameras, so he started filming his friends instead.

“Para lang mabilang ako doon sa group (Just so I could be counted in that group),” he said.

That was how his passion for filmmaking began. His full-length skate film, What The Sigma, was later named Skate Film of the Year 2025 at the first Silog Skate Awards, according to Silog Skate Magazine.

Today, he believes what keeps skaters going is having a crew that believes you can do it. It is also why he wants to bring the scene back.

“Gusto ko talaga buhayin ‘yung scene dito (I really want to bring the scene here back to life),” he said.

Their stories show two sides of the same gap. Banchi remembers a scene worth saving. Jules is still waiting to find one.

Still misunderstood

Banchi wants to change how people see skaters.

“Ayoko lang talagang ma-discriminate ‘yung mga skater (I just really don’t want skaters to be discriminated against),” he said.

Jules also sees skaters as a “very stigmatized community, very misunderstood.”

Within the community itself, there is debate over what skating should be. According to Banchi, some older skaters want younger ones to become competition skaters, partly so the sport looks more proper and gets judged less.

He disagrees. Not every Filipino can afford a skateboard, he said, and he believes there are too few skateparks in the country. Pushing kids to become athletes also goes against what skating meant to those same older skaters when they were young, he added.

Banchi sees skating as closer to art than sport. It is a lifestyle, something done freely, the way someone might draw.

“Wala kasi dapat pressure pag nags-skate (There shouldn’t be any pressure when you skate),” he said.

What a skatepark could change

Banchi has thought about what a skatepark could do for Los Baños. Skaters from other places would start coming to town, he said, and the local skater population would grow.

He believes a park would also give parents, including professors, a safer place than the streets to bring kids who want to skate.

He points to the skatepark in Quezon City, which he said was built beside a pickleball court. Many passersby, he said, grew curious about why it was there. A park in Los Baños could spark the same curiosity, he added, and show young people there is more to sports than basketball.

“Hindi lang basketball ang buhay (Life isn’t just about basketball),” he said.

Jules sees a park as a way to change minds. Skateboarding is still a niche sport in the Philippines, they said. Placing a park in a busy area could clear up some of the stigma and misunderstanding around it.

Until then, Banchi and his friends keep searching for spots around campus, while Jules practices wherever he can.

Some people may still call them tambay. They keep skating anyway.

Banchi’s advice to fellow students is to open their minds and unlock skills they never got to try as kids.

“Enjoy mo lang ‘yung buhay mo (Just enjoy your life),” he said. – Rappler.com

Arabella Grace Sta. Ana is a Rappler intern studying BA Philosophy at UP Los Baños.

World.title: Catching up with the relentless Ronnie Lazaro
World.content:
An old friend looks back on the quiet grit and gallantry of veteran Filipino actor Ronnie Lazaro

Who is the real Ronnie Lazaro?

After a few decades, Ronnie Lazaro shows up on my radar with an invitation to attend the opening of his mobile photography exhibit, Lies The Truth.

It was set in the Avellana Art Gallery in Pasay, and going through the charmingly wooded complex of the Henry Hotel with houses dating back to the ’50s, I am sent back to a place called Cool Malate in the ’80s.

No such place exists anymore, but it exists in every artist’s heart of that generation who used to hang out in Hobbit House, the Penguin Café, Coco Banana, and Bistro Remedios. And the ultimate survivor, Café Adriatico.

So, there’s Ronnie, at his exhibit opening, fussing about the white wine not being cold enough and why the red wine was in the cooler. He seems to be the same man running about the set of City After Dark, a determined art director keeping up with the demands of the director, Ishmael Bernal, and the production designer, Peque Gallaga.

City After Dark was originally titled Manila By Night, but Imelda Marcos objected to Manila being depicted as a decadent city with drugs, gay bars, and prostitution on just about every corner (which it was). This was Ronnie’s fifth assignment as art director.

Age has not done too much to Ronnie. Maybe he was leaner during the City After Dark days, but he looks down at me with the same soulful eyes. Or maybe he didn’t recognize me and was trying to place me in his memory?

Ronnie casually opens the exhibition. Friendly, but definitely in charge.

FAMILY FIRST. Ronnie Lazaro (left) with his wife Lola and son Gabriel. Contributed photo

One has to think about the message with this collection of photographs of artists covering their faces with both hands. Eyes are the mirror of the soul they say, but Ronnie’s subjects cover them up with both hands. Is it intimacy because they’re close-ups? Or the opposite, because they’re all covering their faces with their hands?

“The world is full of lies!” he moans.

Uprooting himself from his native Sagay, Negros Occidental, he set down to do the hard work in Manila. With a natural acting talent and an ability to adapt to any situation, Ronnie says, “I had to work hard. I could not go back a failure.”

So, coming up from the School of Hard Knocks, and living by his work philosophy, “Just show up,” Ronnie has certainly arrived.

“I went to every single art opening to learn, meet people, and also to eat. Hahaha,” he shakes his head, almost amused at himself thinking about those gritty days in the ’80s.

Needless to say, Peque was a major influence on Ronnie as an actor, but other artists like Cesare Syjuco and Jean Syjuco molded a new artist’s perspective in Ronnie, venturing out of his comfort zone and doing dozens of performance art around the city.

In Mendiola, he did Eto Ka, Eto Ako, Ngayon Na where he held up a mirror to each member of the audience. This was in 1984, if memory serves. We can certainly use some of that these days.

It’s not a surprise that the latest Fifth Wall Fest (@fifthwall.ph) invited him to comment on James Clar’s performance art centered around City After Dark.

“Bing, you have to come. Tayo na lang naiiwan (We’re the only ones left).”

After one production meeting for City After Dark, he gallantly escorted me to my car and we discovered I had a flat. Of course, he had to change the tire for me. Gallant as he was.

As he tightened the bolts, he said, “Ibig mo sabihin Bing, nakasalalay ang buhay mo sa akin? (Do you mean, Bing, that your life depends on me?)”

Well yes, I say.

“Then I better get this right.”

On another occasion, we were walking in Sagada, why there was only the two of us, I have no idea. Where was everyone? I was rattling on about some such nonsense, yadayadayada, when he stopped me in my tracks because a snake was crossing our path!

He was looking out for danger this whole time! (Or wasn’t listening at all).

Thank you for that, Ronnie.

Yes, a true galante (gallant) — somewhat soft spoken and introspective.

When you’ve had decades of work experience, it’s hard to name that defining moment. And yet, Ronnie says, the defining moment for him was when Mitch Valdez invited him to her group Reach for Inner Self, a spiritual workshop.

“That is where I learned to forgive and love myself.”

Ronnie hangs back for a beat, enjoying the memories this interview is bringing back. He talked about the time Mitch invited him to be on the board of OPM.

There was an awards night to be held in Tahiti. Everyone was busy so Ronnie had to take one for the team and attended the festival. He was to be a judge and Heber Bartolome was the talent. His eyes sparkled as he said, “Lots of nice girls there.”

His proudest moment, among several, was his directorial debut Edna (2014), with screenplay by Lally Bucoy. The film received glowing critical reviews as it moved away from the typical OFW story, but rather goes inward, exposing the tragic result of a family growing without a mother.

We both contemplate the depth of isolation and loneliness one feels when separated from family and home.

Ronnie has tackled his career as an actor like a man on a mission. In 2012, I reminded him, he had 11 projects listed in his filmography, not to mention the dizzying number of projects in television and theater.

Of note would be his Urian Award for Best Actor, Yanggaw (Affliction) in 2008, Urian Best Supporting Actor for Bagong Buwan (2001) and The Gospel of the Beast (2023).

Raymond Red’s Anino brought him to Cannes where it won Best Short Feature Film (2000), and in 2024, Ronnie attended the Venice International Film Festival as lead actor of Lav Diaz’s Phantosmia.

We put all of that aside for a moment and exchanged ideas for a new movie perhaps, exploring themes, fiction or non-fiction choices, perhaps a period piece. And just when I was saying to myself, how refreshing it was to just sit and shoot the creative breeze with someone so imaginative and passionate, a fire broke out!

Makati Cinema Square was on fire! I told him to quickly get out before the fire trucks completely blocked the road. No need to be galante this time. There were enough firemen to keep me safe. – Rappler.com

World.title: Abu Dhabi OFW turns to cleaning toilets for a living after losing job
World.content:
Dubbed ‘Banyo Boy’ online, a laid-off Filipino worker in Abu Dhabi cleans toilets for AED10 to afford a new visa — sparking an outpouring of community support alongside legal warnings

ABU DHABI, United Arab Emirates – An overseas Filipino worker (OFW) who recently lost his job has resorted to cleaning the toilets of fellow Filipinos for AED10 (P173.67) to raise funds for a new visa to stay in the country.

The good news is that 24-year-old Jaime Herrera (not his real name), who has until November 26 to legally remain in the United Arab Emirates, has been receiving numerous messages for toilet cleanups. Those he has serviced have been paying more than his asking rate and giving him groceries, he said. Others have been offering food and help finding a job.

The bad news is that under UAE law, it is illegal to engage in any form of work during a grace period after a visa has expired or been canceled unless the worker secures a new employment contract and visa.

A grace period, usually one month, only allows a foreign worker to legally remain in the country to process a status change, transition to a new employer, or exit the UAE. Working illegally during this window can result in daily overstay fines, legal action, or a reentry ban.

Herrera’s previous employment contract has been revoked.

A high school graduate, Herrera said he cannot risk becoming undocumented or flying home empty-handed.

Herrera, who hails from Dasmariñas in Cavite, has to exit to nearby Oman while a new two-month visa authorizing his stay in the UAE is processed. The entire process costs around AED4,000 – AED1,200 for the visa, and the rest for transportation and accommodation while waiting for his reentry document.

‘Too bad’

Herrera, who arrived in the UAE on July 4 this year, previously held an employment visa as a house cleaner in Dubai.

“Talagang sayang (It was really too bad),” said Herrera, adding that he was earning AED2,500 a month at that job.

He said he is currently only able to clean one toilet a day.

“Nakakapagod maglinis ng kubeta. Pero okay lang sa akin. Nagme-message sila (customers) sa akin, magko-conversation kami, ‘pag okay, kukunin ko,” Herrera shared.

“‘Yung unang customer ko, Dhs50 (P871) ang binayad sa akin, tapos binigyan ako ng mga prutas. Daming tumatawag, sa isang araw, may limang missed calls ako.”

(It’s tiring to clean a toilet, but I’m okay with that. Customers send me a message, we talk, and if it’s okay, I take the job. My first customer paid me Dhs50 and gave me some fruit. I’ve been getting lots of calls; I receive around five missed calls a day.)

Herrera said he started cleaning toilets in Abu Dhabi on October 26.

“Naghahanap ako ng trabaho. Okay naman dito. Dami kong nakikitang hiring. Nag-iipon ako ng pang-exit. Maganda rin dito sa UAE, pumalpak lang ang mga plano ko. Unang sahod ko, bumili ako ng scooter, naibenta rin, sayang,” he said.

(I’m looking for a job. It’s okay here. I see a lot of hiring. I’m saving up for my exit. Life is good here in the UAE; my plans just went wrong. I bought a scooter with my first paycheck, but I ended up selling it — what a waste.)

Talk of the town

Herrera became the talk of the town when a vlogger, Mercy Dimalanta (not her real name), came across his social media post offering toilet-cleaning services and shared it on her Facebook account.

“(K)ung may labis naman po kayong budget, ibigay ‘nyo na po ang paglilinis ng CR ‘nyo sa kanya dahil napakalaking tulong po sa kanya ang AED10 para makatawid siya sa araw-araw niyang pamumuhay dito sa Abu Dhabi. Higit na marangal ang ginagawa niya kumpara sa ginagawa ng iba. Noong nakita ko ang post niya, alam ko na kailangang-kailangan niya ng tulong kaya agad akong nag-message at ang bilis niyang nag-reply, patunay na abang na abang siya sa kung sinuman ang gusto magpalinis upang may pagkunan siya ng pagkain niya sa araw na ‘yun,” she wrote on Facebook.

(If you happen to have some extra budget, please consider hiring him to clean your bathroom; the AED10 would be a huge help for his daily survival here in Abu Dhabi. The work he does is far more honorable than what some others might resort to. When I saw his post, I knew he was in desperate need of help, so I reached out immediately. He replied right away — proof that he is eagerly waiting for anyone who might need cleaning services, just so he can afford a meal for the day.)

Dimalanta gave him the moniker “Banyo Boy.” And Herrera’s sudden influx of customer calls is largely attributed to her viral Facebook post.

“Tumutulo ang luha ko sa awa pero lamang ang paghanga. Kaya naman pagkatapos niyang maglinis, ibinigay ko ang bayad ko lakip ang munting grocery na dapat sana ay para sa amin,” she added.

“Naitanong ko rin kung may trabaho ba siya at sabi niya ay wala, kaya bukod sa pagpapalinis ng CR ‘nyo, inilalapit ko rin po na sana tulungan natin siya magkaroon ng trabaho.”

(Tears streamed down my face out of pity, but my admiration for him was even greater. So, after he finished cleaning, I handed him my payment, along with some small grocery items that were supposed to be for us. I also asked if he had a job, and he said he didn’t; so, aside from having him clean your bathrooms, I’m also appealing to everyone to help him find a job.) – Rappler.com

World.title: ‘A new imperial age’: Yuval Harari warns Philippines of foreign AI dependence
World.content:
FUTURE. Rappler CEO and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa and historian Yuval Noah Harari talk about the future of AI for humanity.

The best-selling author of 'Sapiens' and 'Nexus' warns that AI could usher in a new age of empires and leave countries like the Philippines dependent on foreign powers

MANILA, Philippines – As the Philippines finds its place in the global artificial intelligence (AI) industry, historian and best-selling author Yuval Noah Harari warned that countries outside the world’s leading technology powers risk losing control of critical infrastructure unless they develop their own capabilities or cooperate with regional partners.

Speaking with Rappler CEO and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa at a pre-recorded conversation for the 2026 Social Good Summit, Harari said the concentration of AI technology in superpowers like the United States and China could usher in a new era of economic and political dependence.

“We are entering a new imperial age,” Harari said. “The empires are back.”

And this time, he warned, could be even worse. Consider how the Romans and the British – powerful as their empires were – remained constrained by geography and physical resources. But now with AI, control of its infrastructure and frontier models could concentrate economic and military power in ways previously impossible.

As lesser powers become dependent on foreign AI systems to run hospitals, airports, and military equipment, that could raise their vulnerability to decisions made abroad.

“In that situation, you’re no longer independent, you are a vassal state,” Harari said.

For the Philippines, which Ressa described as having been a testing ground for social media platforms, the concern revives many old fears.

“We were the petri dish for social media,” Ressa said, recalling how Facebook became a breeding ground for disinformation and political manipulation during Rodrigo Duterte’s rise to power in 2016.

Could the specter of what Harari calls “data colonialism” be coming back to haunt the Philippines, this time through its ambitions under Pax Silica?

Where should the Philippines stand?

The US-led initiative promises to strengthen supply chains for semiconductors, critical minerals, advanced manufacturing, and AI technologies. After joining the initiative in April 2026, the Philippines unveiled plans for a roughly 1,600-hectare advanced manufacturing hub in New Clark City, Tarlac. As of November, Manila and Washington were still working toward a framework agreement. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has sought to allay concerns by saying no data centers would be built in the area.

But beyond concerns over its energy and water use is another question often missing from discussions on Pax Silica. Would joining global AI supply chains give the Philippines greater control over the technology, or merely a role in manufacturing it?

For Harari, countries outside the US and China face three choices. They could remain dependent on foreign AI infrastructure, spend enormous sums building their own, or pool resources with other countries to develop shared capabilities.

He suggested the last option for the Philippines—working alongside partners such as Japan and Australia. Such cooperation could be cheaper than developing independent infrastructure, but would require closer political coordination.

‘Too late for politics?’

Harari rejected the argument that AI development was already beyond political intervention.

“What the companies are now trying to do is to convince us that it’s too late to do politics,” he said. “It’s not yet deterministic, it’s not inevitable, there are still choices to be made.”

AI, Harari said, is particularly dangerous because an agent is capable of making decisions, rather than being just a tool fully controlled by humans. And that leash used to keep autonomous AI under human control has already begun to slip.

In July 2026, agents powered by OpenAI models broke out of a restricted test environment and accessed live systems at AI platform Hugging Face, apparently seeking answers to a cybersecurity evaluation.

Anthropic, the company behind Claude, also reported that its models had gone rouge and hacked computer systems of other organizations. Months later, that same company went on to raise $81 billion in the world’s largest IPO in November, beating the record that Elon Musk’s SpaceX had set just months earlier.

In light of all this, Harari argued that governments need not halt AI development outright, but should reconsider the race toward superintelligence and invest more in safety. He urged greater focus on practical uses in healthcare, education, transportation, and public services.

“A product which is not safe is just not useful,” he said. – Rappler.com

World.title: 3 Inquirer correspondents win big at Bright Leaf awards
World.content:
TRIPLE RECOGNITIONS Three Inquirer correspondents received recognition at the 19th Bright Leaf Agriculture Journalism Awards in Makati City on Thursday. Joanna Rose Aglibot wins Agriculture Story of the Year, Willie Lomibao (left) was inducted into the Bright Leaf Awards Hall of Fame, and Ray Zambrano wins Tobacco Photo of the Year. —CONTRIBUTED PHOTO

Inquirer correspondent Joanna Rose Aglibot took top honors at the 19th Bright Leaf Agriculture Journalism Awards, winning the prize for “Agriculture Story of the Year” for reporting extensively on the struggles of local fishermen amid tensions in the West Philippine Sea.

Aglibot’s three-part special report, “From shore to shoal: Zambales fishers fight to sustain livelihood,” showed how China’s restrictions and harassment in the WPS affected the livelihood not only of fishermen but also traders and buyers in Subic, Zambales.

READ: Inquirer report on PH debt wins CMMA

Article continues after this 

Her entry won over more than 400 submissions. At the awards ceremony held in Makati City on Thursday, Aglibot received a trophy, P100,000 in cash, a MacBook and an all-expenses-paid trip to an Asian destination.

Also at this year’s Bright Leaf, Inquirer photo correspondent Willie Lomibao was inducted into the awards’ Hall of Fame after winning five times (2018, 2019, 2021, 2023 and 2025) in the annual competition by clinching either the “Tobacco Photo of the Year” or the “Agriculture Photo of the Year.”

Lomibao became the 10th journalist to be inducted into the Bright Leaf Awards Hall of Fame since 2010.

Fellow Inquirer photo correspondent Ray Zambrano also won the “Tobacco Photo of the Year” award, his first from Bright Leaf, for his shot of a farmer inspecting tobacco leaves laid out to dry in a barn in Barangay Amamperez, Villasis, Pangasinan.

Both Lomibao and Zambrano also received trophies, cash prizes and trips to an Asian destination.

Article continues after this 

READ: Former DA chief joins ‘Kapatid Angat Lahat’ program

In her speech, Aglibot acknowledged the Zambales fishermen and their families “who have continued to trust us with their stories.”

Article continues after this 

“This recognition belongs as much to them as it does to us,” she said.

“This award comes at a meaningful time as we mark the 10th anniversary of the arbitral ruling (against China’s nine-dash-line claim over the South China Sea).”

“My hope is that our fishermen will finally experience that victory—not just on paper, but through their freedom to return to sea without fear, earn a living, provide for their families, and enjoy the rights that have long been affirmed,” she added.

‘Important platform’

Aglibot thanked the Inquirer for providing an “important platform” for stories that highlight the struggles of fishing communities, as well as the Philippine Center for Investigative Journalism and Internews for supporting the series.

She dedicated her first Bright Leaf Award win to her mother, Juliet; brother, Jonathan Jorge, and her late father Jorge, who was her biggest supporter.

Aglibot, Lomibao and Zambrano also acknowledged the award’s organizer, Philip Morris Philippines, “for bringing the Bright Leaf Awards to life.”

In her opening remarks, Chita Herce, senior director for corporate affairs at Philip Morris Philippines, said this year’s entries brought “new challenges, new perspectives and new stories worth telling.”

“You are the voices behind the stories that matter. You shine a light on the aspirations of our farming, fishing and rural communities,” she said.

Herce noted that through the journalists’ work, “stories that might otherwise go unheard” are able to inspire awareness, action and progress.

“Tonight, we celebrate not only your achievements but also the dedication and purpose behind every story you tell. To your colleagues, families and supporters, thank you for continuing to champion agricultural journalism in the Philippines,” she said.

Agriculture Undersecretary Arrey Perez, the event’s guest speaker, said the future of the sector remained “bright” despite current challenges.

“The problems faced by our farmers are that they don’t have places to store [their produce], they don’t have roads to transport [them], and they don’t have avenues to sell [their products],” he said.

World.title: UN chief Guterres marvels at Ifugao rice terraces
World.content:
NORTHERN EXPOSURE United Nations Secretary General Antonio Guterres is a special guest of Ifugao province, where he spent two days after attending the Asean Summit in Manila. —DOT PHOTOS

United Nations Secretary General António Guterres expressed admiration for the centuries-old rice terraces and local traditions in Ifugao during a two-day visit to the province following his attendance at the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) Summit in Manila.

According to a statement released by the Department of Tourism-Cordillera Administrative Region (DOT-CAR), Guterres was in Ifugao from Nov. 18 to Nov. 19.

READ: UN chief Guterres visits Ifugao rice terraces after Asean Summit

Article continues after this 

“I just spent some time with a family here in Ifugao and it’s amazing—their culture, traditions, and very strong connection to their land,” Guterres said, as quoted in the DOT-CAR statement.

NORTHERN EXPOSURE United Nations Secretary General Antonio Guterres is a special guest of Ifugao province, where he spent two days after attending the Asean Summit in Manila. —DOT PHOTOS

The UN chief visited the Batad, Bangaan and Hapao rice terraces, as well as the Aguian View Deck, during his trip.

Reflecting on the history of the rice terraces, Guterres compared their age with that of his home country, Portugal.

“When these rice fields were built, my country did not exist yet. It shows the importance of culture and civilization of the Philippines and Asia,” he said.

NORTHERN EXPOSURE United Nations Secretary General Antonio Guterres is a special guest of Ifugao province, where he spent two days after attending the Asean Summit in Manila. —DOT PHOTOS

Guterres was accompanied by Tourism Undersecretary Maria Victoria Jasmin and DOT-CAR Regional Director Jovita Ganongan throughout his visit.

Article continues after this 

The Rice Terraces of the Philippine Cordilleras entered the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (Unesco) World Heritage List in 1995.

The World Heritage property comprises five rice terrace clusters in Ifugao, recognized for their cultural significance and traditional agricultural practices maintained by generations of local communities. INQ

World.title: Agri losses due to El Niño up further past P10 billion
World.content:
File photo. ‘Very strong’ El Nino is now active in tropical Pacific, says Pagasa. (Photo Courtesy of OMH-Hilongos,Leyte)

The El Niño phenomenon continues to drain the country’s agriculture sector, with losses inching up further past the P10-billion level, according to the Department of Agriculture (DA).

In its bulletin on Friday evening, the DA said the farm sector incurred P10.44 billion in damage, 4.5 percent higher than the P9.99 billion reported by the agency on Nov. 11.

READ: Food stockpiling eyed amid El Niño, other crises

Article continues after this 

In the previous month, the agency already pegged damage and losses at P8.57 billion, from P6.87 billion initially recorded in September.

The prolonged drought impacted the livelihood of 338,066 farmers and fisherfolk across seven of the eight regions in Luzon (Cordillera, Ilocos, Cagayan Valley, Central Luzon, Calabarzon, Mimaropa and Bicol), all four regions in the Visayas (Western Visayas, Negros Island Region, Central Visayas and Eastern Visayas) and five of the six regions in Mindanao (Zamboanga Peninsula, Northern Mindanao, Davao, Soccsksargen and Caraga).

About 311,289 metric tons of local harvests have been damaged, spanning 332,726 hectares of agricultural land.

Corn, rice losses

According to the agency, corn and rice comprised more than 92 percent of the overall losses.

Losses in corn amounted to P5.67 billion, accounting for 54.25 percent of the total. Rice followed with P4.05 billion, equivalent to 38.74 percent.

Article continues after this 

The majority of rice and corn crops that have been damaged are in the vegetative and reproductive stages.

El Niño likewise hit high-value crops (P665.08 million), livestock and poultry (P40.95 million), fisheries and aquatic resources (P20.38 million) and cassava (P5.60 million).

Article continues after this 

DA funding

The DA set aside P18.64 billion worth of interventions to help affected farmers and fisherfolk nationwide, such as P10.82 billion worth of production support that will be distributed through its regional field offices.

About 2.69 million beneficiaries are entitled to financial assistance through the Presidential Assistance for Farmers and Fisherfolk Program.

Affected farm producers may secure funding from the Agricultural Credit Policy Council’s “AgriRecover” program, which earmarked P31.08 million worth of financial assistance for 1,127 borrowers.

Meanwhile, the Philippine Crop Insurance Corp. will provide P703.06 million in indemnification to 77,522 affected farmers.

The DA previously outlined a P61.99-billion action plan to reduce the impact of El Niño on the agriculture sector.

These include P6.2 billion in fuel and fertilizer subsidies under the Unified Package for Livelihoods, Industry, Food and Transport, or Uplift program, as well as cloud seeding operations and measures to curb the spread of red-striped soft scale insects that are affecting sugarcane production.

World.title: NBI: Romualdez co-accused surrendered at Forbes Park church
World.content:
CUSTODY Felicito Guevarra turns himself in at the Santuario de San Antonio Parish outside Forbes Park. —SCREENGRAB FROM NBI FOOTAGE

Martin Romualdez’s co-accused in his P7.44-billion plunder case surrendered last Thursday at a church in a Makati village, according to the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI).

The bureau said on Friday its agents served the arrest warrant on Felicito Guevarra at the Santuario de San Antonio Parish on McKinley Road in Forbes Park when he showed up at around 10 a.m. as had been arranged with his counsel.

READ: NBI: Romualdez’s co-accused surrendered in Forbes Park

Article continues after this 

“Through counsel, Guevarra conveyed his intention to surrender, and the NBI coordinated with counsel to arrange the time and place of his surrender,” the NBI said in a statement.

Also on Friday, the agency presented Guevarra before the Sandiganbayan’s Third Division, which is hearing the former Speaker’s plunder case and had issued the warrant for Guevarra’s arrest.

Conditional immunity

Guevarra is president of Samchan Foreign Exchange Corp., which was allegedly used to funnel kickbacks from government infrastructure projects to beneficiaries identified by Romualdez, incumbent Leyte representative and a first cousin of President Marcos.

In a July 20 supplemental complaint-affidavit, the Office of the Ombudsman alleged that Samchan directors “knowingly participated in, facilitated, or otherwise aided in the laundering, concealment, transfer, conversion, and disposition” of funds from “unlawful activities.”

The NBI said it had returned the arrest warrant upon presenting Guevarra in court.

Article continues after this 

But following his surrender, the Ombudsman granted Guevarra conditional immunity under Section 17 of Republic Act No. 6770 or the Ombudsman Act of 1989.

It said Guevarra’s “testimony and records are necessary to establish the truth in this case.”

Article continues after this 

“Mr. Guevarra personally handled Samchan’s operations,” the Ombudsman also said in a statement. “His testimony and records will help the prosecution trace the movement of funds.”

‘Questioned transactions’

Samchan had already returned to the Bureau of the Treasury all earnings from the company’s “questioned transactions,” according to the Ombudsman.

World.title: Shedding stigma of conflict, Sulu opens doors to tourism
World.content:
The white sands of Man’s Beach in Luuk is Sulu’s coastalattractions being promoted to visitors. —PHOTOS BY LEAH D. AGONOY

JOLO, SULU—For decades, Sulu was more often associated with security concerns than with the natural landscapes, cultural traditions and local enterprises that make up its tourism potential.

Now, as years of peacebuilding begin to open new opportunities, the island province is working to change that perception—and invite travelers to discover what it has to offer. Backed by improved peace and order, infrastructure upgrades and a renewed push to validate tourism destinations, Sulu is positioning itself as one of Mindanao’s emerging tourism frontiers.

READ: DOT backs Sulu’s push for ‘culture-sensitive’ tourism

Article continues after this 

Tourism officials, local executives and business owners highlighted Sulu’s readiness to receive domestic and foreign travelers during a validation tour for the “Isabela de Basilan and Sulu Cultural Confidence-Building Experience” under the Zamboanga Peninsula’s Southern Corridor tourism initiative and was held from Nov. 12 to Nov. 15.

The scenic Mang Sali Beach in Parang is Sulu’s coastalattractions being promoted to visitors. —PHOTOS BY LEAH D. AGONOY

Tourism Assistant Secretary Ferdinand Jose Bagcal, who visited Basilan and Sulu provinces for the first time, said the trip dispelled long-held misconceptions about the provinces’ security situation.

“Growing up, in school, we’ve always known these areas to be risky,” Bagcal said in a mix of English and Filipino, noting that even his family initially worried about his trip.

He added: “There’s nothing to worry about anymore. Everybody is at peace, and it’s something [security forces] are committed to keeping for the rest of their lives.”

Bagcal said the Department of Tourism (DOT) is validating potential tourism circuits across the province, eyeing nature-based, farm-based and cultural heritage offerings—including intricate local weaving communities, birdwatching sites, a lobster farm and potential expansions of Tourist Rest Areas through the Tourism Infrastructure and Enterprise Zone Authority.

Article continues after this 

Confidence

Women weavers highlight the province’s rich cultural heritage and tourism potential. —PHOTOS BY LEAH D. AGONOY

DOT Zamboanga Peninsula Regional Director Dara Mae Cataluña said the validation tour—conducted alongside the Philippine Army, local government units, weavers’ associations and local stakeholders—aimed to test site readiness and reshape public perception through direct visitor experience.

“Confidence is the infrastructure of tourism. No matter how much development you put in a place, if people lack confidence, they won’t come,” Cataluña said during a courtesy call at the Jolo municipal hall.

Article continues after this 

READ: DOT pushes Basilan, Sulu as Mindanao tourism spots

She introduced the regional office’s “Dear” framework for the Southern Corridor—discover living heritage, embrace host communities, accept and respect the region’s tri-people identity and return to bring more visitors back—under its broader “Discover More to Love” campaign.

Local officials attributed the province’s opening to years of sustained peacebuilding by the military, police and local leaders.

Jolo Mayor Edsir Tan said the provincial capital, which serves as Sulu’s primary gateway via its seaport and airport, has moved past the instability that once dominated national headlines.

Cultural performers highlight the province’s rich cultural heritage and tourism potential. —PHOTOS BY LEAH D. AGONOY

Connectivity

“For many years, I thought I wouldn’t live to see this kind of peace and stability in the province,” Tan said. “Now, with peace in place, development follows continuously. What we are safeguarding now is the sustainability of this peace.”

Tan noted that accessibility to Jolo has steadily improved, supported by daily fast craft and regular sea vessel trips, as well as twice-weekly chartered flights—every Tuesday and Saturday—from Zamboanga City carrying up to 80 passengers per flight.

In the municipality of Panamao, Mayor Al-fravha Jairulla said settling longstanding clan feuds (“rido”) and facilitating the surrender of loose firearms allowed displaced residents to return to their farms to cultivate coconut, cassava and fruit-bearing trees.

SCENIC VIEW Bud Agad, a highland resort in Patikul, Sulu, offers visitors a scenic view of the province as it develops its tourism industry amid improving peace and security.

With improved security, Panamao is preparing to welcome investors and develop new tourism infrastructure, including view decks, while the DOT assesses the potential of Lake Seit.

As visitor arrivals pick up, provincial leaders emphasized that tourism growth must remain anchored on cultural respect and environmental protection.

‘Greatest wealth’

Sulu Vice Gov. Abdusakur Tan said the province is strengthening its ecotourism initiatives, such as mangrove reforestation in areas like the Ipil Mangrove, where raised walkways overlook thriving mud crab and clam habitats. He also pointed to recent Philippine Statistics Authority data showing Sulu’s exit from the list of the country’s poorest provinces as proof of improving local livelihoods.

However, Tan reminded prospective visitors to observe local customs and Islamic traditions, noting that public drinking and the sale of liquor are prohibited in Sulu, and urging tourists—particularly beachgoers—to dress modestly.

COASTAL BOUNTY Fresh sea urchins offer visitors a taste of Sulu’s coastal bounty in Parang.

“Our culture is Sulu’s greatest wealth, and it is our identity that must never be lost,” Tan said.

Improved stability has also spurred local entrepreneurship in neighboring towns like Patikul.

Yves Schuck, owner of Bud Agad Resort in Patikul, said what began in 2019 as a trail site for airsoft and motocross enthusiasts overlooking downtown Jolo has grown into an ecotourism complex complete with a provincial government-backed view deck, pool, restaurant, hotel rooms, convention center and pickleball court.

Charging P100 entrance fee for site maintenance while preserving decades-old fruit trees, the resort now draws peak crowds—including foreign tourists and content creators—during the annual Bangsa Sug festivities.

Meanwhile, Mahruffa Halud Yail-Puntukan, who opened Sulu Coffee Backyard by Katribo in Patikul in August 2026, said growing visitor foot traffic gives young locals a reason to build their careers at home.

World.title: This week’s milestones: Nov. 22 to Nov. 28
World.content:
Nov. 23, 2023

The National Museum of the Philippines (NMP) formally inaugurated its component museum in Uyugan, Batanes, featuring exhibitions on Ivatan Cultural Heritage. The museum occupies the former Long Range Navigation (Loran) Station of the United States Coast Guard. Built in 1953, the former Loran station served as a navigational facility that provided an accurate system for the US Coast Guard’s defense operations during the Second World War. It was run by the Philippine Coast Guard until Dec. 31, 1971, and in 2012, the Uyugan local government took over the abandoned property and donated it to the NMP. Currently, the museum features a permanent exhibition titled, “Ínamuhun: The Natural and Cultural Heritage of Batanes,” which highlights archaeological artifacts and ethnological collections from the Ivatan culture, as well as geological, zoological and botanical specimens present in the archipelago.

Nov. 25, 2018

The National Historical Commission of the Philippines installed a historical marker in Calbayog City, Samar, to commemorate the Calbayog Cathedral. It was first established by the Jesuits in Jibatan and became a visita of the parish of Capul in 1599. Later on, it was moved to the seacoast near the Calbayog River. In 1768, it was placed under the care of the Franciscan missionaries, and then became a parish under the patronage of Our Lady of Nativity in 1785. The present stone and brick church was built in 1840 during the term of Fr. Jose Gomez de Huerce. Designed in the Baroque-Romanesque style, it has a cross-shaped ground plan and a circular dome above the center of the transept. By 1855, its length, width and height was expanded. It was renovated again in 1870, while a bell tower was added in 1871. During the term of Fr. Antonio Sanchez from 1894 to 1898, its interior was beautified, the sanctuary was paved with marble, and a retablo was built. In 1900, the church came under the administration of the secular clergy. In 1913, it was designated as the cathedral of the Diocese of Calbayog under the patronage of Saints Peter and Paul. It was regarded as the largest church in Samar and Leyte and one of the most beautiful cathedrals in the Visayas.

READ: This week’s milestones: Nov. 15 to Nov. 21

Article continues after this 

This week’s festivals

Kabkaban Festival (Nov. 22)

The Kabkaban Festival is a cultural and religious celebration in Carcar City, Cebu, honoring St. Catherine of Alexandria, the city’s patroness. It also showcases locally produced products and features ritual dances (which are traditionally performed to drive away bad spirits), along with presentations incorporating elements of the city’s history, arts and local traditions. The festival derives its name from “kabkab,” which is a fern historically associated with the area and linked to an earlier name of the city. Now in its 25th year, the festival forms part of the annual fiesta celebration and will hold a street dancing competition and a grand ritual showdown.

Guipao Festival (Oct. 31 to Nov. 30)

The Guipao Festival in Sagñay, Camarines Sur, is an annual celebration honoring the town’s patron saint, St. Andrew the Apostle, whose feast day falls on Nov. 30. The festival features activities depicting greatness and thanksgiving for the God-given wealth of the sea. This year’s celebration will include a parade, a mass wedding, a fun run, a cleanup drive, Derby sa Nayon, a basketball tournament and a billiard competition. The highlight of the festival—the street dancing competition—will be held on Nov. 28.

Dana Gracielle Quirante, Inquirer Research

World.title: Seafarers urge compensation release after SC voids bond rule
World.content:
Representatives of the Concerned Seafarers of the Philippines (CSP), the Federation of Free Workers (FFW), and AMOR-Seaman, along with lawyers representing seafarers, hold placards during a press conference on Friday, urging the government to release pending compensation awards for Filipino seafarers following the Supreme Court’s decision to strike down the bond requirement under the Magna Carta of Filipino Seafarers. INQUIRER / Chelsy Claire Perez

MANILA, Philippines—Labor groups are urging government agencies to release pending compensation awards for Filipino seafarers after the Supreme Court struck down a requirement that forced them to post a bond before collecting disputed monetary awards while their cases were under appeal.

Former Bayan Muna Rep. Neri Colmenares, a lawyer for the Concerned Seafarers of the Philippines (CSP), said many injured seafarers had been waiting for compensation because of the provision under the Magna Carta of Filipino Seafarers, which took effect in October 2024.

READ: SC strikes down portions of Magna Carta of seafarers

Article continues after this 

“This law has been in place for two years. Many seafarers need compensation for their injuries, but they cannot get it because of this law,” Colmenares said during a press conference on Friday.

He urged the National Labor Relations Commission (NLRC), the National Conciliation and Mediation Board (NCMB), and the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) to execute pending compensation awards dating back to the law’s effectivity.

“Execute all pending compensation awards from the time the law took effect. Do not make it difficult or prolong the process. Seafarers have been waiting for two years,” he said.

Section 59 of Republic Act No. 12021, or the Magna Carta of Filipino Seafarers, required seafarers to post a bond before they could collect disputed monetary awards while an employer’s appeal was pending.

The Supreme Court ruled that the requirement violated due process and equal protection because it imposed a financial burden on seafarers that was not required of other workers.

Article continues after this 

The court also struck down the use of the AKSYON Fund to pay for bond premiums, ruling that public funds could not be used for private interests.

Colmenares said the bond requirement effectively prevented injured seafarers from accessing compensation even after winning their labor cases. He clarified that employers still had the right to appeal, but said that right should not prevent workers from receiving the compensation awarded to them.

Article continues after this 

Not to appeal ruling

The Federation of Free Workers (FFW) also urged President Marcos and the Office of the Solicitor General not to seek reconsideration of the Supreme Court ruling.

FFW national president Sonny Matula said the government should allow seafarers to benefit from the decision without further delay.

He also called on DOLE to revise its implementing rules to remove provisions that conflict with the Supreme Court ruling, so labor arbiters, voluntary arbitrators, workers and employers would have clear guidance on executing compensation awards.

Matula likewise urged the government to implement final and executory decisions issued by voluntary arbitrators and the NLRC.

Stronger action

Matula said the invalidation of provisions regulating the practice of law should not prevent the government from addressing abusive legal practices targeting seafarers.

He pointed to Republic Act No. 10706, or the Seafarers Protection Act, which prohibits ambulance chasing under Section 3 and provides penalties under Section 5.

Matula said the government should establish a system for acting on pending complaints against lawyers accused of abusing seafarers.

World.title: Dizon to meet transport groups as Manibela readies 2-day strike
World.content:
Transportation Secretary Vince Dizon during the airport inspection. INQUIRER / GABRYELLE DUMALAG

MANILA, Philippines — Transportation Secretary Vince Dizon said he would meet with transport groups next week to discuss their concerns, as one group prepares to stage a two-day transport strike over the possible replacement of the Land Transportation Office (LTO) chief.

“I will talk to the transport groups next week,” Dizon told reporters.

READ: Palace urges Manibela to hold a dialog with DOTr chief

Article continues after this 

Asked about the possible agenda, Dizon said the meeting would cover “everything,” referring to the various concerns raised by transport groups in recent weeks.

He also said he had no objection to the planned protest, stressing that staging a transport strike was within the group’s rights.

“The transport strike is okay. For me, it’s up to them. You have the right to do everything,” he said.

The statement came after transport group Manibela announced a two-day strike on Nov. 23 and Nov. 24, accompanied by a protest outside the LTO Central Office along East Avenue in Quezon City on Monday.

The group is opposing the possible removal of LTO Assistant Secretary Markuz Lacanilao, whom it credited with introducing reforms and improving the agency’s services.

Article continues after this 

In its Nov. 19 media advisory, Manibela questioned the rationale behind the reported possibility of replacing Lacanilao, saying the agency had only recently begun implementing reforms among its personnel and improving the delivery of public services.

“It is only now that the LTO has started getting its act together, with ongoing reforms among its personnel and efforts to speed up services for the public,” the group said.

Article continues after this 

“Do we not want continued change and reforms in government agencies?” it added.

Manibela also appealed to President Marcos not to remove or reassign Lacanilao, whom it described as one of the few effective officials in the administration.

“Only a few officials in your administration who are effective in their jobs remain, and now another one is about to be removed,” the group said.

It also criticized what it described as patronage politics, arguing that an official who had performed well and introduced reforms was at risk of being replaced.

Asked whether Lacanilao’s removal was already being considered, Dizon urged the public to wait for a formal announcement from the Office of the President.

He had earlier said there were no changes or decisions yet concerning the LTO chief’s position, amid reports of a possible leadership shake-up.

Marcos appointed Lacanilao as LTO chief in October 2025.
