World.title: Human health should factor in antibiotic decision, AMA says
World.content:
The nation's peak doctors' group has urged a federal regulator to consider the human health and environmental risks of antibiotic resistance, as it assesses an emergency request to treat farmed salmon with the antibiotic florfenicol in Tasmania.

The Australian Medical Association (AMA) has said antimicrobial resistance is one of "the most serious global health threats of the 21st century", and should be considered by the Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority (APVMA) as it assesses Salmon Tasmania's application.

Lobster fishers rail against salmon industry's antibiotic plans Tensions have escalated between Tasmania's salmon industry and the wild seafood sector over plans to close some fishing areas when antibiotics are used in salmon pens.

The AMA's submission said: "Our concern is that the consequences for human health, the environment and market access are being underestimated, and that health and trade cannot be separated."

The drug florfenicol was first used in the state's south-eastern waters in November last year after an emergency permit was approved by the APVMA.

That was in response to a bacterial disease that led to the deaths of 15,000 tonnes of salmon in early 2025, and resulted in fish chunks washing up on beaches.

Tasmania's farmed Atlantic salmon stocks were hit hard by bacterial outbreaks last year. (Supplied: Bob Brown Foundation)

But the regulator revoked the emergency permit in March this year, on the basis of "unacceptable risk of residue exposure to non-target species".

The permit was repealed after traces of the antibiotic were detected in wild fish species up to 10 kilometres from the nearest salmon pen in which the antibiotic had been used.

Florfenicol was later found in abalone up to 14km away.

Insufficient data, but antibiotic use approved anyway Tasmania's health department and environment watchdog questioned the scientific rigour behind an application to use the antibiotic florfenicol in salmon farms, including a lack of evidence about its impact on humans, documents show.

Salmon Tasmania recently sought the APVMA's approval for another emergency-use permit with the same dose rates and treatment frequency as its previously revoked permit.

The previous permit allowed for 10 to 20 milligrams per kilogram of fish per day for 10 consecutive days, with no re-treatment permitted.

The APVMA recently sought public feedback on Salmon Tasmania's request. Submissions closed last on Monday, November 16, with the agency expected to make a decision as early as this coming week.

Salmon Tasmania chief executive John Whittington said salmon famers agreed with the AMA "that antimicrobial resistance is a serious global health issue".

"That is why the industry's first line of defence is vaccination and selective breeding, not antibiotics," Dr Whittington said.

"Antibiotics are used only to treat diagnosed disease, under veterinary prescription, consistent with growers' legal duty to care for their animals. There is no routine or preventative antibiotic use in Tasmanian salmon farming."

Tasmania's salmon industry says florfenicol is its preferred treatment method to combat Piscirickettsia salmonis. (Facebook: Salmon Tasmania)

The Tasmanian Health Department has previously said: "There are no reports of adverse human health effects from eating seafood with florfenicol residues."

The department said that if a "person chooses to avoid eating finfish that may contain florfenicol residue, they could choose to avoid eating wild finfish caught within 3km of a treated lease for 21 days after treatment finishes".

But the AMA said in its submission that florfenicol given in medicated feed to salmon pens cannot be contained, that antibiotic exposure in the aquatic environment favours resistant bacteria and that aquatic workers and divers, fish processors, fishers and coastal communities "may be exposed to resistant organisms".

"Resistant infections are harder to treat, prolong illness, increase the use of last-line antibiotics and add to the burden on health systems," the AMA's submission said.

Florfenicol was previously used in south-east Tasmania's salmon farms. (Supplied: EPA)

The AMA urged the agency to put the drug through a full assessment rather than grant "repeated emergency permits" with independent environmental and human health risk evaluations made public.

It said the assessment should consider the risk to human health from resistant bacteria and resistance genes "reaching people through water, seafood and occupational contact".

The AMA says there should be a full evaluation of the cumulative environmental and public health effects of repeated, large-scale use, including on wild species, coastal communities, aquaculture workers and fishers.

Yet the AMA said in its submission it "is not suggesting that this use will inevitably produce unacceptable resistance, or that importing countries currently require testing for resistance genes."

The APVMA is also considering a separate "minor use permit" application from florfenicol manufacturer Abbey Labs.

AbbeyFlor florfenicol premix for pigs was initially licensed for use on Atlantic salmon in Tasmania. (Supplied: Abbey Laboratories)

A Senate estimates hearing in October heard Abbey Labs' application was for higher dose rates of florfenicol in the south-eastern and eastern biosecurity zones.

The AMA recently warned antibiotic resistance in Australia was rising and could threaten the foundations of modern medicine.

Antibiotic use expected to fall

Dr Whittington said much of what the AMA was asking for was already in place or underway.

"Samples to support research on antibiotic resistance genes in the marine environment have been collected, and in collaboration with IMAS and the EPA a comprehensive research program has been developed," he said.

"As the AMA notes, florfenicol is not used to treat human infections in Australia. The Director of Public Health has advised there is no evidence of harm to human health from consuming traces of florfenicol."

He said antibiotic use had been "very low to zero for most of the past decade", and while it had been used last summer in response to a new disease, P. salmonis, vaccines and selective breeding were being "rapidly progressed".

"As these take effect in coming seasons, the industry expects its need for antibiotics for this disease to fall back to close to zero," he said.

The Tasmanian Environment Department closed the commercial rock lobster and commercial dive fisheries in parts of the state's south-east for three months to "mitigate trade risks" linked to antibiotic use by the salmon industry.

The move is designed to reduce international trade risks linked to the use of the antibiotic oxytetracycline (OTC) in salmon farms in the area.

Some of those affected fishers describe the decision as "completely unfair", with "one or two businesses ruining it for everyone else".

World.title: Drivers warn shouting for a taxi may become a catchcry of the past
World.content:
Anyone who has dropped a beer in a country pub will have heard the familiar shout of "taxi".

But drivers and operators are warning the call may become a relic if changes are not made to protect the sector.

More than 20 taxi services across NSW have closed in the past few years, with many under significant strain.

Wagga Taxis CEO Tim Peachy, who operates in the NSW Riverina, said since rideshare companies arrived in Australia 10 years ago, operating a taxi business has become unfair.

Tim Peachy is concerned about the future of taxis in NSW. (ABC NEWS: Rachel Holdsworth)

"Our running costs compared to their running costs, it's getting very hard to compete and very hard to keep our cars on the road," he said.

"Our green slips are over $5,000 in regional areas, in the cities even more.

"Rideshares are under private sector green slips and they're paying $500 to $700 a year."

A spokesperson for Uber, which represents 70 per cent of the rideshare market, said in a statement the company "recognises the cost pressures facing drivers and operators across the transport industry, and the important role point-to-point transport plays in keeping the community moving".

"We share the goal of keeping CTP insurance affordable, and sustainable."

Taxis call to 'level the playing field'

Mr Peachey, along with other advocates, rallied at NSW Parliament earlier this week about inequity between the sector and rideshare companies, and the costs incurred to run a registered on-demand, point-to-point transport service.

Taxi operators and advocates converged at the State Parliament House in Macquarie Street to prompt change in the sector. (Supplied: Tim Peachey)

He said the government needed to "level the playing field" because registered taxi services spent more to insure the cars, but setting up the service was more than just downloading an app.

Taxicabs are fitted with cameras as a legal requirement and the company must hold a license issued through the Point To Point Transport Commissioner.

"We go through a lot of checks at the start to become accredited as a taxi driver, most drivers work under a network and networks have very tight rules and regulations," Mr Peachey said.

"We do find a lot of female customers are coming back to us because they feel more safe and secure, especially with what's happened recently in rideshares without cameras.

"Drivers are more trained, and they are more watched."

In a statement, a NSW government spokesperson said it recognised the complexity of the issue and was conducting a statutory review of the Point to Point Act.

The spokesperson said the government's review would consider the issue in detail, including recommendations made in the NSW Legislative Council's review of the CTP scheme.

"Any reform to the CTP scheme must ensure it remains a vital safety net for people injured in a motor crash," the spokesperson said.

"Transport for NSW works closely with both rideshare operators and the taxi industry to improve services across NSW and ensure they continue to meet customer needs."

Towns without a taxi

Mr Peachey said many towns in NSW had lost their taxi services in recent years, and more were being pushed to the brink.

"Just in the last two weeks, the Southern Highlands [Taxis] have closed their doors," he said.

"Twenty taxis, gone."

Tim Peachey says many towns in NSW no longer have a taxi service. (Datawrapper)

On Wednesday, Leeton Radio Cabs announced it would be forced to close due to rising costs.

"The fuel, and the CTP slip, they're all going up," co-owner Graeme Ahern said.

"They've all been going up for a while now, and it's just not worth it."

He said he still hoped to sell the business and did have an interested buyer.

Taxi drivers say the heavy regulations they face compared to rideshare companies is making it hard to compete. (ABC News: Rachel Holdsworth)

In Temora, the taxi service closed down about two years ago, leaving locals to rely on only public transport.

Resident Sue Smith said the loss of the service was devastating, especially for older people who relied on the service.

"There's just been no interest in anyone setting up a cab [business] here at all, which is very difficult for older people," she said.

"We have a bus but that's just within the town."

World.title: Tasmania Police officer shot on Flinders Island
World.content:
A Tasmania Police officer shot "by an unknown person" while on duty is receiving medical treatment.

Emergency services were notified about 9:45pm yesterday that an officer had "received a gunshot wound ... while on duty at Whitemark Police Station" on Flinders Island.

Tasmania Police said the officer was in a serious-but-stable condition and is receiving treatment on Flinders Island, off Tasmania's north-east coast.

The shooter is yet to be found.

"The community is advised there will be an increased police and emergency services presence on Flinders Island in the Whitemark area as investigations get underway, and to ensure community safety," police said in a statement.

Police are expected to provide an update later this morning.

World.title: Historic images reveal life of workhouse poor sent to Queensland island
World.content:
The mention of workhouses usually conjures Dickensian images of foggy, grimy, Victorian London, not a subtropical island off the Brisbane coast.

Yet the quiet bayside township of Dunwich, on North Stradbroke Island, once included a workhouse that operated for 80 years, and saw about 21,000 inmates pass through its doors.

The government-run Dunwich Benevolent Asylum opened in 1865, using former convict and quarantine station buildings to house the inmates.

The benevolent asylum, pictured in 1938, was 30km across Moreton Bay from Brisbane. (Supplied: State Library of Queensland)

It expanded to include dozens of wards, farms, a dairy, and a power station where inmates worked before it closed just after World War Two.

"It was a home for poor, sick people generally who couldn't care for themselves and had no other means of support," said Elisabeth Gondwe, curator of the North Stradbroke Island Museum.

Most of the inmates were single men who needed shelter. (Supplied: State Library of Queensland)

It was hard life, and men outnumbered women at the asylum by six to one.

"There were no bed sheets until after the First World War, and often fresh fruit and vegetables or fresh eggs or milk and fresh produce was not on the menu," Ms Gondwe said.

The asylum's mess hall in 1912. (Supplied: State Library of Queensland)

Historian Tracy Ryan says the need for an asylum grew after the penal settlement closed in 1842, and the region now known as Brisbane was thrown open to free settlers.

"There was a very big push to bring labourers (usually from the UK) out here to provide a workforce … so there was a big influx of men — usually single, usually unskilled," she said.

Historian Tracy Ryan says the workhouse operated on the same principles as British workhouses. (ABC News: Lucy Loram)

"Whenever the population grows, you are inevitably going to end up with people who are unable to care for themselves through accident, through disability, through circumstances.

"These people were considered not very desirable, so let's get them out of sight, out of mind."

The decision was made to ship them off to North Stradbroke Island, a 30-kilometre boat trip across Moreton Bay from Brisbane.

About 21,000 people, mainly single men, lived out their later years at the asylum. (Supplied: State Library of Queensland)

Men gathered outside the library, which was staffed by inmates. (Supplied: State Library of Queensland)

On arrival, inmates were put to work.

"That very much mirrors the workhouse model that Australia inherited from Britain … that the poor needed to work," Ms Ryan said.

"There was deserving poor and undeserving poor, and in order to be deserving, you had to earn your keep."

Food bearers at the asylum in 1931. (Supplied: State Library of Queensland)

First Aboriginal equal-pay case

The Island's Indigenous Quandamooka people staffed the asylum, working in a range of domestic and trade roles, and in unloading the supply boat.

"They were paid in rations — usually salt, flour, sugar and so on — and a small amount in money and that money was put into bank accounts that the so-called Protector of Aborigines was the administrator of," Ms Ryan said.

"In order to get access to those funds they had to jump through the hoops, and they had to prove that they weren't spending it on something the protector didn't approve of."

This 1942 plan shows the male quarters, left, and female quarters of the asylum, where men outnumbered women six to one. (Source: Queensland Historical Atlas/State Library of Queensland)

But the Aboriginal workers were angry they weren't paid the same amount as white workers.

"They knew perfectly well how unfair it was, so they did a long campaign of letter writing, protests, petition signing," Ms Ryan said.

" There was a strike in 1918 when the boat workers refused to unload the supply boat, which meant the asylum just ground to a halt. "

Indigenous workers were used to unload supply boats and fulfil other duties at the asylum but did not receive equal pay. (Supplied: State Library of Queensland)

After a 30-year campaign, they were awarded equal wages in 1944.

"We are pretty confident it is the first case in Australia of equal wages for First Nations people," Ms Ryan said.

Layers of the past

Remnants of the asylum can be found around Dunwich, including a handful of buildings that are now on Queensland's heritage register.

Elisabeth Gondwe says inmates of the asylum lived in harsh conditions, but often had no alternative options. (ABC News: Kirrin McKechnie)

"When you walk around, if you look at these places, you can see the layers of the past on the present landscape," Ms Gondwe said.

" And I always imagine the thousands of men who lived and died here. "

About 9,000 inmates were buried in unmarked graves at the Dunwich cemetery.

Unmarked asylum inmate graves on North Stradbroke Island. (Supplied: State Library of Queensland)

Despite it being a hard life, Ms Ryan insists that for many of the inmates, it was better than the alternative.

"I think we need to be careful about thinking it was nothing but a terrible, terrible thing, because … it was better than dying on the streets," she said.

"Even though they were very, very controlled … they had a bed, they had food, it might be meagre but they did have a bed, so … they could survive."

World.title: Intervention not jail: youth crime plea ahead of Victorian election
World.content:
After migrating from New Zealand with her family as a child, Falé changed schools constantly.

"It was difficult making friends if I was always moving, so at year 8, I just stopped getting comfortable," she said.

Then her father died.

Grieving and caring for six siblings while her mother went back to NZ to care for her own parents, Falé left her studies and began working to pay the bills.

She says "a mix of grief, anger and stress" eventually led to violence.

"It was a one-time altercation," she said, adding that — in retrospect — "there were better ways of handling the situation".

Juveniles account for 11.6 per cent of the state's total alleged offending.

Recently released Crime Statistics Agency data for the year to June 2026 showed alleged youth offender incidents dropped 8.1 per cent compared with the previous year.

The Youth Junction drop-in centre aims to provide safe, inclusive services to young people. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

However, a series of high-profile violent crimes by young people in recent years has kept the issue in the spotlight, fuelling election promises of tighter bail and tougher sentences.

Labor has a new "tough love" policy of mandatory youth rehabilitation detention with low- and mid-level offenders to be held in a "secure residential youth justice facility" for up to 12 months.

The Liberals have pledged to send some juveniles to "boot camp" in regional Victoria.

The key policies on offer from parties in the 2026 Victorian state election Political parties are laying out their visions for the state's future, as voters prepare to head to the polls on November 28.

Labor, the Coalition and One Nation also support "adult time for violent crime", with juveniles given the same sentences as adults for serious crimes such as home invasion, carjacking, burglary and armed robbery.

The Greens strongly oppose these policies and both major parties have pledged some support for community-based intervention programs.

But Victorian youth service providers say there is too much focus on incarceration.

Blake Edwards is the CEO of the Youth Junction Inc, a youth services provider in Sunshine in Melbourne's western suburbs.

Mr Edwards said there needed to be "high levels of consequences" for violent crime, but argued there should be equal amounts of funding for early intervention.

Blake Edwards says intervention is cheaper and more effective than imprisonment. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

"The support services are stretched [and] underfunded, and that's a real concern," Mr Edwards said.

" If we take an approach where we're throwing young people in prison, we're never going to get positive outcomes. "

Jamie Crosby from the Centre for Excellence in Child and Family Welfare, a peak body, said increasing the number of child offenders sent to detention was not only costly but did not work.

"It's really about intervening at the first sign of trouble," Mr Crosby said.

"How do we divert them away from escalating the type of offending behaviour which is putting communities on edge?"

Jamie Crosby says locking up youth offenders only keeps the community safe temporarily. (ABC News: Sacha Payne)

Mr Crosbie said detention might keep the community safe while the offender is in custody, but the problems often escalate when they get out.

"When they reintegrate into the community … there's a much higher likelihood that the very type of behaviour that's causing people to be concerned is perpetuated."

Victoria is one of the highest spending jurisdictions in the country when it comes to juvenile detention.

The latest Productivity Commission Report on Government Services found that detaining a single youth in Victoria costs $7,304 a day, or more than $2.6 million per detainee per year.

That is more than twice the national average of $3,600 per youth prisoner a day.

Mr Edwards said intervention was cheaper, more effective and had better outcomes for offenders and victims.

"It costs $11 per person per day (for community-based programs) and the outcomes that we're seeing are quality," he said.

Falé says the Youth Junction program stopped her from spiralling after the death of her father. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

'Performance and accountability gaps' in current approach

Since 2016, the Victorian government has allocated about $40 million to organisations that provide mentoring and case-management services to at-risk young people under its Youth Crime Prevention Program (YCPP).

But a recent report from the Victorian Auditor-General's Office found no evidence the YCPP led to a reduction in offending.

The report said numbers for most organisations were too small to draw strong conclusions from, and record-keeping was poor, which raised the risk of "performance and accountability gaps".

However, it said results from a number of organisations, including Youth Junction, were "encouraging".

Mr Edwards argued that re-offending should not be the only way of measuring success.

"Offending behaviour is a really important part, but we also need to look at the level of risk that a young person presents with," he said.

"Have they re-engaged with education and employment? Have they reconnected with their family and their communities? Have they disengaged from harmful peers?

"If we're seeing positive changes in those spaces, then what will eventually happen is offending behaviour will reduce.

"Intervention takes time."

One Nation also wants to lower the age of criminal responsibility from 12 to 10, arguing that a child "knows the difference between right and wrong".

But Mr Edwards said children were not physiologically capable of making complex decisions.

"A young person's brain is under rapid development and the area of responsibility for complex thought is diverted to the area that's responsible for how you feel," he said.

" When a kid makes a decision, it's one based on feelings. "

The Youth Junction program is based in Sunshine. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Now 24, Falé said coming to Youth Junction stopped her life spiralling further.

"It was a big difference because, coming here, I was focusing on myself and I didn't have to worry about my siblings," she said.

"This is probably the first place that made me think about what I really wanted to do for my future."

The auditor-general's report also singled out the programs at Banksia Gardens Community Services in Broadmeadows as showing promise.

Falé says spending time at Youth Junction allowed her to focus on her future. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Banksia Gardens youth program manager Paul Atkinson told the ABC there was no evidence that harsher punishments reduced crime.

"Accountability is important," he said.

"But if we concentrate all of our efforts at the end point after a serious crime has been done, we're not actually addressing the issue of crime, we're just making ourselves feel better."

Mr Atkinson said spending time in custody often led to further offending.

"They become associated with other people who are also offending. They're developing a self-identity as an offender," he said.

Maw says he was at a delinquent before a church youth justice program intervened. (ABC News: Sacha Payne)

Maw is a 25-year-old father of two with a passion for music and his Christian faith.

But as a 14-year-old with time on his hands, he drifted into drugs and crime.

"I was disengaged from school," Maw said.

"My mum was working, so often I was left at home by myself, and one day I just came across the wrong crowd."

Maw dropped out of basketball due to a lack of funds. (Supplied)

He soon began coming into contact with police, but it had little impact on his behaviour.

He ended up at rock bottom.

"I was a delinquent," he said.

" I didn't care about the outcome. Being young, you don't really comprehend the consequences. "

Eventually Maw found his way to a church youth justice program.

He is now a youth leader, along with 24-year-old Nachida, who also got into serious trouble as a teen.

"I started to get myself involved in the wrong crowd — smoking, drinking, partying," Nachida explained.

"Starts off small, but one thing leads to another and things got worse along the line."

Nachida says he wishes he had received support earlier. (ABC News: Sacha Payne)

Nachida and Maw both believed early intervention and support could have helped them, and others, avoid a lot of grief.

"It does take time," Nachida said. "But I knew that I wanted to change."

World.title: Alcaraz digs deep to beat Shelton and reach ATP Finals decider
World.content:
Seven-times grand slam champion Carlos Alcaraz battled back from a set down to beat American Ben Shelton 3-6, 6-3, 7-6 (7-1) in their ATP Finals semifinal to charge into ​Sunday's showcase for the ‌second consecutive year.

Alcaraz, beaten by Shelton in the US Open quarterfinals on the Spaniard's return from a four-month injury break, stretched his winning run to 13 matches after ‌back-to-back titles in Vienna and Paris.

He will face either world number ⁠one Alexander Zverev or Daniil Medvedev of Russia, who meet ‌in the other semifinal.

"I was a ​little bit frustrated at ‌the beginning because I didn't start the match the way I wanted to," said Alcaraz, unbeaten on indoor courts this season.

"Just happy that I came back in the second set playing such great tennis, step by step, ​focused ‌on all my things and ended up playing good tennis. The third set was even closer."

Shelton, making his second consecutive appearance in the ⁠season finale, grabbed an early break to ‌race to a 3-0 lead.

Alcaraz, ‌whose fitness had come under scrutiny after he left the court with heavy ‌strapping on his left leg following Wednesday's win over Medvedev, had his thigh wrapped heavily against Shelton.

He upped his game and ‌started ​moving the American around ⁠more, engaging him in longer rallies. He earned two break points at 4-2 but could not convert either, with Shelton's booming serve getting him out of trouble.

The world number four fired a second-serve ace ⁠on his first set point to move ahead but Alcaraz went 5-3 up in the second before ‌serving out the ‌second set.

The pair traded blows in the third set ​before Alcaraz eased through the tie-break, sealing the win with a return winner.

World.title: Meet the scientists working to save the corpse flower from extinction
World.content:
Rotting fish. Dirty socks. Mouldy carpet. Dead Rat. None of these things smell very nice, but they are some of the words used to describe the stench of a corpse flower in bloom in the Geelong Botanic Gardens this week.

Thousands of Victorians lined up to get into a humid 27-degrees-Celsius green house, putting up with persistent mosquitos and intermittent mist from the overhead watering system.

"People say it's like rotten flesh, but I would say it's a little bit more like just general funk stench, like the bottom of a teenage boy's school bag," said John Tucker from Geelong.

The excitement among the crowds was palpable.

The plant, named Pete by his keepers, did not disappoint.

John Tucker says the corpse flower smells like a "teenage boy's school bag". (ABC News: Jonathon Kendall)

"It's quite impressive," Mr Tucker said.

"I didn't think it was going to be as impressive as it is.

"And the stench when you come in is a little bit overpowering."

An imposing presence, Pete was the star of the show and refused to be overawed by the moment.

When he had finished flowering he even took a bow, collapsing on Friday morning.

The titan arum only blooms for up to two days every seven to 10 years. (ABC News: Jonathon Kendall)

Saving the flower

Corpse flowers, also known as titan arums or Amorphophallus titanum, do not just have a rare odour: scientists estimate there are fewer than 1,000 left in their native jungles of Indonesia.

They have become endangered because of poaching, climate change and deforestation for palm oil, timber or agriculture.

Their stubbornly infrequent reproductive cycle has also played a role, with the flower only blooming for up to two days every seven to 10 years.

Behind the scenes, Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria research scientist Dr Rebecca Miller has been working on a conservation mission to make sure others can experience the rare corpse flower bloom.

Rebecca Miller cut a window into the plant and monitored its temperature. (ABC News: Jonathon Kendall)

She monitored the plant's condition and temperature before performing some stinky surgery, using a scalpel to harvest Pete's pollen so it could be kept safe as an insurance policy against extinction.

It is the first time pollen from the corpse flower will be stored at the Victorian Conservation Seedbank at the Royal Botanic Gardens of Victoria in Melbourne.

Dr Miller said she planned to experiment with how to store it best.

Yellow male flowers on the inside of the titan arum releasing pollen with the darker female flowers below. (Supplied: Dr Rebecca Miller)

"We'll be storing it at different temperatures, minus 20, minus 80, changing the relative humidity or moisture content of the pollen," she said.

"Hopefully we're able to store it for a few years and it can be used to pollinate flowers that might flower in other botanic gardens around the world."

But Dr Miller said corpse flowers in captivity often had the equivalent of "a low sperm count".

"I think the viability will be low, which is what seems to be typical of the species and what's been found elsewhere with these titan arums," she said.

"But I'm hopeful that we'll be able to retain some that we can use going forward."

Lucy Griffiths predicted in May the plant would flower this year. (ABC News/Jonathon Kendall)

The Geelong Botanic Gardens staff said they were proud of the role they were playing in saving the corpse flower from extinction.

"I think the fact that this plant is endangered in the wild creates a bit more interest and people want to learn about why that is and it makes us feel special that we can house it and be a part of the conservation effort of this plant," said Geelong Botanic Gardens horticulturalist Lucy Griffiths.

Dr Miller is hoping having Pete in the spotlight will also bring attention to Australia's natives that use similar reproductive techniques, such as Lazarum wilbertii, which is endemic to northern Australia.

It mimics the smell of herbivore dung to trick flies into providing pollination services.

"They're rare and they're beautiful," Dr Miller said.

"The Arum family, the Araceae family, is distributed globally and we have a really special contribution to that family within Australia that I think are underappreciated."

World.title: Far from home and family, islanders find community in SA's food bowl
World.content:
Blue and white strips of fly screen flap in the breeze as island reggae music spills out on to the street.

In the afternoon sun, a group of weary workers laugh and joke as they tuck into lunch: fish lolo, goat curry and taro.

The shop, with its street dining, is officially called the Pacifics Food and Gift store but for Pacific Australian Labour Mobility (PALM) scheme workers, it is a home away from home.

The PALM scheme draws on labour from nine Pacific Island countries and Timor Leste to fill short- and long-term workforce shortages, predominantly in the agricultural industry.

It was not that long ago store owner, Sione Fahoko, was one of those workers. He remembers what it was like to arrive in South Australia's Riverland and, not knowing anyone, he felt isolated.

Sione Fahoko grew up eating homegrown produce in the village of Lotofoa in the Haʻapai islands of Tonga. (ABC Rural: Eliza Berlage)

It was 2020 when he first came to Australia from Tonga. Three years later he met his wife Helen at a local pub.

Mr Fahoko's life looks very different now, swapping long days in the sun picking fruit to owning and running his own shop with his wife, Helen; the two of them creating the very place he could have used when he first arrived in the country.

"It's all for my little family and all for my Pacific people," he reflected.

" We want them to come [here] and feel like they come home from home. "

What is the PALM scheme? With its origins in the Pacific seasonal worker program established in 2008, it helps fill labour shortages in regional Australia by recruiting workers from Pacific nations and Timor-Leste.

The federal government says it is beneficial for both employers and workers, but critics argue the scheme can leave participants vulnerable because their employment, accommodation and visa status are closely linked.

Creating a village

More than 32,000 men and women were employed through the PALM scheme this year, which promotes economic growth for participants and their families.

But Mr Fahoko said he was worried about the social wellbeing of workers who felt disconnected from their culture while away from home.

"There is nothing to do. We just fish and drink," he said.

It's a sentiment shared by other Pacific Islanders, feeling both homesick and ill from the drastic change in diet.

"When I first met my wife, I feel sick, I feel broke most of the time," Mr Fahoko said.

"I asked my wife, I begged my wife, 'Love, can you please go hunting for Pacific food?'"

Helen Fahoko says stocking specialty food from Fiji is costly but worth it to see the smile on customers' faces. (ABC Rural: Em Jensen)

For Helen Fahoko, opening the store has also opened her heart to her husband's culture and she has been proud to see the impact it has had on the people who walk through the doors.

Cooking meals from his home country has also allowed her to connect more deeply with him and see him in his element.

"We just love seeing [customers] come in and be like, 'Oh my gosh, it's like being at home in my village'," she said.

"They definitely need something to make them feel a part of this community and not just that they're here to work and get their money.

"[Sione] gets quite excited about it because he's able to be like, 'This is me providing our home food to my own Pacific brothers and sisters'."

Helen Fahoko says the local community have responded positively to the store. (ABC Rural: Em Jensen)

Big boost to small businesses

In the next town over, PALM workers have also become a mainstay of Tushar Patel's supermarket and laundromat business at Renmark.

After 4pm most days, a flock of white transit vans pull up outside his shop, signalling a rush hour he has grown accustomed to.

Tushar Patel (left) appreciates the winter boost in trade PALM scheme workers provide. (ABC Riverland: Oliver Brown)

To serve this customer base, Mr Patel has added specialty grocery items and also expanded his money transfer options, from one platform to three to better cater for different home countries.

"Winter is always slow for any retailers … [during] that time they [PALM workers] come here and they push your business up. That's very important," he said.

" When they have a pay day, probably a hundred or more customers [come in]. "

Charity by the container full

Nearby, Annette Axon helps run the Renmark opportunity shop, the proceeds from which go towards community organisation Renmark Paringa Independent Living, which builds units for the aging population.

A PALM worker browses the racks at the Renmark op shop. (ABC Rural: Eliza Berlage)

The charity store manager said their business has been welcomed, and she has befriended many PALM workers.

"They're in nearly every day, every week and they just want everything," she laughed.

"They buy things like clothes and shoes to send home in shipping containers because it's very expensive over there to get anything, apparently."

For many workers who first arrive in the region, Ms Axon said her shop was often their first port of call to buy jackets and blankets to handle the colder winter.

"They're walking around with dressing gowns and beanies on and they're quite happy to just be comfy and they're not shy," she said.

Customers find all sorts of treasures in the op shop. (ABC Rural: Eliza Berlage)

"It's been a blast having them come in all year. They go home and then some of them come back and they're so lovely, so polite."

Back at the Pacific store, Mr and Ms Fahoko dream about expanding their small business.

Sione and Helen Fahoko care for four children and have another one on the way. (ABC Rural: Em Jensen)

Additionally, Mr Fahoko has his sights set on starting a touch football competition, to give Pacific Islanders more fun when they are not working.

"I'm very happy," he said.

"I'm so excited to live with my beautiful wife in Australia and run our business."

World.title: Wallabies v Wales LIVE updates: Welsh score stunner to take lead

Les Kiss will be satisfied by that first half effort. Yes, they’re in front. But more than that is that the Wallabies were convincingly beaten in that half of rugby yet they still lead. At dusk, the domes of the New Mosque glow above the ferry piers at Eminonu, and the Spice Bazaar next door, built to pay for the mosque’s upkeep, is still trading. Istanbul was capital to two empires, Rome’s and then the Ottomans’, and two nights here come before Allura sails west through the ancient worlds of Greece and Italy. Mediterranean in full colour. Oceania calls its style Small Ship Luxury. Launched in 2025 for guests 18 and over, Allura keeps one chef for every eight passengers, a history and heritage speaker briefs you on sea days, and in a French Veranda Stateroom, the floor-to-ceiling glass door slides open to the sea. One temple, many empires From below, the Parthenon’s columns look ruler-straight. Almost none are: they swell slightly and lean inwards. Built as Athena’s temple in the 5th century BC, it later served as a church, a mosque and an Ottoman gunpowder store, until a Venetian mortar blew the roof off in 1687.



At Olympia, walk through the vaulted stone tunnel into the stadium where about 45,000 spectators once watched from the earth banks. You can still race the 192+ metre marble track today. 



From Messina, a day trip climbs to Taormina’s ancient theatre, built by Greeks in the 3rd century BC and rebuilt by Romans, who turned its orchestra into an arena. From the top tiers, Etna rises behind the ruined stage and the Ionian coast curves away below. Pizza, then Pompeii Pompeii is a 35-minute train ride from Naples. Its streets still have the raised stepping stones Romans used to keep their feet out of the mud, spaced so cart wheels could pass between. Come evening, Allura’s poolside grill becomes a Neapolitan pizzeria. Brave, in the Bay of Naples. When in Rome Civitavecchia is about an hour and 45 minutes from Rome by train. At the Pantheon, light falls through a nine-metre opening in the dome, and on wet days so does the rain. Around the corner, Sant’Eustachio Il Caffe opened as a wood-fired coffee roaster in 1938. Its gran caffe arrives already sweetened, from a blend that’s still a secret today.



In Florence the next day, swap the espresso for a gelato and eat it on the Ponte Vecchio, where jewellers replaced the butchers in 1593 because the Medici disliked the smell. Two nights in Barcelona close the trip, time enough for the Boqueria, trading on La Rambla since 1217. Before that, on the last morning aboard, order breakfast to your stateroom, slide the glass door open on one last city. World.title: Naivety, larrikins and ‘blood in the water’: Inside the chaotic triumph of Melbourne 1956
World.content:
Betty Cuthbert winning the women s 100m track final at the 1956 Olympics, from And The Crowd Went Wild Sporting Days that Thrilled a Nation by Ian Heads and Gary Lester.

Barely more than a colony, a little over 50 years since federation, Melbourne was surprised when the world came for the Olympics – and even more surprised when they went stunningly well.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

If the world was sceptical in 1954 that a small colonial outpost in the southern hemisphere could host the world’s biggest sporting event, they were not alone. There was the least doubt about whether Australia’s athletes were world class. It was the rest of Australia they worried about. In July that year, two years before the 1956 Olympics, the Melbourne lord mayor, Robert Solly, summoned a meeting of the city’s key women’s groups. Representatives from the Country Women’s Association, the National Council of Women, the Girl Guides Association, the Young Women’s Christian Association and the Housewives Association (yes, you read that correctly) all gathered at the Town Hall. Then-premier John Cain snr spoke, partly to urge the women to understand their role at the forthcoming Games would be to make visitors welcome, but also to assuage the fears of hordes of foreigners in the city. The athletes’ village in 1955. THE AGE It was agreed a committee would be formed to co-ordinate the women’s groups of Melbourne during the Olympics. The Olympics Civics Committee was formed. No women were on it. The volunteer Housewives Brigade (again, not a typo) was also created to help make 6000 beds and tidy the rooms in the athletes’ village in Heidelberg.



The organisers were further worried there would be too few hotel beds for visitors for the Olympics and the city would need to encourage households to be prepared to open their doors to foreign tourists. This was a discussion partly to assuage the fears of locals, but also to ascertain which houses might be suitable for visitors. At the time, a quarter of houses in Melbourne had no refrigerator, two-thirds no hot running water in the bathroom and most had outside toilets. Women were recruited to keep the Olympic village clean for the athletes. The Age (As it turned out, the distance to travel and the price of flights meant few international visitors came for the Games other than the athletes and teams.) Organisers had invited the world, but had precious little idea of what hosting an Olympics involved. Two months from the Games, they didn’t have enough cooks – certainly not enough people who knew how to cook the food the foreign visitors needed. The White Australia Policy was still 10 years from being scrapped. The early influx of European migrants after World War II had begun to alter the vegetables seen in shops, but it had not yet shifted the regular evening meal far from chops and three veg. Roast lamb was as exotic as it got. It was August, barely more than two months before athletes were due to arrive, and the Olympic Organising Committee had still had not hired “Asiatic cooks” to prepare appropriate food. At the last minute, 10 cooks arrived, provided by a shipping line. It was emblematic of the Games being hastily cobbled together. The Indian Olympic team at the village. The Age



It was never certain the MCG would be the venue for the main stadium. There was discussion of the Showground, of St Kilda, and of building a 150,000-seat venue in Princes Park. Even Carlton’s No.1 ticket holder, prime minister Robert Menzies, saw the financial folly of that and agreed with Cain snr when he said it would be at the MCG or nowhere. That still did not best please the Victorian Cricketers Association and the MCC, which were uncomfortable with ripping up the pitch where Donald Bradman had played. When they did rip it up and lay a track, it did not best please the visiting athletes. The cinder track was poor. An aerial view of the opening ceremony. The Age But they got a track built in time. They had found a way. As they did finding cooks. As they did getting the Olympic torch to Melbourne, buying local maps from Shell service stations along the way to navigate a route from Cairns. As they did when the second-to-last torch relay runner was to enter Punt Road Oval to hand the torch to Ron Clarke – only to discover the gate padlocked (they had to shimmy through another turnstile). As they did cobbling together an equestrian event to be staged in Stockholm, Sweden, because quarantine laws would not allow the horses into Australia in time. Historian and journalist Dr Nick Richardson, author of the excellent book 1956, observed the city’s “naïveté was its greatest asset”. Australia was barely more than 50 years from Federation when it invited the world to visit. Sport would be the enticement but also the vehicle to hesitantly seek the world’s approval for the fledgling city and federated country.



Moving furniture into the Olympic village. The Age An Olympic arts festival was opened before the Games began. The Victorian governor, Sir Dallas Brooks, addressed the opening, saying: “Australia is only a young country and we are very proud of our achievements, but we are fully conscious of our shortcomings. So we hope you will find something to enjoy and admire in the exhibitions, and we all look forward to learning something from your friendly criticisms.” The journalist A.A. Phillips had coined the term “cultural cringe” in a Meanjin article six years earlier. Perhaps Sir Dallas considered it advice, not criticism. “There was an attitude that they knew what we were not, but they wanted the world to come and tell us we were OK,” Richardson said. “It was that desperate search for a pat on the head.” The grasping need for international approval partly missed a shift already occurring in Australia. Ray Lawler’s Summer of the Seventeenth Doll was showing, though the cast had to be persuaded to perform with Australian accents and not affect their voices with grand English flourish. It was for the Games that Barry Humphries debuted Edna Everage in an “Olympic Sketch”, turning a mocking mirror on suburban Australia. The arrival of TV in Australia also presented the housewife from Moonee Ponds to a national audience, lampooning the same cringe A.A. Phillips had chronicled. Progress map of the Olympic torch relay. The Age



It spoke to a larrikinism that was drawn out by the Games. As the convoy of Olympic torchbearers wended through the streets of Sydney, a university student called Barry Larkin – a surname deserving of an extra, silent R and I – dressed in the same long grey trousers, white shirt and green tie of the official relay runners, appeared on the streets with friends. He was bearing a torch made from a plum pudding tin atop a chair leg and carrying a flame lit from three pairs of army-issue underpants soaked in kerosene. The police duly provided him and his cohort of friends an escort. At the town hall, he handed the “torch” over to lord mayor Pat Hills, who began a short speech as silver paint from the chair leg flecked onto his hands. Alerted to the hoax, the unamused mayor chastised “our friends at the university who apparently think this is funny”. (Pat, it still is.) The real torch arrived minutes later. Those who had been in Helsinki for the Games four years earlier recalled the excoriating critique of US journalist Tom Van Dycke in Variety magazine that the midnight sun was the height of entertainment in a city with no licensed cafes or bars and only government-controlled venues selling alcohol. Henry Bolte at a meeting at the MCG new construction in 1955. Age Archives Even the Victorian government feared what would be made of the six o’clock swill. The pubs of the state closed at 6pm, creating the nightly rush to drink as many beers in as short a time as possible after work and before the pub doors closed. NSW had extended opening hours to 10pm the year before and Victorian premier Henry Bolte held a referendum in early 1956 proposing the same change in time for the Olympics. It was voted down by 60 per cent of voters. Only six of the state’s 66 electoral zones voted in favour of change. The suburbs were not for turning, or for late drinking.

World.title: The one topic no one wants to talk about at the Rabbitohs
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Opinion The one topic no one wants to talk about at the Rabbitohs Danny Weidler Sport columnist November 22, 2026 — 5:30am

November 22, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

If rugby league superstar Latrell Mitchell is re-signed by the Rabbitohs, we will know undoubtedly that the club’s ultimate power broker is Wayne Bennett. Forget the high-profile owners, the brainy board members, the combative chief executive Blake Solly and anyone else you can name. South Sydney coach Wayne Bennett is backing Latrell Mitchell to stay at the club beyond 2028. Sitthixay Ditthavong Mitchell is at the centre of a back-room split at Maroubra. On one side is Bennett, the most experienced coach in rugby league and the man who has championed Mitchell since he joined the club from the Roosters in 2020.



On the other, Souths officials and heavies who are not convinced Mitchell should be retained by the Rabbitohs beyond his deal, which expires at the end of 2027. It’s a topic not many want to flesh out because of the backlash. Latrell Mitchell in camp with Australia’s World Cup squad. Getty Images In the middle is the talented player, who is well aware of where his friends are, who is working for him and who isn’t. Bennett has unwavering faith in Mitchell that is not shared by some at the club.



Mitchell has had it relayed to him to ignore the talk that he is up for sale next year. Some at Souths have been actively hoping Mitchell has a poor off-season so the decision to take a wait-and-see approach to his re-signing is vindicated. Latrell Mitchell has had an injury-disrupted few seasons for South Sydney. Getty Images Here is where it gets interesting. Mitchell, who was named on Australia’s extended bench, was a late scratching from the Kangaroos squad for the World Cup final last Sunday due to a virus. There were suggestions he missed the game for other reasons, but this was denied by team management, the coach Kevin Walters and Mitchell. Souths were aware of the rumours, and to be frank, they weren’t exactly trying to hose down the situation.



Related Article Analysis

NRL 2027 Every team’s 2027 draw ranked – why the Bears are cheering and rivals left crying Expect the Rabbitohs to strongly deny the contents of this article, but what is important is that anything written here will not be news to Mitchell or those close to him. Mitchell cut a lonely figure when he travelled back to Sydney from Brisbane by himself. I bumped into him at the airport, but he was not interested in chatting. I aimed to ask him about entering the off season without a deal for 2028. He took his ear pods out, paused his chat, had a brief conversation and shook my hand. “I’m on holidays bra,” was his official denial of any contract unease.



In the past, Souths would’ve leapt to Mitchell’s defence when his name was being tossed up as a potential person to exit the club to make way for possible targets, such as Roosters half Sam Walker. But it appears Souths are either happy for that narrative to be spread or are fuelling it themselves. Mitchell cryptically posted on social media a picture of a coffee cup with the Souths emblem on it on Wednesday morning, indicating he was back in the Bunnies’ set-up. His love for the club, or should I say, its playing group and Bennett, is not to be questioned. It’s been an uncomfortable few seasons for Mitchell in the back channels. You remember Sam Burgess kicked up a stink with Souths management in 2023 about rules for some and rules for others, in particular the perceived favourable treatment by the club towards Mitchell and Cody Walker.



Mitchell knows he has not been value for money because of injury. And the club has stood by him through situations he has caused himself, including in 2024 after a photograph of him standing over a white substance in a Dubbo hotel room emerged. He has also had to deal with horrendous racism on social media. The person who has not lost faith in Mitchell is Bennett. His voice and opinion carry enormous weight. The word out of South Sydney headquarters is Mitchell is determined to prove Bennett right and the doubters wrong. It would be a surprise if he didn’t decide to hit the training paddock early.



The 29-year-old is entitled to stay on leave until the new year after being part of the Kangaroos squad for the past month. However, it’s likely he’ll be back training within the next three weeks to show how serious he is about making himself an irresistible option to keep at the Rabbitohs. That may be enough to save his Rabbitohs career and win officials over. Souths seem like the natural home for Mitchell, but with everything going on behind the scenes, he may look elsewhere. Shades of Gray at Rabbitohs The names tossed up to make room in the salary cap to allow the Rabbitohs to bid for Sam Walker have not included Jye Gray.



Until now. The tiny Souths fullback has been offered to rivals quietly. Just like with Latrell Mitchell, there is a difference of opinion between Bennett and Souths management. South Sydney fullback Jye Gray in action this season. Getty Images Bennett is known to have doubts over Gray and that showed with the use of Matt Dufty last season. If a club made a play for Gray, it would be interesting to see who would win the internal power struggle at Souths. Gray is on about $650,000 a year and while many admire his courage, it’s unknown exactly which clubs would pay that sort of money for him.



Manly lowball Turbo Manly’s salary cap crunch we told you about last week doesn’t just impact the players they are trying to shift. The Sea Eagles are looking to free up space in the $12 million cap, with Jamal Fogarty, Luke Brooks and Ethan Bullemor among players they are prepared to release early. Manly’s Tom Trbojevic does not want to leave the Sea Eagles. Getty Images They have also lowballed one of their best, Tom Trbojevic. He has a deal of $850,000 a year sitting in front of him. There is no ratchet clause as part of that deal. So when the new salary cap kicks in from 2028 at possibly $15 million, the “old money” equivalent for the Manly superstar would be $700,000.



That’s mildly insulting for a player of his standing. His agent is working through that offer, but as it stands, there is no way he will accept it. Trbojevic is not one to complain, and every time I’ve asked him, he has said he wants to stay with Manly. He said as much when I interviewed him at the airport on Monday. Fox could be on the run Eels winger Josh Addo-Carr was expected back at training last Thursday, but by mutual agreement he didn’t attend. Josh Addo-Carr at Parramatta’s HQ earlier this month. Wolter Peeters



Addo-Carr is contracted for next season, but is free to find a new club. The former NSW and Australia winger produced a false-positive result for cocaine at a random police roadside test in September. Both the NRL and the club cleared him to return next season. In an ideal world, he will never return to the Eels and start with his new club. That would suit everyone. Gus’ Bulldogs business Phil Gould’s hectic work schedule may be in part why he collapsed at Paul Langmack’s funeral. It’s all part of his constant efforts to make the Bulldogs the strongest club possible.



Loading Gould met with Roosters chair Nick Politis last Thursday and if Sam Walker’s name was not mentioned, we’d be stunned. Gould’s view has been that Walker should be a Rooster in 2027. What is interesting, though, Gould is organising a meeting for Politis and the Bulldogs’ major sponsor, pub baron Arthur Laundy, this week. It would be incredible to hear what two of Sydney’s biggest businessmen have to say. Storm could lose big names Melbourne are bracing themselves for the loss of at least one of their big three off-contract players, with Stefano Utoikamanu expected to join the Roosters.



Related Article Analysis

NRL 2026 These subtle ploys proved Grant is the best. But is he what the Titans need? The concern is also real around Harry Grant as well, with the Titans interested in the Kangaroos hooker, and Cameron Munster may also move on. Meanwhile, the Roosters have had their eyes on Herbie Farnworth, but they are also one of 10 clubs looking at Jack Bostock. The Dolphins are speaking with confidence about retaining Farnworth, which is a shock. Why Teddy’s the best Now, a moment to pay tribute to champion Roosters, NSW and Australia fullback James Tedesco, who has retired from representative footy.



It’s not a widely held view, but he is the best fullback I’ve seen. He owns two of the greatest moments in Blues history, he’s won every award going, he’s skippered his country and he’s captained his team to a premiership. James Tedesco and Australia teammates at full-time last Sunday night. Cameron Spencer/Getty Images The bad games I’ve seen him play, you can count on one hand. The Billy Slater admirers can come at me, but I’d take Tedesco every day of the week.



Inspiring Fiji’s next generation We received a lovely email from Dean Sharman, the co-founder of the Vuvale Pacific 9s, scheduled to be held in Fiji in June 2027. The tournament, for under 9s, will honour retired Melbourne Storm star Tui Kamikamica through the Vuvale Pacific Rugby League Development Program. The tournament will feature nine teams from Fiji and an Australian side. Sharman said their aim was to grow the game in Fiji for children under 12, to create pathways into the Kaiviti Silvertails, who compete in the NSW Rugby League’s Jersey Flegg competition, and “ultimately, NRL clubs”.



“We regularly hold gala days and coaching clinics throughout Fiji,” Sharman wrote. “This December, we are creating history by introducing the first-ever rugby league team from Taveuni, the island where Tui grew up. “We will be travelling to Fiji on December 2 before holding a special jersey presentation in Tui’s village, officially welcoming the Taveuni Warriors into our development program.” Sharman said the program will see Kamikamica and 12 children from Taveuni fly to Lautoka for a coaching clinic on December 5.



“For these children, it’s an incredible opportunity to represent their island, develop their skills and experience opportunities that haven’t previously been available to them,” Sharman wrote. “It’s also a special moment for Tui, being able to give back to his community and inspire the next generation of Fijian rugby league players.” Teflon Todd’s dumb idea “Looking for the perfect truth doesn’t exist and we are not looking for that.” That was Cricket Australia boss Todd Greenberg spinning better than the late, great Shane Warne at the announcement of the dumbest idea we have heard for some time: a sandpaper forum where players can speak in a safe space, without repercussions, regarding the events of the 2018 Newlands Test.



Whoever thought of the forum should fess up. If it was Greenberg, he should make a quiet exit. Cricket Australia CEO Todd Greenberg speaks to the media. Getty Images In his rugby league days, both at club level at the Bulldogs and when he was NRL chief executive, Greenberg was known as “Teflon Todd”. He is a brilliant media performer, but at the press conference on Wednesday, not even Greenberg could sell the forum in a poor performance. Additionally, in typical Cricket Australia fashion, they called the media to Hobart and gave them one hour’s notice.



Not surprisingly, many credible reporters could not attend and ask the tough questions. And apart from a radio interview before his presser, Greenberg has been invisible during this two-week scandal following Usman Khawaja’s account in his autobiography that everyone on that tour in South Africa was aware of the use of sandpaper on the ball. Cummins’ crack at Smith It’s a side issue now given Cameron Bancroft’s recollections this week, but Pat Cummins′ comments nine days ago about team leadership and the way they were approaching Test cricket in 2018 were a slap in the face for the man who was captain of that side, Steve Smith. It was largely overlooked as everyone focused on who did what and when in terms of ball tampering. Cummins did not miss the regime that he was playing under in the early part of his Test career during his 69-minute press conference. It was impossible not to see that as a crack at Smith.

World.title: Cummins helped rebuild Australia’s cricket culture. It’s being tested now
World.content:
SportCricketBall tampering Opinion Cummins helped rebuild Australia’s cricket culture. It’s being tested now Geoff Lawson Cricket columnist November 22, 2026 — 5:30am

November 22, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The term “culture” could be a synonym for “behaviour”. The term gets overused and teams of all sorts get over diagnosed, and right now, it is over here beating Australian cricket to a comatose. The punters, the common people, the fans want our businesses, politicians and sporting bodies to be bound by an appropriate culture. Loading Winning cultures lead to winning athletes and productive people. Organisations create sound cultures though ethical leadership, that communicate clear guidelines as to what is expected of its people and what is unacceptable.



Sometimes the people listen, but don’t take much notice, humans being an irascible bunch who often value individuality over team. Much of a community’s ethics may be left unsaid, made obvious by years of compliance and examples set by antecedents. To live the behaviour is to carry the culture forward, the visible behaviour being the message and the method. Pat Cummins, Steve Smith, David Warner and Usman Khawaja in 2023. Getty Images In theory every cricketer is a guardian of the spirit of the game. It’s a nice theory that is tested continuously, and it’s being put under the microscope today. Watching the Rugby League World Cup, the culture of Pasifika peoples was revelatory.



During the matches powerful athletes crashed with a brutal physicality; there were no compromises on personal welfare – tough, relentless, driven by the fever of representing their nation and culture. To see the joy in the stands and on the streets from the followers and players themselves warmed the heart and gave relief from the conflicts of the suburbs and the cricket fields. Samoan and Tongan fans watch their teams battle in the Rugby League World Cup. Getty Images There was whooping and hollering, blasting of horns and seemingly trillions of flags leaping from lamp posts and car aerials fluttering with the message that trying to win is wonderful, and so is losing. It is a culture that will endure.



Australia’s Test team’s culture improved enormously, first under Tim Paine and now Pat Cummins, driven from within the squad rather than being left to the administrators. Those leaders at the top of Cricket Australia in 2018 should have been the people who outlined the expectations of the real owners of the sport – the fans – but they failed excruciatingly. The players were virtually given carte blanche to do as they pleased, and they did so with little reference to their long and exultant history. Noble, Bradman, Miller, Benaud and Border be buggered, what would those ancients know? The game is in flux now, but the speculations on the past aren’t going to help the transition for the next generation.





Cameron Green prods forward across his pads and is unable to play confidently off the back foot. He ducks his head while trying to hit the short stuff. His all-round package that looked so inspiring three years ago is not there. He doesn’t bowl any more. He is not an all-rounder. Cooper Connolly needs high regular bouncing pitches to prosper and a lot more time in the Sheffield Shield finishing school, finding ways to make runs and bowling with the red ball – he is not an all-rounder yet. The selectors have done him no favours by throwing him in at the deep end. Anchorman Steve Smith needs to settle in a silo with a bowling machine and zero outside noise. The batting needs a revamp now, youth is required, young men who will bring their own fresh bodies and minds.



Related Article Opinion

Australian cricket While the past haunts Australian cricket, its future is piling on runs in the Sheffield Shield Geoff Lawson Cricket columnist The bowlers have been mighty, but all are wounded by the Khawaja shrapnel. They will have to find reserves of motivation as their bodies fight the attrition of age. Arguments have been presented recently as to how the “age profile” (coach Andrew McDonald’s words) will be reformed, that notion may have to be moulded somewhat sooner if the Sandpapergate scandal fall-out spreads. Culture-driven selections could result in a messy and destructive watershed, echoing a period from 1977 to 1979 when World Series Cricket saw 35 first-class players take Kerry Packer’s offer of a decent living. The replacement Australian team fell back on Kim Hughes, Graham Yallop, Dav Whatmore, Graeme Wood and Rodney Hogg, and provided Allan Border the continuity that proved the pathway to become a legend. The culture of that team was adlib, the “Australian way” of toughness, resilience and individuality was the unstated foundation stone.



They played for each other and to prove that they were good enough to wear the baggy green, even while their selections were based on availability rather than performance. Allan Border in 1978. Fairfax Media They did well. The rebel tours of South Africa in 1985 and ’86 took another 16 players out of the talent pool and that hurt the Ashes series in 1985, the Richard Hadlee dominance for New Zealand of ’86 and the home Ashes loss in 86/87. Australia rebounded under Border to win the 1987 World Cup. The Border way was one of selfless, honest, unrelenting toil. He was the living, leading example of that culture. Years earlier, the underarm incident of 1981 under captain Greg Chappell rocked the spirit of the game but was hardly a failure of the cricket community culture. It was an individual’s lapse of judgment under pressure.



That’s about as human as it gets. Related Article Updated

Australian cricket Why Cricket Australia board provided ‘unanimous support’ for Cummins to remain as Test captain Pat Cummins has done a fine job in shaping the culture of today’s group. It doesn’t seem entirely fair that he should stand in the spotlight and be responsible for an event eight years ago, but it comes with the territory of his role as the captain. If he were to resign, then we may find the comparison between those previous turbulent times. I will leave you with the words of Australia’s most successful professional male golfer, Peter Thomson.



“In sport you will learn things on the way. You’ll learn about life and human frailty and all of the shortcuts that man has contrived. If you’re lucky you’ll learn about honour and trust and other high levels of behaviour – most of all you’ll learn about yourself.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: People often ask me why I go to church
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsReligion Opinion People often ask me why I go to church

Bronwyn Pike November 22, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

People often ask me why I go to church. After all, church attendance is in freefall in Australia with less than 39 per cent of people claiming any Christian affiliation. My parents were very committed evangelical Methodists and living as a Christian was the centre of our family life. Sundays were fully occupied with church-related activities, my bedtime songs were Christian choruses and I was well versed in Bible stories from an early age. Even as a young adult my friendships and social life were nearly all connected through the church. The question is often asked: why go to church. There are many answers. Getty Images Influenced by the radical Christian discipleship movement of the ’70s, I began to draw connections between political activism and the social justice underpinning of the gospel, but was less and less comfortable with the other attributes and beliefs assigned to being a good Christian. How could I sing Onward Christian Soldiers as a pacifist? How could I refer to God a father and male? How could I support a homophobic church? And how could I say the Apostles Creed when I didn’t believe in the virgin birth, that Jesus rose from the dead and that somehow after ascending to heaven he would come back to earth again?



What I do believe in is a just, compassionate and forgiving world which upholds the inherent equality and dignity of every single human being. This is the core of most of the world’s religions and in the hearts of many who have no religious adherence at all; I just happened to have been born in a country with Christian heritage. When I became a member of parliament, I worked with so many politicians, public servants and others who shared the same aspirations for a fairer society and were prepared to work in the complex and often unforgiving political environment for positive change. Like all institutions, including the church, it was imperfect, mistakes were made, priorities were not always noble, but frail humans put their best foot forward. Related Article Faith

Religion Two Americans, two journeys, but how many roads? Which leads me to why I go to church now. I believe it’s the narrative that I find most compelling and inspiring. It reminds me that there is much I can do to heal and build relationships, forgive and love others and those actions will hopefully make the world a better place. I am drawn to the life story of the man Jesus, who constantly reminded all who would listen that humans were closer to the divine when they cast aside selfishness, self-righteousness, jealously and prejudice in favour of harmony and acceptance. Jesus didn’t just say these words; he lived them and was prepared to sacrifice his own life for those beliefs.



As we grapple with the deep polarisation with our community, this message is even more powerful and potentially transformative. Going to church is not for everyone, but when I go the material world is silenced for a moment and I am prodded and nudged to be a better version of myself. Bronwyn Pike was a state Labor MP from 1999 to 2012 and a minister in the Bracks government.

World.title: I’m retired with two super funds. Should I move both into pension mode?
World.content:
November 22, 2026 — 5:03am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

I am a retired 66-year-old and have two industry super funds. I converted one to pension mode and receive about $70,000 per year, which is enough for me. The other one is still in accumulation mode. I know I pay tax on it. Should I move it into the pension fund (I know there is a series of steps to do this), or should I leave it to continue accumulating? If I moved it, my total minimum drawdown pension would be $90,000, which is too much, even with travel plans. I’d put the overflow in a term deposit. Doubling up on your super? That’s fine, as long as you know your numbers. Simon Letch Thanks for your question, this is a common source of debate. Typically, this decision is presented as very black and white, with those leaving funds in accumulation doing so out of ignorance. Yet, I’ve seen many people who, deliberately and after consideration, have chosen to leave some funds in accumulation post-retirement. Conventional wisdom would state that you should convert whatever accumulation accounts you can into a pension given the tax-free status pensions provide. Often, however, people have some hesitation in making this move where they do not require the minimum income they would then be required to draw.



The key to solving this conundrum is thinking through what you will do with the excess income. Which is where I’m pleased that in your question you have specified that you would put the excess in a term deposit. Editor's pick Opinion

Ask an expert My mum died last year. Do we need to file her last tax return? Noel Whittaker Money columnist Given you have stated that shifting your remaining accumulation account across to pension will add $20,000 per year to your minimum income requirement, I can assume that this means your accumulation balance is approximately $400,000. If we use an assumption that this sum earns 7 per cent, with 15 per cent tax applicable on the earnings, then keeping it in accumulation results in tax payable by the fund of $4,200. Almost certainly this is overstated due to the impact of franking credits, but it will suffice for this exercise. As I mentioned, the key is deciding what you will do next with the excess income. If we assume that you place this money in a term deposit, where you earn 5 per cent, then you have forgone two percentage points of return that would have occurred had the money been left in superannuation.



Given $20,000 of income, this 2 per cent of forgone earnings is equivalent to $400 per year. Now this is only for year one, returns both inside super and on term deposits vary from year to year, and perhaps you have some tax to pay on the term deposit interest (although for most retirees that is not the case). Nonetheless, the difference ($3800) is sufficient to make the shift to pension sensible, I would have thought. The differential in earnings between super and what you would do with the surplus funds is the most important input here, but it is not the only consideration. Other factors are your personal tax position, your long-term goals, your investment time frame, and most importantly in my experience, your preference with regards to simplicity. Despite the numbers I have shared above, some people still prefer to leave excess funds in accumulation because it aligns with their goal of having a pool of funds growing, and it is administratively simple – they don’t have to deal with a personal tax return, and the money is professionally managed, with no input required from them. For many, paying a small amount of extra tax to keep things simple is a fair trade.



Paul Benson is a Certified Financial Planner at Guidance Financial Services – Retirement Planning specialists. He hosts the Financial Autonomy podcast. Questions to: paul@financialautonomy.com.au Advice given in this article is general in nature and not intended to influence readers’ decisions about investing or financial products. They should always seek their own professional advice that takes into account their own personal circumstances before making any financial decisions.
