World.title: Jensen Huang could lose half his fortune. Who says it was all his to begin with?
World.content:
MoneyInvestingExecutive shake-up Opinion Jensen Huang could lose half his fortune. Who says it was all his to begin with? Victoria Devine Money columnist November 22, 2026 — 5:01am

November 22, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

It’s been quite a couple of weeks for Jensen Huang. The billionaire co-founder of Nvidia, the company powering much of the artificial intelligence boom, has resigned as chief executive following revelations about his extramarital affairs. And while the technology industry has been busy debating what his departure means for the company, another conversation has caught my attention. How much money could his wife get if they divorce? Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang and his wife, Lori Huang, walk to the White House in September to attend a state dinner hosted for China’s President Xi Jinping. AP Some of the headlines have been extraordinary. With Huang’s fortune estimated in the hundreds of billions of dollars, commentators are speculating about whether his wife, Lori, could walk away with half. There’s a particular tone to some of this coverage that I find fascinating, as though we’re witnessing a man potentially lose an enormous portion of everything he’s worked for. Except Jensen and Lori have been married for more than 40 years. They met while studying engineering, married years before Nvidia was founded in 1993 and raised two children together.



Lori is an engineer in her own right, and the family lived through the company’s early struggles long before artificial intelligence made her husband one of the wealthiest people on the planet. I don’t pretend to know the private financial arrangements of their marriage. There’s no confirmed divorce, and the existence or terms of any prenuptial agreement haven’t been established publicly. But I find the assumption that this is entirely his fortune rather telling. What I am questioning is why our instinct is to describe a potential settlement as a man losing part of his fortune. Because who decided that the person whose name is on the company is the only person who built the wealth? Coincidentally, this week I answered a question on my podcast from a woman whose circumstances couldn’t be further removed from Silicon Valley billionaires, but whose story raised almost the same issue.



Her husband wanted them to enter into a binding financial agreement stipulating that if their marriage ended, he would receive 70 per cent of their home, and she would receive 30 per cent. His reasoning, as she explained it, was that he earned more money while she took responsibility for the domestic work. I had a pretty strong reaction to that. Not because I think every couple should automatically split everything down the middle. There are plenty of legitimate reasons to discuss how assets would be divided, particularly where one person brings substantially more into a relationship. I’m a big believer in couples having honest financial conversations and getting proper legal advice. What bothered me was the suggestion that because her contribution didn’t arrive in the family bank account every fortnight, it somehow counted for less. If one person is managing the household, caring for children, organising appointments, doing the school runs and generally keeping family life functioning, that frees up an extraordinary amount of time for the other person to focus on their career. Time they can spend working longer hours, pursuing promotions, travelling for business or building a company.



That arrangement might suit both people perfectly. But it’s still an arrangement in which both people contribute to the family’s financial position. Editor's pick Opinion

Budgeting We want to know if a recession is coming. It’s the wrong question Victoria Devine Money columnist And the person doing the unpaid work often pays a very real price for it. Reduced working hours can mean missed promotions, slower salary growth, smaller superannuation balances and fewer opportunities to develop a career. Those consequences don’t disappear simply because the couple has agreed that one person’s job is to earn the money and the other’s is to look after everything else. As someone who has worked in financial advice and now mortgage broking, I’ve seen how easily couples fall into describing money as belonging to whoever earns it. We discuss his salary or her business without always acknowledging the decisions and sacrifices that made those things possible. I also think we need to be honest about the fact that this isn’t exclusively a women’s issue. There are men who put their careers on hold to raise children or support a higher-earning partner, and their contributions deserve the same recognition. The principle shouldn’t change depending on who’s doing the laundry.



Australian family law, thankfully, takes a broader view than simply comparing payslips. When courts determine property settlements, they consider financial and non-financial contributions, including homemaking and parenting, alongside the parties’ circumstances and future needs. There is no automatic entitlement to a 50-50 split, and properly made binding financial agreements can alter how property is dealt with. That’s precisely why anyone considering one should obtain independent legal advice before signing. When it comes to a divorce, don’t expect a 50-50 split. istock But the fact that our legal system recognises unpaid contributions doesn’t mean our attitudes have caught up. We still have a tendency to celebrate the person with the impressive salary, the successful business or the enormous investment portfolio, while treating the work happening behind the scenes as something separate from the financial success.



And I find that particularly frustrating because the value of that work becomes painfully obvious the moment someone has to pay another person to do it. Childcare, cleaning, cooking, household administration. None of these services is free when you outsource them. Yet when they’re performed by a partner, we somehow become reluctant to recognise their economic value. I’m not suggesting Jensen Huang didn’t build something extraordinary. He did. Nor am I suggesting Lori Huang is automatically entitled to any particular share of their wealth. Those are questions for the people involved and, if necessary, their lawyers. What I am questioning is why our instinct is to describe a potential settlement as a man losing part of his fortune, rather than two people working out how to divide wealth accumulated during a very long marriage. It’s the same thinking that allows an ordinary Australian woman to be offered 30 per cent of her family home because the work she’s been doing apparently doesn’t count as earning. Perhaps we need to stop asking who brought home the most money and start asking what each person contributed to making that money possible.



Because if your partner’s career depends on you taking care of everything they don’t have time to do, you’re not standing on the sidelines of their financial success. You’re part of how it happened. Victoria Devine is an award-winning retired financial adviser, a bestselling author and host of Australia’s No.1 finance podcast, She’s on the Money. She is also founder and director of Zella Money. World.content:

At dusk, the domes of the New Mosque glow above the ferry piers at Eminonu, and the Spice Bazaar next door, built to pay for the mosque’s upkeep, is still trading. Istanbul was capital to two empires, Rome’s and then the Ottomans’, and two nights here come before Allura sails west through the ancient worlds of Greece and Italy. Mediterranean in full colour. Oceania calls its style Small Ship Luxury. Launched in 2025 for guests 18 and over, Allura keeps one chef for every eight passengers, a history and heritage speaker briefs you on sea days, and in a French Veranda Stateroom, the floor-to-ceiling glass door slides open to the sea. One temple, many empires From below, the Parthenon’s columns look ruler-straight. Almost none are: they swell slightly and lean inwards. Built as Athena’s temple in the 5th century BC, it later served as a church, a mosque and an Ottoman gunpowder store, until a Venetian mortar blew the roof off in 1687.



At Olympia, walk through the vaulted stone tunnel into the stadium where about 45,000 spectators once watched from the earth banks. You can still race the 192+ metre marble track today. 



From Messina, a day trip climbs to Taormina’s ancient theatre, built by Greeks in the 3rd century BC and rebuilt by Romans, who turned its orchestra into an arena. From the top tiers, Etna rises behind the ruined stage and the Ionian coast curves away below. Pizza, then Pompeii Pompeii is a 35-minute train ride from Naples. Its streets still have the raised stepping stones Romans used to keep their feet out of the mud, spaced so cart wheels could pass between. Come evening, Allura’s poolside grill becomes a Neapolitan pizzeria. Brave, in the Bay of Naples. When in Rome Civitavecchia is about an hour and 45 minutes from Rome by train. At the Pantheon, light falls through a nine-metre opening in the dome, and on wet days so does the rain. Around the corner, Sant’Eustachio Il Caffe opened as a wood-fired coffee roaster in 1938. Its gran caffe arrives already sweetened, from a blend that’s still a secret today.



In Florence the next day, swap the espresso for a gelato and eat it on the Ponte Vecchio, where jewellers replaced the butchers in 1593 because the Medici disliked the smell. Two nights in Barcelona close the trip, time enough for the Boqueria, trading on La Rambla since 1217. Before that, on the last morning aboard, order breakfast to your stateroom, slide the glass door open on one last city. World.title: Naivety, larrikins and ‘blood in the water’: Inside the chaotic triumph of Melbourne 1956
World.content:
Betty Cuthbert winning the women s 100m track final at the 1956 Olympics, from And The Crowd Went Wild Sporting Days that Thrilled a Nation by Ian Heads and Gary Lester.

Barely more than a colony, a little over 50 years since federation, Melbourne was surprised when the world came for the Olympics – and even more surprised when they went stunningly well.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

If the world was sceptical in 1954 that a small colonial outpost in the southern hemisphere could host the world’s biggest sporting event, they were not alone. There was the least doubt about whether Australia’s athletes were world class. It was the rest of Australia they worried about. In July that year, two years before the 1956 Olympics, the Melbourne lord mayor, Robert Solly, summoned a meeting of the city’s key women’s groups. Representatives from the Country Women’s Association, the National Council of Women, the Girl Guides Association, the Young Women’s Christian Association and the Housewives Association (yes, you read that correctly) all gathered at the Town Hall. Then-premier John Cain snr spoke, partly to urge the women to understand their role at the forthcoming Games would be to make visitors welcome, but also to assuage the fears of hordes of foreigners in the city. The athletes’ village in 1955. THE AGE It was agreed a committee would be formed to co-ordinate the women’s groups of Melbourne during the Olympics. The Olympics Civics Committee was formed. No women were on it. The volunteer Housewives Brigade (again, not a typo) was also created to help make 6000 beds and tidy the rooms in the athletes’ village in Heidelberg.



The organisers were further worried there would be too few hotel beds for visitors for the Olympics and the city would need to encourage households to be prepared to open their doors to foreign tourists. This was a discussion partly to assuage the fears of locals, but also to ascertain which houses might be suitable for visitors. At the time, a quarter of houses in Melbourne had no refrigerator, two-thirds no hot running water in the bathroom and most had outside toilets. Women were recruited to keep the Olympic village clean for the athletes. The Age (As it turned out, the distance to travel and the price of flights meant few international visitors came for the Games other than the athletes and teams.) Organisers had invited the world, but had precious little idea of what hosting an Olympics involved. Two months from the Games, they didn’t have enough cooks – certainly not enough people who knew how to cook the food the foreign visitors needed. The White Australia Policy was still 10 years from being scrapped. The early influx of European migrants after World War II had begun to alter the vegetables seen in shops, but it had not yet shifted the regular evening meal far from chops and three veg. Roast lamb was as exotic as it got. It was August, barely more than two months before athletes were due to arrive, and the Olympic Organising Committee had still had not hired “Asiatic cooks” to prepare appropriate food. At the last minute, 10 cooks arrived, provided by a shipping line. It was emblematic of the Games being hastily cobbled together. The Indian Olympic team at the village. The Age



It was never certain the MCG would be the venue for the main stadium. There was discussion of the Showground, of St Kilda, and of building a 150,000-seat venue in Princes Park. Even Carlton’s No.1 ticket holder, prime minister Robert Menzies, saw the financial folly of that and agreed with Cain snr when he said it would be at the MCG or nowhere. That still did not best please the Victorian Cricketers Association and the MCC, which were uncomfortable with ripping up the pitch where Donald Bradman had played. When they did rip it up and lay a track, it did not best please the visiting athletes. The cinder track was poor. An aerial view of the opening ceremony. The Age But they got a track built in time. They had found a way. As they did finding cooks. As they did getting the Olympic torch to Melbourne, buying local maps from Shell service stations along the way to navigate a route from Cairns. As they did when the second-to-last torch relay runner was to enter Punt Road Oval to hand the torch to Ron Clarke – only to discover the gate padlocked (they had to shimmy through another turnstile). As they did cobbling together an equestrian event to be staged in Stockholm, Sweden, because quarantine laws would not allow the horses into Australia in time. Historian and journalist Dr Nick Richardson, author of the excellent book 1956, observed the city’s “naïveté was its greatest asset”. Australia was barely more than 50 years from Federation when it invited the world to visit. Sport would be the enticement but also the vehicle to hesitantly seek the world’s approval for the fledgling city and federated country.



Moving furniture into the Olympic village. The Age An Olympic arts festival was opened before the Games began. The Victorian governor, Sir Dallas Brooks, addressed the opening, saying: “Australia is only a young country and we are very proud of our achievements, but we are fully conscious of our shortcomings. So we hope you will find something to enjoy and admire in the exhibitions, and we all look forward to learning something from your friendly criticisms.” The journalist A.A. Phillips had coined the term “cultural cringe” in a Meanjin article six years earlier. Perhaps Sir Dallas considered it advice, not criticism. “There was an attitude that they knew what we were not, but they wanted the world to come and tell us we were OK,” Richardson said. “It was that desperate search for a pat on the head.” The grasping need for international approval partly missed a shift already occurring in Australia. Ray Lawler’s Summer of the Seventeenth Doll was showing, though the cast had to be persuaded to perform with Australian accents and not affect their voices with grand English flourish. It was for the Games that Barry Humphries debuted Edna Everage in an “Olympic Sketch”, turning a mocking mirror on suburban Australia. The arrival of TV in Australia also presented the housewife from Moonee Ponds to a national audience, lampooning the same cringe A.A. Phillips had chronicled. Progress map of the Olympic torch relay. The Age



It spoke to a larrikinism that was drawn out by the Games. As the convoy of Olympic torchbearers wended through the streets of Sydney, a university student called Barry Larkin – a surname deserving of an extra, silent R and I – dressed in the same long grey trousers, white shirt and green tie of the official relay runners, appeared on the streets with friends. He was bearing a torch made from a plum pudding tin atop a chair leg and carrying a flame lit from three pairs of army-issue underpants soaked in kerosene. The police duly provided him and his cohort of friends an escort. At the town hall, he handed the “torch” over to lord mayor Pat Hills, who began a short speech as silver paint from the chair leg flecked onto his hands. Alerted to the hoax, the unamused mayor chastised “our friends at the university who apparently think this is funny”. (Pat, it still is.) The real torch arrived minutes later. Those who had been in Helsinki for the Games four years earlier recalled the excoriating critique of US journalist Tom Van Dycke in Variety magazine that the midnight sun was the height of entertainment in a city with no licensed cafes or bars and only government-controlled venues selling alcohol. Henry Bolte at a meeting at the MCG new construction in 1955. Age Archives Even the Victorian government feared what would be made of the six o’clock swill. The pubs of the state closed at 6pm, creating the nightly rush to drink as many beers in as short a time as possible after work and before the pub doors closed. NSW had extended opening hours to 10pm the year before and Victorian premier Henry Bolte held a referendum in early 1956 proposing the same change in time for the Olympics. It was voted down by 60 per cent of voters. Only six of the state’s 66 electoral zones voted in favour of change. The suburbs were not for turning, or for late drinking.

World.title: The one topic no one wants to talk about at the Rabbitohs
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Opinion The one topic no one wants to talk about at the Rabbitohs Danny Weidler Sport columnist November 22, 2026 — 5:30am

November 22, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

If rugby league superstar Latrell Mitchell is re-signed by the Rabbitohs, we will know undoubtedly that the club’s ultimate power broker is Wayne Bennett. Forget the high-profile owners, the brainy board members, the combative chief executive Blake Solly and anyone else you can name. South Sydney coach Wayne Bennett is backing Latrell Mitchell to stay at the club beyond 2028. Sitthixay Ditthavong Mitchell is at the centre of a back-room split at Maroubra. On one side is Bennett, the most experienced coach in rugby league and the man who has championed Mitchell since he joined the club from the Roosters in 2020.



On the other, Souths officials and heavies who are not convinced Mitchell should be retained by the Rabbitohs beyond his deal, which expires at the end of 2027. It’s a topic not many want to flesh out because of the backlash. Latrell Mitchell in camp with Australia’s World Cup squad. Getty Images In the middle is the talented player, who is well aware of where his friends are, who is working for him and who isn’t. Bennett has unwavering faith in Mitchell that is not shared by some at the club.



Mitchell has had it relayed to him to ignore the talk that he is up for sale next year. Some at Souths have been actively hoping Mitchell has a poor off-season so the decision to take a wait-and-see approach to his re-signing is vindicated. Latrell Mitchell has had an injury-disrupted few seasons for South Sydney. Getty Images Here is where it gets interesting. Mitchell, who was named on Australia’s extended bench, was a late scratching from the Kangaroos squad for the World Cup final last Sunday due to a virus. There were suggestions he missed the game for other reasons, but this was denied by team management, the coach Kevin Walters and Mitchell. Souths were aware of the rumours, and to be frank, they weren’t exactly trying to hose down the situation.



Related Article Analysis

NRL 2027 Every team’s 2027 draw ranked – why the Bears are cheering and rivals left crying Expect the Rabbitohs to strongly deny the contents of this article, but what is important is that anything written here will not be news to Mitchell or those close to him. Mitchell cut a lonely figure when he travelled back to Sydney from Brisbane by himself. I bumped into him at the airport, but he was not interested in chatting. I aimed to ask him about entering the off season without a deal for 2028. He took his ear pods out, paused his chat, had a brief conversation and shook my hand. “I’m on holidays bra,” was his official denial of any contract unease.



In the past, Souths would’ve leapt to Mitchell’s defence when his name was being tossed up as a potential person to exit the club to make way for possible targets, such as Roosters half Sam Walker. But it appears Souths are either happy for that narrative to be spread or are fuelling it themselves. Mitchell cryptically posted on social media a picture of a coffee cup with the Souths emblem on it on Wednesday morning, indicating he was back in the Bunnies’ set-up. His love for the club, or should I say, its playing group and Bennett, is not to be questioned. It’s been an uncomfortable few seasons for Mitchell in the back channels. You remember Sam Burgess kicked up a stink with Souths management in 2023 about rules for some and rules for others, in particular the perceived favourable treatment by the club towards Mitchell and Cody Walker.



Mitchell knows he has not been value for money because of injury. And the club has stood by him through situations he has caused himself, including in 2024 after a photograph of him standing over a white substance in a Dubbo hotel room emerged. He has also had to deal with horrendous racism on social media. The person who has not lost faith in Mitchell is Bennett. His voice and opinion carry enormous weight. The word out of South Sydney headquarters is Mitchell is determined to prove Bennett right and the doubters wrong. It would be a surprise if he didn’t decide to hit the training paddock early.



The 29-year-old is entitled to stay on leave until the new year after being part of the Kangaroos squad for the past month. However, it’s likely he’ll be back training within the next three weeks to show how serious he is about making himself an irresistible option to keep at the Rabbitohs. That may be enough to save his Rabbitohs career and win officials over. Souths seem like the natural home for Mitchell, but with everything going on behind the scenes, he may look elsewhere. Shades of Gray at Rabbitohs The names tossed up to make room in the salary cap to allow the Rabbitohs to bid for Sam Walker have not included Jye Gray.



Until now. The tiny Souths fullback has been offered to rivals quietly. Just like with Latrell Mitchell, there is a difference of opinion between Bennett and Souths management. South Sydney fullback Jye Gray in action this season. Getty Images Bennett is known to have doubts over Gray and that showed with the use of Matt Dufty last season. If a club made a play for Gray, it would be interesting to see who would win the internal power struggle at Souths. Gray is on about $650,000 a year and while many admire his courage, it’s unknown exactly which clubs would pay that sort of money for him.



Manly lowball Turbo Manly’s salary cap crunch we told you about last week doesn’t just impact the players they are trying to shift. The Sea Eagles are looking to free up space in the $12 million cap, with Jamal Fogarty, Luke Brooks and Ethan Bullemor among players they are prepared to release early. Manly’s Tom Trbojevic does not want to leave the Sea Eagles. Getty Images They have also lowballed one of their best, Tom Trbojevic. He has a deal of $850,000 a year sitting in front of him. There is no ratchet clause as part of that deal. So when the new salary cap kicks in from 2028 at possibly $15 million, the “old money” equivalent for the Manly superstar would be $700,000.



That’s mildly insulting for a player of his standing. His agent is working through that offer, but as it stands, there is no way he will accept it. Trbojevic is not one to complain, and every time I’ve asked him, he has said he wants to stay with Manly. He said as much when I interviewed him at the airport on Monday. Fox could be on the run Eels winger Josh Addo-Carr was expected back at training last Thursday, but by mutual agreement he didn’t attend. Josh Addo-Carr at Parramatta’s HQ earlier this month. Wolter Peeters



Addo-Carr is contracted for next season, but is free to find a new club. The former NSW and Australia winger produced a false-positive result for cocaine at a random police roadside test in September. Both the NRL and the club cleared him to return next season. In an ideal world, he will never return to the Eels and start with his new club. That would suit everyone. Gus’ Bulldogs business Phil Gould’s hectic work schedule may be in part why he collapsed at Paul Langmack’s funeral. It’s all part of his constant efforts to make the Bulldogs the strongest club possible.



Loading Gould met with Roosters chair Nick Politis last Thursday and if Sam Walker’s name was not mentioned, we’d be stunned. Gould’s view has been that Walker should be a Rooster in 2027. What is interesting, though, Gould is organising a meeting for Politis and the Bulldogs’ major sponsor, pub baron Arthur Laundy, this week. It would be incredible to hear what two of Sydney’s biggest businessmen have to say. Storm could lose big names Melbourne are bracing themselves for the loss of at least one of their big three off-contract players, with Stefano Utoikamanu expected to join the Roosters.



Related Article Analysis

NRL 2026 These subtle ploys proved Grant is the best. But is he what the Titans need? The concern is also real around Harry Grant as well, with the Titans interested in the Kangaroos hooker, and Cameron Munster may also move on. Meanwhile, the Roosters have had their eyes on Herbie Farnworth, but they are also one of 10 clubs looking at Jack Bostock. The Dolphins are speaking with confidence about retaining Farnworth, which is a shock. Why Teddy’s the best Now, a moment to pay tribute to champion Roosters, NSW and Australia fullback James Tedesco, who has retired from representative footy.



It’s not a widely held view, but he is the best fullback I’ve seen. He owns two of the greatest moments in Blues history, he’s won every award going, he’s skippered his country and he’s captained his team to a premiership. James Tedesco and Australia teammates at full-time last Sunday night. Cameron Spencer/Getty Images The bad games I’ve seen him play, you can count on one hand. The Billy Slater admirers can come at me, but I’d take Tedesco every day of the week.



Inspiring Fiji’s next generation We received a lovely email from Dean Sharman, the co-founder of the Vuvale Pacific 9s, scheduled to be held in Fiji in June 2027. The tournament, for under 9s, will honour retired Melbourne Storm star Tui Kamikamica through the Vuvale Pacific Rugby League Development Program. The tournament will feature nine teams from Fiji and an Australian side. Sharman said their aim was to grow the game in Fiji for children under 12, to create pathways into the Kaiviti Silvertails, who compete in the NSW Rugby League’s Jersey Flegg competition, and “ultimately, NRL clubs”.



“We regularly hold gala days and coaching clinics throughout Fiji,” Sharman wrote. “This December, we are creating history by introducing the first-ever rugby league team from Taveuni, the island where Tui grew up. “We will be travelling to Fiji on December 2 before holding a special jersey presentation in Tui’s village, officially welcoming the Taveuni Warriors into our development program.” Sharman said the program will see Kamikamica and 12 children from Taveuni fly to Lautoka for a coaching clinic on December 5.



“For these children, it’s an incredible opportunity to represent their island, develop their skills and experience opportunities that haven’t previously been available to them,” Sharman wrote. “It’s also a special moment for Tui, being able to give back to his community and inspire the next generation of Fijian rugby league players.” Teflon Todd’s dumb idea “Looking for the perfect truth doesn’t exist and we are not looking for that.” That was Cricket Australia boss Todd Greenberg spinning better than the late, great Shane Warne at the announcement of the dumbest idea we have heard for some time: a sandpaper forum where players can speak in a safe space, without repercussions, regarding the events of the 2018 Newlands Test.



Whoever thought of the forum should fess up. If it was Greenberg, he should make a quiet exit. Cricket Australia CEO Todd Greenberg speaks to the media. Getty Images In his rugby league days, both at club level at the Bulldogs and when he was NRL chief executive, Greenberg was known as “Teflon Todd”. He is a brilliant media performer, but at the press conference on Wednesday, not even Greenberg could sell the forum in a poor performance. Additionally, in typical Cricket Australia fashion, they called the media to Hobart and gave them one hour’s notice.



Not surprisingly, many credible reporters could not attend and ask the tough questions. And apart from a radio interview before his presser, Greenberg has been invisible during this two-week scandal following Usman Khawaja’s account in his autobiography that everyone on that tour in South Africa was aware of the use of sandpaper on the ball. Cummins’ crack at Smith It’s a side issue now given Cameron Bancroft’s recollections this week, but Pat Cummins′ comments nine days ago about team leadership and the way they were approaching Test cricket in 2018 were a slap in the face for the man who was captain of that side, Steve Smith. It was largely overlooked as everyone focused on who did what and when in terms of ball tampering. Cummins did not miss the regime that he was playing under in the early part of his Test career during his 69-minute press conference. It was impossible not to see that as a crack at Smith.

World.title: Cummins helped rebuild Australia’s cricket culture. It’s being tested now
World.content:
SportCricketBall tampering Opinion Cummins helped rebuild Australia’s cricket culture. It’s being tested now Geoff Lawson Cricket columnist November 22, 2026 — 5:30am

November 22, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The term “culture” could be a synonym for “behaviour”. The term gets overused and teams of all sorts get over diagnosed, and right now, it is over here beating Australian cricket to a comatose. The punters, the common people, the fans want our businesses, politicians and sporting bodies to be bound by an appropriate culture. Loading Winning cultures lead to winning athletes and productive people. Organisations create sound cultures though ethical leadership, that communicate clear guidelines as to what is expected of its people and what is unacceptable.



Sometimes the people listen, but don’t take much notice, humans being an irascible bunch who often value individuality over team. Much of a community’s ethics may be left unsaid, made obvious by years of compliance and examples set by antecedents. To live the behaviour is to carry the culture forward, the visible behaviour being the message and the method. Pat Cummins, Steve Smith, David Warner and Usman Khawaja in 2023. Getty Images In theory every cricketer is a guardian of the spirit of the game. It’s a nice theory that is tested continuously, and it’s being put under the microscope today. Watching the Rugby League World Cup, the culture of Pasifika peoples was revelatory.



During the matches powerful athletes crashed with a brutal physicality; there were no compromises on personal welfare – tough, relentless, driven by the fever of representing their nation and culture. To see the joy in the stands and on the streets from the followers and players themselves warmed the heart and gave relief from the conflicts of the suburbs and the cricket fields. Samoan and Tongan fans watch their teams battle in the Rugby League World Cup. Getty Images There was whooping and hollering, blasting of horns and seemingly trillions of flags leaping from lamp posts and car aerials fluttering with the message that trying to win is wonderful, and so is losing. It is a culture that will endure.



Australia’s Test team’s culture improved enormously, first under Tim Paine and now Pat Cummins, driven from within the squad rather than being left to the administrators. Those leaders at the top of Cricket Australia in 2018 should have been the people who outlined the expectations of the real owners of the sport – the fans – but they failed excruciatingly. The players were virtually given carte blanche to do as they pleased, and they did so with little reference to their long and exultant history. Noble, Bradman, Miller, Benaud and Border be buggered, what would those ancients know? The game is in flux now, but the speculations on the past aren’t going to help the transition for the next generation.





Cameron Green prods forward across his pads and is unable to play confidently off the back foot. He ducks his head while trying to hit the short stuff. His all-round package that looked so inspiring three years ago is not there. He doesn’t bowl any more. He is not an all-rounder. Cooper Connolly needs high regular bouncing pitches to prosper and a lot more time in the Sheffield Shield finishing school, finding ways to make runs and bowling with the red ball – he is not an all-rounder yet. The selectors have done him no favours by throwing him in at the deep end. Anchorman Steve Smith needs to settle in a silo with a bowling machine and zero outside noise. The batting needs a revamp now, youth is required, young men who will bring their own fresh bodies and minds.



Related Article Opinion

Australian cricket While the past haunts Australian cricket, its future is piling on runs in the Sheffield Shield Geoff Lawson Cricket columnist The bowlers have been mighty, but all are wounded by the Khawaja shrapnel. They will have to find reserves of motivation as their bodies fight the attrition of age. Arguments have been presented recently as to how the “age profile” (coach Andrew McDonald’s words) will be reformed, that notion may have to be moulded somewhat sooner if the Sandpapergate scandal fall-out spreads. Culture-driven selections could result in a messy and destructive watershed, echoing a period from 1977 to 1979 when World Series Cricket saw 35 first-class players take Kerry Packer’s offer of a decent living. The replacement Australian team fell back on Kim Hughes, Graham Yallop, Dav Whatmore, Graeme Wood and Rodney Hogg, and provided Allan Border the continuity that proved the pathway to become a legend. The culture of that team was adlib, the “Australian way” of toughness, resilience and individuality was the unstated foundation stone.



They played for each other and to prove that they were good enough to wear the baggy green, even while their selections were based on availability rather than performance. Allan Border in 1978. Fairfax Media They did well. The rebel tours of South Africa in 1985 and ’86 took another 16 players out of the talent pool and that hurt the Ashes series in 1985, the Richard Hadlee dominance for New Zealand of ’86 and the home Ashes loss in 86/87. Australia rebounded under Border to win the 1987 World Cup. The Border way was one of selfless, honest, unrelenting toil. He was the living, leading example of that culture. Years earlier, the underarm incident of 1981 under captain Greg Chappell rocked the spirit of the game but was hardly a failure of the cricket community culture. It was an individual’s lapse of judgment under pressure.



That’s about as human as it gets. Related Article Updated

Australian cricket Why Cricket Australia board provided ‘unanimous support’ for Cummins to remain as Test captain Pat Cummins has done a fine job in shaping the culture of today’s group. It doesn’t seem entirely fair that he should stand in the spotlight and be responsible for an event eight years ago, but it comes with the territory of his role as the captain. If he were to resign, then we may find the comparison between those previous turbulent times. I will leave you with the words of Australia’s most successful professional male golfer, Peter Thomson.



“In sport you will learn things on the way. You’ll learn about life and human frailty and all of the shortcuts that man has contrived. If you’re lucky you’ll learn about honour and trust and other high levels of behaviour – most of all you’ll learn about yourself.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: People often ask me why I go to church
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsReligion Opinion People often ask me why I go to church

Bronwyn Pike November 22, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

People often ask me why I go to church. After all, church attendance is in freefall in Australia with less than 39 per cent of people claiming any Christian affiliation. My parents were very committed evangelical Methodists and living as a Christian was the centre of our family life. Sundays were fully occupied with church-related activities, my bedtime songs were Christian choruses and I was well versed in Bible stories from an early age. Even as a young adult my friendships and social life were nearly all connected through the church. The question is often asked: why go to church. There are many answers. Getty Images Influenced by the radical Christian discipleship movement of the ’70s, I began to draw connections between political activism and the social justice underpinning of the gospel, but was less and less comfortable with the other attributes and beliefs assigned to being a good Christian. How could I sing Onward Christian Soldiers as a pacifist? How could I refer to God a father and male? How could I support a homophobic church? And how could I say the Apostles Creed when I didn’t believe in the virgin birth, that Jesus rose from the dead and that somehow after ascending to heaven he would come back to earth again?



What I do believe in is a just, compassionate and forgiving world which upholds the inherent equality and dignity of every single human being. This is the core of most of the world’s religions and in the hearts of many who have no religious adherence at all; I just happened to have been born in a country with Christian heritage. When I became a member of parliament, I worked with so many politicians, public servants and others who shared the same aspirations for a fairer society and were prepared to work in the complex and often unforgiving political environment for positive change. Like all institutions, including the church, it was imperfect, mistakes were made, priorities were not always noble, but frail humans put their best foot forward. Related Article Faith

Religion Two Americans, two journeys, but how many roads? Which leads me to why I go to church now. I believe it’s the narrative that I find most compelling and inspiring. It reminds me that there is much I can do to heal and build relationships, forgive and love others and those actions will hopefully make the world a better place. I am drawn to the life story of the man Jesus, who constantly reminded all who would listen that humans were closer to the divine when they cast aside selfishness, self-righteousness, jealously and prejudice in favour of harmony and acceptance. Jesus didn’t just say these words; he lived them and was prepared to sacrifice his own life for those beliefs.



As we grapple with the deep polarisation with our community, this message is even more powerful and potentially transformative. Going to church is not for everyone, but when I go the material world is silenced for a moment and I am prodded and nudged to be a better version of myself. Bronwyn Pike was a state Labor MP from 1999 to 2012 and a minister in the Bracks government.

World.title: I’m retired with two super funds. Should I move both into pension mode?
World.content:
November 22, 2026 — 5:03am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

I am a retired 66-year-old and have two industry super funds. I converted one to pension mode and receive about $70,000 per year, which is enough for me. The other one is still in accumulation mode. I know I pay tax on it. Should I move it into the pension fund (I know there is a series of steps to do this), or should I leave it to continue accumulating? If I moved it, my total minimum drawdown pension would be $90,000, which is too much, even with travel plans. I’d put the overflow in a term deposit. Doubling up on your super? That’s fine, as long as you know your numbers. Simon Letch Thanks for your question, this is a common source of debate. Typically, this decision is presented as very black and white, with those leaving funds in accumulation doing so out of ignorance. Yet, I’ve seen many people who, deliberately and after consideration, have chosen to leave some funds in accumulation post-retirement. Conventional wisdom would state that you should convert whatever accumulation accounts you can into a pension given the tax-free status pensions provide. Often, however, people have some hesitation in making this move where they do not require the minimum income they would then be required to draw.



The key to solving this conundrum is thinking through what you will do with the excess income. Which is where I’m pleased that in your question you have specified that you would put the excess in a term deposit. Editor's pick Opinion

Ask an expert My mum died last year. Do we need to file her last tax return? Noel Whittaker Money columnist Given you have stated that shifting your remaining accumulation account across to pension will add $20,000 per year to your minimum income requirement, I can assume that this means your accumulation balance is approximately $400,000. If we use an assumption that this sum earns 7 per cent, with 15 per cent tax applicable on the earnings, then keeping it in accumulation results in tax payable by the fund of $4,200. Almost certainly this is overstated due to the impact of franking credits, but it will suffice for this exercise. As I mentioned, the key is deciding what you will do next with the excess income. If we assume that you place this money in a term deposit, where you earn 5 per cent, then you have forgone two percentage points of return that would have occurred had the money been left in superannuation.



Given $20,000 of income, this 2 per cent of forgone earnings is equivalent to $400 per year. Now this is only for year one, returns both inside super and on term deposits vary from year to year, and perhaps you have some tax to pay on the term deposit interest (although for most retirees that is not the case). Nonetheless, the difference ($3800) is sufficient to make the shift to pension sensible, I would have thought. The differential in earnings between super and what you would do with the surplus funds is the most important input here, but it is not the only consideration. Other factors are your personal tax position, your long-term goals, your investment time frame, and most importantly in my experience, your preference with regards to simplicity. Despite the numbers I have shared above, some people still prefer to leave excess funds in accumulation because it aligns with their goal of having a pool of funds growing, and it is administratively simple – they don’t have to deal with a personal tax return, and the money is professionally managed, with no input required from them. For many, paying a small amount of extra tax to keep things simple is a fair trade.



Paul Benson is a Certified Financial Planner at Guidance Financial Services – Retirement Planning specialists. He hosts the Financial Autonomy podcast. World.title: Jensen Huang could lose half his fortune. Who says it was all his to begin with?
World.content:
MoneyInvestingExecutive shake-up Opinion Jensen Huang could lose half his fortune. Who says it was all his to begin with? Victoria Devine Money columnist November 22, 2026 — 5:01am

November 22, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

It’s been quite a couple of weeks for Jensen Huang. The billionaire co-founder of Nvidia, the company powering much of the artificial intelligence boom, has resigned as chief executive following revelations about his extramarital affairs. And while the technology industry has been busy debating what his departure means for the company, another conversation has caught my attention. How much money could his wife get if they divorce? Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang and his wife, Lori Huang, walk to the White House in September to attend a state dinner hosted for China’s President Xi Jinping. AP Some of the headlines have been extraordinary. With Huang’s fortune estimated in the hundreds of billions of dollars, commentators are speculating about whether his wife, Lori, could walk away with half. There’s a particular tone to some of this coverage that I find fascinating, as though we’re witnessing a man potentially lose an enormous portion of everything he’s worked for. Except Jensen and Lori have been married for more than 40 years. They met while studying engineering, married years before Nvidia was founded in 1993 and raised two children together.



Lori is an engineer in her own right, and the family lived through the company’s early struggles long before artificial intelligence made her husband one of the wealthiest people on the planet. I don’t pretend to know the private financial arrangements of their marriage. There’s no confirmed divorce, and the existence or terms of any prenuptial agreement haven’t been established publicly. But I find the assumption that this is entirely his fortune rather telling. What I am questioning is why our instinct is to describe a potential settlement as a man losing part of his fortune. Because who decided that the person whose name is on the company is the only person who built the wealth? Coincidentally, this week I answered a question on my podcast from a woman whose circumstances couldn’t be further removed from Silicon Valley billionaires, but whose story raised almost the same issue.



Her husband wanted them to enter into a binding financial agreement stipulating that if their marriage ended, he would receive 70 per cent of their home, and she would receive 30 per cent. His reasoning, as she explained it, was that he earned more money while she took responsibility for the domestic work. I had a pretty strong reaction to that. Not because I think every couple should automatically split everything down the middle. There are plenty of legitimate reasons to discuss how assets would be divided, particularly where one person brings substantially more into a relationship. I’m a big believer in couples having honest financial conversations and getting proper legal advice. What bothered me was the suggestion that because her contribution didn’t arrive in the family bank account every fortnight, it somehow counted for less. If one person is managing the household, caring for children, organising appointments, doing the school runs and generally keeping family life functioning, that frees up an extraordinary amount of time for the other person to focus on their career. Time they can spend working longer hours, pursuing promotions, travelling for business or building a company.



That arrangement might suit both people perfectly. But it’s still an arrangement in which both people contribute to the family’s financial position. Editor's pick Opinion

Budgeting We want to know if a recession is coming. It’s the wrong question Victoria Devine Money columnist And the person doing the unpaid work often pays a very real price for it. Reduced working hours can mean missed promotions, slower salary growth, smaller superannuation balances and fewer opportunities to develop a career. Those consequences don’t disappear simply because the couple has agreed that one person’s job is to earn the money and the other’s is to look after everything else. As someone who has worked in financial advice and now mortgage broking, I’ve seen how easily couples fall into describing money as belonging to whoever earns it. We discuss his salary or her business without always acknowledging the decisions and sacrifices that made those things possible. I also think we need to be honest about the fact that this isn’t exclusively a women’s issue. There are men who put their careers on hold to raise children or support a higher-earning partner, and their contributions deserve the same recognition. The principle shouldn’t change depending on who’s doing the laundry.



Australian family law, thankfully, takes a broader view than simply comparing payslips. When courts determine property settlements, they consider financial and non-financial contributions, including homemaking and parenting, alongside the parties’ circumstances and future needs. There is no automatic entitlement to a 50-50 split, and properly made binding financial agreements can alter how property is dealt with. That’s precisely why anyone considering one should obtain independent legal advice before signing. When it comes to a divorce, don’t expect a 50-50 split. istock But the fact that our legal system recognises unpaid contributions doesn’t mean our attitudes have caught up. We still have a tendency to celebrate the person with the impressive salary, the successful business or the enormous investment portfolio, while treating the work happening behind the scenes as something separate from the financial success.



And I find that particularly frustrating because the value of that work becomes painfully obvious the moment someone has to pay another person to do it. Childcare, cleaning, cooking, household administration. None of these services is free when you outsource them. Yet when they’re performed by a partner, we somehow become reluctant to recognise their economic value. I’m not suggesting Jensen Huang didn’t build something extraordinary. He did. Nor am I suggesting Lori Huang is automatically entitled to any particular share of their wealth. Those are questions for the people involved and, if necessary, their lawyers. What I am questioning is why our instinct is to describe a potential settlement as a man losing part of his fortune, rather than two people working out how to divide wealth accumulated during a very long marriage. It’s the same thinking that allows an ordinary Australian woman to be offered 30 per cent of her family home because the work she’s been doing apparently doesn’t count as earning. Perhaps we need to stop asking who brought home the most money and start asking what each person contributed to making that money possible.



Because if your partner’s career depends on you taking care of everything they don’t have time to do, you’re not standing on the sidelines of their financial success. You’re part of how it happened. Victoria Devine is an award-winning retired financial adviser, a bestselling author and host of Australia’s No.1 finance podcast, She’s on the Money. She is also founder and director of Zella Money.
